subtopic_detail: Investigating young onset hepatitis with a movement disorder and a low alkaline phosphatase
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 22-year-old university student referred by his general practitioner with abnormal liver tests found during an insurance medical.

Over the past 6 months his handwriting has become larger and untidy and his housemates have noticed his hands shake when he holds a cup. He has also become withdrawn and has failed a semester after previously passing comfortably. He denies alcohol beyond two drinks a month and takes no paracetamol, supplements or recreational drugs.

His alanine aminotransferase is 96 U/L (less than 40), aspartate aminotransferase 70 U/L (less than 35), alkaline phosphatase 42 U/L (30-110), bilirubin 28 micromol/L (less than 20) and international normalised ratio 1.1. Hepatitis B and C serology are negative, autoimmune liver serology is negative, ferritin and transferrin saturation are within normal limits, and alpha-1 antitrypsin is normal.

His haemoglobin is 108 g/L (130-180) with a direct antiglobulin test that is negative. On examination he has a coarse postural tremor of both arms and mildly slurred speech, with no rigidity and normal power.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Coarse postural tremor of both arms, mildly slurred speech, no rigidity, normal power and reflexes
data_table.Investigations: Alanine aminotransferase 96 U/L (less than 40), aspartate aminotransferase 70 U/L (less than 35), alkaline phosphatase 42 U/L (30-110), bilirubin 28 micromol/L (less than 20), international normalised ratio 1.1, haemoglobin 108 g/L (130-180), direct antiglobulin test negative, hepatitis B and C serology negative, autoimmune liver serology negative, iron studies and alpha-1 antitrypsin within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Liver biopsy with histological staging and quantitative tissue iron measurement
options.rationale: Biopsy with quantitative metal measurement can be informative but is invasive and would be arranged only after non-invasive testing is equivocal; iron studies are already normal, so measuring tissue iron answers the wrong question. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Wilson disease clinical resources)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Wilson disease clinical resources

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain with susceptibility weighted sequences performed first
options.rationale: Brain imaging can show basal ganglia changes and supports the diagnosis, but it is not the confirmatory test and is arranged alongside or after the biochemical assessment rather than in place of it. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Wilson disease clinical resources)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Wilson disease clinical resources

options.text: Repeat autoimmune liver serology with immunoglobulin subclasses and coeliac antibodies
options.rationale: Repeating a negative autoimmune panel is unlikely to change the answer and does not explain the neurological signs, the anaemia with a negative direct antiglobulin test, or the low alkaline phosphatase. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

options.text: Serum copper level alone, with a repeat measurement in 4 weeks for confirmation
options.rationale: Total serum copper largely reflects the copper bound to caeruloplasmin, so it falls as caeruloplasmin falls and can appear normal despite a high free copper fraction; it is not a useful standalone test. This is the near-pair to distinguish from caeruloplasmin and urinary copper. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Wilson disease clinical resources)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Wilson disease clinical resources

options.text: Serum caeruloplasmin with a 24 hour urinary copper collection and slit lamp examination
options.rationale: Hepatitis with a movement disorder and a psychiatric or academic decline in a young adult, alongside Coombs negative anaemia and a disproportionately low alkaline phosphatase, is the combination that points to Wilson disease, and the diagnosis is built from a low caeruloplasmin, raised 24 hour urinary copper and Kayser-Fleischer rings. No single one of these is sufficient alone, which is why they are requested together. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Wilson disease clinical resources)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Wilson disease clinical resources

explanation.summary: Wilson disease is an autosomal recessive disorder of copper transport caused by ATP7B mutations, in which copper accumulates in the liver and then spills into other tissues, notably the basal ganglia and cornea. It should be considered in anyone under 40 with unexplained liver disease, particularly when neurological or psychiatric features accompany it, because the neurological form is frequently misattributed to a primary psychiatric disorder for years. No single test is diagnostic: caeruloplasmin is low in most but not all patients and is an acute phase reactant that can be falsely normal, urinary copper is raised, and Kayser-Fleischer rings are present in almost all patients with neurological involvement but in only about half of those presenting with liver disease alone. Two supporting clues are Coombs negative haemolytic anaemia from copper release and a disproportionately low alkaline phosphatase. Treatment with chelation using penicillamine or trientine, or with zinc to block absorption, is lifelong and highly effective if started before irreversible damage, and first-degree relatives require screening.
key_points: Consider Wilson disease in anyone under 40 with unexplained liver disease, especially with neurological or psychiatric features
Diagnosis combines low caeruloplasmin, raised 24 hour urinary copper and slit lamp examination for Kayser-Fleischer rings
Total serum copper is unhelpful alone because it tracks caeruloplasmin
Coombs negative haemolysis and a low alkaline phosphatase are supportive clues
Treatment is lifelong chelation or zinc, and first-degree relatives must be screened
explanation.pearls: A ratio of alkaline phosphatase to total bilirubin below 4 in acute liver failure is highly suggestive of Wilson disease and should prompt immediate transplant unit referral, since fulminant Wilsonian failure is almost always fatal without transplantation.

sources.label: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Wilson disease clinical resources

subtopic_detail: Proximal weakness with autonomic features and post exercise facilitation in a smoker
stem:
You are the neurology registrar seeing a 62-year-old man referred with 4 months of difficulty getting out of a low chair and climbing the stairs at home.

He has smoked 20 cigarettes a day for 40 years. He also mentions a persistently dry mouth that has made him carry a water bottle everywhere, and erectile difficulty that began around the same time. He has lost 3 kg without trying.

He has no double vision, no drooping eyelids, no difficulty swallowing and no change to his speech, and his symptoms do not fluctuate through the day.

On examination hip flexion and shoulder abduction are both reduced. When he grips your hand and sustains the effort for 15 seconds, his grip strength improves. His knee reflexes are absent on first testing but become obtainable after he contracts the quadriceps for 15 seconds. Sensation is normal. His creatine kinase is within normal limits and his thyroid function is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Symmetrical proximal weakness of hip flexion and shoulder abduction, grip improves after 15 seconds of sustained effort, knee reflexes absent initially but obtainable after sustained quadriceps contraction, normal sensation, no ptosis or ophthalmoplegia
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase within normal limits, thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Request acetylcholine receptor antibodies and arrange computed tomography of the mediastinum
options.rationale: This is the workup for myasthenia gravis, which characteristically involves ocular and bulbar muscles, worsens with sustained effort rather than improving, and preserves reflexes; the thymus rather than the lung is the associated structure. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists clinical resources)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists clinical resources

options.text: Request voltage gated calcium channel antibodies and arrange computed tomography of the chest
options.rationale: Proximal weakness that improves with sustained effort, reflexes that return after contraction, and autonomic features such as dry mouth and erectile dysfunction describe Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome, confirmed by antibodies to the presynaptic voltage gated calcium channel. About half of cases are paraneoplastic and almost always from small cell lung cancer, so chest imaging is part of the same request in a heavy smoker. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists clinical resources)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists clinical resources

options.text: Request nerve conduction studies with low frequency repetitive stimulation of a distal nerve
options.rationale: Low frequency repetitive stimulation at 2 to 3 Hz demonstrates the decrement of myasthenia gravis; the presynaptic disorder here requires high frequency stimulation or brief maximal voluntary contraction to show the characteristic post-exercise increment. The distinguishing feature is decrement versus increment. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists clinical resources)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists clinical resources

options.text: Arrange a muscle biopsy of the vastus lateralis with immunohistochemistry and electron microscopy
options.rationale: Muscle biopsy investigates an inflammatory or metabolic myopathy, which a normal creatine kinase and the post-exercise facilitation of both power and reflexes make improbable. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Start prednisolone 50 mg daily and review his proximal strength in the clinic in 4 weeks
options.rationale: Empirical immunosuppression before a diagnosis risks masking or delaying identification of an underlying malignancy, which is the priority in a 62-year-old smoker with this syndrome. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists clinical resources)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists clinical resources

explanation.summary: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome is a disorder of the presynaptic neuromuscular junction caused by antibodies against voltage gated calcium channels, which reduce the quantal release of acetylcholine. The clinical signature is the mirror image of myasthenia gravis: proximal lower limb weakness dominates, ocular and bulbar involvement is mild or absent, autonomic features such as dry mouth, constipation and erectile dysfunction are common, and both power and reflexes improve transiently after sustained contraction as calcium accumulates in the nerve terminal. Around half of cases are paraneoplastic, overwhelmingly associated with small cell lung cancer, and the neurological syndrome commonly precedes the radiological detection of the tumour by months, so surveillance imaging is repeated if the initial scan is clear. Treatment of the tumour often improves the neurological syndrome, and symptomatic treatment uses amifampridine to prolong nerve terminal depolarisation, with immunosuppression or immunoglobulin for more severe disease. Recognising the syndrome matters practically because these patients are exquisitely sensitive to neuromuscular blocking agents during anaesthesia.
key_points: Proximal weakness, autonomic features and areflexia that reverses after contraction distinguish it from myasthenia gravis
Antibodies to voltage gated calcium channels confirm the diagnosis
About half of cases are paraneoplastic, almost always small cell lung cancer, so chest imaging is mandatory
Electrophysiology shows an increment after high frequency stimulation or brief maximal contraction, not a decrement
Patients are highly sensitive to neuromuscular blocking agents, which matters before any anaesthetic
explanation.pearls: If the initial chest computed tomography is clear in a smoker with confirmed Lambert-Eaton syndrome, repeat imaging every 3 to 6 months for at least 2 years, since the neurological syndrome commonly precedes detectable small cell lung cancer.

sources.label: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists clinical resources

subtopic_detail: Confirmatory testing before commencing targeted therapy for suspected pulmonary arterial hypertension
stem:
You are the registrar in a respiratory clinic. A 46-year-old woman is referred with 14 months of progressive exertional breathlessness, now limiting her to walking 200 m on the flat, and two episodes of light-headedness on climbing stairs.

She has limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis diagnosed 9 years ago with Raynaud phenomenon and sclerodactyly. She has never smoked and takes nifedipine and a proton pump inhibitor.

On examination there is a loud pulmonary component of the second heart sound, a left parasternal heave and a jugular venous pressure 5 cm above the sternal angle. The chest is clear. Spirometry is normal with a diffusing capacity 44 per cent predicted. High resolution computed tomography shows no interstitial disease and no evidence of emphysema. Ventilation perfusion scanning shows no mismatched segmental defects. Echocardiography estimates pulmonary artery systolic pressure at 62 mmHg with a dilated right ventricle and normal left ventricular size and function. Brain natriuretic peptide is 410 ng/L (<100).

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92/min, blood pressure 112/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 94% on room air, temperature 36.5 °C
data_table.Examination: Loud pulmonary component of the second heart sound, left parasternal heave, jugular venous pressure 5 cm above the sternal angle, chest clear, sclerodactyly and Raynaud phenomenon
data_table.Investigations: Spirometry normal with diffusing capacity 44 per cent predicted. High resolution computed tomography: no interstitial disease or emphysema. Ventilation perfusion scan: no mismatched segmental defects. Echocardiography: estimated pulmonary artery systolic pressure 62 mmHg, dilated right ventricle, normal left ventricular size and function. Brain natriuretic peptide 410 ng/L (<100)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Right heart catheterisation with vasoreactivity testing before any targeted therapy is commenced
options.rationale: Echocardiography estimates pulmonary pressures indirectly and cannot measure pulmonary capillary wedge pressure, which is what separates pre-capillary pulmonary arterial hypertension from post-capillary disease due to left heart pathology. Targeted vasodilator therapy is harmful in post-capillary disease and is only subsidised and justified once catheterisation has confirmed the haemodynamic diagnosis. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia: Pulmonary hypertension)

options.text: Commence an endothelin receptor antagonist and arrange repeat echocardiography in 3 months
options.rationale: Starting targeted therapy on echocardiographic estimates alone risks treating post-capillary hypertension, in which pulmonary vasodilation increases transpulmonary flow into a congested left atrium and precipitates pulmonary oedema. It becomes appropriate once catheterisation confirms pre-capillary haemodynamics. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia: Pulmonary hypertension)

options.text: Commence high dose calcium channel blocker therapy and arrange repeat echocardiography in 3 months
options.rationale: High dose calcium channel blockade benefits only the small minority who demonstrate acute vasoreactivity at catheterisation, and vasoreactive responders are very rare in connective tissue disease associated disease. Empirical use in non-responders causes systemic hypotension and right ventricular decompensation. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia: Pulmonary hypertension)

options.text: Commence therapeutic anticoagulation with a direct oral anticoagulant and arrange repeat imaging in 3 months
options.rationale: Anticoagulation is directed at chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension, which the ventilation perfusion scan has effectively excluded by showing no mismatched segmental defects. It would be indicated if that scan had shown mismatched defects warranting pulmonary angiography. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia: Pulmonary hypertension)

options.text: Commence long term oxygen therapy and arrange repeat arterial blood gas measurement in 3 months
options.rationale: Long term oxygen is prescribed for sustained resting hypoxaemia with an arterial oxygen tension at or below 55 mmHg, and her saturation is 94 per cent on room air. Oxygen would become appropriate if she developed resting hypoxaemia meeting those criteria. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia: Pulmonary hypertension)

explanation.summary: Pulmonary arterial hypertension complicating connective tissue disease, particularly systemic sclerosis, carries a worse prognosis than the idiopathic form, and an isolated reduction in diffusing capacity with normal lung volumes and no parenchymal disease is the classic early signal. The diagnostic pathway is deliberately sequential because the treatment is expensive, the drugs are hazardous in the wrong group, and the differential spans five distinct haemodynamic groups. Echocardiography is the screening test but systematically over and under-estimates pressures and cannot distinguish pre-capillary from post-capillary disease, which requires a measured pulmonary capillary wedge pressure. Before catheterisation, lung disease must be excluded by imaging and function testing and chronic thromboembolic disease by ventilation perfusion scanning, which is the test of choice because computed tomography angiography misses chronic organised thrombus. Screening annually with echocardiography and diffusing capacity in systemic sclerosis is recommended precisely because earlier treatment improves outcomes.
key_points: An isolated fall in diffusing capacity with normal volumes suggests pulmonary vascular disease
Echocardiography screens but cannot separate pre-capillary from post-capillary hypertension
Right heart catheterisation with wedge pressure measurement is required before targeted therapy
Ventilation perfusion scanning excludes chronic thromboembolic disease more reliably than computed tomography angiography
Systemic sclerosis warrants annual screening because early treatment improves outcomes
explanation.pearls: Giving a pulmonary vasodilator to a patient whose hypertension is post-capillary can precipitate acute pulmonary oedema, which is why a measured wedge pressure at or below 15 mmHg is required before targeted therapy begins.

subtopic_detail: Management of a congenital repolarisation disorder found during investigation of exertional syncope
stem:
You are the registrar in a cardiology clinic. A 19-year-old woman is referred after collapsing twice, once while swimming at a carnival and once when a fire alarm sounded unexpectedly at work.

On each occasion she lost consciousness without warning and recovered fully within a minute with no confusion afterward and no tongue biting or incontinence. Her mother describes brief jerking of the limbs during the second episode, lasting a few seconds while she was on the ground.

She takes no medicines and a urine drug screen is negative. A maternal aunt drowned at 22 while swimming in calm water. On examination the cardiovascular examination is normal with no murmur. Electrolytes including potassium, magnesium and calcium are within normal limits, as are thyroid function and full blood count. Echocardiography shows a structurally normal heart with normal biventricular function. Electrocardiogram shows sinus rhythm at 62 beats per minute with a corrected QT interval of 496 ms and broad-based T waves in the precordial leads. An electroencephalogram is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 62/min, blood pressure 110/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Cardiovascular examination normal, no murmur
data_table.Investigations: Electrocardiogram: sinus rhythm 62/min, corrected QT interval 496 ms, broad-based precordial T waves. Echocardiography structurally normal with normal biventricular function. Potassium, magnesium, calcium, thyroid function and full blood count within normal limits. Electroencephalogram normal. Urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence an antiseizure medicine, advise against competitive swimming and refer relatives for screening
options.rationale: The brief jerking described occurred after the patient was already on the ground and is typical of convulsive syncope from cerebral hypoperfusion rather than of a primary seizure. Rapid recovery without postictal confusion and a normal electroencephalogram argue against epilepsy, which is a common misdiagnosis in this condition. (Source: CSANZ: Genetic heart disease)

options.text: Commence a non-selective beta blocker, advise against competitive swimming and refer relatives for screening
options.rationale: Syncope triggered by swimming and by sudden auditory startle with a prolonged corrected QT interval and a family history of unexplained drowning indicates congenital long QT syndrome, in which beta blockade substantially reduces cardiac events. Non-selective agents such as nadolol and propranolol are preferred over selective agents, and cascade screening of first-degree relatives is essential because inheritance is autosomal dominant. (Source: CSANZ: Genetic heart disease)

options.text: Arrange a permanent pacemaker, advise against competitive swimming and refer relatives for screening
options.rationale: Pacing does not prevent the polymorphic ventricular tachycardia that causes syncope in this condition and does not address the repolarisation abnormality. Pacing has a limited role in pause-dependent arrhythmia or in symptomatic bradycardia resulting from beta blockade. (Source: CSANZ: Genetic heart disease)

options.text: Arrange catheter ablation, advise against competitive swimming and refer relatives for cardiac screening
options.rationale: Ablation targets a discrete arrhythmic focus or circuit, and this is a diffuse genetic disorder of ion channel repolarisation with no such target. Ablation would be appropriate for an accessory pathway or a focal ventricular tachycardia in a structurally normal heart. (Source: CSANZ: Genetic heart disease)

options.text: Commence oral magnesium supplementation, advise against competitive swimming and refer relatives for screening
options.rationale: Intravenous magnesium terminates established torsades de pointes but oral supplementation does not prevent events in congenital long QT syndrome, and her magnesium is already normal. Magnesium would be given acutely for polymorphic ventricular tachycardia in progress. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

explanation.summary: Congenital long QT syndrome is regularly misdiagnosed as epilepsy, because the cerebral hypoperfusion of a self-terminating polymorphic ventricular tachycardia produces brief limb jerking that observers describe as a fit. The distinguishing features are the abruptness of onset without aura, the speed of full recovery without postictal confusion, and above all the trigger. Trigger patterns map onto genotype with unusual fidelity: exertion and particularly swimming point to the potassium channel subtype, sudden auditory startle to the sodium-potassium subtype, and events during sleep or rest to the sodium channel subtype. A family history of drowning in a competent swimmer, of sudden infant death, or of unexplained single-vehicle accidents is highly relevant and should be sought explicitly. Beta blockade is the foundation of treatment, with non-selective agents outperforming selective ones, while an implantable defibrillator is reserved for aborted cardiac arrest or recurrent syncope despite adequate beta blockade, and avoidance of QT-prolonging drugs is a lifelong requirement.
key_points: Convulsive syncope with rapid full recovery and no postictal confusion suggests arrhythmia rather than epilepsy
Swimming and sudden auditory startle are characteristic triggers in specific genotypes
Family history of drowning, sudden infant death or unexplained accidents is highly relevant
Non-selective beta blockers are preferred over selective agents such as metoprolol
Cascade screening of first-degree relatives is required because inheritance is autosomal dominant
explanation.pearls: A competent swimmer who drowns in calm water should raise suspicion of the potassium channel subtype of long QT syndrome in the family, since swimming is its signature trigger and the diagnosis is frequently made only after a relative presents.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Long QT syndrome

subtopic_detail: Acute management when a febrile illness unmasks a type 1 coved ST elevation pattern
stem:
You are the registrar in an emergency department. A 32-year-old man of Vietnamese background presents with 2 days of fever and productive cough. He mentions that he briefly blacked out this morning while getting out of bed and hit his shoulder.

He has had two previous unexplained blackouts at night over 3 years, each attributed to a vasovagal cause. His older brother died suddenly in his sleep at 35 with a normal autopsy.

He takes no regular medicines. On examination the chest has coarse crackles at the right base and the cardiovascular examination is normal. Temperature is 39.1 °C. Chest radiograph shows right lower lobe consolidation. Electrocardiogram shows sinus rhythm at 104 beats per minute with coved ST elevation of 3 mm followed by an inverted T wave in leads V1 and V2, and a corrected QT interval of 400 ms. Potassium is 4.1 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), calcium and magnesium are within normal limits, and troponin is not elevated. An electrocardiogram from 2 years ago, taken when he was afebrile, showed only 1 mm of saddleback ST elevation in V1.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 104/min, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 24/min, SpO2 94% on room air, temperature 39.1 °C
data_table.Examination: Coarse crackles at the right base, cardiovascular examination normal
data_table.Investigations: Electrocardiogram: sinus rhythm 104/min, coved ST elevation 3 mm with inverted T waves in V1 and V2, corrected QT interval 400 ms. Prior afebrile electrocardiogram 2 years ago: 1 mm saddleback ST elevation in V1 only. Chest radiograph right lower lobe consolidation. Potassium 4.1 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), calcium and magnesium within normal limits, troponin not elevated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Activate the catheter laboratory for primary percutaneous coronary intervention for anterior infarction
options.rationale: The ST elevation is confined to the right precordial leads with a coved morphology and inverted T waves, the troponin is not elevated and there is no chest pain, so this is not an occlusive infarction. Reperfusion would be correct for regional ST elevation with reciprocal change and a compatible ischaemic history. (Source: CSANZ: Genetic heart disease)

options.text: Commence an intravenous amiodarone infusion and admit to a monitored bed with cardiology referral
options.rationale: Amiodarone does not prevent arrhythmia in this condition and sodium channel blocking antiarrhythmics accentuate the electrocardiographic pattern and the arrhythmic risk. Isoprenaline is the agent used for recurrent ventricular fibrillation in this setting, by increasing calcium current and heart rate. (Source: CSANZ: Genetic heart disease)

options.text: Treat the fever aggressively with antipyretics and admit to a monitored bed with cardiology referral
options.rationale: Fever unmasks the type 1 coved pattern of Brugada syndrome by accentuating sodium channel dysfunction, and the arrhythmic risk is at its highest while the temperature is elevated, so aggressive antipyresis is itself an antiarrhythmic intervention. Continuous monitoring is required because ventricular fibrillation can occur without warning, and the syncope with a family history of nocturnal sudden death marks him as high risk. (Source: CSANZ: Genetic heart disease)

options.text: Administer a flecainide challenge to confirm the diagnosis and admit to a monitored bed for observation
options.rationale: Provocation testing is used to unmask the pattern when the baseline tracing is non-diagnostic, and the diagnostic type 1 pattern is already present, so the challenge would add arrhythmic risk without diagnostic gain. It would be appropriate in an afebrile patient with only a saddleback pattern and a suggestive history. (Source: CSANZ: Genetic heart disease)

options.text: Arrange urgent cardiac magnetic resonance imaging and admit to a monitored bed with cardiology referral
options.rationale: Imaging is used to exclude structural mimics such as arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy but does not change the immediate priority of controlling the fever that is driving current risk. It would be a reasonable part of the subsequent workup once he is stable and afebrile. (Source: CSANZ: Genetic heart disease)

explanation.summary: Brugada syndrome is an inherited sodium channelopathy in which reduced inward sodium current creates a transmural voltage gradient in the right ventricular outflow tract, producing the coved ST elevation of the type 1 pattern and a substrate for phase 2 reentry and ventricular fibrillation. Its defining clinical feature is that the electrocardiogram is dynamic: the pattern waxes and wanes, and fever is the most important and most treatable unmasking factor because elevated temperature further impairs sodium channel kinetics. This makes a febrile illness a genuine emergency in an affected patient rather than an incidental finding, and antipyresis is therapeutic rather than merely symptomatic. Events characteristically occur at rest or during sleep and in males of South East Asian background at disproportionate rates, which is the opposite pattern to the exertional syncope of long QT syndrome or hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Sodium channel blocking drugs, cocaine and excess alcohol all accentuate the phenotype and must be avoided lifelong, while an implantable defibrillator remains the only proven treatment for those with aborted arrest or arrhythmic syncope.
key_points: Fever unmasks the type 1 coved pattern and markedly increases arrhythmic risk
Aggressive antipyresis is an antiarrhythmic intervention, not merely symptomatic care
Events occur at rest or during sleep rather than with exertion
Sodium channel blockers, cocaine and excess alcohol accentuate the phenotype and are avoided
An implantable defibrillator is the only proven therapy after arrhythmic syncope or aborted arrest
explanation.pearls: Give paracetamol early and at full dose for any febrile illness in a patient with a Brugada pattern, and record a repeat electrocardiogram once afebrile, because the type 1 morphology may disappear entirely and the diagnosis be wrongly discarded.

subtopic_detail: Timing intervention for rheumatic mitral stenosis presenting with pulmonary oedema in mid-pregnancy
stem:
You are the registrar in a coronary care unit. A 27-year-old woman at 26 weeks in her first pregnancy is admitted with 4 days of worsening breathlessness, now orthopnoeic and unable to lie flat.

She arrived in Australia from the Pacific at 14 and recalls being told as a child that she had a heart murmur after a febrile illness with sore joints. She has had no cardiology follow-up.

She has responded partially to intravenous furosemide and oxygen in the emergency department. On examination the pulse is 112 beats per minute and irregularly irregular. There is a loud first heart sound, an opening snap and a low-pitched mid-diastolic murmur at the apex. There are crackles to the mid zones bilaterally. Electrocardiogram shows atrial fibrillation at 112 beats per minute. Transthoracic echocardiography reports a mitral valve area of 0.9 cm2 with a mean gradient of 16 mmHg, pliable non-calcified leaflets with commissural fusion, no mitral regurgitation, no left atrial thrombus and estimated pulmonary artery systolic pressure 58 mmHg. Fetal cardiotocography is normal and growth is on the 45th centile.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal pulse 112/min irregularly irregular, blood pressure 104/66 mmHg, respiratory rate 26/min, SpO2 93% on 4 L/min oxygen, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Loud first heart sound, opening snap, low-pitched mid-diastolic apical murmur, bilateral crackles to the mid zones
data_table.Investigations: Electrocardiogram: atrial fibrillation at 112/min. Echocardiography: mitral valve area 0.9 cm2, mean gradient 16 mmHg, pliable non-calcified leaflets with commissural fusion, no mitral regurgitation, no left atrial thrombus, estimated pulmonary artery systolic pressure 58 mmHg. Cardiotocography normal, growth 45th centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate definitive management?

options.text: Open mitral valve replacement on cardiopulmonary bypass after rate control and anticoagulation
options.rationale: Cardiopulmonary bypass in pregnancy carries fetal mortality of roughly 20 to 30 per cent through non-pulsatile placental perfusion, so it is reserved for valves unsuitable for percutaneous treatment. Replacement would be appropriate for a heavily calcified valve, significant mitral regurgitation or left atrial thrombus. (Source: CSANZ: Valvular heart disease)

options.text: Continued diuresis with beta blockade alone and planned reassessment in the third trimester
options.rationale: Medical therapy is the correct first step but she has already failed it while cardiac output demands continue to rise until around 32 weeks, so deferring intervention allows further deterioration. Ongoing medical management alone would be reasonable for moderate stenosis with symptoms controlled on rate control and diuretics. (Source: CSANZ: Valvular heart disease)

options.text: Emergency caesarean birth at 26 weeks followed by valve intervention in the postpartum period
options.rationale: Delivery at 26 weeks commits the infant to extreme prematurity and the immediate haemodynamic stress of birth and autotransfusion is poorly tolerated in severe mitral stenosis. Delivery would be the priority if the fetus were near term or if maternal collapse were imminent and irreversible. (Source: CSANZ: Valvular heart disease)

options.text: Percutaneous balloon mitral valvuloplasty after rate control and anticoagulation are established
options.rationale: Severe mitral stenosis with pulmonary oedema refractory to medical therapy in pregnancy warrants mechanical relief of the obstruction, and pliable non-calcified leaflets with commissural fusion, no regurgitation and no left atrial thrombus make this valve ideally suited to balloon valvuloplasty. The percutaneous route avoids cardiopulmonary bypass, which carries substantial fetal loss rates, and rate control plus anticoagulation are established first because the new atrial fibrillation is driving the decompensation. (Source: CSANZ: Valvular heart disease)

options.text: Direct current cardioversion to sinus rhythm alone with anticoagulation and no valve intervention
options.rationale: Restoring sinus rhythm improves diastolic filling time and is a valuable adjunct, but it leaves a valve area of 0.9 cm2 obstructing flow and recurrence of atrial fibrillation is likely while the left atrium remains pressurised. Cardioversion alone would suffice if the underlying valve lesion were mild. (Source: CSANZ: Valvular heart disease)

explanation.summary: Rheumatic mitral stenosis remains an important cause of maternal morbidity in Australia, disproportionately affecting Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities and people who grew up in the Pacific and South East Asia, and pregnancy is frequently the event that unmasks it. The physiology explains why: cardiac output rises by up to half by the early third trimester and tachycardia shortens diastole, and since the stenotic valve fills only during diastole, both changes raise left atrial pressure steeply. New atrial fibrillation compounds this by removing atrial systole and shortening filling time further, which is often the final trigger for pulmonary oedema. Medical management with rate control, cautious diuresis and anticoagulation is first-line, but failure of medical therapy in severe stenosis before term requires mechanical relief because the haemodynamic burden will only increase. Percutaneous balloon valvuloplasty is strongly preferred over surgery, with abdominal shielding and minimised screening time, and valve morphology determines suitability, while anticoagulation matters because left atrial stasis with atrial fibrillation carries a high thromboembolic risk in an already prothrombotic pregnancy.
key_points: Cardiac output rises through pregnancy and tachycardia shortens diastolic filling, worsening the gradient
New atrial fibrillation removes atrial systole and often precipitates decompensation
Balloon valvuloplasty suits pliable non-calcified valves without regurgitation or left atrial thrombus
Cardiopulmonary bypass carries fetal mortality of roughly 20 to 30 per cent and is a second choice
Anticoagulate for atrial fibrillation with mitral stenosis regardless of any risk score
explanation.pearls: Atrial fibrillation with rheumatic mitral stenosis is an absolute indication for warfarin rather than a direct oral anticoagulant, since the direct agents have not been shown safe in this valve lesion and are specifically excluded from that indication.

subtopic_detail: Deciding between infective and immune causes of diarrhoea on checkpoint inhibitor therapy
stem:
You are the registrar in an oncology day unit. A 61-year-old man receiving combination immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy for metastatic melanoma presents 5 weeks after his second cycle with 8 days of increasing diarrhoea, now 9 loose stools daily with abdominal cramping and visible blood on two occasions.

He has been opening his bowels twice overnight. He has had no recent travel, no antibiotic exposure and no unwell contacts, and no fever at home.

On examination the abdomen is soft with generalised tenderness and no guarding and no rebound. Bowel sounds are present. Stool testing is negative for Clostridioides difficile toxin, negative on bacterial culture and negative on viral and parasite polymerase chain reaction panel. Cytomegalovirus serology shows past exposure. C-reactive protein is 78 mg/L (<5), albumin 29 g/L (35-50), white cell count 9.2 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), haemoglobin 122 g/L (130-180) and faecal calprotectin markedly elevated. Computed tomography of the abdomen shows diffuse colonic wall thickening with mesenteric fat stranding and no perforation and no abscess.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96/min, blood pressure 116/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 37.2 °C
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft with generalised tenderness, no guarding, no rebound, bowel sounds present
data_table.Investigations: Stool Clostridioides difficile toxin negative, bacterial culture negative, viral and parasite panel negative. C-reactive protein 78 mg/L (<5), albumin 29 g/L (35-50), white cell count 9.2 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), haemoglobin 122 g/L (130-180), faecal calprotectin markedly elevated. Computed tomography: diffuse colonic wall thickening with mesenteric fat stranding, no perforation or abscess
data_table.Treatment: Combination immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy, second cycle 5 weeks ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue immunotherapy and commence loperamide with dietary modification and outpatient review
options.rationale: Antimotility agents are appropriate for mild grade 1 diarrhoea but risk masking progression and precipitating toxic dilatation in established immune colitis. Loperamide would be reasonable for fewer than four extra stools daily with no blood, no nocturnal symptoms and normal inflammatory markers. (Source: eviQ: Immune-related adverse events)

options.text: Withhold immunotherapy and commence oral vancomycin with repeat stool toxin testing in 48 hours
options.rationale: Clostridioides difficile is an important differential in this population but the toxin assay is negative and there has been no antibiotic exposure or healthcare contact to support it. Vancomycin would be indicated if toxin or nucleic acid testing were positive alongside compatible symptoms. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Withhold immunotherapy and commence infliximab as initial therapy with gastroenterology referral
options.rationale: Infliximab is the standard second-line agent for immune colitis but is reserved for patients who fail to improve after roughly 3 days of adequate corticosteroid. Starting it first exposes the patient to infection risk before establishing whether steroid alone will control the colitis. (Source: eviQ: Immune-related adverse events)

options.text: Withhold immunotherapy and arrange urgent colonoscopy with biopsies before commencing any treatment
options.rationale: Endoscopy usefully assesses severity and excludes cytomegalovirus colitis, but deferring treatment until it can be arranged risks progression in a patient with an established clinical and radiological diagnosis. Colonoscopy should proceed alongside, not before, corticosteroid therapy in grade 3 disease. (Source: eviQ: Immune-related adverse events)

options.text: Withhold immunotherapy and commence high dose systemic corticosteroid with gastroenterology referral
options.rationale: Nine stools daily with blood, nocturnal symptoms and radiological colitis after infection has been excluded is grade 3 immune-related colitis, which requires immunotherapy to be withheld and high dose corticosteroid started promptly. Delay is the principal driver of perforation and death in this complication, so treatment begins on clinical and radiological grounds rather than awaiting endoscopy. (Source: eviQ: Immune-related adverse events)

explanation.summary: Immune-related colitis is among the most common serious toxicities of checkpoint inhibition and is substantially more frequent and more severe with combination cytotoxic T-lymphocyte antigen 4 and programmed death 1 blockade than with either agent alone. Onset is typically weeks to months after starting treatment and can occur after the drug has been stopped, since the immune activation outlasts drug exposure, so the diagnosis must be considered in any patient who has ever received these agents. Grading drives management: mild disease is managed symptomatically while continuing treatment, moderate disease prompts withholding the drug and starting corticosteroid, and severe disease requires admission, high dose corticosteroid and early escalation. Infection must be excluded because the treatment is immunosuppression, but exclusion should not delay therapy when the clinical picture is convincing, and cytomegalovirus reactivation should be reconsidered in anyone who fails to respond. Corticosteroid non-response by around day 3 is the trigger for infliximab or vedolizumab, and untreated or slowly treated colitis progresses to perforation, which carries high mortality in this population.
key_points: Combination checkpoint blockade causes more frequent and more severe colitis than single agent therapy
Onset is typically weeks to months after initiation and can follow drug cessation
Blood in stool, nocturnal symptoms and more than six extra stools daily indicate severe disease
Exclude infection but do not delay corticosteroid when the clinical picture is convincing
Escalate to infliximab or vedolizumab if there is no response after about 3 days of corticosteroid
explanation.pearls: Reconsider cytomegalovirus colitis by requesting tissue polymerase chain reaction on colonic biopsies in any patient whose immune colitis fails to respond to corticosteroid, because serology showing past exposure does not distinguish latent infection from active reactivation unmasked by immunosuppression.

subtopic_detail: Investigation sequencing for progressive dysphagia to solids and liquids with a normal endoscopy
stem:
You are the resident in a gastroenterology clinic. A 41-year-old woman describes 14 months of food sticking behind the sternum, now occurring with both solid food and drinks including water.

She regurgitates undigested food onto her pillow at night and has started sleeping propped up. She has lost 5 kg over the past year. She has taken a proton pump inhibitor at full dose for 6 months with no benefit, and says antacids have never helped.

She has no odynophagia, no haematemesis and no hoarseness. She has never smoked and drinks minimal alcohol. On examination she is thin with a body mass index of 19.2 kg/m2, the chest is clear and there is no lymphadenopathy. Gastroscopy performed last week was reported as showing a normal oesophageal mucosa with no stricture and no mass, with mild resistance passing the scope through the gastro-oesophageal junction that yielded with gentle pressure. Oesophageal biopsies showed fewer than 5 eosinophils per high power field.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Anthropometry: Body mass index 19.2 kg/m2, 5 kg weight loss over 12 months
data_table.Investigations: Gastroscopy: normal oesophageal mucosa, no stricture or mass, mild resistance at the gastro-oesophageal junction yielding to gentle pressure. Oesophageal biopsies fewer than 5 eosinophils per high power field

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Repeat gastroscopy with dilatation of the gastro-oesophageal junction under direct vision
options.rationale: Empirical dilatation treats a presumed structural narrowing, and the endoscopy specifically found no stricture, so this intervenes before the mechanism is known. Dilatation would be appropriate for a confirmed peptic or fibrotic stricture causing solid food dysphagia. (Source: GESA: Dysphagia)

options.text: Ambulatory 24 hour oesophageal pH and impedance monitoring off acid suppression therapy
options.rationale: Reflux monitoring quantifies acid exposure in suspected gastro-oesophageal reflux disease, and her symptoms did not respond to full dose acid suppression and are not reflux-typical. It would be indicated for refractory heartburn or regurgitation where reflux remains the leading hypothesis. (Source: GESA: Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease)

options.text: Computed tomography of the chest and abdomen with intravenous contrast to stage a suspected malignancy
options.rationale: Staging imaging follows a tissue diagnosis of malignancy, and endoscopy with biopsy has already excluded a mucosal lesion in the segment being imaged. It would be the next step if endoscopy had shown an infiltrating mass or ulcerated lesion. (Source: GESA: Dysphagia)

options.text: High resolution oesophageal manometry to characterise peristalsis and sphincter relaxation
options.rationale: Dysphagia to both solids and liquids from the outset points to a motility disorder rather than a mechanical obstruction, which typically begins with solids alone and progresses. With endoscopy having excluded mucosal and structural disease, manometry is the definitive test and is required to make the diagnosis and to subtype it. (Source: GESA: Dysphagia)

options.text: Videofluoroscopic swallow study with a speech pathologist to assess the oropharyngeal phase
options.rationale: Videofluoroscopy assesses oropharyngeal swallowing, which produces coughing, choking and nasal regurgitation at the moment of swallowing rather than food lodging retrosternally. It would be the right test for a patient with a neurological cause of transfer dysphagia. (Source: GESA: Dysphagia)

explanation.summary: The single most useful discriminator in dysphagia is whether solids alone or solids and liquids are affected, because mechanical obstruction narrows a lumen progressively and therefore troubles solids first, while a motility disorder disrupts coordinated transit and affects both from the outset. Nocturnal regurgitation of undigested food, weight loss and a complete lack of response to acid suppression all reinforce that picture here. Endoscopy remains the necessary first investigation in any adult with dysphagia because malignancy must be excluded and eosinophilic oesophagitis is now a common finding requiring biopsies even when the mucosa looks normal. A normal endoscopy in this setting is an informative result rather than a dead end, and high resolution manometry then classifies the disorder and, in achalasia, identifies the subtype that predicts response to pneumatic dilatation and to myotomy. Pseudoachalasia from a tumour infiltrating the gastro-oesophageal junction remains an important mimic, particularly with short symptom duration and rapid weight loss in an older patient.
key_points: Dysphagia to solids and liquids from the outset indicates a motility disorder
Solid food dysphagia progressing to liquids suggests mechanical narrowing
Endoscopy is the necessary first test to exclude malignancy and eosinophilic oesophagitis
Take oesophageal biopsies even when the mucosa appears normal
High resolution manometry is the definitive test and subtypes achalasia to guide treatment
explanation.pearls: Failure to respond to a full dose proton pump inhibitor trial in a patient with regurgitation should prompt manometry rather than dose escalation, because achalasia is regularly mislabelled as refractory reflux for years before the correct test is ordered.

subtopic_detail: Next therapeutic step after a proton pump inhibitor trial fails in oesophageal eosinophilia
stem:
You are the resident in a gastroenterology clinic. A 27-year-old man attends for review after an episode 3 months ago in which a piece of steak lodged in his oesophagus and required endoscopic removal.

He has a long history of asthma, hay fever and childhood eczema. He describes years of food sticking that he had adapted to by chewing extensively, cutting food finely and drinking water with every mouthful.

At the index endoscopy the oesophagus showed concentric rings and longitudinal furrows with white exudate, and biopsies from the proximal and distal oesophagus each showed 45 eosinophils per high power field. He was commenced on a proton pump inhibitor at full dose twice daily. A repeat endoscopy last week, after 10 weeks of therapy, shows persisting rings and furrows and biopsies showing 38 eosinophils per high power field. He reports no improvement in his swallowing.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Investigations: Index endoscopy: concentric rings, longitudinal furrows, white exudate; proximal and distal biopsies 45 eosinophils per high power field. Repeat endoscopy after 10 weeks of twice daily proton pump inhibitor: persisting rings and furrows, biopsies 38 eosinophils per high power field
data_table.History: Asthma, allergic rhinitis, childhood eczema; food impaction requiring endoscopic removal 3 months ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Commence a long-acting inhaled corticosteroid by metered dose inhaler and repeat endoscopy after 8 to 12 weeks
options.rationale: The corticosteroid must be swallowed rather than inhaled so that it coats the oesophageal mucosa, and inhaled delivery sends the drug to the lungs where it does nothing for this condition. Inhaled delivery is correct for his asthma, which is a separate indication. (Source: GESA: Eosinophilic oesophagitis)

options.text: Commence oral prednisolone at a weaning dose and repeat endoscopy with biopsies after 8 to 12 weeks
options.rationale: Systemic corticosteroid is effective but exposes a young man to cumulative toxicity for a chronic relapsing condition that topical therapy controls. Oral steroid is reserved for severe disease with malnutrition or stricturing requiring rapid control. (Source: GESA: Eosinophilic oesophagitis)

options.text: Arrange skin prick testing to guide a targeted food elimination diet and repeat endoscopy after 8 to 12 weeks
options.rationale: Allergy testing predicts food triggers poorly in this condition, so elimination diets are structured empirically, most commonly by removing the six or the two most common trigger food groups. Dietary therapy is a legitimate alternative to topical steroid but should not be directed by skin prick results. (Source: GESA: Eosinophilic oesophagitis)

options.text: Arrange endoscopic oesophageal dilatation and repeat endoscopy with biopsies after 8 to 12 weeks
options.rationale: Dilatation relieves fibrostenotic narrowing mechanically but does nothing for the underlying eosinophilic inflammation, which will continue to remodel the oesophagus. It is appropriate for a persistent stricture causing symptoms despite adequate anti-inflammatory therapy. (Source: GESA: Eosinophilic oesophagitis)

options.text: Commence a swallowed topical corticosteroid preparation and repeat endoscopy with biopsies after 8 to 12 weeks
options.rationale: Persisting symptoms with more than 15 eosinophils per high power field after an adequate proton pump inhibitor trial confirms eosinophilic oesophagitis not responsive to acid suppression, and swallowed topical corticosteroid is the standard next-line therapy. Histological reassessment is required because symptoms correlate poorly with inflammation and untreated inflammation drives progressive fibrostenotic remodelling. (Source: GESA: Eosinophilic oesophagitis)

explanation.summary: Eosinophilic oesophagitis is now the commonest cause of food impaction in young adults and is strongly associated with the atopic diathesis of asthma, rhinitis and eczema. The history of long-standing adaptive eating behaviour, such as chewing excessively, cutting food finely and drinking with every mouthful, is characteristic and frequently goes unreported unless asked about directly, because patients regard it as normal. Diagnosis requires at least 15 eosinophils per high power field on oesophageal biopsy with symptoms of oesophageal dysfunction, and biopsies must be taken from both proximal and distal oesophagus since the disease is patchy. Proton pump inhibitors are now understood as a treatment rather than a diagnostic filter, resolving inflammation in a meaningful proportion of patients, and non-response simply moves therapy along. The three established options are topical corticosteroids, dietary elimination and, in refractory disease, biologic therapy, with dilatation reserved for fixed strictures, and the treatment goal is histological remission because ongoing inflammation drives the fibrosis that ultimately causes strictures.
key_points: Suspect the diagnosis in any young adult with food impaction, especially with an atopic history
Diagnosis requires 15 or more eosinophils per high power field with oesophageal symptoms
Take biopsies from both proximal and distal oesophagus because involvement is patchy
Proton pump inhibitors are a treatment, not a diagnostic filter; non-response moves therapy on
Corticosteroid must be swallowed, not inhaled, and histological remission is the treatment target
explanation.pearls: Rinse the mouth and avoid eating or drinking for 30 minutes after a swallowed corticosteroid dose, because oesophageal candidiasis is the main adverse effect and adherence to that instruction largely prevents it.

subtopic_detail: Deciding which patient with airflow obstruction warrants testing for an inherited protease inhibitor deficiency
stem:
You are the resident in a respiratory clinic. A 43-year-old woman is referred with 2 years of progressive exertional breathlessness and a daily cough productive of clear sputum.

She has never smoked and has worked as a primary school teacher. She has no history of childhood asthma and no occupational dust or fume exposure. Her brother was diagnosed with emphysema at 47 and her father died of liver cirrhosis at 58 with no history of alcohol use.

She takes no regular medicines. On examination the chest is hyperinflated with quiet breath sounds throughout and no wheeze. Spirometry shows forced expiratory volume in 1 second 1.52 L (58 per cent predicted), forced vital capacity 3.40 L (94 per cent predicted), ratio 0.45, with a 4 per cent improvement after bronchodilator. Chest radiograph shows hyperinflation. High resolution computed tomography of the chest reports panlobular emphysema most marked in the lower zones. Full blood count, C-reactive protein and liver function tests are within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82/min, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 95% on room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Hyperinflated chest with quiet breath sounds throughout, no wheeze
data_table.Investigations: Spirometry: forced expiratory volume in 1 second 1.52 L (58 per cent predicted), forced vital capacity 3.40 L (94 per cent predicted), ratio 0.45, 4 per cent post-bronchodilator improvement. Chest radiograph hyperinflation. High resolution computed tomography: panlobular lower zone emphysema. Full blood count, C-reactive protein and liver function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Serum alpha-1 antitrypsin concentration, with phenotyping if the level is reduced
options.rationale: Emphysema in a lifelong non-smoker under 45 with lower zone panlobular distribution and a family history of both early emphysema and unexplained cirrhosis is the classic presentation of alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency. Serum concentration is the appropriate screening test and phenotyping or genotyping follows a low result to characterise the variant. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia: COPD-X Plan)

options.text: Serum total immunoglobulin E with specific aeroallergen testing, and skin prick testing if elevated
options.rationale: Allergic assessment supports an asthma diagnosis, and the fixed obstruction with only 4 per cent bronchodilator reversibility and emphysema on imaging argues against that. Testing would be appropriate for variable airflow obstruction with significant bronchodilator response and a compatible history. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia: COPD-X Plan)

options.text: Sweat chloride testing, with cystic fibrosis gene panel analysis if the result is elevated
options.rationale: Cystic fibrosis produces bronchiectasis with upper lobe predominance, purulent sputum and pancreatic and gastrointestinal features rather than isolated lower zone panlobular emphysema. It would be worth testing for bronchiectasis with recurrent infections and malabsorption. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia: COPD-X Plan)

options.text: Serum angiotensin converting enzyme, with tissue biopsy if the level is elevated
options.rationale: Sarcoidosis causes upper zone predominant interstitial change with hilar lymphadenopathy and a restrictive or mixed pattern, not obstructive physiology with panlobular emphysema. It would be considered for bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy with reticulonodular infiltrates. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)

options.text: Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody testing, with renal biopsy if the titre is elevated
options.rationale: Vasculitis affecting the lung presents with nodules, cavities, haemorrhage or infiltrates alongside renal or upper airway involvement, none of which is present. Testing would be appropriate for haemoptysis with pulmonary infiltrates and an active urinary sediment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

explanation.summary: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency is substantially underdiagnosed, with typical delays of many years between first symptoms and recognition, largely because emphysema is assumed to require smoking. The protein is a protease inhibitor produced in the liver that protects alveolar tissue from neutrophil elastase, so deficiency allows unopposed proteolysis in the lower zones where perfusion and neutrophil traffic are greatest, producing the characteristic basal panlobular pattern that contrasts with the upper zone centrilobular emphysema of smoking. The same mutation causes liver disease through accumulation of misfolded protein in hepatocytes, which is why unexplained cirrhosis in a relative is such a useful clue. Testing is recommended for all patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and particularly those presenting young, never-smokers, those with a basal predominant distribution and those with a suggestive family history. Diagnosis changes management: smoking avoidance becomes critical, family members warrant testing and counselling, and augmentation therapy may be considered in selected patients.
key_points: Suspect deficiency in emphysema that is early onset, in a never-smoker, or basal predominant
Panlobular lower zone emphysema contrasts with upper zone centrilobular disease from smoking
Unexplained liver disease in the patient or family is an important associated clue
Serum concentration is the screening test, followed by phenotyping or genotyping
Diagnosis has implications for family screening and counselling as well as for the patient
explanation.pearls: Alpha-1 antitrypsin is an acute phase reactant, so a level measured during an infection or exacerbation can be falsely normal in a deficient patient; recheck when the C-reactive protein has settled.

subtopic_detail: Confirming a workplace cause for adult onset asthma before recommending removal from exposure
stem:
You are the resident in a respiratory clinic. A 34-year-old man is referred with 8 months of cough, chest tightness and wheeze that began 2 years after he started work as a spray painter in a vehicle repair shop.

He reports symptoms build through the working week and are noticeably better on weekends and were absent during a 3 week holiday. He uses a supplied respirator inconsistently. He has never smoked and had no childhood asthma or atopy.

On examination the chest is clear today, having been reviewed on a Monday morning. Spirometry today shows forced expiratory volume in 1 second 3.62 L (96 per cent predicted) with a ratio of 0.79 and a 6 per cent bronchodilator response. Chest radiograph is normal. Full blood count shows an eosinophil count of 0.4 x10^9/L (0.0-0.5). He is worried about losing his job and asks whether he really has to leave the trade.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Chest clear on auscultation, assessed on a Monday morning
data_table.Investigations: Spirometry: forced expiratory volume in 1 second 3.62 L (96 per cent predicted), ratio 0.79, 6 per cent bronchodilator response. Chest radiograph normal. Eosinophil count 0.4 x10^9/L (0.0-0.5)
data_table.Occupational: Spray painter for approximately 3 years; symptoms build across the working week, resolve at weekends and during a 3 week holiday; inconsistent respirator use

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Advise immediate permanent removal from spray painting work and commence inhaled corticosteroid therapy
options.rationale: Removing a worker from their trade has major financial and legal consequences and should follow objective confirmation rather than history alone, which is unreliable in isolation. Immediate removal would be justified once the diagnosis is objectively established, since continued exposure worsens long-term outcome. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia: Occupational asthma)

options.text: Arrange serial peak expiratory flow recordings across periods at work and away from work
options.rationale: A single normal spirometry taken after a weekend away from exposure cannot exclude occupational asthma, because airflow obstruction recovers between exposures early in the disease. Serial peak flow diaries across at least 2 weeks at work and 2 weeks away demonstrate the work-related pattern objectively, which is required before advising a change that will end his livelihood. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia: Occupational asthma)

options.text: Commence inhaled corticosteroid with a long-acting beta agonist and continue current work practices
options.rationale: Treating the inflammation while exposure continues allows progressive airway remodelling and permanent impairment, which is what distinguishes this from ordinary asthma management. Controller therapy is appropriate but only alongside exposure control, not as a substitute for it. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia: Occupational asthma)

options.text: Arrange high resolution computed tomography of the chest to assess for an interstitial process
options.rationale: Cross-sectional imaging investigates hypersensitivity pneumonitis or interstitial disease, which cause breathlessness with crackles and restrictive physiology rather than episodic wheeze with normal spirometry. It would be indicated if there were crackles, hypoxaemia or a restrictive pattern. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)

options.text: Arrange skin prick testing to common aeroallergens to establish an atopic basis for the symptoms
options.rationale: Common aeroallergen testing does not address workplace sensitisers such as isocyanates, and a negative result would not exclude occupational asthma. Specific immunological testing to the workplace agent, where available, is the relevant investigation rather than a standard environmental panel. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia: Occupational asthma)

explanation.summary: Occupational asthma accounts for a meaningful share of adult onset asthma and is important because it is potentially curable if exposure ceases early, while continued exposure leads to fixed airflow obstruction. Isocyanates in two-pack spray paints are among the commonest Australian causes, alongside flour, wood dusts, latex and laboratory animal proteins. The history of symptoms improving away from work and on holidays is suggestive but not sufficient, since recall is unreliable and the consequences of a diagnosis are severe for the worker. Serial peak flow monitoring, ideally four or more readings daily across at least 2 weeks working and 2 weeks away, is the accessible objective test, with specific inhalation challenge available only in specialised centres, and timing of assessment matters because spirometry performed after a break from exposure is frequently normal, as happened here. Prognosis depends heavily on the interval between symptom onset and removal from exposure, so investigation should be prompt rather than leisurely.
key_points: Adult onset asthma with symptoms improving away from work should prompt an occupational assessment
Isocyanates in two-pack spray paints are a common Australian sensitiser
Normal spirometry after time away from exposure does not exclude the diagnosis
Serial peak flow diaries across periods at and away from work provide objective confirmation
Prognosis depends on how early exposure ceases, so avoid delay in investigating
explanation.pearls: Ask what day of the week the patient is being assessed: a Monday morning clinic after a weekend away from exposure is the least likely time to capture the airflow obstruction that confirms occupational asthma.

sources.label: Safe Work Australia: Occupational respiratory disease

subtopic_detail: Bedside manoeuvres separating dynamic outflow obstruction from fixed valvular stenosis
stem:
You are the resident in a cardiology clinic. A 24-year-old man is referred after collapsing while playing football. He describes a few seconds of greying vision as he sprinted, then waking on the ground with bystanders around him.

He has had two similar near-collapses while exercising over the past year, each resolving within a minute of stopping. He has no chest pain at rest and no palpitations. His father died suddenly at 41 while swimming and no autopsy findings were ever discussed with the family.

On examination the pulse is sharp with a rapid upstroke. The apex beat is forceful and undisplaced with a palpable double impulse. There is a harsh mid-systolic murmur at the left lower sternal edge that does not radiate to the carotids. The murmur becomes louder when he stands from squatting and softer during a sustained handgrip. There is no ejection click. Electrocardiogram shows deep narrow Q waves in the inferolateral leads with left ventricular hypertrophy by voltage criteria.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 68/min, blood pressure 122/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Sharp pulse with rapid upstroke, forceful undisplaced apex with palpable double impulse, harsh mid-systolic murmur at the left lower sternal edge without carotid radiation, louder on standing from squatting, softer with sustained handgrip, no ejection click
data_table.Investigations: Electrocardiogram: deep narrow Q waves inferolaterally with left ventricular hypertrophy by voltage criteria

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Fixed valvular aortic stenosis from a calcified congenitally bicuspid valve
options.rationale: A fixed valvular lesion produces a murmur that softens rather than intensifies on standing, because reduced stroke volume decreases flow across the fixed orifice, and it characteristically radiates to the carotids with a slow rising pulse. The near-pair distinction is that both give a harsh mid-systolic murmur with exertional syncope, but the pulse character and response to manoeuvres are opposite. (Source: CSANZ: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy)

options.text: Ventricular septal defect with left to right shunting across a perimembranous defect
options.rationale: A septal defect produces a pansystolic rather than mid-systolic murmur and would not generate exertional syncope with a double apical impulse and inferolateral Q waves. It would be the diagnosis for a harsh pansystolic murmur at the left sternal edge with a thrill and a normal pulse character. (Source: CSANZ: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy)

options.text: Dynamic left ventricular outflow tract obstruction from asymmetric septal hypertrophy
options.rationale: A murmur that intensifies with standing from squatting and softens with handgrip indicates dynamic obstruction, because reduced preload and afterload bring the hypertrophied septum and mitral apparatus closer together. The sharp rapid upstroke pulse, double apical impulse, absence of carotid radiation and inferolateral Q waves complete the picture. (Source: CSANZ: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy)

options.text: Mitral valve prolapse with late systolic regurgitation through a myxomatous valve
options.rationale: Prolapse produces a mid-systolic click with a late systolic murmur at the apex, and although the click moves earlier on standing there is no click described here. It would be the diagnosis with an audible click and an apical late systolic murmur. (Source: CSANZ: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy)

options.text: Pulmonary valve stenosis with right ventricular overload and post-stenotic dilatation
options.rationale: Pulmonary stenosis produces an upper left sternal edge murmur with an ejection click and right ventricular hypertrophy on the electrocardiogram, not left ventricular hypertrophy with inferolateral Q waves. It would be suggested by right axis deviation and a click varying with respiration. (Source: CSANZ: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy)

explanation.summary: Exertional syncope in a young person with a family history of sudden death is a presentation that demands explanation rather than reassurance, and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is the leading cardiac cause of sudden death in young athletes. The physical signs follow directly from the physiology: a hypertrophied septum narrows the outflow tract during systole, and anything that reduces ventricular cavity size increases the obstruction. Standing from squatting drops preload and makes the murmur louder, while squatting and sustained handgrip increase preload and afterload respectively and make it quieter, which is the exact reverse of a fixed valvular lesion. The electrocardiogram is abnormal in the great majority of patients and deep narrow Q waves reflect septal hypertrophy rather than infarction. Echocardiography confirms the diagnosis and quantifies the gradient, after which risk stratification determines whether an implantable defibrillator is indicated, and first-degree relatives require screening because inheritance is autosomal dominant.
key_points: Exertional syncope with a family history of sudden death requires cardiac investigation, not reassurance
Reduced preload increases dynamic obstruction, so standing from squatting makes the murmur louder
Handgrip increases afterload and softens a dynamic murmur while intensifying a regurgitant one
A sharp rapid upstroke pulse without carotid radiation contrasts with the slow rising pulse of valvular stenosis
Inheritance is autosomal dominant, so first-degree relatives require screening
explanation.pearls: Deep narrow Q waves in the inferolateral leads of a young patient represent septal hypertrophy rather than prior infarction, and their presence alongside left ventricular hypertrophy should prompt echocardiography before any exercise clearance is given.

subtopic_detail: Obligations and screening after silicosis is identified in an engineered stone benchtop worker
stem:
You are the registrar in a respiratory clinic. A 38-year-old man is referred with 10 months of exertional breathlessness and a dry cough. He has cut and polished engineered stone benchtops in a fabrication workshop for 9 years, frequently dry cutting without water suppression.

He has never smoked. He reports no fever, no weight loss and no night sweats, and no joint pain, rash or dry eyes.

On examination there is no clubbing, no lymphadenopathy and fine inspiratory crackles at both bases. Spirometry shows forced expiratory volume in 1 second 2.68 L (72 per cent predicted), forced vital capacity 3.24 L (70 per cent predicted), ratio 0.83, with a diffusing capacity 62 per cent predicted. High resolution computed tomography reports multiple small centrilobular and subpleural nodules with an upper zone predominance, with enlarged hilar nodes showing peripheral calcification. Interferon gamma release assay for tuberculosis is negative, and antinuclear antibody and rheumatoid factor are negative.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84/min, blood pressure 124/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: No clubbing or lymphadenopathy, fine inspiratory crackles at both bases
data_table.Investigations: Spirometry: forced expiratory volume in 1 second 2.68 L (72 per cent predicted), forced vital capacity 3.24 L (70 per cent predicted), ratio 0.83, diffusing capacity 62 per cent predicted. High resolution computed tomography: small centrilobular and subpleural nodules with upper zone predominance, hilar nodes with peripheral calcification. Interferon gamma release assay negative, antinuclear antibody and rheumatoid factor negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence oral prednisolone at an immunosuppressive dose and continue current work with a fitted respirator
options.rationale: Corticosteroids do not alter the natural history of silicosis and the fibrosis progresses even after exposure ends, so immunosuppression adds risk without benefit. Steroid therapy would be appropriate for sarcoidosis, which can produce a similar nodular pattern but lacks the exposure history. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)

options.text: Commence antifibrotic therapy with nintedanib and continue current work with a fitted respirator
options.rationale: Antifibrotics are established in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and progressive fibrosing phenotypes, not as primary therapy for silicosis, and continuing exposure would undermine any benefit. Nintedanib would be considered for a progressive fibrosing course after specialist assessment, alongside exposure cessation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)

options.text: Commence a standard four drug antituberculous regimen and continue current work with a fitted respirator
options.rationale: Silicosis substantially increases tuberculosis risk and screening is mandatory, but the interferon gamma release assay is negative and there are no clinical features of active disease. Treatment would be indicated for a positive screen with active disease, or preventive therapy for latent infection. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Notify the occupational health authority, remove him from further exposure and screen co-workers
options.rationale: Silicosis is a notifiable occupational disease in Australian jurisdictions and there is no treatment that reverses established fibrosis, so exposure cessation is the only intervention that alters disease trajectory. Notification triggers workplace inspection and screening of co-workers, who share the same exposure and are frequently affected without symptoms. (Source: Safe Work Australia: Silicosis and silica dust)
source_refs: Safe Work Australia: Silicosis and silica dust

options.text: Arrange surgical lung biopsy to confirm the histological pattern before making any workplace recommendation
options.rationale: The occupational history with a characteristic upper zone nodular pattern and calcified hilar nodes makes this a clinical and radiological diagnosis not requiring tissue. Biopsy would be considered only where imaging is atypical and an alternative diagnosis would change management. (Source: Safe Work Australia: Silicosis and silica dust)
source_refs: Safe Work Australia: Silicosis and silica dust

explanation.summary: Australia experienced a marked resurgence of silicosis driven by the engineered stone benchtop industry, where the material contains a far higher crystalline silica content than natural stone and dry cutting generates extremely high respirable dust concentrations. The disease has been seen in young workers after unusually short latency, in contrast to the decades-long course of classical silicosis from mining. Diagnosis rests on occupational history with characteristic imaging showing upper zone predominant small nodules, and calcified hilar nodes are a supportive feature. There is no disease-modifying drug therapy, which makes exposure control and early detection the entire strategy, and notification is both a legal duty and the mechanism by which other exposed workers are identified. Associated risks require active surveillance, since tuberculosis, autoimmune connective tissue disease, chronic kidney disease and lung cancer all occur at increased rates and progression continues for years after exposure ceases.
key_points: Engineered stone has very high crystalline silica content and dry cutting produces extreme dust exposure
Silicosis is notifiable in Australian jurisdictions and notification triggers co-worker screening
No pharmacological therapy alters the disease, so exposure cessation is the primary intervention
