Upper zone predominant nodules with calcified hilar nodes are characteristic on imaging
Screen for tuberculosis, autoimmune disease, renal impairment and lung cancer on an ongoing basis
explanation.pearls: Tuberculosis risk is increased several-fold in silicosis and remains elevated for life, so annual screening continues even after the worker has left the industry and regardless of how well the lung disease appears to be behaving.

sources.label: Safe Work Australia: Silicosis and silica dust

subtopic_detail: Separating pericardial constriction from myocardial restriction after mediastinal radiotherapy
stem:
You are the registrar in a cardiology clinic. A 54-year-old woman presents with 8 months of progressive abdominal swelling and ankle oedema. She was treated for Hodgkin lymphoma at age 26 with mediastinal radiotherapy and remains in remission.

She describes breathlessness on climbing one flight of stairs but sleeps flat on one pillow. She has had two paracenteses at another hospital, each time being told the fluid was a transudate, and was investigated for liver disease with a normal liver biopsy.

On examination the jugular venous pressure is elevated 8 cm above the sternal angle and rises on inspiration. There is tense ascites, pitting oedema to both knees and a firm non-pulsatile liver edge. Heart sounds are normal with an added early diastolic sound. Echocardiography reports normal left ventricular wall thickness, ejection fraction 58 per cent, normal valve appearances, a respirophasic ventricular septal shift and marked respiratory variation in mitral inflow velocity. Brain natriuretic peptide is 128 ng/L (<100).

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88/min, blood pressure 108/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Jugular venous pressure elevated 8 cm above the sternal angle and rising on inspiration, tense ascites, pitting oedema to both knees, firm non-pulsatile liver edge, added early diastolic sound
data_table.Investigations: Echocardiography: normal left ventricular wall thickness, ejection fraction 58 per cent, normal valves, respirophasic ventricular septal shift, marked respiratory variation in mitral inflow velocity. Brain natriuretic peptide 128 ng/L (<100)

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Restrictive cardiomyopathy from infiltration producing impaired myocardial relaxation and compliance
options.rationale: Infiltrative myocardial disease typically thickens the ventricular walls and produces a markedly elevated natriuretic peptide, whereas the walls are normal here and the peptide is only marginally raised. The near-pair distinction is that both cause right-sided failure with preserved ejection fraction, but respiratory interdependence with septal shift is a pericardial phenomenon absent in myocardial restriction. (Source: CSANZ: Pericardial disease)

options.text: Cirrhosis with portal hypertension producing ascites and secondary peripheral fluid retention
options.rationale: Hepatic ascites is not accompanied by an elevated jugular venous pressure, and the liver biopsy was normal, so the liver is congested rather than diseased. Cirrhosis would be the diagnosis with a normal venous pressure, stigmata of chronic liver disease and confirmatory histology. (Source: GESA: Ascites)

options.text: Severe tricuspid regurgitation producing systolic venous congestion and secondary hepatic enlargement
options.rationale: Significant tricuspid regurgitation produces a pansystolic murmur, large venous v waves and a pulsatile liver, and the echocardiogram reported normal valves. It would be the diagnosis with those examination findings and regurgitation demonstrated on colour Doppler. (Source: CSANZ: Pericardial disease)

options.text: Pulmonary arterial hypertension producing right ventricular pressure overload and systemic congestion
options.rationale: Pulmonary hypertension causes right ventricular dilatation and hypertrophy with a raised estimated pulmonary artery systolic pressure, none of which is described on the echocardiogram. It would also be expected to cause exertional syncope and a loud pulmonary component of the second heart sound. (Source: CSANZ: Pericardial disease)

options.text: Pericardial constriction producing equalisation of diastolic pressures between the cardiac chambers
options.rationale: A rigid pericardium isolates the heart from intrathoracic pressure changes, producing the respirophasic septal shift and exaggerated mitral inflow variation seen here as the ventricles compete for a fixed total volume. A jugular venous pressure that rises on inspiration and prior mediastinal radiotherapy, a well recognised cause with a latency of decades, complete the picture. (Source: CSANZ: Pericardial disease)

explanation.summary: Constrictive pericarditis is one of the most frequently missed causes of right heart failure, and patients commonly accumulate years of gastroenterological investigation for ascites before the venous pressure is examined properly. The physiology is distinctive: a thickened non-compliant pericardium prevents transmission of intrathoracic pressure changes to the cardiac chambers, so inspiration no longer augments right-sided filling and the jugular venous pressure paradoxically rises, and the two ventricles become interdependent within a fixed total volume so that inspiratory right ventricular filling displaces the septum leftward. Distinguishing it from restrictive cardiomyopathy matters enormously because constriction is surgically curable by pericardiectomy while myocardial restriction is not. Helpful discriminators include normal wall thickness, a natriuretic peptide that is normal or only slightly elevated, and respiratory variation in inflow velocities. Prior cardiac surgery, mediastinal radiotherapy and tuberculosis are the leading causes, and radiation-induced constriction may appear decades after treatment.
key_points: A jugular venous pressure that rises on inspiration is highly suggestive of constriction
Respirophasic septal shift and exaggerated mitral inflow variation reflect ventricular interdependence
Normal wall thickness with a normal or minimally raised natriuretic peptide favours constriction over restriction
Mediastinal radiotherapy, prior cardiac surgery and tuberculosis are the main causes
Constriction is surgically curable by pericardiectomy, unlike restrictive cardiomyopathy
explanation.pearls: A brain natriuretic peptide that is normal or only marginally elevated in a patient with florid right heart failure argues strongly for constriction, because the normal myocardium is not stretched, whereas infiltrative restriction drives the peptide substantially higher.

subtopic_detail: Timing of ventilatory support in motor neuron disease using supine vital capacity and nocturnal symptoms
stem:
You are the medical registrar in a neurology clinic reviewing a 61-year-old man diagnosed with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis fourteen months ago. He has been taking riluzole since diagnosis and attends a multidisciplinary clinic every three months.

He tells you he now sleeps 'propped up on four pillows' because lying flat makes him feel he cannot get enough air, wakes two or three times a night, and has a dull headache for the first hour after waking that clears by mid-morning. He dozes off in the afternoon, which is new.

He has wasting of both hands with fasciculations, brisk reflexes and mild dysarthria, but swallows normally and his weight is stable. Forced vital capacity is 68 per cent predicted sitting and falls to 52 per cent predicted when supine. Daytime arterial carbon dioxide tension is 44 mmHg. Overnight oximetry shows the oxygen saturation below 90 per cent for 24 per cent of the recording.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84/min, blood pressure 130/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 96 per cent on room air seated, temperature 36.7°C
data_table.Respiratory symptoms: Orthopnoea requiring four pillows, two to three nocturnal awakenings, morning headache clearing by mid-morning, new daytime somnolence
data_table.Lung function: Forced vital capacity 68 per cent predicted sitting, falling to 52 per cent predicted supine
data_table.Gas exchange: Daytime arterial carbon dioxide tension 44 mmHg; overnight oximetry with saturation below 90 per cent for 24 per cent of the recording
data_table.Neurological and nutritional: Wasted fasciculating hands, brisk reflexes, mild dysarthria, normal swallow, stable weight

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start riluzole and review his respiratory function again in three months
options.rationale: He has taken riluzole since diagnosis, and in any case it extends survival by a few months without altering diaphragmatic weakness or nocturnal hypoventilation. Deferring for three months allows a further substantial fall in vital capacity. (Source: MND Australia: Clinical guidance)

options.text: Arrange a percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy before any other intervention
options.rationale: Gastrostomy is indicated for dysphagia with weight loss or unsafe swallowing, and his swallow is normal with a stable weight. Placing a tube once vital capacity has fallen below 50 per cent predicted also becomes substantially more hazardous, which is an argument for doing it earlier when it is genuinely needed, not for doing it now. (Source: MND Australia: Clinical guidance)

options.text: Start nocturnal oxygen by nasal prongs at 2 L/min and review him in one month
options.rationale: Oxygen alone treats the saturation without supporting ventilation and can worsen carbon dioxide retention by reducing hypoxic respiratory drive in a patient whose problem is pump failure. Supplemental oxygen is used only alongside ventilatory support or in the palliative phase. (Source: MND Australia: Clinical guidance)

options.text: Refer now for assessment and initiation of non-invasive nocturnal ventilation
options.rationale: Orthopnoea, disturbed sleep, morning headache and daytime somnolence with a supine fall in vital capacity to 52 per cent predicted and significant nocturnal desaturation indicate diaphragmatic weakness with nocturnal hypoventilation, which is the trigger for non-invasive ventilation. Started at this point it improves survival by several months and improves quality of life more than any other intervention in this disease, and a normal daytime carbon dioxide does not exclude the diagnosis because hypoventilation appears first during sleep. (Source: MND Australia: Clinical guidance)

options.text: Start morphine and a benzodiazepine for breathlessness and review in a month
options.rationale: Opioids and benzodiazepines are the mainstay of symptom control for dyspnoea in the terminal phase or when ventilation has been declined or withdrawn. Used now they would suppress an already failing respiratory drive in a man who is ambulant, eating normally and has months to years of useful function ahead. (Source: MND Australia: Clinical guidance)

explanation.summary: Respiratory failure is the usual cause of death in motor neuron disease and arises from progressive weakness of the diaphragm and accessory muscles rather than from lung pathology. Because the diaphragm is loaded most when supine, the earliest measurable abnormality is a fall in vital capacity on lying flat and the earliest symptoms are orthopnoea, fragmented sleep, morning headache and daytime sleepiness, all of which precede any daytime rise in carbon dioxide. Monitoring therefore uses seated and supine forced vital capacity, sniff nasal inspiratory pressure and overnight oximetry at each clinic visit, because a single seated measurement will miss the transition. Non-invasive ventilation started at the point of nocturnal hypoventilation prolongs survival and improves quality of life and cognition, with the benefit greatest in patients without severe bulbar involvement. Discussions about ventilation, gastrostomy and advance care planning are held early while communication is intact, and are revisited as the disease progresses.
key_points: Supine vital capacity falls before seated vital capacity because the diaphragm is loaded lying flat
Morning headache, orthopnoea and daytime somnolence indicate nocturnal hypoventilation
A normal daytime carbon dioxide does not exclude nocturnal hypoventilation
Non-invasive ventilation improves both survival and quality of life when started at this stage
Oxygen without ventilatory support can worsen carbon dioxide retention
explanation.pearls: Place a gastrostomy while forced vital capacity is still above 50 per cent predicted; beyond that point the procedure carries a markedly higher risk of respiratory complications and radiologically inserted gastrostomy under non-invasive ventilation becomes the safer route.

subtopic_detail: Choosing the initial screening test when acral and facial change suggests growth hormone excess
stem:
You are the medical registrar seeing a 44-year-old man referred with bilateral hand numbness that wakes him at night and is worst in the thumb and index finger. He mentions in passing that he has had his wedding ring enlarged twice and has gone up two shoe sizes in five years.

His wife, who attends with him, says his jaw 'looks heavier' and produces a photograph from eight years ago that shows noticeably finer features and a smaller nose.

On examination his hands are broad with doughy soft tissue, there is an interdental gap that he says is new, and the tongue appears enlarged. Tinel sign is positive bilaterally at the wrist. Blood pressure is 158/94 mmHg on two occasions and fasting glucose is 6.6 mmol/L. He has no headache and no visual symptoms, and confrontation visual fields are full.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78/min, blood pressure 158/94 mmHg on two occasions, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6°C
data_table.Examination: Broad hands with doughy soft tissue, new interdental separation, enlarged tongue, coarsened facial features against a photograph from eight years ago
data_table.Neurological: Tinel sign positive bilaterally at the wrist; confrontation visual fields full
data_table.Investigations: Fasting glucose 6.6 mmol/L (3.5-5.5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial investigation?

options.text: Measure a random serum growth hormone level as the initial screening test
options.rationale: Growth hormone is secreted in pulses with a short half-life, so a random level overlaps between health and disease and a normal value cannot exclude the diagnosis. Growth hormone is measured meaningfully only during a dynamic suppression test. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary as the initial investigation
options.rationale: Imaging follows biochemical confirmation because incidental pituitary lesions are found in around 10 per cent of the population and an unconfirmed abnormality generates unnecessary surgery. Once excess secretion is proven, magnetic resonance imaging defines the adenoma and its relation to the optic chiasm. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Measure a serum insulin-like growth factor 1 as the initial screening test
options.rationale: Insulin-like growth factor 1 is produced by the liver in response to integrated growth hormone exposure and has a long half-life, so a single age-matched measurement reflects average secretion over the preceding day and is the recommended screening test. A raised result is confirmed by failure of growth hormone to suppress below 1 microgram/L during a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test, after which imaging is arranged. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Measure an early morning serum cortisol as the initial screening investigation
options.rationale: Cortisol screening addresses Cushing syndrome, which shares hypertension and impaired glucose tolerance with this presentation but produces central obesity, proximal myopathy, thin skin and striae rather than acral enlargement. Acral growth and coarsened features are not features of cortisol excess. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Arrange a 48 hour low dose dexamethasone suppression test as the first step
options.rationale: This is a confirmatory test for cortisol excess and is used after an abnormal first-line screen such as late night salivary cortisol or 24 hour urinary free cortisol. It examines an axis that is not implicated by the clinical findings here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Acromegaly is caused in almost all cases by a growth hormone secreting pituitary adenoma, and diagnosis is typically delayed by 7 to 10 years because the changes are insidious and the patient sees themselves daily. Comparison with old photographs is one of the most useful bedside manoeuvres available. Presenting complaints are often the complications rather than the appearance: carpal tunnel syndrome, obstructive sleep apnoea, hypertension, impaired glucose tolerance or type 2 diabetes, arthropathy and cardiomyopathy. Insulin-like growth factor 1 is the screening test because it integrates pulsatile growth hormone secretion, and confirmation uses failure of growth hormone suppression during an oral glucose tolerance test, with imaging reserved for after biochemical proof. Transsphenoidal surgery is first-line treatment, with somatostatin analogues, the growth hormone receptor antagonist pegvisomant, dopamine agonists and radiotherapy used for residual disease, and mortality, which is increased mainly through cardiovascular disease, returns towards normal once growth hormone and insulin-like growth factor 1 are brought into the target range.
key_points: Insulin-like growth factor 1 is the screening test; random growth hormone is uninterpretable
Confirm with failure of growth hormone suppression during an oral glucose tolerance test
Image the pituitary only after biochemical confirmation
Compare with old photographs, since the changes are too gradual for the patient to notice
Screen for sleep apnoea, diabetes, hypertension, cardiomyopathy and colonic neoplasia
explanation.pearls: Colonoscopy is recommended at diagnosis in acromegaly and repeated according to findings and disease control, because growth hormone excess raises the risk of colonic adenomas and carcinoma independently of other factors.

sources.label: Endocrine Society of Australia: Pituitary disorders

subtopic_detail: Dorsal column signs with a serum cobalamin inside the reference range in a recreational inhalant user
stem:
You are the medical registrar seeing a 24-year-old hospitality worker referred with six weeks of numbness and tingling that began in both feet and has ascended to just below both knees. He says he now has to 'watch my feet to know where they are' and stumbles badly in a dark corridor.

He eats a mixed diet including meat and dairy, has had no gastrointestinal surgery and takes no metformin or proton pump inhibitor. When asked directly about recreational drugs he tells you he inhales nitrous oxide from cream chargers, roughly a hundred bulbs a week for the past eight months.

On examination vibration sense is absent at both ankles and reduced at both knees, joint position sense is impaired at both great toes, and Romberg test is positive. Ankle reflexes are absent while both plantar responses are extensor. Power is preserved. Investigations are shown.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Neurological examination: Vibration absent at ankles and reduced at knees, impaired joint position sense at the great toes, Romberg positive, ankle reflexes absent with extensor plantar responses, power preserved
data_table.Investigations: Serum vitamin B12 210 pmol/L (150-700), haemoglobin 146 g/L (130-180), mean cell volume 92 fL (80-98), no hypersegmented neutrophils on film
data_table.Metabolites: Serum homocysteine 42 micromol/L (5-15), methylmalonic acid 1.9 micromol/L (less than 0.4)
data_table.Exposure: Nitrous oxide inhalation, approximately 100 bulbs weekly for eight months

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure him that the vitamin B12 level is normal and repeat it in three months
options.rationale: Nitrous oxide irreversibly oxidises the cobalt core of cobalamin, inactivating the vitamin while leaving the serum assay, which measures total cobalamin, within the reference range. Functional deficiency is demonstrated by the raised methylmalonic acid and homocysteine, which are the appropriate tests when the level is normal but the clinical picture is not. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Start oral cyanocobalamin 1000 microgram daily and review him in three months
options.rationale: High dose oral replacement is effective for dietary and even for absorptive deficiency in the absence of neurological signs, and it acts too slowly for subacute combined degeneration where the window for recovery is measured in weeks. Parenteral loading is used whenever neurological involvement is present. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the spine before starting any treatment
options.rationale: Imaging may show the characteristic inverted V signal change in the dorsal columns and is useful to document severity, but the biochemical and clinical picture is already diagnostic and treatment should not wait for a scan slot. Delay while imaging is arranged converts reversible deficit into permanent disability. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Start oral folic acid 5 mg daily and review his neurological signs in one month
options.rationale: Folate corrects the megaloblastic anaemia of cobalamin deficiency while allowing the neurological damage to progress unchecked, which is why folate is never given first when cobalamin deficiency is possible. His homocysteine is raised through the cobalamin dependent pathway, not from folate deficiency. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Start intramuscular hydroxocobalamin now and advise him to stop the nitrous oxide
options.rationale: Dorsal column loss with a positive Romberg sign, absent ankle reflexes and extensor plantar responses is subacute combined degeneration of the cord, and parenteral hydroxocobalamin is started immediately because recovery depends on how long the deficit has been present. Cessation of nitrous oxide is equally essential, since continued exposure will inactivate each replacement dose as it is given. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Nitrous oxide inactivates cobalamin by oxidising its cobalt centre, which blocks methionine synthase and produces a functional deficiency regardless of dietary intake or absorption. The consequence is subacute combined degeneration of the dorsal columns and corticospinal tracts, giving the distinctive combination of sensory ataxia and absent ankle reflexes with extensor plantar responses, and a peripheral neuropathy often coexists. Serum cobalamin is frequently within the reference range because the assay measures total rather than active vitamin, so methylmalonic acid and homocysteine are the tests that establish functional deficiency. Haematological changes are commonly absent, and the neurological syndrome can occur with an entirely normal blood film, so a normal full blood count is no reassurance. Treatment is immediate parenteral hydroxocobalamin with cessation of exposure, and recovery is good when treatment starts within weeks but incomplete once the deficit has been established for months.
key_points: Nitrous oxide inactivates cobalamin directly, so serum levels are often normal
Methylmalonic acid and homocysteine demonstrate functional deficiency when the level is normal
Neurological disease can occur without anaemia or macrocytosis
Sensory ataxia with absent ankle jerks and extensor plantars is the classic cord syndrome
Treat with parenteral hydroxocobalamin immediately; oral replacement is too slow
explanation.pearls: Never give folate before cobalamin when both may be deficient: correcting the megaloblastic anaemia removes the haematological signal while methylmalonic acid continues to accumulate, and the cord lesion progresses silently.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Vitamin B12 deficiency

subtopic_detail: Anticoagulant choice for venous thrombosis in a patient with an unresected luminal gastrointestinal tumour
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 67-year-old man on the oncology ward. He was diagnosed six weeks ago with a locally advanced gastric adenocarcinoma and started neoadjuvant chemotherapy, and today his left calf and thigh have become swollen and painful.

His endoscopy report describes a large ulcerated antral lesion, and he has needed two units of red cells since diagnosis for a slow drop in haemoglobin attributed to tumour ooze. He has had no melaena or haematemesis this admission.

Doppler ultrasound confirms occlusive thrombus in the left femoral and popliteal veins. His platelet count is 120 x10^9/L, creatinine clearance is 78 mL/min and liver function is within normal limits. He is taking no antiplatelet drugs and has a central venous access device in the right arm.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92/min, blood pressure 122/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 36.9°C
data_table.Imaging: Doppler ultrasound shows occlusive thrombus in the left femoral and popliteal veins
data_table.Tumour: Large ulcerated gastric antral adenocarcinoma, unresected, on neoadjuvant chemotherapy
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 120 x10^9/L (150-400), creatinine clearance 78 mL/min, liver function within normal limits, haemoglobin 98 g/L (130-180) after two units of red cells
data_table.Other: No antiplatelet drugs; central venous access device in the right arm

lead_in: What is the most appropriate anticoagulation?

options.text: Start oral apixaban at a treatment dose and continue while the cancer is active
options.rationale: Direct oral anticoagulants are a reasonable choice for most cancer associated thrombosis and apixaban has the lowest bleeding signal of the class, but the trials consistently show excess major bleeding in patients with unresected luminal gastrointestinal tumours. An ulcerated antral lesion that is already bleeding is the specific situation in which the oral agents are avoided. (Source: eviQ: Cancer associated thrombosis)

options.text: Start subcutaneous low molecular weight heparin at a treatment dose and continue
options.rationale: Low molecular weight heparin remains the preferred agent for cancer associated thrombosis when there is an unresected luminal gastrointestinal tumour, active tumour bleeding, significant thrombocytopenia or concerns about oral absorption, all of which apply here. It is continued for at least 6 months and for as long as the cancer remains active or treatment continues, with the dose reduced rather than stopped if the platelet count falls further. (Source: eviQ: Cancer associated thrombosis)

options.text: Start warfarin with heparin bridging and target a ratio of 2 to 3 thereafter
options.rationale: Warfarin performs worse than low molecular weight heparin in cancer, with higher recurrence and bleeding rates, because chemotherapy, vomiting, altered nutrition and drug interactions make the international normalised ratio unstable. It is used when neither heparin nor an oral agent is feasible. (Source: eviQ: Cancer associated thrombosis)

options.text: Insert a retrievable inferior vena cava filter and withhold anticoagulation
options.rationale: A filter is reserved for patients in whom anticoagulation is absolutely contraindicated, such as active uncontrolled haemorrhage or recent intracranial bleeding, and he has had no overt bleeding this admission. Filters prevent pulmonary embolism but increase recurrent deep vein thrombosis and do not treat the existing clot. (Source: eviQ: Cancer associated thrombosis)

options.text: Start oral rivaroxaban at a treatment dose and continue for three months only
options.rationale: Rivaroxaban carries the clearest excess of gastrointestinal bleeding of the oral agents in cancer trials, which is the wrong profile for an ulcerated gastric tumour. Three months is also too short, since anticoagulation continues while the malignancy is active. (Source: eviQ: Cancer associated thrombosis)

explanation.summary: Venous thromboembolism is several times more common in people with cancer than in the general population, and it is the second commonest cause of death in patients receiving chemotherapy. Risk is driven by tumour type, with pancreatic, gastric, brain, lung and haematological malignancies at the top, and by the presence of a central venous access device, recent surgery, immobility and certain chemotherapy and antiangiogenic agents. The treatment landscape shifted with trials showing direct oral anticoagulants are at least as effective as low molecular weight heparin, so they are now first choice for many patients, but the same trials identified a consistent excess of gastrointestinal and genitourinary bleeding in patients with unresected luminal tumours at those sites. Low molecular weight heparin therefore retains a clear place where mucosal bleeding risk is high, where absorption is unreliable from vomiting or gastrointestinal resection, and where drug interactions with anticancer therapy are a concern. Anticoagulation continues for a minimum of 6 months and indefinitely while the cancer remains active, with the platelet count guiding dose reduction rather than cessation.
key_points: Direct oral anticoagulants are first choice for many cancer associated thromboses
Avoid them with unresected luminal gastrointestinal or genitourinary tumours because of bleeding
Low molecular weight heparin is preferred when absorption or mucosal bleeding is a concern
Continue for at least 6 months and while the cancer remains active
Reduce the heparin dose rather than stopping it when the platelet count falls
explanation.pearls: Anticoagulate catheter associated upper limb thrombosis and keep the line in place if it is functioning and still needed; removal is required only for infection, malfunction or persistent symptoms despite anticoagulation.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Cancer associated thrombosis

subtopic_detail: High anion gap acidosis with a raised osmolar gap and urinary crystals in a patient with no visual symptoms
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar receiving a 47-year-old man found drowsy on his garage floor by his brother, who says he drinks heavily and has been low since losing his job. He last ate yesterday morning.

He opens his eyes to voice, is confused and is breathing deeply and rapidly. He has vomited twice since arrival. He tells you his vision is completely normal and reads the wall clock across the room without difficulty, and his pupils are 4 mm and briskly reactive with normal fundi.

His brother brings in a partly empty 2 litre container of engine coolant from beside him and also a bottle of methylated spirits, and does not know whether either was opened today. Point-of-care glucose is 5.4 mmol/L. Investigations are shown. Urine microscopy reports abundant envelope shaped crystals and the urine fluoresces under a Wood lamp.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118/min, blood pressure 104/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 34/min and deep, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.1°C
data_table.Arterial blood gas: pH 7.06, arterial carbon dioxide tension 18 mmHg, bicarbonate 7 mmol/L (22-32), lactate 2.1 mmol/L (0.5-2.2)
data_table.Biochemistry: Sodium 141 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 4.8 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), chloride 102 mmol/L (95-110), urea 8.2 mmol/L (3.0-8.0), creatinine 198 micromol/L (60-110), glucose 5.4 mmol/L, serum ketones 0.2 mmol/L (less than 0.6)
data_table.Osmolality: Measured serum osmolality 340 mOsm/kg (275-295); calculated osmolarity 302 mOsm/L
data_table.Urine and vision: Abundant envelope shaped crystals on microscopy, urine fluoresces under a Wood lamp; visual acuity normal, pupils 4 mm and briskly reactive, fundi normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Give fomepizole now and arrange urgent haemodialysis with the renal team
options.rationale: An anion gap of 32 with an osmolar gap of 38, an undetectable ethanol, calcium oxalate crystalluria and fluorescent urine identifies ethylene glycol rather than methanol, and preserved vision with normal fundi argues against the methanol optic neuropathy. Fomepizole blocks alcohol dehydrogenase and stops further conversion to glycolic and oxalic acid, while haemodialysis is indicated here by a pH of 7.06 with acute kidney injury and removes both the parent alcohol and the accumulated metabolites. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

options.text: Give intravenous sodium bicarbonate alone and repeat the blood gas in an hour
options.rationale: Bicarbonate is a useful adjunct that reduces tissue distribution of the acid metabolites and is given alongside definitive therapy, but on its own it does nothing to stop ongoing metabolite production. Buffering a toxic alcohol poisoning while the parent compound continues to be converted is treating the number rather than the poisoning. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

options.text: Give intravenous thiamine and dextrose and repeat the blood gas in an hour
options.rationale: Thiamine and glucose are given to every unwell person who drinks heavily and are entirely appropriate, but alcoholic ketoacidosis has been excluded by serum ketones of 0.2 mmol/L and cannot explain an osmolar gap of 38. Relying on this alone would allow renal failure and death from the acidosis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

options.text: Give oral activated charcoal 50 g and observe him in the short stay unit
options.rationale: Charcoal binds alcohols poorly, the ingestion is clearly hours old given the established metabolic acidosis and renal injury, and administering it to a confused vomiting patient risks aspiration. Decontamination has no role in toxic alcohol poisoning. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

options.text: Give intravenous N-acetylcysteine and arrange urgent liver function testing
options.rationale: Acetylcysteine treats paracetamol poisoning, which produces hepatic injury with transaminase rise rather than an early high anion gap acidosis with an osmolar gap. Massive paracetamol ingestion can cause a lactic acidosis, but the lactate here is 2.1 mmol/L. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

explanation.summary: Toxic alcohol poisoning is suspected whenever a high anion gap metabolic acidosis is accompanied by a raised osmolar gap, calculated as measured osmolality minus calculated osmolarity with a normal value below about 10. The gap is largest early, when the parent alcohol is still present, and falls as it is metabolised while the anion gap rises, so a normal osmolar gap late in the course does not exclude the diagnosis. Ethylene glycol and methanol are separated clinically by the target organ: ethylene glycol produces calcium oxalate crystalluria, hypocalcaemia and acute kidney injury, while methanol produces blurred vision, central scotomata and a hyperaemic optic disc from formic acid toxicity to the optic nerve. Treatment for both is blockade of alcohol dehydrogenase with fomepizole, or with an ethanol infusion where fomepizole is not immediately available, combined with bicarbonate and cofactor therapy, thiamine and pyridoxine for ethylene glycol and folinic acid for methanol. Haemodialysis is added for severe acidosis, end-organ injury or a high measured concentration, and it clears both the parent alcohol and its acid metabolites.
key_points: A high anion gap acidosis with an osmolar gap above 10 suggests toxic alcohol ingestion
The osmolar gap falls and the anion gap rises as the parent alcohol is metabolised
Oxalate crystalluria and renal injury indicate ethylene glycol; visual loss indicates methanol
Alcohol dehydrogenase blockade with fomepizole or ethanol stops metabolite production
Dialyse for severe acidosis, end-organ injury or a high measured concentration
explanation.pearls: Sodium fluorescein is added to many automotive coolants, which is why the urine can fluoresce under a Wood lamp in ethylene glycol ingestion; the finding supports the diagnosis when positive but is too unreliable to exclude it when negative.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Ethylene glycol poisoning

subtopic_detail: Timeframe for colonoscopy after a positive immunochemical faecal occult blood test in the national program
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 62-year-old man who has brought in a letter reporting a positive result from his National Bowel Cancer Screening Program kit. He completed it three weeks ago and says he 'nearly threw the envelope out because I feel completely fine'.

He has no rectal bleeding, no change in bowel habit and no abdominal pain. His weight has been stable for years. There is no family history of bowel cancer or polyps and he has never had a colonoscopy.

He takes perindopril for hypertension and no antiplatelet or anticoagulant drugs. Examination including abdominal and rectal examination is unremarkable. A full blood count taken last month for another reason showed a haemoglobin of 148 g/L (130-180) with a mean cell volume of 89 fL (80-98).

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Screening result: Positive immunochemical faecal occult blood test through the National Bowel Cancer Screening Program
data_table.Symptoms: No rectal bleeding, no change in bowel habit, no abdominal pain, weight stable
data_table.Examination: Abdominal and rectal examination unremarkable
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 148 g/L (130-180), mean cell volume 89 fL (80-98)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Repeat the immunochemical faecal occult blood test in twelve months' time
options.rationale: A positive screening test is not repeated to confirm it, because a repeat negative does not exclude the lesion that caused the original bleed and intermittent bleeding from a tumour is the rule rather than the exception. Repeat testing is for people whose kit was inadequate or spoiled. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Colorectal cancer guidelines)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Colorectal cancer guidelines

options.text: Arrange a computed tomography colonography within the next thirty days
options.rationale: Computed tomography colonography is the alternative when colonoscopy is incomplete, refused or unsafe, and it cannot take biopsies or remove polyps, so any abnormality still requires colonoscopy afterwards. It is not the first choice in a fit 62-year-old. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Colorectal cancer guidelines)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Colorectal cancer guidelines

options.text: Refer for colonoscopy to be performed within thirty days of the result
options.rationale: Around one in 20 people with a positive immunochemical faecal occult blood test has a colorectal cancer and about a third have an advanced adenoma, so colonoscopy is the required follow-up test regardless of whether symptoms are present. Australian guidance is that it should occur within 30 days of the positive result, and outcomes worsen measurably once the interval exceeds about 120 days. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Colorectal cancer guidelines)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Colorectal cancer guidelines

options.text: Check a full blood count and iron studies and refer only if he is anaemic
options.rationale: Anaemia is neither sensitive nor specific for colorectal neoplasia, and most screen-detected cancers are found in people with a normal haemoglobin, as his result illustrates. Using a normal blood count to withhold colonoscopy is a recognised route to delayed diagnosis. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Colorectal cancer guidelines)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Colorectal cancer guidelines

options.text: Refer for flexible sigmoidoscopy to be performed within thirty days
options.rationale: Sigmoidoscopy examines only to the splenic flexure and would miss the proximal lesions that account for a substantial minority of screen-detected cancers. The whole colon must be visualised after a positive faecal occult blood test. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Colorectal cancer guidelines)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Colorectal cancer guidelines

explanation.summary: The National Bowel Cancer Screening Program offers a free immunochemical faecal occult blood test every two years, with eligibility now extending from age 45 to 74 following the lowering of the starting age. The test detects human globin and so does not require dietary restriction, unlike the older guaiac based tests. Participation remains well below target and a substantial number of positive results are never followed up with colonoscopy, which is the single greatest weakness in the program and where general practice makes the most difference. Roughly 5 per cent of positive tests correspond to a cancer and a further third to an advanced adenoma, and the absence of symptoms carries no reassurance because the program exists precisely to find disease before symptoms appear. Colonoscopy is recommended within 30 days, with evidence of worsening stage at diagnosis and survival as the interval lengthens beyond about 120 days.
key_points: A positive immunochemical faecal occult blood test requires colonoscopy, not a repeat test
Target interval is within 30 days, with outcomes worsening beyond about 120 days
About 5 per cent of positive tests correspond to a cancer and a third to an advanced adenoma
Absence of symptoms and a normal haemoglobin do not reduce the need for colonoscopy
The program now covers ages 45 to 74 with two yearly testing
explanation.pearls: The immunochemical test detects human globin and is therefore specific to lower gastrointestinal bleeding, because globin from an upper gastrointestinal source is digested before reaching the colon; this is why it needs no dietary preparation and why a positive result should not be attributed to reflux or peptic ulcer disease.

sources.label: Cancer Council Australia: Colorectal cancer guidelines

subtopic_detail: Choosing a repeat intravenous iron preparation after symptomatic hypophosphataemia from the previous infusion
stem:
You are the medical registrar in a haematology clinic seeing a 44-year-old woman with iron deficiency anaemia from heavy menstrual bleeding. She has a levonorgestrel intrauterine system in place and is awaiting gynaecological review.

Oral ferrous sulfate caused severe nausea and constipation at every dose she tried, including alternate day dosing, and she stopped it after two months. She was given an intravenous infusion of ferric carboxymaltose three months ago.

Two weeks after that infusion she developed profound fatigue, aching in both thighs and pain in her ribs when she coughed, and a serum phosphate taken at the time was 0.42 mmol/L. The symptoms and the phosphate normalised over eight weeks without specific treatment. Her haemoglobin has now fallen again and she needs further parenteral iron.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Current investigations: Haemoglobin 96 g/L (115-155), mean cell volume 72 fL (80-98), ferritin 8 microgram/L (15-200), transferrin saturation 6 per cent (15-45)
data_table.Previous episode: Serum phosphate 0.42 mmol/L (0.75-1.50) two weeks after ferric carboxymaltose, with fatigue, thigh ache and rib pain; normalised over eight weeks
data_table.Oral iron history: Ferrous sulfate caused severe nausea and constipation including on alternate day dosing; stopped after two months
data_table.Renal and bone profile: Creatinine, corrected calcium and vitamin D within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Repeat ferric carboxymaltose and check the serum phosphate two weeks later
options.rationale: Repeating the same preparation reproduces the mechanism that caused the problem, since ferric carboxymaltose raises intact fibroblast growth factor 23 and drives renal phosphate wasting, and recurrence rates on rechallenge are high. Monitoring the phosphate detects the complication rather than preventing it. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Give ferric derisomaltose instead and check the serum phosphate afterwards
options.rationale: Ferric carboxymaltose is the intravenous iron most strongly associated with fibroblast growth factor 23 mediated hypophosphataemia, and head to head trials show substantially lower rates with ferric derisomaltose, which delivers an equivalent single high dose. Switching preparation addresses the mechanism while still correcting the iron deficit in one visit, with a phosphate check to confirm the change has worked. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Restart oral ferrous sulfate daily and check the haemoglobin in three months
options.rationale: She has already failed oral iron on intolerance grounds including a trial of alternate day dosing, which is the usual strategy for improving tolerance and absorption. Returning to it would leave her anaemic while ongoing menstrual losses continue. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Give oral phosphate supplements and repeat the ferric carboxymaltose today
options.rationale: Oral phosphate does not prevent the renal wasting driven by fibroblast growth factor 23 and can worsen it by further stimulating the hormone. Supplementation is used to treat symptomatic hypophosphataemia once it has occurred, not to enable a rechallenge. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Transfuse two units of red cells and check the serum ferritin afterwards
options.rationale: Transfusion is reserved for haemodynamic compromise or symptomatic anaemia that cannot wait for iron repletion, and a stable woman with a haemoglobin of 96 g/L does not meet that threshold. It also fails to replenish the iron stores that the marrow needs. (Source: National Blood Authority: Patient Blood Management Guidelines)
source_refs: National Blood Authority: Patient Blood Management Guidelines

explanation.summary: Intravenous iron is indicated when oral iron is not tolerated or not absorbed, when losses exceed what oral replacement can match, or when repletion is needed quickly before surgery. Hypophosphataemia is an under-recognised complication that is specific to certain carbohydrate shells, occurring because they increase intact fibroblast growth factor 23, which causes renal phosphate wasting and suppresses calcitriol. It is far more frequent with ferric carboxymaltose than with ferric derisomaltose, iron sucrose or iron polymaltose, and although most cases are asymptomatic and transient, repeated infusions can produce persistent hypophosphataemia with proximal myopathy, bone pain and osteomalacic fractures. Phosphate is checked a fortnight after infusion in anyone receiving repeated doses, in malabsorption, malnutrition or vitamin D deficiency, and in those with existing bone disease. All modern preparations carry a low rate of hypersensitivity and the transient Fishbane reaction of flushing and back or chest tightness, which settles with stopping the infusion and does not by itself contraindicate re-exposure.
key_points: Hypophosphataemia after intravenous iron is mediated by fibroblast growth factor 23
The risk is substantially higher with ferric carboxymaltose than with other preparations
Repeated exposure can cause proximal myopathy, bone pain and osteomalacic fracture
Check phosphate about two weeks after infusion in those needing repeated doses
Switching preparation, rather than supplementing phosphate, is the way to prevent recurrence
explanation.pearls: The Fishbane reaction of facial flushing with chest or back tightness during an iron infusion is not anaphylaxis: there is no urticaria, wheeze or hypotension, and it settles within minutes of pausing the infusion, which can then be restarted at a slower rate.

sources.label: National Blood Authority: Patient Blood Management Guidelines
BMJ Best Practice: Iron deficiency anaemia

subtopic_detail: Initiating iron removal in a C282Y homozygote with a markedly raised ferritin and no fibrosis
stem:
You are the medical registrar in a liver clinic seeing a 48-year-old man referred after abnormal blood tests taken for life insurance. He says he feels 'a bit flat and achy in the knuckles' but has no other complaints.

He drinks four standard drinks a week and takes no regular medications, vitamins or iron supplements. His father died at 61 of liver disease that was never fully investigated.

His fasting transferrin saturation is 62 per cent with a ferritin of 1150 microgram/L, repeated on a second fasting sample with the same values. HFE genotyping reports homozygosity for the C282Y variant. Alanine aminotransferase is mildly raised, C-reactive protein is within normal limits and transient elastography reports a liver stiffness of 4.8 kPa. Fasting glucose and an echocardiogram are both normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Iron studies: Fasting transferrin saturation 62 per cent (15-45), ferritin 1150 microgram/L (30-300), confirmed on a repeat fasting sample
data_table.Genetics: HFE genotype homozygous for the C282Y variant
data_table.Liver assessment: Alanine aminotransferase 68 U/L (less than 45), C-reactive protein within normal limits, transient elastography 4.8 kPa
data_table.Other results: Fasting glucose and echocardiogram within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Start oral deferasirox and repeat the ferritin measurement in three months
options.rationale: Chelation is reserved for iron overload in people who cannot be venesected, principally those with transfusion dependent anaemias, and it carries renal, hepatic and gastrointestinal toxicity. Venesection is cheaper, faster and better tolerated in a man with normal haemoglobin. (Source: GESA: Haemochromatosis)

options.text: Start weekly venesection aiming for a ferritin of 50 to 100 microgram/L
options.rationale: C282Y homozygosity with a fasting transferrin saturation above 45 per cent and a ferritin above the reference range, in the absence of inflammation or alcohol excess, establishes iron overload that warrants treatment. Weekly removal of 450 to 500 mL continues until the ferritin reaches 50 to 100 microgram/L, after which maintenance venesection every 3 to 4 months keeps it in that range. (Source: GESA: Haemochromatosis)

options.text: Advise dietary iron restriction and repeat the ferritin in twelve months
options.rationale: Dietary measures cannot remove the iron already deposited and have only a marginal effect on ongoing absorption, so they are an adjunct rather than a treatment. Avoiding iron and vitamin C supplements and uncooked shellfish is sensible advice alongside venesection. (Source: GESA: Haemochromatosis)

options.text: Arrange liver biopsy before any decision about starting iron removal
options.rationale: Biopsy is used to assess fibrosis when the ferritin exceeds 1000 microgram/L with raised transaminases and non-invasive assessment is equivocal, and here transient elastography at 4.8 kPa already indicates the absence of significant fibrosis. Venesection is started regardless of the fibrosis stage. (Source: GESA: Haemochromatosis)

options.text: Repeat the iron studies fasting in three months before starting treatment
options.rationale: Repeat fasting testing is the right step when a single raised ferritin could reflect inflammation, alcohol or metabolic syndrome, and that has already been done with concordant results and a normal C-reactive protein. Further delay allows continued deposition in liver, pancreas, heart and joints. (Source: GESA: Haemochromatosis)

explanation.summary: Hereditary haemochromatosis in people of northern European ancestry is overwhelmingly caused by homozygosity for the C282Y variant in HFE, which reduces hepcidin production and allows unregulated intestinal iron absorption. Penetrance is incomplete, so many homozygotes never develop clinical disease, and the decision to treat rests on the iron indices rather than on the genotype alone. Transferrin saturation rises first and is the more specific marker, while ferritin is an acute phase reactant that is also raised by alcohol, inflammation and metabolic dysfunction, which is why both are measured fasting and interpreted together with a C-reactive protein. Venesection is remarkably effective and, when started before cirrhosis develops, restores a normal life expectancy; established cirrhosis does not reverse and carries an ongoing hepatocellular carcinoma risk that requires six monthly surveillance. First-degree relatives are offered genetic and biochemical screening, since identifying them before organ damage occurs is the main benefit of making the diagnosis.
key_points: Transferrin saturation rises before ferritin and is the more specific marker of iron loading
Treat on the basis of the iron indices, not on the genotype alone, since penetrance is incomplete
Weekly venesection until ferritin reaches 50 to 100 microgram/L, then maintenance every 3 to 4 months
Life expectancy is normal if treatment starts before cirrhosis develops
Screen first-degree relatives genetically and biochemically
explanation.pearls: Arthropathy of the second and third metacarpophalangeal joints is the one manifestation that does not improve with venesection and can progress despite normal iron indices, so its presence should not be used to judge the adequacy of treatment.

subtopic_detail: Action on a first isolation of Pseudomonas aeruginosa in stable bronchiectasis
stem:
You are the medical registrar in a respiratory clinic seeing a 56-year-old woman with bronchiectasis confirmed on high resolution computed tomography five years ago following childhood pertussis. She attends for a routine review and says she is 'about the same as always'.

She produces around 20 mL of mucoid sputum daily, has had no increase in volume or change in colour, no fever and no new breathlessness, and has not had an exacerbation for eight months. She performs airway clearance twice daily and her forced expiratory volume in one second is unchanged from six months ago at 72 per cent predicted.

Her previous sputum cultures over five years have consistently grown Haemophilus influenzae. The routine sputum sample collected at her last visit has grown Pseudomonas aeruginosa for the first time, sensitive to ciprofloxacin and to tobramycin.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Symptoms: 20 mL mucoid sputum daily, unchanged; no fever, no new breathlessness, no exacerbation for eight months
data_table.Lung function: Forced expiratory volume in one second 72 per cent predicted, unchanged from six months ago
data_table.Microbiology: First isolation of Pseudomonas aeruginosa, sensitive to ciprofloxacin and tobramycin; all previous cultures grew Haemophilus influenzae

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Attempt eradication with oral ciprofloxacin and nebulised tobramycin
options.rationale: A first isolation of Pseudomonas aeruginosa in bronchiectasis is treated with an eradication attempt even when the patient is clinically stable, because chronic infection is independently associated with more exacerbations, faster lung function decline and higher mortality. The usual Australian regimen combines two weeks of oral ciprofloxacin with a course of nebulised tobramycin, with repeat cultures to confirm clearance. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia: Bronchiectasis Toolbox)

options.text: Start long term azithromycin three times weekly and repeat the sputum culture
options.rationale: Long term macrolide therapy reduces exacerbation frequency in patients having three or more exacerbations a year, and she has had none for eight months. Starting a macrolide also requires excluding non-tuberculous mycobacterial infection first, or resistance may be induced. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia: Bronchiectasis Toolbox)

options.text: Observe and repeat the sputum culture in three months if she remains well
options.rationale: Waiting allows the organism to establish a biofilm, after which eradication becomes much less likely and treatment shifts to lifelong suppression. Observation is appropriate for organisms of low pathogenic significance in bronchiectasis, which Pseudomonas aeruginosa is not. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia: Bronchiectasis Toolbox)

options.text: Start inhaled corticosteroid with a long-acting beta agonist and review her
options.rationale: Inhaled corticosteroids are not routinely indicated in bronchiectasis without coexisting asthma or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and they increase the risk of respiratory infection including Pseudomonas colonisation. They do nothing to clear an established isolate. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia: Bronchiectasis Toolbox)

options.text: Refer for surgical resection of the most affected bronchiectatic segment
options.rationale: Resection is considered for localised disease causing recurrent severe exacerbations or massive haemoptysis that has failed medical management. Her disease is stable and this would not address an organism present throughout the airway. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia: Bronchiectasis Toolbox)

explanation.summary: Bronchiectasis management rests on four pillars: airway clearance and exercise, treatment of exacerbations, long term suppression where exacerbations are frequent, and identification and treatment of the underlying cause. Pseudomonas aeruginosa occupies a special position because chronic infection with it marks a distinct trajectory, with more frequent exacerbations, greater sputum volume, accelerated decline in forced expiratory volume and increased mortality independent of other severity markers. For that reason a first isolation triggers an eradication attempt even in a clinically stable patient, borrowing the strategy established in cystic fibrosis, typically oral ciprofloxacin combined with an inhaled antipseudomonal agent. Once biofilm formation has occurred the organism is rarely cleared and management shifts to long term suppression with nebulised antibiotics. Investigation for a treatable underlying cause continues alongside, including immunoglobulins, allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis serology, cystic fibrosis testing where appropriate, and consideration of primary ciliary dyskinesia.
key_points: Chronic Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection independently predicts decline and mortality
A first isolation warrants an eradication attempt even when the patient is stable
Typical regimen is oral ciprofloxacin plus a nebulised antipseudomonal agent with repeat cultures
Long term macrolides are for three or more exacerbations a year, after excluding mycobacteria
Inhaled corticosteroids are not routine in bronchiectasis without asthma or airflow obstruction
explanation.pearls: Exclude non-tuberculous mycobacterial infection with three sputum cultures before starting long term azithromycin in bronchiectasis: macrolide monotherapy against an unrecognised Mycobacterium avium complex infection induces resistance and removes the most effective drug from any future regimen.

subtopic_detail: Withdrawing a long standing nightly benzodiazepine after recurrent falls in an older woman
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing an 82-year-old woman in a falls clinic. She has fallen twice in three months, once in the hallway on the way to the toilet at 2 am and once getting out of bed in the morning, and says she 'just went down' both times with no warning and no chest pain or palpitations.

She lives alone in a single storey unit and manages her own shopping. She has taken temazepam 20 mg every night for eleven years, originally started after her husband died, and says she 'could not possibly sleep without it'. She also takes sertraline 50 mg daily and perindopril.

Lying and standing blood pressures show no postural drop. Gait is slow but steady with a normal timed up and go test, visual acuity is corrected to 6/9 bilaterally and cognition is intact. Her estimated glomerular filtration rate is 48 mL/min/1.73m2. An electrocardiogram and a vitamin D level are both within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72/min, blood pressure 132/76 mmHg lying with no postural drop, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6°C
data_table.Medications: Temazepam 20 mg nightly for eleven years, sertraline 50 mg daily, perindopril
data_table.Falls assessment: Timed up and go test within normal limits, gait slow but steady, corrected visual acuity 6/9 bilaterally, cognition intact
data_table.Investigations: Estimated glomerular filtration rate 48 mL/min/1.73m2, electrocardiogram and vitamin D within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Stop the temazepam tonight and start modified release melatonin instead
options.rationale: Abrupt cessation after eleven years of continuous use risks rebound insomnia, anxiety, and in some cases seizures and delirium, and it almost always drives the patient to resume the drug. Melatonin is a reasonable adjunct during a taper but does not make abrupt withdrawal safe. (Source: NPS MedicineWise: Benzodiazepine deprescribing)

options.text: Continue the temazepam and refer her to a falls prevention program only
options.rationale: Exercise based falls prevention reduces falls and should be arranged, but leaving the single most modifiable pharmacological risk factor in place treats around the problem. Benzodiazepine use roughly doubles the risk of falls and hip fracture in older people. (Source: NPS MedicineWise: Benzodiazepine deprescribing)

options.text: Reduce the temazepam by about a quarter every two to four weeks with support
options.rationale: Benzodiazepine withdrawal in long term users is achieved by gradual dose reduction of roughly 10 to 25 per cent every 2 to 4 weeks, slowing further near the end where withdrawal symptoms are most pronounced. Pairing the taper with education and behavioural strategies for insomnia substantially increases the proportion who stop successfully. (Source: NPS MedicineWise: Benzodiazepine deprescribing)

options.text: Switch her to nightly zopiclone at an equivalent dose and review in a month
options.rationale: The so-called Z drugs carry the same falls, fracture and cognitive risks as benzodiazepines in older people and are not a safer substitute. Substitution also resets the dependence rather than reducing total sedative exposure. (Source: NPS MedicineWise: Benzodiazepine deprescribing)

options.text: Switch her to nightly diazepam at an equivalent dose and review in a month
options.rationale: Conversion to a long-acting agent is a recognised technique that smooths withdrawal for short-acting drugs such as alprazolam, but temazepam has an intermediate half-life and tapers adequately in its own right. Diazepam accumulates markedly in older people with reduced renal and hepatic clearance, and the active metabolite prolongs the sedative and falls risk. (Source: NPS MedicineWise: Benzodiazepine deprescribing)

explanation.summary: Falls in older people are multifactorial, and a structured assessment covers gait and balance, vision, postural blood pressure, cognition, continence, footwear, home hazards and medications. Benzodiazepines, Z drugs, antipsychotics, anticholinergics, opioids and antidepressants are the principal culprit medicine classes, and benzodiazepines approximately double the risk of falls and hip fracture in this age group. Long term use is rarely justified for insomnia because tolerance to the hypnotic effect develops within weeks while the daytime psychomotor and cognitive impairment persists. Deprescribing succeeds far more often when the patient understands the rationale, when reduction is gradual rather than abrupt, and when non-pharmacological treatment for insomnia is offered in parallel. Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia outperforms hypnotics for chronic insomnia at every age and its benefit persists after treatment ends.
key_points: Benzodiazepines roughly double the risk of falls and hip fracture in older people
Reduce by about 10 to 25 per cent every 2 to 4 weeks, slowing near the end of the taper
Never stop abruptly after long term use because of rebound, seizure and delirium risk
Z drugs carry the same risks and are not a safer substitute
Offer cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia alongside the taper
explanation.pearls: Switching to diazepam before tapering is genuinely useful for short half-life agents like alprazolam and oxazepam, where interdose withdrawal drives the difficulty, but it is counterproductive in frail older people because the active metabolite desmethyldiazepam has a half-life that can exceed 100 hours.

subtopic_detail: Advising a man in his mid fifties whose father was diagnosed with prostate cancer after age sixty
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 55-year-old man for a routine review of his blood pressure. Towards the end of the consultation he says a colleague has told him to 'get the prostate test' and asks whether he should have it.

His father was diagnosed with prostate cancer at the age of 62 and is alive and well eight years after treatment. He has no brothers. No other family members have had prostate, breast or ovarian cancer.

He passes urine twice a night, which he says has been the same for years, with a normal stream and no haematuria and no bone pain. Digital rectal examination has never been performed. He is otherwise well, works full time, and tells you he would want treatment if something were found.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Family history: Father diagnosed with prostate cancer at age 62 and well eight years after treatment; no brothers; no family history of breast or ovarian cancer
data_table.Urinary symptoms: Nocturia twice nightly, unchanged for years, normal stream, no haematuria
data_table.Other: No bone pain, works full time, would accept treatment if a cancer were found

lead_in: What would you first recommend?

options.text: Arrange a prostate specific antigen test and a digital rectal examination today
options.rationale: Digital rectal examination adds negligible diagnostic value to prostate specific antigen testing in asymptomatic men in primary care and is no longer recommended as part of screening. Ordering the antigen test without first discussing the benefits and harms also bypasses the consent process the guideline requires. (Source: PCFA and Cancer Council Australia: PSA testing guidelines)
source_refs: PCFA and Cancer Council Australia: PSA testing guidelines

options.text: Advise against testing and review him again when he turns sixty years old
options.rationale: Blanket advice against testing is not what Australian guidance recommends for a man aged 50 to 69 who asks about it, and deferring to 60 would forfeit a decade of the age band in which testing offers most benefit. Testing is not recommended in men whose life expectancy is under 7 years, which does not apply here. (Source: PCFA and Cancer Council Australia: PSA testing guidelines)
source_refs: PCFA and Cancer Council Australia: PSA testing guidelines

options.text: Refer him directly to urology for multiparametric magnetic resonance imaging
options.rationale: Multiparametric imaging is used after a raised prostate specific antigen to decide whether and where to biopsy, not as a first-line screening test in an asymptomatic man. Using it up front would generate incidental findings without an antigen result to interpret them against. (Source: PCFA and Cancer Council Australia: PSA testing guidelines)
source_refs: PCFA and Cancer Council Australia: PSA testing guidelines

options.text: Arrange a prostate specific antigen test yearly from now until age seventy
options.rationale: Annual testing increases the detection of indolent disease and the associated overtreatment without a corresponding mortality benefit, which is why the recommended interval is every 2 years. The age band is also to 69 rather than to 70. (Source: PCFA and Cancer Council Australia: PSA testing guidelines)
source_refs: PCFA and Cancer Council Australia: PSA testing guidelines

options.text: Discuss the benefits and harms and recommend two yearly testing to age 69
options.rationale: Australian guidance is that men aged 50 to 69 who decide to be tested after being informed of the benefits and harms should be offered prostate specific antigen testing every 2 years, and a father diagnosed after 60 confers a modestly increased risk that does not change the starting age. The discussion covers the reduction in prostate cancer mortality set against overdiagnosis, biopsy complications, and the incontinence and erectile dysfunction that follow treatment of disease that would never have caused harm. (Source: PCFA and Cancer Council Australia: PSA testing guidelines)
source_refs: PCFA and Cancer Council Australia: PSA testing guidelines

explanation.summary: Prostate specific antigen testing is offered rather than recommended universally, because the mortality benefit is real but modest while overdiagnosis is substantial, and Australian guidance therefore builds the decision around an informed discussion. For men at average risk the recommendation is two yearly testing between 50 and 69 years for those who choose to be tested, with no testing where life expectancy is less than about 7 years. Family history modifies the starting age rather than the interval: a first-degree relative diagnosed under 60, or two or more affected relatives, moves the start to 45, and a very strong family history or a known BRCA2 mutation moves it to 40. A father diagnosed at 62 raises the relative risk modestly and does not by itself bring the start forward. Digital rectal examination is no longer recommended as an addition to antigen testing in asymptomatic men in general practice, and a raised result is now usually followed by multiparametric magnetic resonance imaging before any decision about biopsy.
key_points: Offer two yearly testing between 50 and 69 after discussing benefits and harms
A first-degree relative diagnosed under 60 brings the starting age forward to 45
A relative diagnosed after 60 raises risk modestly without changing the starting age
Digital rectal examination adds little in asymptomatic men and is no longer recommended
Do not test where life expectancy is less than about 7 years
explanation.pearls: A prostate specific antigen above the age specific 95th centile, which is 3.0 microgram/L for men in their fifties, prompts a repeat within 1 to 3 months before referral, because transient rises from ejaculation, cycling, prostatitis or instrumentation are common and a single raised value is not an indication for biopsy.

sources.label: PCFA and Cancer Council Australia: PSA testing guidelines
RACGP: Guidelines for preventive activities in general practice
BMJ Best Practice: Prostate cancer screening

subtopic_detail: Rash with fever, eosinophilia and hepatitis six weeks after starting a urate lowering drug
stem:
You are the medical registrar admitting a 64-year-old man from the emergency department with a rash and fever. He says it started around his neck nine days ago and 'has taken over everywhere', and that his face feels tight and swollen.

He started allopurinol 300 mg daily six weeks ago for recurrent gout. He takes perindopril and has taken no new antibiotics, herbal preparations or over the counter medicines.

On examination there is a confluent morbilliform eruption covering the trunk, both arms and both legs with marked periorbital and facial oedema. The lips, conjunctivae and oral mucosa are unaffected, there is no skin detachment and Nikolsky sign is negative. There is tender cervical and axillary lymphadenopathy. Investigations are shown.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108/min, blood pressure 128/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 38.9°C
data_table.Skin: Confluent morbilliform eruption over trunk and all four limbs with facial and periorbital oedema; mucosae spared; no skin detachment; Nikolsky sign negative
data_table.Investigations: Eosinophils 2.4 x10^9/L (0.0-0.5), white cell count 16.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0) with atypical lymphocytes, alanine aminotransferase 320 U/L (less than 45), creatinine 142 micromol/L (60-110) rising from 88 micromol/L
data_table.Medications: Allopurinol 300 mg daily started six weeks ago; perindopril long term

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Stop the allopurinol and start topical corticosteroid with an oral antihistamine
options.rationale: Topical treatment and antihistamines are appropriate for a simple morbilliform drug eruption, which is confined to the skin without fever, facial oedema, eosinophilia or organ involvement. Restricting treatment to the skin here leaves a hepatitis and an acute kidney injury untreated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

options.text: Continue the allopurinol and start oral prednisolone 0.5 mg/kg each morning
options.rationale: Immediate and permanent withdrawal of the culprit drug is the single most important intervention and determines outcome, so corticosteroid without withdrawal is inadequate. Allopurinol also has a long-acting metabolite, oxipurinol, so the reaction can continue to evolve for weeks after cessation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

options.text: Stop the allopurinol and transfer him to a burns unit for specialist skin care
options.rationale: Burns unit transfer is the pathway for Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis, which present with mucosal erosions, a positive Nikolsky sign and epidermal detachment. His mucosae are spared with no detachment, and the eosinophilia and hepatitis point to a different reaction pattern. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

options.text: Stop the allopurinol and start oral prednisolone 0.5 mg/kg each morning
options.rationale: Rash with fever, facial oedema, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia above 1.5 x10^9/L and hepatic and renal involvement 2 to 8 weeks after starting a drug is a drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms, and allopurinol is among the commonest causes. The drug is withdrawn permanently and systemic corticosteroid at 0.5 to 1 mg/kg is given for organ involvement, weaned slowly over 8 to 12 weeks because rapid reduction provokes relapse. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

options.text: Stop the allopurinol and start intravenous immunoglobulin over five days
options.rationale: Immunoglobulin is used in severe toxic epidermal necrolysis and in some refractory presentations, and it is not first-line treatment for this reaction pattern. Corticosteroid remains the mainstay where there is organ involvement. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

explanation.summary: Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms is a severe delayed hypersensitivity reaction distinguished from other drug eruptions by its long latency of 2 to 8 weeks, its systemic features and its tendency to persist and relapse after the drug is stopped. The characteristic combination is fever, an extensive morbilliform or oedematous eruption, facial oedema, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia or atypical lymphocytosis, and involvement of at least one internal organ, most often the liver. Allopurinol, aromatic anticonvulsants such as carbamazepine, phenytoin and lamotrigine, sulfonamides, vancomycin and minocycline account for the majority of cases. Reactivation of human herpesvirus 6 and other herpesviruses occurs during the illness and contributes to the relapsing course and to the late complications, which include thyroiditis and type 1 diabetes appearing months afterwards. Mortality is around 5 to 10 per cent, mostly from fulminant hepatitis, and long term follow-up with thyroid and glucose monitoring is recommended.
key_points: Latency is 2 to 8 weeks, far longer than a simple morbilliform eruption
Look for fever, facial oedema, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia and organ involvement
Allopurinol and the aromatic anticonvulsants are the commonest culprits
Withdraw the drug permanently and treat organ involvement with systemic corticosteroid
Wean corticosteroid over 8 to 12 weeks and monitor thyroid function for months afterwards
explanation.pearls: Test for HLA-B*58:01 before starting allopurinol in people of Han Chinese, Thai or Korean ancestry: carriage confers a markedly increased risk of severe cutaneous adverse reaction and the alternative urate lowering agent is febuxostat.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms

subtopic_detail: diagnosis and therapy for prolonged fever with hepatitis in an abattoir worker
stem:
You are the general practitioner in a regional town seeing a 38-year-old man with three weeks of fever, drenching sweats, severe retro-orbital headache and profound fatigue. He has lost 5 kg. He works on the kill floor of the local abattoir and helped with a sheep shearing weekend a month ago. He has not travelled overseas.

He has taken two courses of amoxicillin from an after hours service without benefit. Examination shows a temperature of 38.7 degrees Celsius with other vital signs within normal limits, a tender liver edge 2 cm below the costal margin, no lymphadenopathy, no rash and no murmur. Alanine aminotransferase is 186 U/L (less than 40), alkaline phosphatase 168 U/L (30 to 110), bilirubin within normal limits, white cell count 6.8 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0), platelets 128 x10^9/L (150 to 400) and C-reactive protein 84 mg/L (less than 5). Chest radiograph and two sets of blood cultures are negative.

data_table.Vital signs: Temperature 38.7 degrees Celsius with pulse, blood pressure, respiratory rate and oxygen saturation within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Tender liver edge 2 cm below costal margin; no lymphadenopathy, rash, splinter haemorrhages or murmur
data_table.Investigations: Alanine aminotransferase 186 U/L (less than 40); alkaline phosphatase 168 U/L (30 to 110); bilirubin within normal limits; white cell count 6.8 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0); platelets 128 x10^9/L (150 to 400); C-reactive protein 84 mg/L (less than 5); chest radiograph normal; two sets of blood cultures negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Repeat blood cultures while febrile and commence intravenous ceftriaxone empirically pending those culture results
options.rationale: Coxiella burnetii is an obligate intracellular organism that will not grow in standard blood culture bottles, so repeat cultures will again be negative. Cephalosporins have no activity against it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Send paired phase I and phase II serology and commence oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for a two week course
options.rationale: A prolonged febrile illness with hepatitis, thrombocytopenia and a normal white cell count in someone with intensive livestock exposure is Coxiella burnetii infection, which is not detected on routine blood culture and does not respond to beta-lactams.
