Here the parathyroid response is reversibly suppressed and recovers within days of magnesium repletion. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Give intravenous magnesium and stop the proton pump inhibitor as well
options.rationale: Long term proton pump inhibitor use impairs intestinal magnesium absorption, and the resulting deficiency causes both renal potassium wasting and functional hypoparathyroidism, which is why the potassium and calcium will not correct on their own. Repleting magnesium intravenously and removing the cause corrects all three abnormalities together. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Start spironolactone to reduce the ongoing urinary potassium wasting
options.rationale: Potassium sparing diuretics are useful when renal potassium loss is driven by mineralocorticoid excess, which typically presents with hypertension and metabolic alkalosis. He is normotensive and not alkalotic, so the mechanism does not fit. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Proton pump inhibitor associated hypomagnesaemia is an under-recognised complication of long term therapy, typically appearing after a year or more and caused by impaired active intestinal magnesium transport. Magnesium deficiency then produces two secondary problems that dominate the presentation. It causes renal potassium wasting by removing magnesium dependent inhibition of potassium secreting channels, making hypokalaemia refractory to replacement, and it impairs both parathyroid hormone release and end-organ responsiveness, producing hypocalcaemia with an inappropriately normal or low parathyroid hormone. The clinical signs are neuromuscular, with tetany, tremor, weakness and in severe cases seizures and ventricular arrhythmias including torsades de pointes. Treatment is magnesium repletion, usually intravenous when symptomatic, together with withdrawal of the causative drug where possible. Deprescribing acid suppression should be considered in every patient taking it for years without a maintained indication.
key_points: Hypokalaemia will not correct until magnesium is repleted.
Magnesium deficiency causes functional hypoparathyroidism with low or inappropriately normal parathyroid hormone.
Long term proton pump inhibitor use impairs intestinal magnesium absorption.
Severe deficiency causes tetany, seizures and torsades de pointes.
Deprescribing the acid suppressing drug is part of the treatment.
explanation.pearls: Check magnesium in any patient whose potassium or calcium refuses to correct with replacement, and remember that serum magnesium underestimates total body stores because less than 1 per cent is extracellular, so a low normal value in a symptomatic patient still warrants repletion.

subtopic_detail: lymphocytic exudative effusion with nodular pleural thickening and two negative cytology samples
stem:
You are the respiratory registrar reviewing a 68-year-old retired carpenter with three months of increasing breathlessness and a dull ache in the right side of his chest. He built and renovated houses from the mid 1970s and recalls cutting a great deal of fibre sheeting without a mask.

He has had two therapeutic aspirations of a large right pleural effusion in the last six weeks. Both fluid samples were exudative with a lymphocyte predominance, negative cultures including mycobacterial culture, and cytology reported as negative for malignant cells on each occasion. He has never smoked. Computed tomography today shows circumferential nodular pleural thickening extending onto the mediastinal pleura, with the effusion reaccumulating.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 88/min, blood pressure 134/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 94% in room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Investigations: Pleural fluid protein 48 g/L with serum protein 70 g/L, pleural lactate dehydrogenase above two thirds the upper serum limit, lymphocyte predominant differential, cultures including mycobacterial culture negative, cytology negative on two samples
data_table.Imaging: Computed tomography showing circumferential nodular pleural thickening involving the mediastinal pleura with a reaccumulating right effusion

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Repeat the pleural fluid cytology a third time before any further step
options.rationale: Cytological yield is low for tumours that shed few cells into the fluid, and a third sample adds little after two negatives when imaging shows nodular thickening. Repeat cytology is worthwhile for suspected adenocarcinoma, where yield is considerably higher. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia: Pleural disease)

options.text: Start empirical antituberculous therapy for a lymphocytic exudate now
options.rationale: Tuberculous pleuritis also produces a lymphocytic exudate, but smooth rather than nodular thickening, and mycobacterial cultures are negative here. Empirical therapy would delay tissue diagnosis of a condition with major compensation implications. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Arrange a positron emission tomography scan and review in four weeks
options.rationale: Functional imaging can direct a biopsy and assist staging but cannot provide the histological subtype and immunohistochemistry required for diagnosis, treatment and compensation claims. It is an adjunct to tissue sampling rather than an alternative. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia: Pleural disease)

options.text: Start a trial of diuretics and repeat the chest radiograph in one month
options.rationale: Diuresis is appropriate for a transudate from heart failure, but the fluid here meets exudative criteria on protein and lactate dehydrogenase ratios. Treating an exudate as a transudate wastes a month in a time-critical diagnosis. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia: Pleural disease)

options.text: Arrange image guided pleural biopsy to obtain tissue for histology
options.rationale: Nodular circumferential thickening with mediastinal pleural involvement in a man with heavy occupational fibre exposure requires tissue, and image guided cutting needle biopsy of the thickened pleura has a far higher yield than repeated fluid cytology. Thoracoscopic biopsy is the alternative when image guided sampling is non-diagnostic or drainage and pleurodesis are needed at the same time. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia: Pleural disease)

explanation.summary: Australia has one of the highest rates of asbestos related disease in the world because of decades of domestic use in building products, and the latency from exposure to malignant pleural disease is typically 20 to 50 years, so presentations continue well after the ban. The imaging features that should raise concern are circumferential pleural thickening, nodularity, thickening greater than 1 cm and involvement of the mediastinal pleura, all of which distinguish malignant from benign pleural disease. Fluid cytology is insufficiently sensitive for mesothelioma, so tissue is required, obtained either by image guided cutting needle biopsy or at thoracoscopy, which has the advantage of allowing drainage and talc pleurodesis in the same procedure. Histological subtype has prognostic and therapeutic implications and is also essential for dust diseases compensation, which in most states does not require the person to prove which employer was responsible. Every case warrants referral to a specialist multidisciplinary service and a discussion about compensation entitlements.
key_points: Latency from asbestos exposure to malignant pleural disease is typically 20 to 50 years.
Nodular circumferential thickening with mediastinal involvement suggests malignancy.
Fluid cytology has low sensitivity for mesothelioma, so tissue is required.
Thoracoscopy allows biopsy, drainage and pleurodesis in a single procedure.
Histological confirmation is needed for treatment decisions and for dust diseases compensation.
explanation.pearls: Record a detailed occupational and home renovation exposure history at the first visit, including the years and the materials handled, because compensation schemes in each state rely on that account and it becomes far harder to reconstruct once the patient deteriorates.

subtopic_detail: markedly elevated low density lipoprotein cholesterol with tendon thickening and premature coronary disease in a parent
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 41-year-old man who came for a workplace health check. He has no symptoms, does not smoke, walks daily and drinks four standard drinks a week.

His fasting lipid profile has been repeated on two occasions eight weeks apart with consistent results. On examination both Achilles tendons feel thickened and nodular, and there are no xanthelasmata. His father had a myocardial infarction at 46 and his paternal grandmother died suddenly at 52. His blood pressure is 126/78 mmHg, his body mass index is 24 kg/m2, and he has two brothers and a 16-year-old daughter.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Bilateral Achilles tendon thickening with nodularity, no xanthelasmata, no corneal arcus
data_table.Investigations: Total cholesterol 9.6 mmol/L (<5.5), low density lipoprotein cholesterol 7.4 mmol/L (<3.5), high density lipoprotein cholesterol 1.3 mmol/L (>1.0), triglycerides 1.4 mmol/L (<1.7), thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, HbA1c 5.2 per cent (<6.0), liver function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start a low dose statin and recheck the lipid profile in twelve months
options.rationale: Low intensity therapy will not approach the target reduction of at least 50 per cent from baseline needed in this condition, and a year of untreated exposure adds to a lifetime cholesterol burden that began at birth. Dose intensity, not simply the presence of a statin, determines outcome here. (Source: Heart Foundation and FH Australasia Network: Familial hypercholesterolaemia)
source_refs: Heart Foundation and FH Australasia Network: Familial hypercholesterolaemia

options.text: Advise dietary change alone and repeat the lipid profile in six months
options.rationale: Diet lowers low density lipoprotein cholesterol by roughly 10 per cent at best and cannot correct a genetic receptor defect. Lifestyle measures remain part of management but are never sufficient as sole therapy in this disorder. (Source: Heart Foundation and FH Australasia Network: Familial hypercholesterolaemia)
source_refs: Heart Foundation and FH Australasia Network: Familial hypercholesterolaemia

options.text: Start a high intensity statin and arrange cascade testing of relatives
options.rationale: Untreated low density lipoprotein cholesterol above 6.5 mmol/L with tendon xanthomata and premature coronary disease in a first degree relative makes familial hypercholesterolaemia the working diagnosis, and treatment is a high intensity statin aiming for at least a 50 per cent reduction, with ezetimibe added if needed. Cascade testing of first degree relatives identifies affected family members, each of whom has a one in two chance of carrying the variant. (Source: Heart Foundation and FH Australasia Network: Familial hypercholesterolaemia)
source_refs: Heart Foundation and FH Australasia Network: Familial hypercholesterolaemia

options.text: Start ezetimibe alone and arrange a coronary calcium score this month
options.rationale: Ezetimibe lowers cholesterol by about 15 to 20 per cent and is used as an addition to a statin rather than as monotherapy except in statin intolerance. Calcium scoring can refine risk in intermediate risk patients but does not change the need to treat this degree of elevation. (Source: Heart Foundation and FH Australasia Network: Familial hypercholesterolaemia)
source_refs: Heart Foundation and FH Australasia Network: Familial hypercholesterolaemia

options.text: Refer for lipoprotein apheresis before starting any medical treatment
options.rationale: Apheresis is reserved for homozygous disease or for severe heterozygous disease with progressive coronary disease despite maximal drug therapy. It is not a first line intervention in an asymptomatic patient who has not yet been treated. (Source: Heart Foundation and FH Australasia Network: Familial hypercholesterolaemia)
source_refs: Heart Foundation and FH Australasia Network: Familial hypercholesterolaemia

explanation.summary: Familial hypercholesterolaemia affects about one in 250 Australians and remains largely undiagnosed, despite carrying a risk of premature coronary disease many times that of the general population because arterial exposure to high cholesterol begins at birth. Diagnosis is clinical, using criteria that combine untreated low density lipoprotein cholesterol level, physical signs such as tendon xanthomata and corneal arcus before 45, personal or family history of premature coronary disease, and genetic testing where available. Standard absolute cardiovascular risk calculators must not be applied, because they systematically underestimate risk in this group and would justify inaction in a young patient. Treatment is a high intensity statin from diagnosis, with ezetimibe and then a PCSK9 inhibitor added to reach targets, and treatment in children is generally started from around 8 to 10 years of age. Cascade testing of first degree relatives is the single highest yield public health action, since each has a 50 per cent chance of being affected.
key_points: Untreated low density lipoprotein cholesterol above 6.5 mmol/L strongly suggests the diagnosis.
Tendon xanthomata and premature coronary disease in relatives support it.
Absolute risk calculators underestimate risk and should not guide treatment here.
High intensity statin therapy aims for at least a 50 per cent reduction from baseline.
Each first degree relative has a 50 per cent chance of being affected and should be tested.
explanation.pearls: Palpate the Achilles tendons in any patient with a low density lipoprotein cholesterol above 5 mmol/L: tendon xanthomata are close to specific for this diagnosis and take the clinical score straight into the definite range, whereas corneal arcus only counts if it appears before the age of 45.

sources.label: Heart Foundation and FH Australasia Network: Familial hypercholesterolaemia

subtopic_detail: urethral discharge with intracellular Gram negative diplococci on the smear while nucleic acid testing is pending
stem:
You are the doctor in a sexual health clinic seeing a 24-year-old man with four days of burning on passing urine and a thick discharge that is staining his underwear.

He had condomless anal and oral sex with a new male partner ten days ago and has had two other partners in the last three months. He has no fever, no rash, no joint pain and no testicular pain. He takes no pre-exposure prophylaxis and his last testing was nine months ago and negative. A Gram stained smear of the urethral discharge taken in the clinic shows polymorphs containing Gram negative diplococci. Nucleic acid amplification testing on a first pass urine sample and on throat and rectal swabs has been sent and will take two days.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Purulent urethral discharge, no scrotal tenderness or swelling, no skin lesions, no lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Urethral Gram stain showing intracellular Gram negative diplococci, nucleic acid amplification testing pending on urine and on throat and rectal swabs, serology for human immunodeficiency virus and syphilis sent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management today?

options.text: Give oral doxycycline for seven days and await the nucleic acid results
options.rationale: Doxycycline covers chlamydia and is part of many urethritis regimens, but it does not reliably treat gonococcal infection and Australian resistance patterns make it unsuitable as sole therapy. It is the correct choice when only chlamydia is identified. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Give a single dose of oral azithromycin alone and review in one week
options.rationale: Azithromycin monotherapy is inadequate for gonorrhoea and drives macrolide resistance, which is why Australian guidance pairs it with an injectable cephalosporin. The pairing, not either drug alone, is what achieves cure. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Await the nucleic acid results before starting any antibiotic treatment
options.rationale: Waiting two days leaves a symptomatic and infectious man untreated, risks loss to follow up, and ignores a smear finding that is highly specific in symptomatic urethral discharge. Deferring treatment is reasonable only for asymptomatic screening. (Source: ASHM: Australian STI management guidelines)

options.text: Give ceftriaxone with azithromycin now and arrange partner notification
options.rationale: Intracellular Gram negative diplococci in a symptomatic man are sufficient to treat presumptively, and Australian practice uses intramuscular ceftriaxone with oral azithromycin, which covers the gonococcal infection, limits resistance emergence and treats coexisting chlamydia. Partner notification for contacts in the preceding two months is part of the treatment episode, not an optional extra. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Give oral ciprofloxacin as a single dose and repeat the testing in a week
options.rationale: Quinolone resistance in Australian gonococcal isolates is high enough that ciprofloxacin is used only when susceptibility has been demonstrated on culture. That makes it a directed rather than an empirical option. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Symptomatic urethral discharge in a man is treated presumptively at the first visit, because delay prolongs infectivity and risks the patient not returning. A Gram stain showing intracellular Gram negative diplococci has high specificity in this setting and justifies treating for gonorrhoea immediately, while nucleic acid testing confirms the organism and identifies coinfection. Australian practice uses dual therapy with an injectable third generation cephalosporin plus azithromycin, which addresses both the rising cephalosporin minimum inhibitory concentrations seen internationally and the high rate of chlamydial coinfection. Culture should be collected before treatment where possible, since it is the only way to obtain susceptibility data for surveillance and for treatment failures. Every episode requires testing at all exposed sites, partner notification covering contacts from the preceding two months, a full sexually transmissible infection screen including syphilis and human immunodeficiency virus serology, discussion of pre-exposure prophylaxis, and a test of cure where pharyngeal infection or treatment failure is a concern.
key_points: Symptomatic urethral discharge is treated presumptively at the first visit.
Intracellular Gram negative diplococci on smear are highly specific in symptomatic men.
Australian therapy is dual, with an injectable cephalosporin plus azithromycin.
Culture before treatment provides the susceptibility data that nucleic acid testing cannot.
Partner notification and a full screen including syphilis and human immunodeficiency virus are part of the episode.
explanation.pearls: Test all exposed sites rather than urine alone, because pharyngeal and rectal gonorrhoea are usually asymptomatic, are missed by urine testing, and are the reservoir from which both onward transmission and cephalosporin resistance emerge.

subtopic_detail: symmetrical polyarthralgia with a rash after mosquito exposure on an inland river camping trip
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 34-year-old warehouse supervisor with ten days of pain and stiffness in both wrists, both ankles and both knees. She says she is covered in bites from a camping trip along an inland river system three weeks ago, where mosquitoes were dreadful at dusk.

The stiffness is worst for the first hour of the morning and the fatigue is profound enough that she has taken a week off work. A blotchy pink rash appeared over her trunk and arms four days ago and is fading. She has no fever now, though she felt hot and shivery in the first few days. She has no tick bite or eschar, no genital or eye symptoms, no recent diarrhoea and no overseas travel in the last two years.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 78/min, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99% in room air, temperature 36.9 °C
data_table.Examination: Symmetrical tenderness of wrists, ankles and knees with mild soft tissue swelling and no large effusions, fading maculopapular rash on trunk and arms, no eschar or lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 6.4 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), C-reactive protein 18 mg/L (<5), creatinine and liver function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start prednisolone 25 mg daily for two weeks and review the joints then
options.rationale: Corticosteroid is not indicated for a self-limiting post-infectious arthropathy and may prolong symptoms while exposing her to adverse effects. It is reserved for inflammatory arthritis once that diagnosis is established. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Start doxycycline for a presumed tick borne infection and review in a week
options.rationale: Rickettsial infection is worth considering after bush exposure but classically produces fever, headache and often an eschar at the bite site, none of which is present ten days into a symmetrical polyarthralgia. Doxycycline would be appropriate if an eschar or ongoing fever were found. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Refer for urgent joint aspiration of both wrists to exclude sepsis today
options.rationale: Septic arthritis is almost always monoarticular with a hot, exquisitely tender joint, fever and marked inflammatory response. Symmetrical polyarticular involvement with mild inflammatory markers and no fever makes aspiration unnecessary. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Start methotrexate for probable early inflammatory arthritis this month
options.rationale: Disease modifying therapy is started when persistent inflammatory arthritis is confirmed over weeks with supportive serology and imaging, not at ten days in a post-infectious picture that usually resolves. Starting it now would treat a disease she probably does not have. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Early arthritis)

options.text: Send arbovirus serology and manage with analgesia and graded activity
options.rationale: Symmetrical polyarthralgia with profound fatigue and a transient maculopapular rash three weeks after intense mosquito exposure in an inland river region is the classic Australian arboviral pattern, confirmed by serology showing specific immunoglobulin M with a rising immunoglobulin G titre. Management is symptomatic with simple analgesia, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and graded return to activity, and the illness is notifiable. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Ross River and Barmah Forest viruses are the commonest arboviral infections in Australia, transmitted by mosquitoes with reservoirs in macropods, and outbreaks follow flooding and high tides in coastal and inland river systems. The illness typically begins one to three weeks after exposure with symmetrical polyarthralgia affecting wrists, ankles, knees and small joints, accompanied by profound fatigue, myalgia and often a transient maculopapular rash. Diagnosis is serological, with specific immunoglobulin M plus either a rising immunoglobulin G titre or supportive epidemiology, and single immunoglobulin M positivity can persist for many months and must be interpreted cautiously. There is no specific treatment and no vaccine, so management is analgesia, education and graded activity, with most people recovering over three to six months although fatigue and arthralgia occasionally persist longer. The main clinical trap is mistaking it for the onset of rheumatoid arthritis and starting disease modifying therapy, or conversely attributing persistent symptoms to the virus when a genuine inflammatory arthritis is evolving.
key_points: Incubation is typically one to three weeks after mosquito exposure.
Symmetrical polyarthralgia with profound fatigue and a transient rash is the typical picture.
Diagnosis is serological, and isolated immunoglobulin M can persist for months.
Management is symptomatic, as there is no specific therapy or vaccine.
Most recover within three to six months, with fatigue the last symptom to settle.
explanation.pearls: Warn patients at diagnosis that fatigue and joint pain commonly persist for three to six months, because the single most common reason these patients return distressed is an expectation of recovery within a fortnight.

sources.label: CDNA: Ross River virus infection national guidelines

subtopic_detail: high anion gap ketoacidosis with a normal blood glucose after several days of vomiting and no oral intake
stem:
You are the emergency registrar seeing a 44-year-old man with three days of vomiting and abdominal pain. He has drunk a bottle of spirits most days for 15 years, drank heavily until four days ago, and has eaten almost nothing since.

He is tremulous with a mild tachycardia and is breathing deeply. His abdomen is soft with mild epigastric tenderness and no guarding. He has no fever, no melaena and no jaundice. His blood alcohol concentration is undetectable and his lipase is normal. He has never been diagnosed with diabetes and his HbA1c is 4.9 per cent.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 112/min, blood pressure 106/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 28/min, SpO2 98% in room air, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Investigations: pH 7.24 (7.35-7.45), bicarbonate 12 mmol/L (22-32), anion gap 24 mmol/L (8-16), glucose 4.1 mmol/L (3.5-5.5), blood ketones 5.2 mmol/L (<0.6), lactate 2.1 mmol/L (<2.0), potassium 3.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), creatinine 118 micromol/L (60-110), blood alcohol undetectable, lipase within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Give intravenous saline with glucose plus thiamine and replace potassium
options.rationale: Ketoacidosis with a normal glucose after a binge followed by starvation and vomiting is driven by glycogen depletion and a high ratio of reduced nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide, and it resolves with volume replacement and carbohydrate, which restores insulin secretion and switches off ketogenesis. Thiamine is given before the glucose load and potassium is replaced because it falls further as ketosis clears. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Start an intravenous insulin infusion with fluid at the usual protocol rates
options.rationale: Insulin is the cornerstone of diabetic ketoacidosis, where hyperglycaemia is present and endogenous insulin is absent, but here the glucose is normal and insulin would cause dangerous hypoglycaemia and hypokalaemia. The distinguishing feature between these two ketoacidoses is the glucose, not the ketone level. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Give intravenous sodium bicarbonate to correct the metabolic acidosis now
options.rationale: Bicarbonate does not improve outcomes in ketoacidosis at this pH and worsens hypokalaemia and intracellular acidosis. It is reserved for extreme acidaemia, conventionally a pH below 6.9, or for specific poisonings. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Give intravenous saline alone and recheck the ketones in eight hours
options.rationale: Saline restores volume but without a carbohydrate source the ketogenic drive persists, so recovery is slower and hypoglycaemia may supervene. Saline alone is the right approach in hyperglycaemic states where fluid is the first priority. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Arrange urgent haemodialysis for a severe high anion gap acidosis today
options.rationale: Dialysis is indicated for toxic alcohol ingestion, severe salicylate poisoning or refractory acidosis with kidney failure, none of which applies to a ketoacidosis that reverses within hours of simple treatment. The osmolar gap and toxicology history are what separate those causes from this one. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

explanation.summary: Alcoholic ketoacidosis develops after a heavy drinking episode ends and is followed by vomiting and starvation, at which point glycogen is depleted, insulin secretion falls, counterregulatory hormones rise and free fatty acids are mobilised. Alcohol metabolism generates a high ratio of reduced to oxidised nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide, which favours beta hydroxybutyrate over acetoacetate, so bedside ketone strips measuring acetoacetate can underestimate the severity while blood beta hydroxybutyrate is markedly raised. The acid base picture is frequently mixed, with vomiting adding a metabolic alkalosis and alcohol withdrawal adding a respiratory alkalosis, so the pH can be deceptively close to normal and the anion gap is the more reliable signal. Treatment is dextrose containing saline with thiamine given first, potassium replacement, and treatment of withdrawal, with resolution usually within 12 to 24 hours. Failure to improve should prompt a search for pancreatitis, sepsis, gastrointestinal bleeding or toxic alcohol ingestion.
key_points: A normal or low glucose with a high anion gap ketoacidosis is the defining pattern.
Beta hydroxybutyrate predominates, so acetoacetate based bedside tests underestimate severity.
Treatment is dextrose containing fluid, thiamine first, and potassium replacement.
Insulin is not required and risks hypoglycaemia and hypokalaemia.
Failure to resolve within 24 hours suggests an alternative or additional diagnosis.
explanation.pearls: Give thiamine before any glucose containing fluid in a malnourished drinker, since a carbohydrate load consumes the last of the thiamine as a cofactor and can precipitate acute thiamine deficient encephalopathy within hours.

subtopic_detail: seizure then a broad complex bradyarrhythmia minutes after a large volume regional block
stem:
You are the emergency registrar. You have just performed an ultrasound guided fascia iliaca block with a large volume of ropivacaine for a 58-year-old woman with a fractured neck of femur, after negative aspiration at each step.

Eight minutes later she complains that her lips feel numb and there is a metallic taste in her mouth, then becomes agitated and says the room sounds strange. Two minutes after that she has a generalised tonic clonic seizure lasting 90 seconds, terminated with intravenous midazolam. Her monitor now shows a broad complex rhythm at 38 beats per minute with a systolic pressure of 68 mmHg. The resuscitation trolley and airway equipment are at the bedside and a second doctor is calling for help.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 38/min, blood pressure 68/40 mmHg, respiratory rate 8/min with bag mask support, SpO2 93% on 15 L/min oxygen, temperature 36.5 °C
data_table.Examination: Post-ictal with reduced conscious state, airway supported with a bag and mask, no external haemorrhage
data_table.Electrocardiogram: Broad complex bradycardia with QRS duration 180 ms and no discernible P waves

lead_in: What is the most important specific treatment to give now?

options.text: Give intravenous flumazenil and prepare for immediate endotracheal intubation
options.rationale: Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepine sedation but would remove seizure control in a patient at high risk of further convulsions, and it does nothing for the cardiac toxicity. Airway support is essential but is standard care rather than the specific treatment. (Source: ANZCA and ASA: Local anaesthetic systemic toxicity)
source_refs: ANZCA and ASA: Local anaesthetic systemic toxicity

options.text: Give intravenous lipid emulsion while continuing standard resuscitation measures
options.rationale: Perioral numbness, metallic taste and auditory change progressing to seizure and then cardiovascular collapse after a large volume block is local anaesthetic systemic toxicity, and 20 per cent lipid emulsion is the specific antidote, given as a bolus followed by an infusion. It acts as a lipid sink that draws the drug away from cardiac sodium channels, and it is given alongside, not instead of, airway support and resuscitation. (Source: ANZCA and ASA: Local anaesthetic systemic toxicity)
source_refs: ANZCA and ASA: Local anaesthetic systemic toxicity

options.text: Give intravenous adrenaline at the standard 1 mg arrest dose immediately
options.rationale: Adrenaline is used in this setting but at substantially reduced doses, conventionally 1 microgram per kilogram or less, because large boluses impair resuscitation and worsen arrhythmia in local anaesthetic toxicity. Dose, not the drug, is what makes this option wrong. (Source: ANZCA and ASA: Local anaesthetic systemic toxicity)
source_refs: ANZCA and ASA: Local anaesthetic systemic toxicity

options.text: Give intravenous amiodarone for the broad complex rhythm and observe her
options.rationale: Amiodarone is the preferred antiarrhythmic if ventricular arrhythmia occurs in this setting, so it is not wrong in itself, but it does not remove the drug from the sodium channels and should not displace the antidote. Lidocaine and other local anaesthetic antiarrhythmics are specifically contraindicated because they add to the toxic burden. (Source: ANZCA and ASA: Local anaesthetic systemic toxicity)
source_refs: ANZCA and ASA: Local anaesthetic systemic toxicity

options.text: Give intravenous sodium bicarbonate and repeat the dose after five minutes
options.rationale: Sodium bicarbonate is the treatment for sodium channel blockade from tricyclic antidepressant poisoning and is a reasonable adjunct here, but it is not the specific antidote and should not be given first. The two poisonings share a mechanism but differ in the treatment with the strongest evidence. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

explanation.summary: Local anaesthetic systemic toxicity follows inadvertent intravascular injection or systemic absorption from a large volume block, and its incidence has fallen with ultrasound guidance but has not disappeared. The classic sequence begins with prodromal neurological symptoms including perioral numbness, metallic taste, tinnitus, visual disturbance and agitation, progresses to seizures, and then to cardiovascular toxicity with conduction delay, bradyarrhythmias, ventricular arrhythmias and asystole. Onset is typically within minutes but can be delayed for up to an hour with large volume blocks, so monitoring after the procedure matters. Management combines stopping the injection, airway and ventilation support, seizure control with a benzodiazepine, and lipid emulsion as the specific antidote. Adrenaline is used in reduced doses, propofol is avoided as a lipid substitute, and lidocaine and other sodium channel blocking antiarrhythmics are contraindicated. Prolonged resuscitation is justified because recovery after long arrests has been documented, and every clinician performing blocks should know where the lipid emulsion is kept.
key_points: Prodromal perioral numbness, metallic taste and tinnitus precede seizures and cardiac toxicity.
Onset can be delayed up to an hour after a large volume block.
Lipid emulsion 20 per cent is the specific antidote, given as a bolus then an infusion.
Adrenaline is used at markedly reduced doses and lidocaine is contraindicated.
Prolonged resuscitation is warranted because late recovery has been documented.
explanation.pearls: Keep a dedicated lipid emulsion kit wherever regional blocks are performed and rehearse the dose: 1.5 mL/kg of 20 per cent emulsion as a bolus followed by an infusion at 15 mL/kg/hour, with the bolus repeatable twice if circulation has not returned.

sources.label: ANZCA and ASA: Local anaesthetic systemic toxicity

subtopic_detail: exertional syncope in a young athlete with a murmur that increases on standing and lateral T wave inversion
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 19-year-old semi-professional footballer who blacked out twice in the last month, both times during sprinting at training. Each episode lasted under a minute with rapid full recovery and no confusion afterwards.

He has no chest pain and no palpitations, and he has never fainted while standing still or after standing up. His mother's brother died suddenly at 34 while jogging and no cause was found. On examination there is an ejection systolic murmur at the left sternal edge that becomes louder when he stands up from squatting and softer when he squats down. His electrocardiogram shows voltage criteria for left ventricular hypertrophy with deep T wave inversion in the lateral leads.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 58/min, blood pressure 122/76 mmHg with no postural drop, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99% in room air, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Ejection systolic murmur at the left sternal edge louder on standing from squatting and softer on squatting, brisk carotid upstroke, no radiation to the carotids
data_table.Electrocardiogram: Voltage criteria for left ventricular hypertrophy with deep T wave inversion in leads V5, V6, I and aVL

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure him that exertional syncope in young athletes is usually benign
options.rationale: Syncope during rather than after exertion is a red flag for a structural or arrhythmic cardiac cause and is never reassured away, particularly with a family history of sudden death under 40. Post-exertional syncope on stopping is the pattern more often benign. (Source: CSANZ: Pre-participation screening and genetic heart disease)
source_refs: CSANZ: Pre-participation screening and genetic heart disease

options.text: Arrange an exercise stress test to reproduce the symptoms before imaging
options.rationale: Provoking symptoms in someone with suspected dynamic outflow obstruction risks the very event being investigated, and stress testing is done later, under supervision, for risk stratification once the anatomy is known. Imaging precedes provocation. (Source: CSANZ: Pre-participation screening and genetic heart disease)
source_refs: CSANZ: Pre-participation screening and genetic heart disease

options.text: Arrange transthoracic echocardiography and withhold competitive sport now
options.rationale: A murmur that increases when preload falls on standing, lateral T wave inversion with voltage criteria, exertional syncope and a family history of sudden death under 40 together require urgent imaging to define the myocardium and outflow tract. Sport is suspended immediately because the highest risk period is before the diagnosis is established, and continued training while awaiting a scan is what turns this presentation into a death. (Source: CSANZ: Pre-participation screening and genetic heart disease)
source_refs: CSANZ: Pre-participation screening and genetic heart disease

options.text: Start a beta blocker and allow training to continue while awaiting review
options.rationale: Beta blockade is a reasonable treatment once the diagnosis is confirmed and symptoms require it, but it does not abolish the risk of sudden arrhythmic death and allowing continued competition is the dangerous element of this option. Treatment follows diagnosis and risk stratification. (Source: CSANZ: Pre-participation screening and genetic heart disease)
source_refs: CSANZ: Pre-participation screening and genetic heart disease

options.text: Arrange a 24 hour Holter monitor alone and review the result in one month
options.rationale: Ambulatory monitoring contributes to risk stratification by detecting non-sustained ventricular tachycardia, but it cannot show the structural abnormality and a normal recording would be falsely reassuring. It is part of the assessment after imaging rather than instead of it. (Source: CSANZ: Pre-participation screening and genetic heart disease)
source_refs: CSANZ: Pre-participation screening and genetic heart disease

explanation.summary: Syncope occurring during exertion, as opposed to immediately after stopping, is a cardinal warning sign that demands assessment before any return to sport. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is the commonest inherited cause of sudden cardiac death in young athletes and produces a dynamic outflow murmur that behaves opposite to the murmur of aortic stenosis: it increases when preload or afterload falls, as on standing or during Valsalva, and decreases when preload rises with squatting or handgrip. Electrocardiographic abnormalities precede symptoms in most cases, with deep lateral T wave inversion and voltage criteria being typical, and a completely normal tracing makes the diagnosis unlikely. Echocardiography defines wall thickness, outflow gradient and systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve, with cardiac magnetic resonance imaging used when windows are poor or apical disease is suspected. Family screening of first degree relatives is mandatory, and risk stratification determines whether an implantable defibrillator is required.
key_points: Syncope during exertion is a red flag, unlike syncope after stopping exercise.
The murmur increases on standing and Valsalva and decreases on squatting.
Deep lateral T wave inversion with voltage criteria is the typical electrocardiographic pattern.
Competitive sport is suspended pending diagnosis, not after it.
First degree relatives require clinical and electrocardiographic screening.
explanation.pearls: Any family history of sudden death under 40, including a death attributed to drowning, a single vehicle accident or unexplained epilepsy, should be treated as a possible inherited arrhythmia syndrome and triggers screening of the whole first degree family.

sources.label: CSANZ: Pre-participation screening and genetic heart disease

subtopic_detail: progressive breathlessness with a large inspiratory fall in systolic pressure and low voltage complexes in advanced malignancy
stem:
You are the oncology registrar called to see a 64-year-old woman with metastatic lung adenocarcinoma who has become breathless over five days and cannot lie flat.

She is sitting forward and is anxious. Her jugular venous pressure is visible at the angle of the jaw at 45 degrees and rises further on inspiration. Her heart sounds are quiet and her chest is clear on auscultation with no crackles. Measuring her blood pressure carefully, the systolic falls by 16 mmHg during inspiration. Her electrocardiogram shows small complexes throughout with beat to beat variation in QRS amplitude, and her chest radiograph shows an enlarged globular cardiac silhouette with clear lung fields. A bedside echocardiogram shows a large circumferential pericardial effusion with diastolic collapse of the right atrium.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 124/min, blood pressure 92/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 28/min, SpO2 94% in room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Jugular venous pressure elevated and rising on inspiration, quiet heart sounds, chest clear on auscultation, cool peripheries with capillary refill 3 seconds
data_table.Investigations: Electrocardiogram with low voltage complexes and beat to beat QRS amplitude variation, chest radiograph with globular cardiac silhouette and clear lung fields, echocardiogram with large circumferential pericardial effusion and diastolic right atrial collapse

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Give intravenous furosemide 40 mg and reassess the breathlessness later
options.rationale: Diuresis reduces the filling pressure that is maintaining cardiac output against external compression and can precipitate shock. It is the correct treatment for the pulmonary oedema this presentation mimics, which is excluded by the clear chest and clear lung fields. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Start a glyceryl trinitrate infusion to reduce the pulmonary congestion
options.rationale: Vasodilatation reduces preload and systemic vascular resistance, both of which are supporting circulation in tamponade, so it risks cardiovascular collapse. Nitrates are appropriate for acute pulmonary oedema with a raised blood pressure. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Start high dose dexamethasone and arrange radiotherapy for the tumour
options.rationale: Corticosteroid and radiotherapy have a role in malignant airway or superior vena caval obstruction, but they do nothing for the mechanical problem of fluid under pressure in the pericardial sac. Drainage must come first regardless of the underlying tumour. (Source: eviQ: Oncological emergencies)

options.text: Arrange urgent echocardiography guided pericardiocentesis and drainage
options.rationale: An elevated jugular venous pressure that rises on inspiration, quiet heart sounds, an inspiratory systolic fall above 10 mmHg and diastolic right atrial collapse establish tamponade, which is relieved only by removing the fluid. Echocardiographic guidance with a drain left in place reduces complications and reaccumulation, which is common in malignant effusions. (Source: eviQ: Oncological emergencies)

options.text: Arrange computed tomography of the chest before any further treatment
options.rationale: Cross sectional imaging adds staging information but delays decompression while the patient sits at the steep part of the pressure volume curve, where small further increases in fluid cause abrupt collapse. Imaging follows stabilisation. (Source: eviQ: Oncological emergencies)

explanation.summary: Cardiac tamponade is a clinical diagnosis supported by echocardiography rather than a purely echocardiographic one, and in malignancy it often develops gradually, allowing the pericardium to stretch until a critical volume is reached and decompensation becomes abrupt. The physical signs reflect equalisation of diastolic pressures and exaggerated ventricular interdependence: a raised jugular venous pressure with preserved or exaggerated inspiratory rise, quiet heart sounds, tachycardia, hypotension and an inspiratory fall in systolic pressure greater than 10 mmHg. Electrocardiographic low voltage with beat to beat amplitude variation reflects the heart swinging within the fluid. The management principle is that anything reducing preload is harmful, so diuretics, nitrates and positive pressure ventilation are avoided, while cautious fluid loading can temporise in a hypovolaemic patient. Definitive treatment is drainage, and because malignant effusions reaccumulate, a drain is usually left in place with consideration of a pericardial window or sclerosant for recurrence. Fluid is sent for cytology, which also has staging implications.
key_points: Tamponade is a clinical diagnosis confirmed rather than made by echocardiography.
An inspiratory systolic fall above 10 mmHg is a key physical sign.
Diuretics, nitrates and positive pressure ventilation all reduce preload and are harmful.
Echocardiography guided drainage with a catheter left in place is the treatment.
Malignant effusions frequently reaccumulate and may need a window or sclerosant.
explanation.pearls: Chest radiograph enlargement of the cardiac silhouette requires roughly 200 mL or more of pericardial fluid, so a normal sized heart never excludes tamponade when fluid has accumulated rapidly after a procedure or trauma.

subtopic_detail: headache and nausea in several members of a household that improve away from home, with normal pulse oximetry
stem:
You are the emergency registrar seeing a 35-year-old woman with three days of throbbing headache, nausea and dizziness. It is the middle of a cold winter.

She tells you that both of her housemates have the same headache and one vomited this morning, and that all three feel better by the middle of the day at work and worse again a few hours after they get home. Their unflued gas heater in the living room has been running each evening since the cold weather started, and one housemate noticed sooty marks on the wall above it. She has no neck stiffness, no photophobia, no rash and no fever. Her neurological examination is normal and her pulse oximeter reads 99 per cent in room air.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 96/min, blood pressure 124/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 99% in room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Alert and oriented, no neck stiffness or photophobia, normal fundoscopy, normal neurological examination, no rash
data_table.Investigations: Venous lactate 2.8 mmol/L (<2.0), full blood count and electrolytes within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Give intravenous fluids and metoclopramide for a presumed viral illness
options.rationale: A viral illness does not remit at work and recur at home, and it would not affect three adults with a time course tied to the evenings. Symptomatic treatment here would send her back into the exposure that caused the illness. (Source: NSW Poisons Information Centre: Carbon monoxide)
source_refs: NSW Poisons Information Centre: Carbon monoxide

options.text: Arrange computed tomography of the brain before any specific treatment
options.rationale: Imaging is indicated for focal neurology, altered conscious state or thunderclap onset, none of which is present, and it delays a treatment that is safe to start immediately. Scanning is reasonable later if symptoms fail to resolve with treatment. (Source: NSW Poisons Information Centre: Carbon monoxide)
source_refs: NSW Poisons Information Centre: Carbon monoxide

options.text: Give sumatriptan and advise review if the headaches persist next week
options.rationale: Triptans treat migraine, which does not spread to housemates or follow the geography of a house. Discharging her with an analgesic returns three people to an ongoing source of exposure that can be lethal during sleep. (Source: NSW Poisons Information Centre: Carbon monoxide)
source_refs: NSW Poisons Information Centre: Carbon monoxide

options.text: Arrange lumbar puncture after imaging to exclude subarachnoid bleeding
options.rationale: Subarachnoid haemorrhage presents with sudden severe headache in one person, not with three days of building symptoms shared by a household. The shared exposure history is what redirects the workup. (Source: NSW Poisons Information Centre: Carbon monoxide)
source_refs: NSW Poisons Information Centre: Carbon monoxide

options.text: Give high flow oxygen by non rebreather mask and take a blood gas sample
options.rationale: Headache and nausea affecting a whole household, worse at home and better away from it, with an unflued combustion heater and soot staining, is carbon monoxide exposure, and treatment is 100 per cent oxygen through a non rebreather mask started before any confirmatory result. A blood gas analysed by co-oximetry is required because standard pulse oximetry cannot distinguish carboxyhaemoglobin from oxyhaemoglobin and reads falsely normal. (Source: NSW Poisons Information Centre: Carbon monoxide)
source_refs: NSW Poisons Information Centre: Carbon monoxide

explanation.summary: Carbon monoxide poisoning is the great imitator of winter emergency medicine, presenting with headache, nausea, dizziness, fatigue and confusion that are routinely attributed to viral illness or migraine. Three features should redirect the assessment: more than one person in a household affected, symptoms that improve away from the building and recur on return, and the presence of an unflued or poorly maintained combustion appliance, which in Australia has caused deaths in both rental housing and camping situations with fuel burning devices in enclosed spaces. Standard pulse oximetry is falsely reassuring because it cannot distinguish carboxyhaemoglobin from oxyhaemoglobin, so a blood gas with co-oximetry is required, and the level correlates poorly with symptom severity. Treatment is high flow oxygen, which reduces the elimination half life from several hours in room air to around an hour, continued until symptoms resolve and the level normalises. Hyperbaric therapy is considered for loss of consciousness, neurological signs, myocardial ischaemia, very high levels or pregnancy, and every case requires public health notification and remediation of the source before anyone returns to the building.
key_points: Multiple household members affected with symptoms tied to being at home is the key pattern.
Pulse oximetry reads falsely normal, so co-oximetry on a blood gas is required.
High flow oxygen is started before confirmation and shortens the elimination half life substantially.
Levels correlate poorly with severity, so treatment follows the clinical picture.
The source must be identified and remediated before anyone returns to the premises.
explanation.pearls: Ask explicitly whether the family pet has also been unwell, since small animals with high metabolic rates develop symptoms earlier than people and a sick cat or bird at home is often the first clue to a domestic exposure.

sources.label: NSW Poisons Information Centre: Carbon monoxide

subtopic_detail: day three assessment of response to intravenous corticosteroid in an acute severe colitis admission
stem:
You are the gastroenterology registrar reviewing a 28-year-old woman on day three of an admission with ulcerative colitis. She came in with nine bloody stools a day, cramping and fatigue, and has been on intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg four times daily since admission.

Today she reports seven bloody stools in the last 24 hours, including two overnight. Her abdomen is soft with mild tenderness and no guarding, and bowel sounds are present. Stool testing for Clostridioides difficile and enteric pathogens is negative, and sigmoidoscopy on admission showed deep ulceration without cytomegalovirus inclusions on biopsy. Her abdominal radiograph today shows a transverse colon diameter of 4 cm with no free gas. She has had no previous biologic therapy and her tuberculosis and hepatitis screening sent on admission are negative.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 98/min, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99% in room air, temperature 37.4 °C
data_table.Investigations: C-reactive protein 52 mg/L (<5, was 68 on admission), haemoglobin 98 g/L (115-155), albumin 28 g/L (35-50), stool testing negative for Clostridioides difficile and enteric pathogens, transverse colon diameter 4 cm on abdominal radiograph
data_table.Medications: Intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg four times daily since admission, enoxaparin prophylaxis

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management now?

options.text: Start rescue therapy with infliximab and involve the colorectal surgeons
options.rationale: More than eight stools a day on day three, or three to eight stools with a C-reactive protein above 45 mg/L, predicts a high likelihood of colectomy during that admission and defines failure of intravenous corticosteroid. Rescue therapy with infliximab or ciclosporin is started at that point, with concurrent surgical review so that a timely operation follows if rescue fails. (Source: GESA: Acute severe ulcerative colitis)

options.text: Continue intravenous corticosteroid for a further five days and reassess
options.rationale: Continuing beyond day three in a non-responder delays rescue therapy and surgery, and prolonged corticosteroid exposure increases postoperative complications if colectomy becomes necessary. Response is formally assessed on day three precisely to prevent this drift. (Source: GESA: Acute severe ulcerative colitis)

options.text: Switch to oral prednisolone 40 mg daily and plan discharge in two days
options.rationale: Stepping down to oral therapy is appropriate for a patient who has responded, with stool frequency falling and inflammatory markers normalising. Discharging a patient still passing seven bloody stools a day risks readmission with perforation. (Source: GESA: Acute severe ulcerative colitis)

options.text: Start oral mesalazine at maximal dose and continue the corticosteroid
options.rationale: Aminosalicylates maintain remission and treat mild to moderate disease but have no role in acute severe colitis, where they do not alter the trajectory. They are reintroduced once the acute episode is controlled. (Source: GESA: Acute severe ulcerative colitis)

options.text: Start oral loperamide to reduce stool frequency and continue the steroid
options.rationale: Antimotility agents are avoided in acute severe colitis because they can precipitate toxic megacolon by masking the very stool frequency used to judge response. They remain useful in quiescent disease with functional diarrhoea. (Source: GESA: Acute severe ulcerative colitis)

explanation.summary: Acute severe ulcerative colitis is defined by six or more bloody stools a day with evidence of systemic upset, and it remains a condition with real mortality, so admissions are managed jointly by gastroenterology and colorectal surgery from day one. Intravenous corticosteroid is first line, along with venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, correction of anaemia and electrolytes, exclusion of superimposed Clostridioides difficile and cytomegalovirus infection, and avoidance of opioids, antimotility agents and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. The day three assessment is the pivot of the admission: persisting high stool frequency, or intermediate frequency with a raised C-reactive protein, identifies patients who will not respond and who need rescue therapy with infliximab or ciclosporin. Rescue therapy is itself assessed at around day seven, and failure at that point means colectomy. Daily abdominal examination and radiographs when there is concern about dilatation are essential, since colonic dilatation beyond 5.5 cm, perforation or massive haemorrhage mandate immediate surgery regardless of the medical plan.
key_points: Acute severe colitis is six or more bloody stools daily with systemic upset.
Response to intravenous corticosteroid is formally assessed on day three.
More than eight stools daily, or three to eight with C-reactive protein above 45 mg/L, predicts colectomy.
Rescue therapy is infliximab or ciclosporin, with surgical involvement in parallel.
Opioids, antimotility drugs and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs are avoided throughout.
explanation.pearls: Colonic diameter above 5.5 cm on abdominal radiograph, or any free gas, converts this from a medical problem to an immediate surgical one, so repeat the film whenever stool frequency falls at the same time as abdominal distension increases, which is the deceptive pattern of evolving toxic megacolon.

subtopic_detail: confusion in an older woman with a near normal pH concealing a high anion gap acidosis and a respiratory alkalosis
stem:
You are the emergency registrar seeing a 72-year-old woman brought in by her son with four days of increasing confusion. He says she has been complaining that her ears are ringing and has been breathing oddly since yesterday.

She takes aspirin 300 mg four times daily, bought over the counter for shoulder pain, and her son thinks she has also been taking a powder from the chemist for the same pain. She is agitated, disoriented to time and place, sweaty and febrile at 38.1 °C, with deep rapid respirations. Her chest is clear, there is no neck stiffness or rash, and her neurological examination shows no focal deficit. She has taken no deliberate overdose according to her son, and her regular tablets are all accounted for.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 112/min, blood pressure 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 34/min, SpO2 98% in room air, temperature 38.1 °C
data_table.Investigations: pH 7.41 (7.35-7.45), pCO2 22 mmHg (35-45), bicarbonate 14 mmol/L (22-32), anion gap 22 mmol/L (8-16), sodium 141 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 3.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), glucose 3.8 mmol/L (3.5-5.5), lactate 2.4 mmol/L (<2.0), creatinine 128 micromol/L (60-110), salicylate 3.9 mmol/L (therapeutic 1.1-2.2)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Give activated charcoal and repeat the drug level in six hours time
options.rationale: Charcoal is useful for recent large ingestions and for ongoing absorption from concretions, but it does nothing for drug already distributed into tissue over four days of accumulation. Using it as the sole measure in a confused patient also risks aspiration. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

options.text: Give sodium bicarbonate with potassium and arrange urgent haemodialysis
options.rationale: Chronic salicylate toxicity with altered mental status is an indication for haemodialysis regardless of the absolute level, and alkalinisation with sodium bicarbonate is started immediately because raising serum and urinary pH keeps salicylate ionised, out of the brain and excreted by the kidney. Potassium must be replaced in the same fluid, since hypokalaemia prevents the kidney from excreting bicarbonate and defeats the alkalinisation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

options.text: Intubate and ventilate for airway protection given her confusion now
options.rationale: Intubation is the classic trap in this poisoning, because her hyperventilation is the compensation keeping her pH survivable, and any period of apnoea or conventional ventilator settings precipitates a catastrophic fall in pH that drives salicylate into the brain. If intubation is unavoidable, it is done with bicarbonate loading and very high minute ventilation matched to her own. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

options.text: Give intravenous fluid alone and monitor her conscious state closely
options.rationale: Volume replacement is necessary because these patients are markedly dehydrated, but fluid alone does not enhance elimination and observation wastes the window in which neurological injury is preventable. Fluid is a component of the correct plan rather than the whole of it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

options.text: Give intravenous acetylcysteine and admit for overnight observation
options.rationale: Acetylcysteine is the antidote for paracetamol poisoning, which is worth excluding given the additional chemist powder, but it has no role against this drug. Confusing the two analgesic poisonings is a recognised error when a patient has been taking several over the counter products. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

explanation.summary: Chronic salicylate toxicity occurs in older patients taking regular over the counter analgesia and is frequently missed because there is no history of overdose and the presentation resembles sepsis, delirium or a respiratory illness. Salicylate stimulates the respiratory centre, producing a primary respiratory alkalosis, and uncouples oxidative phosphorylation, producing a high anion gap metabolic acidosis with fever, sweating and hypoglycaemia, particularly in the brain where cerebrospinal fluid glucose can be low despite a normal serum value. Because the two disturbances oppose each other, the pH can be near normal, so the diagnosis rests on recognising the anion gap and the low carbon dioxide rather than on the pH. Chronic toxicity causes neurological injury at much lower levels than acute overdose, so dialysis criteria are correspondingly lower and altered mental status alone justifies it. Management is alkalinisation with sodium bicarbonate and generous potassium, volume replacement, glucose supplementation even when the serum glucose is normal, and avoidance of intubation wherever possible.
key_points: A near normal pH with a high anion gap and a low carbon dioxide indicates a mixed disorder.
Chronic toxicity produces neurological injury at far lower levels than acute overdose.
Altered mental status is an indication for dialysis regardless of the measured level.
Alkalinisation fails without adequate potassium replacement.
Intubation removes the compensatory hyperventilation and can be rapidly fatal.
explanation.pearls: Give glucose to any salicylate poisoned patient with altered mental status even when the serum glucose is normal, because cerebral glucose use is uncoupled from the serum level and neuroglycopenia occurs with normal peripheral readings.

subtopic_detail: a shuffling wide based gait preceding urinary urgency and mental slowing with enlarged ventricles
stem:
You are the geriatric medicine registrar seeing a 76-year-old man whose daughter says his walking has changed over about nine months. She describes his feet as looking stuck to the floor when he sets off and when he turns in the hallway, and says he takes several small steps to get around a corner.

The walking came first. Over the past three months he has begun rushing to the toilet and has twice not made it, and in the last month she has noticed he is slower to answer questions and has stopped doing the crossword. On examination his stride is short and his feet are wide apart, and he takes six steps to turn 180 degrees. There is no tremor at rest, no bradykinesia of repetitive finger tapping, no cogwheel rigidity and no asymmetry of limb tone. Power, reflexes and sensation are normal and the plantar responses are flexor. His Montreal Cognitive Assessment is 23 out of 30, losing points on attention and executive tasks with preserved delayed recall. Computed tomography shows enlarged lateral ventricles disproportionate to the degree of cortical sulcal widening.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Gait: Short stride with a wide base, hesitation on initiation, six steps to turn 180 degrees
data_table.Symptom sequence: Gait disturbance for nine months, urinary urgency for three months, cognitive slowing for one month
data_table.Movement examination: No rest tremor, bradykinesia, cogwheel rigidity or asymmetry of tone
data_table.Neurological examination: Normal power, reflexes and sensation with flexor plantar responses
data_table.Cognition: Montreal Cognitive Assessment 23 out of 30, deficits in attention and executive function with preserved delayed recall
data_table.Imaging: Enlarged lateral ventricles disproportionate to cortical sulcal widening

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer directly for ventriculoperitoneal shunt insertion on these findings
options.rationale: Shunting is the definitive treatment and this is the near pair to the correct answer, but imaging and clinical features alone predict response poorly and the operation carries risks of subdural haematoma, infection and shunt failure. Demonstrating reversibility first is what selects the patients who benefit. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Start an anticholinergic for the urinary symptoms and review in two months
options.rationale: Treating the bladder in isolation ignores the gait and cognitive features that share a single cause, and anticholinergic drugs worsen cognition in older adults and add falls risk. The urinary urgency here is a central rather than a bladder problem. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Perform a high volume lumbar puncture with gait testing before and after
options.rationale: Gait disturbance preceding urinary and cognitive symptoms, with ventriculomegaly out of proportion to atrophy, is the picture of normal pressure hydrocephalus. Removing 30 to 50 mL of cerebrospinal fluid with timed and videoed gait assessment either side is the standard test of reversibility and predicts response to shunting. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Start levodopa and assess the gait response after six weeks of treatment
options.rationale: Parkinson disease is the principal differential because both cause a shuffling gait with start hesitation and turning difficulty, and it is separated here by the absence of rest tremor, bradykinesia, rigidity and asymmetry, and by a wide rather than narrow base. A levodopa trial would delay a potentially reversible diagnosis by six weeks. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Start donepezil and refer to the memory clinic for cognitive follow up
options.rationale: Alzheimer disease impairs delayed recall early and affects gait only late, whereas his memory is preserved and the gait changed first by many months. Treating this as a primary dementia misses the reversible cause. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Normal pressure hydrocephalus is a communicating hydrocephalus in which cerebrospinal fluid pressure measured at a single point is within the normal range, and it matters disproportionately because it is one of the few treatable causes of gait disturbance and cognitive decline in older people. The classic triad of gait apraxia, urinary incontinence and cognitive impairment is present in full in only a minority, and the sequence carries more diagnostic weight than the completeness, since gait almost always comes first and a case where cognition leads should be doubted. The gait is broad based, short strided and magnetic with marked start hesitation and difficulty turning, and it is distinguished from parkinsonian gait by the wide base and by the absence of rest tremor, rigidity and asymmetry, although the overlap is real enough that the two are often confused. Imaging shows ventriculomegaly disproportionate to sulcal atrophy, conventionally with an Evans index above 0.3, but imaging alone cannot distinguish it from the ventricular enlargement of cerebral atrophy, so a cerebrospinal fluid drainage trial is used to demonstrate reversibility. Gait improvement after high volume drainage is the best predictor of benefit from ventriculoperitoneal shunting, and gait responds better than cognition, so realistic expectations are set before surgery.
key_points: Gait disturbance almost always precedes the urinary and cognitive features.
A wide base with no rest tremor, rigidity or asymmetry separates it from Parkinson disease.
Ventriculomegaly alone cannot be distinguished from atrophy without a drainage trial.
Gait responds to shunting better than cognition does, which shapes expectations.
explanation.pearls: Time and video the gait over a fixed distance before and immediately after removing 30 to 50 mL of cerebrospinal fluid, because a measurable improvement in walking speed and turning is the best available predictor of who will benefit from a shunt, and unrecorded clinical impression is unreliable.

subtopic_detail: fever ten days after chemotherapy with a neutrophil count below half a billion per litre
stem:
You are the medical registrar called to the emergency department to see a 58-year-old woman who finished her second cycle of chemotherapy for breast cancer ten days ago. She has felt shivery since this morning and recorded a temperature of 38.4 degrees Celsius at home.

She has no cough, no dysuria, no diarrhoea and no rash. Her central venous access device site is clean with no erythema, tenderness or discharge. On examination her chest is clear, her abdomen is soft and non-tender, and the mouth shows no ulceration or thrush. Her pulse rate is 112 beats per minute, blood pressure 106/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 per cent in air and temperature 38.6 degrees Celsius. Her white cell count is 1.1 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0) with an absolute neutrophil count of 0.3 x10^9/L (2.0-7.5), haemoglobin 98 g/L (115-155), platelets 88 x10^9/L (150-400), creatinine 78 micromol/L (45-90), lactate 1.8 mmol/L (0.5-2.2) and C-reactive protein 94 mg/L (less than 5).

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 112 beats per minute, blood pressure 106/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 per cent in air, temperature 38.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Clear chest, soft non-tender abdomen, no oral ulceration, clean central line site with no erythema or discharge
data_table.Full blood count: White cell count 1.1 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), absolute neutrophil count 0.3 x10^9/L (2.0-7.5), haemoglobin 98 g/L (115-155), platelets 88 x10^9/L (150-400)
data_table.Other investigations: Creatinine 78 micromol/L (45-90), lactate 1.8 mmol/L (0.5-2.2), C-reactive protein 94 mg/L (less than 5)
data_table.Treatment history: Second cycle of chemotherapy completed ten days ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Start oral amoxicillin with clavulanate and review again in the morning
options.rationale: Oral therapy with amoxicillin and clavulanate plus ciprofloxacin is an option only for carefully selected low-risk outpatients with a favourable risk score, adequate support and reliable follow-up. This regimen also lacks pseudomonal cover, which is the reason antipseudomonal agents are mandated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Give granulocyte colony stimulating factor and observe her on the ward
options.rationale: Colony stimulating factor shortens the duration of neutropenia and has a place in primary and secondary prophylaxis, but it does not treat established infection and has no demonstrated mortality benefit in this setting. It is an adjunct, never the initial intervention. (Source: eviQ: Febrile neutropenia)

options.text: Start intravenous vancomycin alone and add gentamicin if she deteriorates
options.rationale: Vancomycin covers Gram positive organisms only and leaves the Gram negative bacilli, particularly Pseudomonas aeruginosa, that cause the most rapidly fatal episodes entirely untreated. It is the near pair to correct empirical therapy, and the distinguishing point is that it is added to a beta lactam for suspected line infection, skin or soft tissue infection or haemodynamic instability rather than used alone. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Take blood cultures and give intravenous piperacillin with tazobactam now
options.rationale: Fever with an absolute neutrophil count below 0.5 x10^9/L is febrile neutropenia, a medical emergency in which empirical broad spectrum antipseudomonal beta lactam therapy is given within an hour of presentation. Cultures are drawn immediately before the first dose, from both a peripheral vein and each lumen of the central device, but they must not delay it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Await the blood culture result before starting any antimicrobial therapy
options.rationale: Cultures take 24 to 48 hours and are negative in around 70 per cent of episodes, while mortality in untreated neutropenic sepsis rises sharply with every hour of delay. Waiting for microbiological confirmation is the central error this presentation tests. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Febrile neutropenia is defined as a single oral temperature of 38.3 degrees Celsius or more, or 38.0 degrees Celsius sustained for an hour, together with an absolute neutrophil count below 0.5 x10^9/L or below 1.0 x10^9/L and predicted to fall. The nadir typically falls between seven and fourteen days after cytotoxic chemotherapy, which makes the timing in the history a diagnostic feature in its own right. Clinical signs of infection are attenuated because the inflammatory response depends on the neutrophils that are absent, so pus, consolidation on auscultation and localised erythema may all be missing, and no source is identified in around half of episodes. Empirical therapy is an antipseudomonal beta lactam such as piperacillin with tazobactam or cefepime given within an hour, with vancomycin added for suspected line or skin infection, for haemodynamic instability or for known resistant Gram positive colonisation, and an aminoglycoside added for shock or known resistant Gram negative organisms. Risk stratification tools such as the Multinational Association for Supportive Care in Cancer score identify a low-risk subgroup suitable for oral therapy and early discharge, but that decision follows the first dose rather than preceding it.
key_points: Fever with a neutrophil count below 0.5 x10^9/L is an emergency requiring antibiotics within an hour.
Signs of infection are blunted because the inflammatory response requires neutrophils.
Empirical cover must include Pseudomonas aeruginosa; vancomycin alone is inadequate.
No source is found in around half of episodes and cultures are often negative.
explanation.pearls: The chemotherapy nadir at 7 to 14 days after treatment means a patient who telephones with fever in that window is told to come in immediately rather than to take paracetamol and see how they go, since antipyretics mask the only reliable sign they have.

subtopic_detail: strictly unilateral periorbital pain with lacrimation and agitation in nightly attacks lasting an hour
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar seeing a 34-year-old man who has come in at two in the morning with severe pain behind his right eye. He says it has woken him about ninety minutes after falling asleep every night for the past eighteen days, lasts around an hour and then goes completely.

He cannot sit still during the attack and paces the cubicle, rocking and pressing his palm into the socket, and tells you he would rather be doing anything than lying down. His right eye is watering and red, the right nostril is running, and the right upper lid is drooping with a smaller pupil on that side. There is no photophobia, no phonophobia and no vomiting, and he says he has been completely well between attacks and has kept working. He smokes 20 cigarettes a day and drinks a beer most evenings, which he has noticed now sets off an attack. Neurological examination including fundoscopy is otherwise normal and he is afebrile with no neck stiffness.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Attack pattern: Nightly strictly right sided periorbital pain waking him 90 minutes after sleep onset, lasting about one hour, for 18 days
data_table.Autonomic features: Right conjunctival injection, lacrimation, rhinorrhoea, partial ptosis and miosis
data_table.Behaviour in attack: Restless and pacing, unable to lie still
data_table.Examination: Normal neurological examination including fundoscopy, no neck stiffness, afebrile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate acute treatment?

options.text: Prescribe oral sumatriptan to be taken at the onset of each further attack
options.rationale: Oral triptans take 30 to 60 minutes to act, by which time an attack is already resolving, and the same drug given subcutaneously acts within about ten minutes. This is the near pair to the correct answer, and the distinction is entirely one of route and pharmacokinetics rather than of drug choice. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Start carbamazepine and titrate the dose against the attack frequency
options.rationale: Carbamazepine is first-line for trigeminal neuralgia, which produces brief electric shock-like paroxysms lasting seconds, triggered by touching the face, and without autonomic features or nocturnal periodicity. The attack duration alone separates the two conditions. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Prescribe regular oral prednisolone for the duration of the current cluster
