options.rationale: A tapering corticosteroid course is a legitimate transitional treatment used to suppress attacks while a preventive agent is titrated, but it does not abort the attack he is having now. Its place is bridging rather than acute relief. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Start propranolol as preventive treatment and review him in eight weeks
options.rationale: Propranolol prevents migraine and has no established role in cluster headache, where verapamil is the preventive agent of choice. Eight weeks is also longer than the bout is likely to last, so the review would follow spontaneous remission. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Give high flow oxygen by non rebreather mask and subcutaneous sumatriptan
options.rationale: Strictly unilateral periorbital pain with ipsilateral cranial autonomic features and agitation in circadian nocturnal attacks is cluster headache, and high flow oxygen with subcutaneous sumatriptan are the two acute treatments with the strongest evidence. Both work within minutes, which matters when attacks peak in under a quarter of an hour. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Cluster headache is the commonest trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia and is defined by severe strictly unilateral orbital, supraorbital or temporal pain lasting 15 to 180 minutes untreated, occurring from every other day to eight times daily, with ipsilateral cranial autonomic features or a sense of restlessness. Three features separate it from migraine at the bedside, namely the restlessness and pacing where migraine sufferers lie still in the dark, the prominent ipsilateral autonomic signs, and the striking circadian and circannual periodicity that wakes patients at the same time each night. A partial Horner syndrome is common and usually resolves between attacks, although it can persist. Acute treatment must act within minutes, which restricts the effective options to oxygen at 12 to 15 litres per minute by non-rebreather mask and to subcutaneous or intranasal triptans, and oral agents of any kind are too slow. Verapamil is the preventive of choice with electrocardiographic monitoring during titration because of dose-related atrioventricular block, a tapering corticosteroid course or greater occipital nerve block can bridge the gap, and smoking cessation and alcohol avoidance during a bout are advised.
key_points: Restlessness during attacks distinguishes cluster headache from migraine, where patients lie still.
Attacks last 15 to 180 minutes with ipsilateral autonomic features and circadian periodicity.
Acute treatment must act in minutes: high flow oxygen and subcutaneous or nasal triptan.
Verapamil is the preventive of choice and requires electrocardiographic monitoring.
explanation.pearls: Oxygen for cluster headache must be 12 to 15 litres per minute through a non-rebreather mask with a reservoir bag, because nasal prongs or a simple mask deliver too low a fraction of inspired oxygen to abort the attack and are the usual reason a patient reports that oxygen did not work.

subtopic_detail: a rising creatinine during a diarrhoeal illness in a woman taking three drugs that each impair renal autoregulation
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 72-year-old woman three days into a diarrhoeal illness that her whole family has had. She has hypertension and osteoarthritis, and takes perindopril, indapamide and ibuprofen, the last of which she buys herself and has been taking regularly for knee pain.

She has kept drinking cordial but has passed urine only twice today. On examination her mucous membranes are dry, the jugular venous pressure is not visible, and there is a postural drop from 128/74 mmHg lying to 104/62 mmHg standing with a pulse rate of 96 beats per minute. There is no rash, no fever, no loin tenderness and no palpable bladder. Creatinine is 186 micromol/L (45-90), up from 76 micromol/L six weeks ago, urea 16.8 mmol/L (3.0-8.0), potassium 5.5 mmol/L (3.5-5.2) and sodium 132 mmol/L (135-145). Urinalysis shows no blood, protein, nitrites or leucocytes, and microscopy shows no casts, no eosinophils and no crystals. A renal tract ultrasound reports normal sized unobstructed kidneys with no hydronephrosis.

data_table.Vital signs: Blood pressure 128/74 mmHg lying and 104/62 mmHg standing, pulse rate 96 beats per minute, afebrile, remaining vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Dry mucous membranes, jugular venous pressure not visible, no rash, no loin tenderness, no palpable bladder
data_table.Renal function: Creatinine 186 micromol/L (45-90) from 76 micromol/L six weeks ago, urea 16.8 mmol/L (3.0-8.0)
data_table.Urine: No blood, protein, nitrites or leucocytes, microscopy showing no casts, eosinophils or crystals
data_table.Imaging: Normal sized unobstructed kidneys with no hydronephrosis

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Withhold the perindopril, indapamide and ibuprofen and rehydrate her
options.rationale: Volume depletion with a bland urinary sediment and an unobstructed tract indicates prerenal acute kidney injury, and all three drugs are contributing by different mechanisms that each disable glomerular autoregulation. Withholding the whole combination while restoring volume is the treatment, with reintroduction once renal function has recovered. (Source: KHA-CARI: Acute kidney injury)

options.text: Withhold the perindopril only and continue the other two medications
options.rationale: Stopping one agent leaves the other two mechanisms operating, with the diuretic continuing to deplete volume and the anti-inflammatory continuing to constrict the afferent arteriole. This is the near pair to the correct answer, and the distinction is that the injury arises from the combination rather than from any single drug. (Source: KHA-CARI: Acute kidney injury)

options.text: Start prednisolone for a presumed acute interstitial nephritis today
options.rationale: Drug-induced interstitial nephritis is worth considering with any new medication, but it typically produces sterile pyuria, white cell casts, eosinophiluria, a rash or fever, and her sediment and examination are bland. Corticosteroid would add hyperglycaemia and immunosuppression without addressing the volume deficit. (Source: KHA-CARI: Acute kidney injury)

options.text: Insert a urinary catheter and arrange renal tract imaging this evening
options.rationale: Catheterisation and imaging are the right moves when obstruction is suspected, and obstruction has already been excluded by an ultrasound showing no hydronephrosis with a non-palpable bladder. An unnecessary catheter carries a real risk of urinary infection in this age group. (Source: KHA-CARI: Acute kidney injury)

options.text: Refer for urgent renal biopsy to establish the underlying diagnosis
options.rationale: Biopsy is reserved for suspected intrinsic glomerular or interstitial disease where the cause remains unclear after non-invasive assessment, particularly with an active sediment or systemic features. A clear precipitant with a bland sediment does not warrant an invasive procedure with a bleeding risk. (Source: KHA-CARI: Acute kidney injury)

explanation.summary: The combination of a renin angiotensin system inhibitor, a diuretic and a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug is often called the triple whammy and is one of the commonest preventable causes of community-acquired acute kidney injury in older Australians. The three act at different points on the same autoregulatory system, since the diuretic depletes intravascular volume, the non-steroidal blocks the prostaglandin-mediated afferent arteriolar vasodilatation that maintains glomerular perfusion when volume is low, and the angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor blocks the efferent arteriolar constriction that would otherwise preserve filtration pressure. Each is well tolerated alone in a euvolaemic patient, which is why the combination is so often overlooked until an intercurrent illness removes the volume reserve, and gastroenteritis, vomiting, febrile illness and hot weather are the usual triggers. A bland urinary sediment with an unobstructed tract and clinical volume depletion establishes a prerenal picture without further investigation, and management is to withhold all three agents and restore volume. Sick day guidance is the durable lesson, with patients on these agents told which medicines to pause during vomiting, diarrhoea or fever, and over-the-counter anti-inflammatory purchase asked about directly since it will not appear on the medication list.
key_points: Diuretic, renin angiotensin inhibitor and non-steroidal disable renal autoregulation together.
An intercurrent illness removing volume reserve is the usual precipitant.
A bland sediment with no obstruction establishes a prerenal cause without further tests.
Over-the-counter anti-inflammatory use must be asked about, as it is absent from the list.
explanation.pearls: Give written sick day guidance to every patient on a renin angiotensin inhibitor plus a diuretic, naming the medicines to pause during vomiting, diarrhoea or fever and when to restart them, because the combination is safe until the day the patient cannot keep fluids down.

subtopic_detail: a falling phosphate on the third day of nutritional support after a fortnight of minimal oral intake
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 74-year-old man admitted eight days ago after a fall at home, where he had been living alone and eating almost nothing for a fortnight because of low mood after his wife died. He weighs 48 kg and his body mass index is 16.2 kg/m2.

Nasogastric feeding was started three days ago at his full estimated energy requirement. This morning he is more short of breath than yesterday, has new peripheral oedema and says his legs feel weak going to the toilet. On examination there are bibasal crackles and a raised jugular venous pressure. His pulse rate is 106 beats per minute, blood pressure 108/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, SpO2 93 per cent in air and temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius. Phosphate is 0.38 mmol/L (0.75-1.50), having been 0.82 mmol/L on admission, potassium 3.0 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), magnesium 0.58 mmol/L (0.70-1.10), corrected calcium 2.26 mmol/L (2.15-2.55) and creatinine 74 micromol/L (60-110). His thiamine status was not assessed before feeding began.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 106 beats per minute, blood pressure 108/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, SpO2 93 per cent in air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Bibasal crackles, raised jugular venous pressure, new peripheral oedema, proximal weakness
data_table.Nutritional status: Weight 48 kg, body mass index 16.2 kg/m2, minimal oral intake for a fortnight before admission
data_table.Electrolytes: Phosphate 0.38 mmol/L (0.75-1.50) from 0.82 mmol/L on admission, potassium 3.0 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), magnesium 0.58 mmol/L (0.70-1.10), corrected calcium 2.26 mmol/L (2.15-2.55)
data_table.Feeding history: Nasogastric feeding at full estimated requirement from day three of admission, thiamine status not assessed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Change to parenteral nutrition and add an insulin infusion for tight control
options.rationale: The route of feeding is not the problem and parenteral nutrition carries higher refeeding risk along with line-related complications. Adding exogenous insulin would drive further intracellular shift of the very electrolytes that are already dangerously low. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

options.text: Reduce the feeding rate, replace phosphate intravenously and give thiamine
options.rationale: A falling phosphate with hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia and new fluid overload after reintroducing nutrition to a severely malnourished patient is refeeding syndrome. Management is to reduce the caloric load, aggressively replace phosphate, potassium and magnesium, and give thiamine, which is consumed rapidly as carbohydrate metabolism resumes. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

options.text: Continue the current feeding rate and replace phosphate by the oral route
options.rationale: Oral phosphate is slow, causes diarrhoea at the doses needed and is inadequate for a level of 0.38 mmol/L with respiratory and cardiac manifestations. Continuing full-rate feeding sustains the insulin-driven intracellular shift that caused the problem. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

options.text: Stop feeding entirely and recommence once the phosphate has normalised
options.rationale: Stopping feeding altogether prolongs malnutrition and sets up a repeat episode when it is restarted, and the evidence supports continuing at a reduced rate while replacing electrolytes. This is the near pair to the correct answer, and the distinction is between reducing and abandoning the feed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

options.text: Increase the feeding rate to correct the underlying malnutrition more quickly
options.rationale: Increasing the caloric load intensifies the insulin surge that drives phosphate, potassium and magnesium into cells and will deepen every abnormality present. Starting at full requirement was itself the precipitant in this case. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

explanation.summary: Refeeding syndrome is the constellation of fluid and electrolyte shifts that follows reintroduction of nutrition after a period of starvation, driven by the switch from fat and protein catabolism back to carbohydrate metabolism and the resulting insulin surge. Insulin drives phosphate, potassium and magnesium into cells at a time when total body stores are already depleted despite normal or near-normal admission levels, and it simultaneously promotes sodium and water retention, producing the oedema and cardiac failure seen here. Hypophosphataemia is the biochemical hallmark and it causes the clinical syndrome, since adenosine triphosphate and 2,3-diphosphoglycerate synthesis both fail, producing respiratory muscle weakness, cardiac failure, rhabdomyolysis, haemolysis, seizures and arrhythmia. Thiamine is a cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase and is consumed rapidly as carbohydrate metabolism restarts, so it is given before or with the first feed to prevent precipitating Wernicke encephalopathy. Prevention is what matters most, with identification of high-risk patients by body mass index, weight loss, duration of negligible intake and pre-existing electrolyte abnormality, starting feeds at a fraction of the requirement and building up over days, with daily electrolyte monitoring throughout the first week.
key_points: Insulin release after refeeding drives phosphate, potassium and magnesium into cells.
Hypophosphataemia impairs adenosine triphosphate synthesis, causing cardiac and respiratory failure.
Thiamine is given before or with the first feed to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy.
Prevention means starting at reduced calories and building up with daily monitoring.
explanation.pearls: Start feeding a patient at high refeeding risk at about 5 to 10 kcal per kilogram per day and build to full requirement over four to seven days, with daily phosphate, potassium and magnesium for the first week, since normal admission electrolytes say nothing about total body stores.

subtopic_detail: excessive daytime sleepiness with witnessed apnoeas in a heavy vehicle driver awaiting a sleep study
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 52-year-old man who drives a semi-trailer on overnight interstate runs. He has come for a repeat prescription and mentions that he nodded off at the wheel for a moment approaching a roundabout last week and put it down to a long shift.

His partner says he snores loudly, stops breathing and then gasps several times a night. His Epworth Sleepiness Scale score is 17 out of 24. His body mass index is 37 kg/m2, his neck circumference is 45 cm and his blood pressure is 152/94 mmHg on two occasions despite perindopril. He has fallen asleep watching television and while sitting in the waiting room today. Examination shows a crowded oropharynx, clear lung fields and no peripheral oedema, and his oxygen saturation is 95 per cent in air. A polysomnogram has been requested and the next available appointment in the public system is in fourteen weeks. He asks you to sign his commercial driving medical certificate today.

data_table.Vital signs: Blood pressure 152/94 mmHg on two occasions, SpO2 95 per cent in air, remaining vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Sleep history: Loud snoring with witnessed apnoeas and gasping, Epworth Sleepiness Scale 17 out of 24
data_table.Anthropometry: Body mass index 37 kg/m2, neck circumference 45 cm
data_table.Recent event: Episode of falling asleep at the wheel while driving a heavy vehicle last week
data_table.Examination: Crowded oropharynx, clear lung fields, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Pending investigation: Polysomnogram requested with a fourteen week wait

lead_in: What is the most appropriate course of action?

options.text: Start modafinil to control the sleepiness while he awaits the sleep study
options.rationale: Wake-promoting agents are reserved for residual sleepiness that persists despite adequate treatment of the underlying disorder, and using one to mask sleepiness in an untreated driver is unsafe. It also has no effect on the apnoeas, the hypoxaemia or the blood pressure. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Refer for bariatric surgery assessment and continue his current work duties
options.rationale: Weight loss is genuinely disease-modifying and bariatric referral is reasonable in the longer term, but surgery is months away at best and does nothing about tomorrow night's shift. The immediate hazard is not addressed. (Source: Austroads: Assessing Fitness to Drive)

options.text: Advise him to stop commercial driving now and document that advice clearly
options.rationale: Severe excessive daytime sleepiness with a recent episode of falling asleep at the wheel means he does not meet the commercial vehicle standard, and the advice to cease driving applies immediately rather than after the sleep study. Australian practice places the reporting obligation on the driver, with the doctor responsible for giving and documenting clear advice. (Source: Austroads: Assessing Fitness to Drive)

options.text: Allow him to keep driving until the sleep study result becomes available
options.rationale: A fourteen week wait means fourteen more weeks of overnight heavy vehicle driving by a man who has already fallen asleep at the wheel, and fitness to drive turns on demonstrated sleepiness rather than on a numerical apnoea index. Deferring the decision to the test misunderstands what the standard measures. (Source: Austroads: Assessing Fitness to Drive)

options.text: Notify the driver licensing authority today without informing the patient
options.rationale: Reporting to the licensing authority is permitted where a driver continues to drive against advice and is the near pair to the correct answer, but it follows rather than replaces giving the advice, and doing it covertly is not supported. The first step is always an explicit conversation with the patient. (Source: Austroads: Assessing Fitness to Drive)

explanation.summary: Obstructive sleep apnoea affects a substantial proportion of commercial drivers and is associated with a two to threefold increase in motor vehicle crash risk, concentrated in those with excessive daytime sleepiness rather than in everyone with a raised apnoea hypopnoea index. The Australian standard set out in Assessing Fitness to Drive is stricter for commercial vehicle drivers than for private drivers and turns primarily on symptoms, so a driver reporting sleepiness while driving, or a recent episode of falling asleep at the wheel, does not meet the standard regardless of what a sleep study eventually shows. The legal framework places the obligation to report a relevant medical condition on the driver, while the treating doctor is responsible for assessing fitness, giving clear advice, and documenting both, with direct notification to the licensing authority permitted and appropriate where a driver continues to drive against advice. Continuous positive airway pressure is the definitive treatment and drivers can usually return to commercial driving once symptoms are controlled and adherence is demonstrated objectively, typically with downloaded device data showing regular use. Weight loss, positional therapy, mandibular advancement splints and treatment of contributory hypothyroidism or alcohol use are adjuncts, and the associated hypertension frequently improves with effective treatment.
key_points: Commercial driving standards turn on daytime sleepiness rather than on the apnoea index alone.
Falling asleep at the wheel means the standard is not met, before any sleep study is done.
The driver holds the reporting obligation; the doctor advises, documents and may notify.
Return to commercial driving requires symptom control with demonstrated device adherence.
explanation.pearls: An Epworth Sleepiness Scale of 16 or more, or any episode of falling asleep at the wheel, disqualifies a commercial driver under the Austroads standard immediately, so the certificate is withheld on the day rather than held open pending the polysomnogram.

subtopic_detail: recurrent oral and genital ulceration with blurred vision and a positive skin prick response
stem:
You are the medical registrar seeing a 29-year-old man born in Turkey who has had crops of painful mouth ulcers for three years, occurring six or seven times a year and taking a fortnight to heal. Over the past year he has also had two episodes of painful scrotal ulceration that left scars.

He now reports three days of blurred vision and floaters in the right eye with some aching around it. On examination there are four shallow ulcers with erythematous rims on the buccal mucosa and two healed scars on the scrotum, and there are several tender erythematous nodules on both shins. A cannula inserted in the emergency department yesterday has developed a sterile pustule at the puncture site. Herpes simplex polymerase chain reaction from an ulcer base is negative, coeliac serology is negative, and his full blood count, iron studies, B12 and folate are all normal. C-reactive protein is 42 mg/L (less than 5) and he is afebrile with otherwise normal vital signs.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Mucocutaneous findings: Four shallow buccal ulcers with erythematous rims, two healed scrotal scars, tender erythematous nodules on both shins
data_table.Needle site: Sterile pustule at a cannula puncture site inserted the previous day
data_table.Ocular symptoms: Three days of blurred vision, floaters and periocular ache in the right eye
data_table.Investigations: Negative herpes simplex polymerase chain reaction and coeliac serology, normal full blood count, iron studies, B12 and folate, C-reactive protein 42 mg/L (less than 5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start topical corticosteroid eye drops and review him in the clinic next month
options.rationale: Topical therapy penetrates adequately for anterior uveitis only, and posterior segment inflammation requires systemic treatment. A month of observation in a condition that causes irreversible visual loss within days is the central hazard here. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Behcet disease)

options.text: Start valaciclovir and swab both ulcer sites for herpes simplex virus again
options.rationale: Recurrent herpetic ulceration is the near pair for oral and genital ulcers occurring together, and it is excluded here by a negative polymerase chain reaction from the ulcer base, by the scarring pattern and by the accompanying erythema nodosum and pathergy, which herpes does not produce. Repeating a negative test delays treatment of the eye. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Start colchicine alone and review the ulcer frequency in three months' time
options.rationale: Colchicine is a reasonable first-line agent for mucocutaneous and joint manifestations and would be appropriate if ulcers were the only problem. It is inadequate as sole therapy once sight-threatening ocular disease is present. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Behcet disease)

options.text: Refer for gastroenterology assessment and colonoscopy before any treatment
options.rationale: Inflammatory bowel disease can produce oral ulceration and erythema nodosum and warrants consideration, but he has no bowel symptoms and endoscopy will take weeks. The eye cannot wait for a differential diagnosis to be narrowed by an unrelated investigation. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Behcet disease)

options.text: Refer urgently for ophthalmology review and start systemic corticosteroid
options.rationale: Recurrent oral and genital ulceration with erythema nodosum, a positive pathergy response and new ocular symptoms indicates Behcet disease with probable posterior uveitis, which is sight-threatening and can destroy vision within days. Same-day ophthalmological assessment with systemic corticosteroid, followed by a steroid-sparing agent, is the appropriate response. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Behcet disease)

explanation.summary: Behcet disease is a variable vessel vasculitis affecting arteries and veins of all sizes, with a marked geographic distribution along the historical Silk Road from the eastern Mediterranean through to East Asia, and a strong association with HLA-B51. The International Study Group criteria require recurrent oral ulceration at least three times a year plus two of recurrent genital ulceration, eye lesions, skin lesions and a positive pathergy test, in which a sterile pustule forms at a needle prick site within 48 hours. Ocular involvement occurs in around half of patients, is typically a bilateral relapsing panuveitis with retinal vasculitis rather than isolated anterior uveitis, and was historically a leading cause of blindness in young adults in endemic regions. Other major manifestations are venous thrombosis, arterial aneurysm including the pulmonary arteries, central nervous system parenchymal and venous sinus disease, and gastrointestinal ulceration that can perforate. Treatment is stratified by organ involvement, with colchicine and topical measures for mucocutaneous disease, and systemic corticosteroid combined with azathioprine, ciclosporin, interferon alfa or a tumour necrosis factor inhibitor for ocular, neurological and vascular disease.
key_points: Recurrent oral ulceration plus two of genital ulcers, eye, skin or pathergy meets criteria.
Pathergy is a sterile pustule forming at a needle prick site within 48 hours.
Ocular disease is a relapsing panuveitis with retinal vasculitis, not isolated anterior uveitis.
Sight-threatening or neurological disease requires systemic immunosuppression, not colchicine alone.
explanation.pearls: Look at the cannula sites before ordering a pathergy test: a sterile pustule that appeared at a venepuncture or cannulation site within 48 hours is the same phenomenon and is often already documented in the nursing notes as a line-site reaction.

subtopic_detail: progressive headache with papilloedema and a focal seizure in a woman taking combined oral contraception
stem:
You are the medical registrar called to the emergency department to see a 31-year-old woman with eight days of headache that has become steadily worse. She takes the combined oral contraceptive pill and returned from a long-haul flight a fortnight ago.

She describes the headache as a constant band that is worse when she lies flat, worse when she coughs or strains, and worst on waking. This afternoon her left arm jerked rhythmically for about ninety seconds while she remained aware throughout, and afterwards the arm felt weak for twenty minutes. On examination there is bilateral papilloedema with blurred disc margins and absent venous pulsation, and visual acuity is 6/6 in each eye. Power, tone, reflexes and sensation are now normal in all four limbs and she is fully oriented. There is no neck stiffness, no fever and no rash. An unenhanced computed tomography scan of the brain shows a small area of haemorrhage in the right parietal region with surrounding low attenuation that does not conform to an arterial territory. Her vital signs are within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Headache pattern: Eight days of progressive headache worse lying flat, on coughing and straining, and on waking
data_table.Seizure: Focal motor seizure of the left arm lasting 90 seconds with retained awareness and 20 minutes of postictal weakness
data_table.Fundoscopy: Bilateral papilloedema with blurred disc margins and absent venous pulsation, visual acuity 6/6 bilaterally
data_table.Neurological examination: Normal power, tone, reflexes and sensation in all four limbs, fully oriented, no neck stiffness
data_table.Computed tomography: Small right parietal haemorrhage with surrounding low attenuation not conforming to an arterial territory
data_table.Risk factors: Combined oral contraceptive use and recent long-haul flight

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange venographic imaging and start therapeutic anticoagulation
options.rationale: Progressive positional headache with papilloedema, a focal seizure and a parenchymal haemorrhage that crosses arterial boundaries in a woman on oestrogen indicates cerebral venous sinus thrombosis. Venography confirms it and therapeutic anticoagulation is the established treatment, since the haemorrhage is venous infarction caused by the clot rather than a contraindication to treating it. (Source: Stroke Foundation: Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management)
source_refs: Stroke Foundation: Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management

options.text: Withhold anticoagulation because of the intracranial haemorrhage present
options.rationale: This is the central trap of the presentation, and randomised and observational evidence both support anticoagulating despite haemorrhagic venous infarction, because relieving the venous outflow obstruction is what stops the bleeding from extending. Withholding treatment allows the thrombus to propagate and the infarct to enlarge. (Source: Stroke Foundation: Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management)
source_refs: Stroke Foundation: Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management

options.text: Start intravenous mannitol and refer for decompressive craniectomy now
options.rationale: Decompressive surgery is reserved for impending herniation from a large venous infarct with a deteriorating conscious state, and she is fully oriented with normal limb power. Osmotic therapy also does not address the underlying occlusion. (Source: Stroke Foundation: Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management)
source_refs: Stroke Foundation: Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management

options.text: Load with levetiracetam and repeat the unenhanced scan in 24 hours
options.rationale: An antiseizure medication is appropriate after a seizure with a supratentorial lesion and is part of the plan, which makes this the near pair to the correct answer. The distinction is that it treats a complication while leaving the thrombosis undiagnosed and untreated, and a repeat unenhanced scan cannot demonstrate the occluded sinus. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Start high dose aspirin and arrange carotid duplex ultrasound tomorrow
options.rationale: Antiplatelet therapy and carotid imaging belong to the workup of arterial ischaemic stroke, which this is not, since the lesion crosses arterial territory boundaries and the presentation is dominated by raised intracranial pressure. Carotid disease is also vanishingly rare at this age. (Source: Stroke Foundation: Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management)
source_refs: Stroke Foundation: Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management

explanation.summary: Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis accounts for under 1 per cent of strokes but occurs in a much younger population, with a median age around 35 and a marked female predominance driven by oestrogen-containing contraception, pregnancy and the puerperium. Presentation is protean and often subacute, and the four recognised syndromes are isolated intracranial hypertension with headache and papilloedema, focal deficits, seizures, and encephalopathy, with headache the presenting symptom in around 90 per cent. Two features on plain imaging should raise the diagnosis, namely a parenchymal haemorrhage or infarct that does not respect arterial territory boundaries, particularly when parasagittal or temporal, and a hyperdense cord or delta sign, though the unenhanced scan is normal in up to a third of cases so a negative scan does not exclude it. Confirmation is by computed tomography venography or magnetic resonance venography, and treatment is therapeutic anticoagulation with low molecular weight heparin even in the presence of haemorrhagic venous infarction, a counterintuitive principle supported by trial and registry data because the bleeding is a consequence of venous congestion that anticoagulation relieves. Endovascular thrombectomy is reserved for deterioration despite anticoagulation, and thrombophilia screening, cessation of oestrogen-containing contraception and three to twelve months of oral anticoagulation follow.
key_points: Oestrogen-containing contraception, pregnancy and the puerperium are the major risk factors.
A haemorrhage or infarct crossing arterial territory boundaries suggests a venous cause.
Anticoagulation is given despite haemorrhagic venous infarction, which is the key principle.
A normal unenhanced scan occurs in up to a third of cases and does not exclude the diagnosis.
explanation.pearls: A headache that is worse lying flat, worse on coughing or straining and worst on waking is the raised intracranial pressure pattern, and in a young woman on the combined pill it should trigger venographic imaging rather than a diagnosis of migraine, whatever the unenhanced scan shows.

sources.label: Stroke Foundation: Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management

subtopic_detail: new back pain with brisk lower limb reflexes and a sensory level in a man with known metastatic disease
stem:
You are the medical registrar called to the emergency department at ten at night to see a 71-year-old man with prostate cancer and known bone metastases, on androgen deprivation therapy. He has had mid back pain for three weeks that is worse lying flat and wakes him, and today he has found the stairs difficult and nearly fell twice.

He says his legs feel heavy rather than painful and that he has had to strain to start passing urine since yesterday. On examination hip flexion is 4 out of 5 bilaterally with normal power in the arms, both knee and ankle reflexes are brisk with sustained ankle clonus, and both plantar responses are extensor. There is a band of reduced pinprick sensation below the level of the umbilicus. The bladder is palpable to three finger breadths above the pubic symphysis. There is percussion tenderness over the mid thoracic spine. His observations are normal, his prostate specific antigen has risen from 12 to 68 micrograms/L over four months, and his corrected calcium is 2.44 mmol/L (2.15-2.55).

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Motor examination: Hip flexion 4 out of 5 bilaterally with normal upper limb power
data_table.Reflexes and tone: Brisk knee and ankle reflexes with sustained ankle clonus, extensor plantar responses bilaterally
data_table.Sensory examination: Band of reduced pinprick sensation below the umbilicus
data_table.Other findings: Palpable bladder three finger breadths above the pubic symphysis, mid thoracic percussion tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Prostate specific antigen risen from 12 to 68 micrograms/L over four months, corrected calcium 2.44 mmol/L (2.15-2.55)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the lumbar spine within the next week
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance imaging is the correct modality, which makes this the near pair to the correct answer, and it fails on two counts. The whole spine must be imaged because a third of patients have compression at more than one level, some of it remote from the symptomatic site, and the timeframe must be hours rather than a week. (Source: eviQ: Malignant spinal cord compression)

options.text: Give high dose dexamethasone and arrange urgent whole spine imaging
options.rationale: Back pain with upper motor neuron signs, a sensory level and urinary retention in a man with bone metastases is malignant spinal cord compression, and neurological outcome depends almost entirely on how much function remains when treatment begins. High dose dexamethasone is given immediately to reduce peritumoural oedema while magnetic resonance imaging of the whole spine is arranged. (Source: eviQ: Malignant spinal cord compression)

options.text: Arrange a plain radiograph of the lumbar spine and review the result first
options.rationale: Plain films miss around a fifth of compressive lesions, cannot show the cord or the epidural space, and would be imaging the wrong region given a sensory level at the umbilicus corresponding to the tenth thoracic dermatome. A normal film would falsely reassure. (Source: eviQ: Malignant spinal cord compression)

options.text: Start opioid analgesia and refer to outpatient radiation oncology clinic
options.rationale: Analgesia is necessary but does nothing for the compression, and an outpatient referral introduces a delay measured in days when the window for preserving ambulation is measured in hours. Established paraplegia is rarely reversible. (Source: eviQ: Malignant spinal cord compression)

options.text: Arrange a radionuclide bone scan and refer for palliative radiotherapy later
options.rationale: A bone scan shows osseous metastatic activity but gives no information about the epidural space or the degree of cord compression, and it cannot guide the radiotherapy field or a surgical decision. It answers a question that has already been answered. (Source: eviQ: Malignant spinal cord compression)

explanation.summary: Malignant spinal cord compression complicates around 5 per cent of cancers, most often from prostate, breast, lung, myeloma and renal primaries, and results from vertebral metastasis expanding into the epidural space or from vertebral collapse. Back pain precedes neurological signs by a median of several weeks and has characteristic features, being worse on lying flat, waking the patient at night and worsened by coughing or straining, which together distinguish it from mechanical pain that eases with rest. The single strongest predictor of whether a patient walks afterwards is whether they were walking when treatment started, so this is a presentation where hours matter and where waiting for the morning list costs function that does not return. Dexamethasone is given immediately at high dose to reduce vasogenic oedema, whole spine magnetic resonance imaging is obtained urgently because multilevel disease is common and changes the treatment field, and definitive treatment is decided jointly between radiation oncology and spinal surgery. Surgical decompression with stabilisation followed by radiotherapy gives better ambulatory outcomes than radiotherapy alone in selected patients with a single level of compression, good performance status, a reasonable prognosis and spinal instability or a radioresistant tumour.
key_points: Pain worse lying flat and waking the patient is the warning that precedes neurological signs.
Ambulatory status at the start of treatment is the strongest predictor of final function.
Image the whole spine, since around a third of patients have multilevel compression.
Dexamethasone is given before imaging, not after it.
explanation.pearls: The sensory level in cord compression sits at or below the compressive lesion and never above it, so a level at the umbilicus corresponding to the tenth thoracic dermatome means imaging the thoracic and cervical spine as well, and a lumbar-only request will miss the lesion entirely.

subtopic_detail: a platelet fall of more than half on day seven of low molecular weight heparin with a new limb thrombosis
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 66-year-old woman who is day seven after an elective total knee replacement and has been on prophylactic enoxaparin since the operation. The nursing staff have called you because her left calf has become swollen and painful overnight.

On examination the left calf is 4 cm larger than the right with pitting oedema and tenderness along the deep veins, and the surgical wound is clean and dry with no erythema or discharge. There is no bleeding from the wound, no bruising and no petechiae anywhere. Her platelet count is 68 x10^9/L today, having been 198 x10^9/L on the day of surgery and 186 x10^9/L on day three. Haemoglobin is 112 g/L (115-155), white cell count 8.2 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), fibrinogen 4.1 g/L (2.0-4.0), prothrombin time and activated partial thromboplastin time are both normal and the blood film shows no schistocytes and no platelet clumping. Compression ultrasound confirms occlusive thrombus in the left popliteal vein. Her temperature is 36.9 degrees Celsius and the remaining vital signs are normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius, remaining vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Left calf 4 cm larger than the right with pitting oedema and deep venous tenderness, clean dry surgical wound, no bleeding, bruising or petechiae
data_table.Platelet trend: 198 x10^9/L on the day of surgery, 186 x10^9/L on day three, 68 x10^9/L today on day seven
data_table.Other haematology: Haemoglobin 112 g/L (115-155), white cell count 8.2 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), fibrinogen 4.1 g/L (2.0-4.0), normal prothrombin and activated partial thromboplastin times
data_table.Blood film: No schistocytes and no platelet clumping
data_table.Imaging: Compression ultrasound showing occlusive thrombus in the left popliteal vein

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Cease heparin and start warfarin at a loading dose on the same evening
options.rationale: Warfarin given before the platelet count has recovered depletes protein C faster than the procoagulant factors and can precipitate venous limb gangrene and skin necrosis, which makes this the most dangerous of the wrong answers. Warfarin is introduced only once the platelet count exceeds 150 x10^9/L, overlapped with the non-heparin agent. (Source: HSANZ: Heparin induced thrombocytopenia)

options.text: Continue enoxaparin and give intravenous immunoglobulin for the low count
options.rationale: High dose immunoglobulin has a role in severe or refractory disease by saturating the Fc receptors that mediate platelet activation, which makes it the near pair to a legitimate adjunct. The distinction is that it never substitutes for stopping the heparin, and continuing the causative drug guarantees progression. (Source: HSANZ: Heparin induced thrombocytopenia)

options.text: Cease all heparin and start a non heparin parenteral anticoagulant
options.rationale: A platelet fall of more than 50 per cent beginning on day five to ten of heparin exposure with new thrombosis and no alternative cause gives a high 4Ts score, and the disorder is profoundly prothrombotic despite the low count. Stopping every heparin preparation and starting a full therapeutic dose of a non-heparin agent such as danaparoid, argatroban or fondaparinux is the immediate step. (Source: HSANZ: Heparin induced thrombocytopenia)

options.text: Cease heparin and transfuse platelets before starting any anticoagulation
options.rationale: Platelet transfusion adds substrate to a process that is driving thrombosis rather than bleeding and has been associated with arterial thrombotic events in this setting. It is reserved for active major bleeding, which is absent here. (Source: HSANZ: Heparin induced thrombocytopenia)

options.text: Change to unfractionated heparin and monitor the platelet count each day
options.rationale: The antibody is directed against platelet factor 4 bound to heparin and cross-reacts across all heparin preparations, so unfractionated heparin perpetuates rather than resolves the process. Unfractionated heparin in fact carries a higher risk of causing the syndrome than the low molecular weight form. (Source: HSANZ: Heparin induced thrombocytopenia)

explanation.summary: Heparin induced thrombocytopenia is an immune reaction in which antibodies form against complexes of platelet factor 4 and heparin, and those immune complexes cross-link platelet Fc receptors to cause platelet activation, thrombin generation and thrombosis, with the thrombocytopenia arising from consumption rather than from impaired production. The paradox that defines it clinically is that bleeding is rare while thrombosis occurs in up to half of untreated patients, so a falling platelet count on heparin is a thrombotic emergency rather than a bleeding one. The 4Ts score structures the pretest assessment using the degree of thrombocytopenia, the timing at five to ten days after first exposure or sooner with recent prior exposure, the presence of thrombosis or skin necrosis, and the absence of other causes, and a high score mandates immediate action before any laboratory confirmation. Confirmatory testing proceeds in two steps, with a sensitive but non-specific immunoassay for platelet factor 4 antibodies followed by a functional assay such as serotonin release or heparin induced platelet activation, but results take days and treatment cannot wait. Anticoagulation continues for at least four weeks in isolated thrombocytopenia and three months where thrombosis has occurred, and the event is documented prominently as an adverse drug reaction because re-exposure years later can provoke rapid-onset recurrence.
key_points: It causes thrombosis rather than bleeding despite a falling platelet count.
The 4Ts score drives immediate management before laboratory confirmation returns.
All heparin preparations cross-react, so switching to unfractionated heparin is futile.
Warfarin before platelet recovery risks venous limb gangrene through protein C depletion.
explanation.pearls: Delay warfarin until the platelet count is above 150 x10^9/L and overlap it with the non-heparin anticoagulant for at least five days, because starting it early depletes protein C before the procoagulant factors fall and has caused venous limb gangrene requiring amputation.

subtopic_detail: tender shin nodules with bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy and ankle arthritis in a woman of thirty
stem:
You are the respiratory registrar seeing a 30-year-old woman referred after a chest radiograph taken for two weeks of ankle pain and swelling. She has crops of tender red raised lumps over both shins that came up ten days ago.

She has had no cough, no breathlessness on climbing two flights, no fever, no night sweats and no weight loss. She was born in Australia, has not travelled overseas, and has had no known contact with anyone with tuberculosis. On examination there are six tender erythematous nodules on both shins, both ankles are warm and swollen with painful dorsiflexion, and the chest is clear on auscultation. There is no lymphadenopathy palpable in the neck, axillae or groins, and there are no skin lesions elsewhere, no red eye and no facial rash. The chest radiograph shows symmetrical bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy with clear lung fields. An interferon gamma release assay is negative, corrected calcium is 2.44 mmol/L (2.15-2.55), and her spirometry and gas transfer are normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Skin examination: Six tender erythematous nodules over both shins present for ten days
data_table.Joint examination: Both ankles warm and swollen with painful dorsiflexion
data_table.Respiratory examination: Clear chest on auscultation, no palpable lymphadenopathy
data_table.Chest radiograph: Symmetrical bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy with clear lung fields
data_table.Investigations: Negative interferon gamma release assay, corrected calcium 2.44 mmol/L (2.15-2.55), normal spirometry and gas transfer

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start standard four drug antituberculous therapy while cultures are awaited
options.rationale: Tuberculous lymphadenopathy is characteristically unilateral or asymmetrical and accompanied by constitutional symptoms, and her interferon gamma release assay is negative with no exposure history. Empirical antituberculous therapy carries substantial hepatotoxicity for a diagnosis that is not supported. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Start high dose oral prednisolone and taper it over the next six months
options.rationale: Corticosteroids are reserved for organ-threatening disease such as significant pulmonary impairment, cardiac or neurological involvement, hypercalcaemia or sight-threatening uveitis, none of which is present given normal lung function and a normal calcium. Steroids may also prolong the course in an otherwise self-limiting presentation. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Sarcoidosis)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Sarcoidosis

options.text: Refer to haematology for excision biopsy to exclude a lymphoproliferative cause
options.rationale: Lymphoma typically produces asymmetrical or bulky mediastinal nodes with constitutional symptoms rather than symmetrical hilar enlargement with erythema nodosum and periarticular ankle inflammation. Surgical biopsy would subject her to a general anaesthetic for a clinical diagnosis. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Sarcoidosis)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Sarcoidosis

options.text: Treat symptomatically with a nonsteroidal drug and review her in six weeks
options.rationale: Erythema nodosum with symmetrical bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy and ankle periarthritis in a well patient is Lofgren syndrome, an acute presentation of sarcoidosis with a distinctive natural history of spontaneous remission in around 90 per cent within two years. The constellation is sufficiently specific that tissue diagnosis is not required, and symptomatic treatment with observation is appropriate. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Sarcoidosis)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Sarcoidosis

options.text: Arrange endobronchial ultrasound guided lymph node sampling within the week
options.rationale: Tissue sampling is indicated where the presentation is atypical, where lymphoma or malignancy is a genuine concern, or where treatment decisions depend on it, and it is the near pair to the correct answer because it is the standard route to a sarcoidosis diagnosis in other presentations. The distinguishing point is that this specific triad is diagnostic on its own and biopsy adds procedural risk without changing management. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Sarcoidosis)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Sarcoidosis

explanation.summary: Lofgren syndrome is an acute form of sarcoidosis defined by the combination of erythema nodosum, bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy and periarticular ankle inflammation, often with fever, and it is one of the few presentations in which the clinical picture alone is considered diagnostic without histology. That exception exists because the specificity of the triad approaches 95 per cent and because the prognosis is excellent, with spontaneous resolution in around 90 per cent within two years, particularly in those carrying HLA-DRB1 03. The ankle involvement is a periarthritis of the soft tissues around the joint rather than a true synovitis, which is why it is warm and tender but not destructive. Initial assessment still includes chest radiography, lung function with gas transfer, serum calcium, renal and liver function, an electrocardiogram and ophthalmological review, because asymptomatic cardiac, renal and ocular involvement determine whether treatment is needed. Corticosteroids are reserved for organ-threatening disease rather than given routinely, and in this presentation non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs with rest and planned review are sufficient, with colchicine or a short steroid course used if symptoms are severe.
key_points: Erythema nodosum, bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy and ankle periarthritis define the syndrome.
The triad is diagnostic without biopsy, unlike other presentations of sarcoidosis.
Around 90 per cent remit spontaneously within two years.
Steroids are reserved for organ-threatening disease, not for the syndrome itself.
explanation.pearls: Symmetry of the hilar lymphadenopathy is what earns the clinical diagnosis: asymmetrical or unilateral hilar nodes, or any accompanying weight loss and night sweats, take the presentation out of Lofgren syndrome and back to tissue sampling for lymphoma and tuberculosis.

sources.label: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Sarcoidosis

subtopic_detail: a rising urate and potassium after induction chemotherapy in a man whose brother haemolysed on primaquine
stem:
You are the medical registrar on call. A 34-year-old man received the first dose of induction chemotherapy for a bulky high grade lymphoma fourteen hours ago and has been on intravenous fluids with allopurinol since admission. He feels nauseated and has cramp in both hands but is otherwise comfortable.

His family came to Australia from Sardinia. He tells you his older brother was admitted with dark urine and jaundice after taking an antimalarial before a trip, and that he was told to avoid the same tablet and fava beans. He has never been tested himself. On examination he has a positive Trousseau sign and is otherwise unremarkable. His pulse rate is 92 beats per minute, blood pressure 124/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent in air and temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius. Potassium is 5.8 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), urate 0.68 mmol/L (0.20-0.42), phosphate 2.4 mmol/L (0.75-1.50), corrected calcium 1.82 mmol/L (2.15-2.55), creatinine 148 micromol/L (60-110) from 82 micromol/L on admission and lactate dehydrogenase 1840 units/L (120-250). His electrocardiogram shows sinus rhythm with normal T wave morphology and a QRS duration of 88 milliseconds. Urine output has been 30 mL per hour for the last three hours.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 92 beats per minute, blood pressure 124/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent in air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Biochemistry: Potassium 5.8 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), urate 0.68 mmol/L (0.20-0.42), phosphate 2.4 mmol/L (0.75-1.50), corrected calcium 1.82 mmol/L (2.15-2.55)
data_table.Renal function: Creatinine 148 micromol/L (60-110), up from 82 micromol/L on admission, urine output 30 mL per hour for three hours
data_table.Electrocardiogram: Sinus rhythm with normal T wave morphology and QRS duration 88 milliseconds
data_table.Examination: Positive Trousseau sign, otherwise unremarkable
data_table.Family history: Brother developed dark urine and jaundice after an antimalarial and was advised to avoid fava beans

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Give intravenous calcium gluconate to correct the low calcium immediately
options.rationale: The hypocalcaemia here is secondary to hyperphosphataemia, and giving calcium while the phosphate is 2.4 mmol/L promotes calcium phosphate precipitation in the renal tubules and soft tissues, worsening the kidney injury. Calcium is reserved for cardiac membrane stabilisation with electrocardiographic changes or for symptomatic tetany or seizures, and a Trousseau sign alone does not meet that threshold. (Source: eviQ: Tumour lysis syndrome)

options.text: Start urinary alkalinisation with sodium bicarbonate and add a loop diuretic
options.rationale: Alkalinisation increases urate solubility but simultaneously reduces calcium phosphate solubility, promoting nephrocalcinosis in a patient whose phosphate is already markedly raised, and it is no longer recommended. A diuretic in a patient who is becoming oliguric with a rising creatinine risks compounding hypovolaemia. (Source: eviQ: Tumour lysis syndrome)

options.text: Arrange urgent haemodialysis before starting any further medical measures
options.rationale: Renal replacement therapy is indicated for refractory hyperkalaemia, severe symptomatic hypocalcaemia, fluid overload or oliguria persisting despite adequate volume expansion, and none of those thresholds has yet been reached with a normal electrocardiogram and fluids not yet maximised. It remains a real possibility over the next hours if the response is inadequate. (Source: eviQ: Tumour lysis syndrome)

options.text: Give intravenous rasburicase and continue the high volume intravenous fluids
options.rationale: Rasburicase is the standard agent for established tumour lysis with a urate this high, and it would be the answer in almost any other patient, which is what makes it the tempting branch here. Its metabolism generates hydrogen peroxide, and in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency, which this family history strongly suggests, it precipitates severe haemolysis and methaemoglobinaemia and is contraindicated. (Source: eviQ: Tumour lysis syndrome)

options.text: Escalate the intravenous fluids, continue allopurinol and test for enzyme deficiency
options.rationale: With urine output falling and creatinine rising, intensified volume expansion is the immediate priority, and allopurinol is continued because it blocks further urate formation without the oxidative risk. Testing glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase status is what determines whether rasburicase can ever be used, and treatment proceeds on the safe assumption of deficiency until it returns. (Source: eviQ: Tumour lysis syndrome)

explanation.summary: Tumour lysis syndrome follows massive release of intracellular contents from rapidly dividing cells, classically in bulky high grade lymphoma and acute leukaemias within 12 to 72 hours of treatment, producing hyperkalaemia, hyperphosphataemia, hyperuricaemia and secondary hypocalcaemia, with acute kidney injury from urate and calcium phosphate deposition. Prevention rests on risk stratification, aggressive hydration and a urate-lowering agent, with allopurinol for intermediate risk and rasburicase for high risk or established disease. Rasburicase is a recombinant urate oxidase that converts urate to the far more soluble allantoin, and because that reaction generates hydrogen peroxide it causes severe haemolysis and methaemoglobinaemia in people who cannot regenerate reduced glutathione, making glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency an absolute contraindication. The deficiency is X-linked and common in people of Mediterranean, African, Middle Eastern and Southeast Asian ancestry, and a family history of haemolysis after primaquine or fava beans is strong enough evidence to withhold the drug while testing proceeds. The management of hypocalcaemia in this syndrome is also counterintuitive, since correcting it in the face of a high phosphate drives calcium phosphate deposition, so calcium is given only for arrhythmia, tetany or seizures rather than for the number.
key_points: Rasburicase generates hydrogen peroxide and is contraindicated in G6PD deficiency.
Hypocalcaemia is treated only for arrhythmia, tetany or seizures, not for the value alone.
Urinary alkalinisation is no longer recommended as it promotes calcium phosphate deposition.
Volume expansion with allopurinol is the safe route when enzyme status is unknown.
explanation.pearls: A family history of haemolysis after primaquine, dapsone, nitrofurantoin or fava beans is enough to withhold rasburicase before any test result is available, because the resulting haemolysis and methaemoglobinaemia are more dangerous than the hyperuricaemia the drug was going to treat.

sources.label: HSANZ: Supportive care in haematological malignancy

subtopic_detail: worsening hand shake in a man whose mood medication was increased three months before the tremor began
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 61-year-old man with a worsening hand tremor. He has spilled his tea twice this week and is embarrassed signing documents at the bank. He tells you the shaking started about six months ago and has become steadily more noticeable.

He has bipolar disorder that has been stable for years, and his sodium valproate was increased from 1000 mg to 1500 mg daily nine months ago after a brief hypomanic episode. He also takes perindopril. He drinks two standard drinks on a Friday and says alcohol makes no difference to the shaking. There is no family history of tremor. On examination there is a symmetrical fine tremor of both outstretched hands that is present throughout finger to nose movement and absent at rest. There is no rigidity, no bradykinesia on rapid alternating movements, no reduction in arm swing and no facial masking. Gait is normal, and there is no head tremor or vocal tremor. Thyroid function and a serum valproate level are within their reference ranges.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Symmetrical fine postural and action tremor of both hands, absent at rest, no head or vocal tremor
data_table.Parkinsonian features: No rigidity, no bradykinesia on rapid alternating movements, preserved arm swing, no facial masking, normal gait
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid function within normal limits, serum valproate concentration within the therapeutic range
data_table.Medications: Sodium valproate 1500 mg daily increased from 1000 mg nine months ago, perindopril

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Request serum caeruloplasmin with a twenty four hour urinary copper and a slit lamp examination
options.rationale: Wilson disease must be excluded in any movement disorder presenting under the age of forty, and it can cause tremor alongside psychiatric symptoms. First presentation at sixty one with a clear temporal relationship to a dose increase makes it very unlikely. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Wilson disease)

options.text: Commence primidone at a low dose at night and increase it gradually over the following month
options.rationale: Primidone is the other established treatment for essential tremor and is effective, so this shares the reasoning error rather than the pharmacology. It adds a second sedating anticonvulsant to a patient already taking one, when the simpler answer is to address the causative dose. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Commence propranolol for essential tremor and titrate the dose according to his response
options.rationale: Propranolol is first line for essential tremor and would help the tremor symptomatically whatever its cause, which makes it tempting. Essential tremor is usually longstanding with a family history and characteristic alcohol responsiveness, and adding a drug to treat another drug's adverse effect is poor practice when the dose can be reduced. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Discuss a reduction of the valproate dose with his treating psychiatrist and review in six weeks
options.rationale: A symmetrical postural and action tremor beginning after a valproate dose increase, with no parkinsonian signs and no alcohol responsiveness, is drug induced. Valproate tremor is dose related and occurs at therapeutic concentrations, so dose reduction in partnership with the prescriber is the first step. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Refer for dopamine transporter imaging to assess for a nigrostriatal degenerative process
options.rationale: Functional dopaminergic imaging is used when a parkinsonian syndrome is suspected but the clinical picture is equivocal. A purely postural and action tremor with no rest component, rigidity or bradykinesia gives no clinical basis for the referral. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Drug induced tremor is among the commonest causes of tremor in adults and is routinely misattributed to essential tremor or to early Parkinson disease. It is characteristically symmetrical, postural and action predominant, and temporally related to starting a drug or increasing a dose. Sodium valproate causes tremor in up to a quarter of patients, it is dose related, and it occurs at therapeutic serum concentrations, so a normal level does not exclude it. Other frequent culprits are lithium, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, beta agonists, corticosteroids, amiodarone, thyroxine and caffeine, while dopamine antagonists including antipsychotics and metoclopramide instead produce a rest tremor with other parkinsonian features. The correct first response to a drug induced tremor is to review the offending medication, ideally with the prescriber where the drug is treating a serious condition, rather than to add a second medication to suppress the symptom.
key_points: Drug induced tremor is symmetrical, postural and action predominant, and dose related.
Valproate tremor occurs at therapeutic levels, so a normal concentration excludes nothing.
Dopamine antagonists cause a rest tremor with other parkinsonian features instead.
Essential tremor suggests itself through duration, family history and alcohol responsiveness.
Review the causative drug before adding a second drug to suppress the symptom.
explanation.pearls: Never reduce or stop a mood stabiliser unilaterally in a patient with bipolar disorder, because relapse risk after abrupt withdrawal is substantial, particularly with lithium where rapid cessation can precipitate mania within weeks; the change is negotiated with the treating psychiatrist.

subtopic_detail: widespread scaly oval trunk rash also involving both palms and soles in a young man
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 26-year-old man with a rash that appeared ten days ago and has spread across his trunk. He is not particularly itchy. He had a mild sore throat and felt tired for a few days beforehand.

He assumed it was a viral rash and has been using a moisturiser. He is otherwise well with no fever now. On examination there are multiple oval salmon pink scaly macules and papules 5 to 15 mm across scattered over the trunk, with the long axis of the lesions following the skin lines over the back. There are similar scaly copper coloured papules on both palms and both soles, and a few on the shaft of the penis. There is no single larger patch preceding the eruption that he can recall. He has non-tender rubbery lymph nodes palpable in both axillae and both groins, and there are a few small moth eaten patches of hair loss on the occipital scalp. He has had four male sexual partners in the past year and last tested for sexually transmitted infections two years ago.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Oval salmon pink scaly papules over the trunk following skin lines, scaly copper coloured papules on both palms and soles, papules on the penile shaft
data_table.Lymph nodes: Non-tender rubbery generalised lymphadenopathy in both axillae and both groins
data_table.Scalp: Patchy moth eaten hair loss over the occipital scalp
data_table.History: Four male sexual partners in the preceding year, last sexually transmitted infection screening two years ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Request a monospot test with a full blood examination and liver function tests this week
options.rationale: Infectious mononucleosis causes a prodrome, lymphadenopathy and occasionally a rash, particularly after aminopenicillin exposure, so it is a fair differential for the systemic features. It does not produce palmoplantar scaly papules or moth eaten alopecia. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Infectious mononucleosis)

options.text: Request syphilis serology together with a full sexually transmitted infection screen today
options.rationale: Palmoplantar involvement, generalised non-tender lymphadenopathy, moth eaten alopecia and mucosal lesions after a flu like prodrome are secondary syphilis, which mimics several common eruptions. Serology confirms it and the full screen is required because of the high rate of coinfection. (Source: Australian STI Management Guidelines)

options.text: Take skin scrapings for fungal microscopy and culture and start topical terbinafine cream
options.rationale: Scrapings investigate tinea corporis, which produces annular lesions with a raised scaly leading edge and central clearing rather than uniformly scaly oval papules. Widespread simultaneous onset with systemic features is not a dermatophyte pattern. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

options.text: Reassure him that this is a self-limiting eruption and review him again in six to eight weeks
options.rationale: Pityriasis rosea is the near pair and does produce oval scaly lesions following skin lines after a viral prodrome, so the trunk appearance alone genuinely fits. It spares the palms and soles and does not cause generalised lymphadenopathy or patchy alopecia, and watchful waiting would leave syphilis untreated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

options.text: Prescribe a moderately potent topical corticosteroid ointment with an emollient twice daily
options.rationale: Topical corticosteroid suits guttate psoriasis or an eczematous eruption, which do not involve the penile shaft in this pattern or produce rubbery generalised lymphadenopathy. Suppressing the rash would also obscure the presentation without treating the cause. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

explanation.summary: Secondary syphilis appears weeks to a few months after the primary chancre and is the great imitator of dermatology, being mistaken for pityriasis rosea, guttate psoriasis, viral exanthem and drug eruption. The findings that should redirect thinking are involvement of the palms and soles, which almost no other papulosquamous eruption shares, generalised non-tender rubbery lymphadenopathy, moth eaten patchy alopecia, mucous patches and condylomata lata. Diagnosis rests on serology, with a treponemal test used for screening and a non treponemal titre such as the rapid plasma reagin used to assess activity and to monitor the response to treatment. Treatment of early syphilis is a single intramuscular dose of benzathine benzylpenicillin, and patients should be warned about the Jarisch Herxheimer reaction in the first 24 hours. Testing for human immunodeficiency virus and other sexually transmitted infections, and partner notification, are integral to management.
key_points: Palmoplantar scaly papules in a widespread eruption should prompt syphilis serology.
Generalised non-tender lymphadenopathy and moth eaten alopecia support the diagnosis.
Pityriasis rosea follows skin lines but spares palms and soles and lacks systemic signs.
Treponemal serology screens; a non treponemal titre monitors treatment response.
Early syphilis is treated with a single dose of intramuscular benzathine benzylpenicillin.
explanation.pearls: Warn every patient treated for early syphilis about the Jarisch Herxheimer reaction, a self-limiting fever, rigors and headache within 24 hours of the first penicillin dose, because it is commonly mistaken for penicillin allergy and leads to unnecessary avoidance of the only recommended treatment.

subtopic_detail: night time hand tingling with flattening of the muscle bulk at the base of the thumb
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 57-year-old cleaner with eighteen months of tingling in her right hand that wakes her most nights and is relieved by shaking the hand over the side of the bed. She has recently started dropping cups and cannot reliably do up buttons or turn a key.

She was given a wrist splint by a physiotherapist a year ago and wore it nightly for three months with some early benefit that has since been lost. She has no neck pain and no pain radiating from the neck. She has no diabetes and thyroid function tested last month was normal. On examination there is visible flattening of the muscle bulk over the ball of the thumb on the right compared with the left, and thumb abduction against resistance is weak on the right. Sensation is reduced to light touch over the palmar surfaces of the thumb, index and middle fingers, with normal sensation over the little finger and over the skin at the base of the thumb. Neck movements are full and painless, and reflexes in both arms are normal and symmetrical.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Visible right thenar wasting with weak thumb abduction against resistance, normal bulk on the left
data_table.Sensory findings: Reduced light touch over the palmar thumb, index and middle fingers, spared little finger and spared thenar eminence skin
data_table.Cervical spine: Full painless neck movements, no radicular pain, normal and symmetrical upper limb reflexes
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid function within normal limits, no diabetes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Inject the carpal tunnel with corticosteroid and review her symptoms again in six weeks
options.rationale: Corticosteroid injection produces useful short term relief in moderate disease and is a legitimate step before surgery in patients without weakness. Its effect wanes over months and it does not address structural compression that has already caused axonal loss. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Commence pregabalin for neuropathic pain and refer her for hand therapy and nerve gliding exercises
options.rationale: Neuropathic agents and hand therapy address symptoms and may improve comfort, and nerve gliding has modest supporting evidence. Neither reverses compression, and treating symptomatically while the thenar muscles waste risks a permanent functional deficit. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Refit a neutral position night wrist splint and arrange a review of her symptoms in three months
options.rationale: Nocturnal neutral splinting is the correct first line for mild to moderate carpal tunnel syndrome without motor signs and often works well. Once there is thenar wasting, splinting will not restore lost motor axons and delays a decompression that becomes less effective the longer it waits. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the cervical spine to assess for nerve root compression
options.rationale: Cervical imaging targets a C6 radiculopathy, the near pair, which gives neck pain, a dermatomal sensory pattern extending above the wrist, and an altered biceps or brachioradialis reflex. Painless full neck movement with normal reflexes and sensory loss confined to the hand argues against it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Refer for nerve conduction studies and surgical assessment for decompression of the nerve
options.rationale: Thenar wasting with weak thumb abduction indicates established motor axonal loss, which does not recover with conservative treatment and can progress to permanent weakness. Surgical release with prior electrophysiological confirmation is indicated rather than further conservative measures. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Carpal tunnel syndrome is the commonest entrapment neuropathy and results from compression of the median nerve beneath the flexor retinaculum. The classic history is nocturnal paraesthesia in the median distribution relieved by shaking the hand, and symptoms are often reported across the whole hand even though the sensory deficit spares the little finger. A useful anatomical clue is that the palmar cutaneous branch leaves the median nerve proximal to the tunnel, so sensation over the thenar eminence skin is preserved, which distinguishes the entrapment from a more proximal median lesion or a C6 radiculopathy. Management is stratified by severity: nocturnal neutral wrist splinting with activity modification for mild to moderate disease, corticosteroid injection as a temporising measure, and surgical decompression for severe disease. The findings that define severe disease and mandate surgical referral are thenar wasting, weakness of thumb abduction, constant rather than intermittent sensory loss, and failure of conservative treatment.
key_points: Nocturnal paraesthesia relieved by shaking the hand is the characteristic history.
Preserved sensation over the thenar eminence skin reflects the spared palmar cutaneous branch.
Thenar wasting and weak thumb abduction define severe disease requiring surgery.
Splinting and injection are for mild to moderate disease without motor signs.
Sensory recovery after decompression is reliable, but motor recovery is slow and incomplete.
explanation.pearls: Test thumb abduction by asking the patient to raise the thumb vertically out of the plane of the palm against your resistance, because this isolates abductor pollicis brevis, the one thenar muscle supplied solely by the median nerve, and its weakness is what converts a conservative management plan into a surgical referral.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Carpal tunnel syndrome

subtopic_detail: painful stiff shoulder in a woman whose passive external rotation is as restricted as her active movement
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 53-year-old woman with six months of right shoulder pain. It began without injury, was worst at night for the first three months and woke her whenever she rolled onto that side, and the night pain has now eased while the stiffness has become the dominant problem.

She can no longer reach behind her back to fasten a bra or reach up to a high cupboard. She has type 2 diabetes treated with metformin and her most recent glycated haemoglobin was 8.4 per cent (target under 7.0). On examination active abduction is limited to 80 degrees and active external rotation to 10 degrees. When you relax her arm and move it passively, external rotation remains restricted at 10 degrees with a firm end point and reproduces her pain. There is no tenderness over the acromioclavicular joint and no painful arc between 60 and 120 degrees. Power in the rotator cuff muscles is preserved within the available range, and a radiograph of the shoulder shows no calcification, no fracture and preserved joint space.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Active abduction limited to 80 degrees and active external rotation to 10 degrees
data_table.Passive movement: Passive external rotation equally restricted at 10 degrees with a firm end point, reproducing the pain
data_table.Other findings: No acromioclavicular tenderness, no painful arc, rotator cuff power preserved within the available range
data_table.Investigations: Shoulder radiograph showing no calcification, fracture or joint space loss, glycated haemoglobin 8.4 per cent (target under 7.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?
