options.text: Offer a subacromial corticosteroid injection with a graded rotator cuff strengthening program
options.rationale: Subacromial injection and cuff strengthening treat subacromial pain syndrome, the near pair, in which passive range is preserved even when active movement is painful and limited. Injecting the subacromial space does not reach an inflamed and contracted glenohumeral capsule. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

options.text: Offer an intra-articular corticosteroid injection with supervised physiotherapy and glycaemic review
options.rationale: Equal restriction of active and passive external rotation with a normal radiograph is adhesive capsulitis, and intra-articular corticosteroid with physiotherapy gives the greatest benefit during the painful and stiffening phases. Optimising glycaemic control matters because diabetes both predisposes to the condition and prolongs it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

options.text: Refer for urgent magnetic resonance imaging of the shoulder to assess for a rotator cuff tear
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance imaging is appropriate for suspected cuff tear with weakness out of proportion to pain, or when surgery is being considered. A full thickness tear reduces active movement while passive range stays free, and imaging is not needed to make this diagnosis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

options.text: Advise rest from overhead activity with regular analgesia and review her again in three months
options.rationale: Analgesia is part of care but immobilisation accelerates capsular contracture and worsens the stiffness that is now her main complaint. Three months of waiting during the stiffening phase loses the window in which injection is most useful. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

options.text: Refer for arthroscopic capsular release and manipulation of the shoulder under anaesthesia
options.rationale: Capsular release is genuinely effective and is the escalation for disabling stiffness persisting beyond six to twelve months despite conservative treatment. Offering it at six months before injection and physiotherapy have been tried is premature for a condition that usually resolves. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Frozen shoulder)

explanation.summary: Adhesive capsulitis is a fibro inflammatory contracture of the glenohumeral joint capsule that classically evolves through a painful freezing phase of two to nine months, a stiff frozen phase of four to twelve months, and a thawing phase over one to three years. The defining physical sign is loss of passive as well as active movement, with external rotation affected earliest and most severely, and a firm capsular end feel rather than pain limited guarding. That single finding separates it from the rotator cuff disorders, in which passive range is preserved, and a normal radiograph excludes glenohumeral osteoarthritis, which gives a similar pattern with joint space loss. Diabetes is the strongest risk factor, increasing incidence roughly fivefold and predicting a longer and more refractory course, and thyroid disease, Dupuytren disease and previous shoulder immobilisation are also associated. Intra-articular corticosteroid combined with supervised physiotherapy gives the best short and medium term outcomes, particularly when given early, and hydrodilatation, capsular release or manipulation under anaesthesia are reserved for disabling stiffness persisting beyond six to twelve months.
key_points: Equal restriction of active and passive movement with a firm end feel is the defining sign.
External rotation is affected earliest and most severely.
Rotator cuff disorders preserve passive range; osteoarthritis shows joint space loss.
Diabetes raises incidence roughly fivefold and predicts a more refractory course.
Intra-articular corticosteroid with physiotherapy is most effective when given early.
explanation.pearls: Stabilise the scapula with one hand while testing external rotation with the elbow at the side, because scapulothoracic substitution otherwise masks up to 30 degrees of lost glenohumeral rotation and makes a frozen shoulder look like a cuff problem.

subtopic_detail: continuous spinning for eighteen hours with a normal head impulse test and a normal early brain scan
stem:
You are the emergency registrar seeing a 63-year-old man who woke yesterday evening with the room spinning and has been continuously dizzy since, unable to stand without help and vomiting repeatedly. He has hypertension and smokes fifteen cigarettes a day.

He has had no hearing loss, no tinnitus and no headache, and he reports no double vision, no slurred speech and no limb weakness. On examination he is distressed and pale but alert and fully oriented. There is horizontal nystagmus with the fast phase to the left when he looks ahead, which reverses direction and beats to the right when he looks to the right. Horizontal head impulse testing produces no corrective saccade in either direction. Alternate cover testing shows a small vertical realignment of the right eye. Limb power, tone and reflexes are normal and there is no dysmetria on finger to nose testing, but he cannot sit unsupported on the trolley without falling to the left. A non contrast computed tomography scan of the brain performed an hour ago is reported as normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76 beats per minute, blood pressure 168/94 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees
data_table.Eye movements: Horizontal nystagmus beating left in primary gaze that reverses to beat right on right gaze, small vertical realignment of the right eye on alternate cover testing
data_table.Head impulse test: No corrective saccade on rapid horizontal head impulse in either direction
data_table.Neurological: Normal limb power, tone and reflexes, no dysmetria on finger to nose testing, unable to sit unsupported without falling to the left
data_table.Imaging: Non contrast computed tomography of the brain reported as normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Perform the Dix Hallpike manoeuvre and treat any positional nystagmus with particle repositioning
options.rationale: Positional testing is for benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, which produces brief paroxysms lasting under a minute on position change rather than eighteen hours of continuous spinning. Repositioning a patient with a posterior fossa infarct offers no benefit and delays imaging. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Admit under the stroke service for magnetic resonance imaging with diffusion weighted sequences
options.rationale: A normal head impulse test, direction changing nystagmus and vertical ocular misalignment together indicate a central cause, and truncal ataxia out of proportion to limb findings supports it. Computed tomography misses most acute posterior fossa infarcts, so diffusion weighted magnetic resonance imaging is required. (Source: Stroke Foundation: Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management)
source_refs: Stroke Foundation: Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management

options.text: Arrange outpatient audiometry and a carotid duplex ultrasound with review in the next week
options.rationale: Carotid imaging assesses the anterior circulation, whereas the vestibular system is supplied by the posterior circulation, so a normal duplex would be falsely reassuring. Discharging a man who cannot sit unsupported is unsafe regardless of the investigation chosen. (Source: Stroke Foundation: Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management)
source_refs: Stroke Foundation: Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management

options.text: Give intravenous prochlorperazine, rehydrate him and reassess his symptoms in four hours
options.rationale: Antiemetic and fluid resuscitation are reasonable supportive measures alongside investigation and will make him more comfortable. Used as the management plan they suppress the vestibular signs that the examination depends on and lose time in a stroke pathway. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Commence a tapering course of oral prednisolone and refer him for vestibular rehabilitation
options.rationale: This treats vestibular neuritis, which is the diagnosis the duration and the continuous vertigo would otherwise suggest. Neuritis gives an abnormal head impulse test with a corrective saccade towards the affected side and unidirectional nystagmus that does not change direction, and this man has neither. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Acute vestibular syndrome describes continuous vertigo lasting more than 24 hours with nystagmus, nausea and gait unsteadiness, and the clinical task is to separate vestibular neuritis from a posterior circulation stroke, which accounts for roughly a quarter of cases in patients with vascular risk factors. The three step bedside examination known by the acronym HINTS comprises the horizontal head impulse test, observation of nystagmus in different gaze positions, and a test of skew using alternate cover. Each component reads counterintuitively: a normal head impulse test is the worrying result, because a peripheral lesion produces a corrective saccade and an intact vestibulo ocular reflex means the periphery is working. Performed in the right patient this combination outperforms early magnetic resonance imaging for detecting stroke, and it vastly outperforms computed tomography, which misses the large majority of acute posterior fossa infarcts. The other high value bedside sign is severe truncal ataxia: inability to sit or stand unsupported is rare in neuritis and should be treated as central until proven otherwise.
key_points: A normal head impulse test in acute vestibular syndrome is a central finding, not a reassuring one.
Direction changing gaze evoked nystagmus and skew deviation both indicate a central lesion.
Computed tomography misses most acute posterior fossa infarcts and cannot exclude one.
Inability to sit or stand unsupported points strongly to a central cause.
HINTS applies only to continuous acute vestibular syndrome, never to episodic vertigo.
explanation.pearls: HINTS is valid only in a patient with continuous vertigo and nystagmus at the time of examination; applying it to someone whose episodic vertigo has already settled produces a falsely reassuring result, because a normal head impulse test in an asymptomatic patient means nothing at all.

sources.label: Stroke Foundation: Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management
BMJ Best Practice: Assessment of vertigo

subtopic_detail: man with a drooping face who cannot raise the eyebrow on the affected side and cannot close that eye
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 42-year-old carpenter who woke yesterday morning with the right side of his face not working. He noticed coffee dribbling from the corner of his mouth and his wife said his face looked crooked. He had noticed some pain behind the right ear the day before.

He says sounds seem uncomfortably loud in the right ear and that food tastes odd. He has had no fever, no rash, no headache, no limb weakness and no difficulty speaking or swallowing. He has not travelled outside Australia and has no tick exposure. On examination the right side of the face is weak throughout: he cannot wrinkle the right forehead, cannot fully close the right eye, and the right nasolabial fold is flattened. Power and reflexes are normal in all four limbs, the pupils are equal and reactive and eye movements are full. The external auditory canal and the tympanic membrane are normal with no vesicles, and the parotid region is normal on palpation.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Cranial nerves: Complete right sided facial weakness including the forehead, incomplete eye closure, hyperacusis and altered taste on the right
data_table.Neurological: Normal power, tone and reflexes in all four limbs, full eye movements, equal reactive pupils, normal speech and swallow
data_table.Ear and parotid: Normal external auditory canal and tympanic membrane with no vesicles, normal parotid on palpation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange serological testing for Lyme disease and defer treatment until the results return
options.rationale: Bilateral or sequential facial palsy with a preceding rash and overseas tick exposure would justify this, but there is no locally acquired Lyme disease in Australia. Waiting for serology would also take him past the window in which steroid works. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Arrange urgent computed tomography of the brain and refer him to the stroke service today
options.rationale: Urgent stroke assessment is the correct response to an upper motor neurone facial weakness, the critical near pair, in which the forehead is spared because it receives bilateral cortical innervation. Complete forehead involvement localises the lesion to the nerve rather than the cortex. (Source: Stroke Foundation: Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management)
source_refs: Stroke Foundation: Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management

options.text: Commence oral valaciclovir alone today and arrange review of his recovery in one week
options.rationale: Antiviral monotherapy is inferior to corticosteroid and is not recommended on its own. Adding an antiviral to prednisolone may give a small additional benefit in severe or complete palsy, but it never substitutes for the steroid. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Commence oral prednisolone today and prescribe lubricating drops with overnight eye taping
options.rationale: Forehead involvement establishes a lower motor neurone facial palsy, and with a normal ear and no other cranial nerve signs this is Bell palsy. Corticosteroid started within 72 hours of onset significantly improves the chance of complete recovery, and eye protection prevents exposure keratopathy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Refer for facial nerve electrophysiological studies before deciding on any drug treatment
options.rationale: Electroneuronography has a role in prognostication for complete palsies that fail to recover, and it is occasionally used to guide decompression decisions. It has no place in the acute phase and delaying treatment for it costs the therapeutic window. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Bell palsy)

explanation.summary: Bell palsy is an acute idiopathic lower motor neurone facial palsy that evolves over hours to three days and accounts for most cases of unilateral facial weakness. The single most important examination step is testing the forehead, because the frontalis receives bilateral cortical input and is therefore spared in an upper motor neurone lesion such as a stroke but involved in a peripheral nerve lesion. Associated features that support a peripheral lesion include hyperacusis from stapedius weakness, altered taste over the anterior two thirds of the tongue from chorda tympani involvement, and postauricular pain. Corticosteroid started within 72 hours of onset improves the probability of complete recovery from roughly 80 to over 90 per cent, and the evidence for adding an antiviral is weaker and limited to severe cases. Features that should prompt reassessment include bilateral palsy, other cranial nerve involvement, vesicles in the ear canal indicating Ramsay Hunt syndrome, a parotid mass, and failure to show any recovery by three weeks.
key_points: Forehead sparing indicates an upper motor neurone lesion and demands urgent stroke assessment.
Hyperacusis, altered taste and postauricular pain support a peripheral facial nerve lesion.
Corticosteroid within 72 hours substantially improves complete recovery rates.
Antivirals are adjunctive at best and never used alone.
Eye protection prevents exposure keratopathy and is part of every prescription.
explanation.pearls: Inspect the external auditory canal, the concha and the palate in every facial palsy, because the vesicles of Ramsay Hunt syndrome change the treatment to combined corticosteroid and antiviral therapy and carry a considerably worse prognosis for complete recovery.

sources.label: Stroke Foundation: Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management

subtopic_detail: acutely hot swollen first toe joint in a man whose kidney function is severely reduced
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 66-year-old man who woke at 3 am with an exquisitely painful right great toe. He cannot bear the weight of the bedsheet on it. He has had two similar episodes in the past three years, each resolving over a week.

He has stage 4 chronic kidney disease from long standing hypertension and takes perindopril, amlodipine and atorvastatin. He is not on a diuretic and takes no anticoagulant. He has no history of peptic ulcer disease, diabetes or heart failure. On examination he is afebrile and systemically well. The right first metatarsophalangeal joint is red, hot, swollen and exquisitely tender with overlying shiny skin, and there is no break in the skin and no ascending erythema or lymphangitis. No other joint is involved. His estimated glomerular filtration rate is 24 mL/min/1.73 square metres, creatinine 248 micromol/L (60 to 110), serum urate 0.54 mmol/L (0.20 to 0.42), C reactive protein 38 mg/L (less than 5) and white cell count 9.4 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0).

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78 beats per minute, blood pressure 138/82 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees
data_table.Examination: Red hot swollen exquisitely tender right first metatarsophalangeal joint with shiny overlying skin, intact skin, no lymphangitis, no other joint involved
data_table.Investigations: Estimated glomerular filtration rate 24 mL/min/1.73 square metres, creatinine 248 micromol/L (60 to 110), serum urate 0.54 mmol/L (0.20 to 0.42)
data_table.Additional: C reactive protein 38 mg/L (less than 5), white cell count 9.4 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0), medications perindopril, amlodipine and atorvastatin

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment for this acute episode?

options.text: A short course of oral prednisolone with review of his symptoms after five days
options.rationale: Severe renal impairment makes non-steroidal agents hazardous and requires substantial colchicine dose reduction, so a short oral corticosteroid course is the preferred option for an acute flare in stage 4 chronic kidney disease. It is effective within 24 to 48 hours in a man with no diabetes or heart failure. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

options.text: A short course of oral indometacin with a proton pump inhibitor for gastric protection
options.rationale: Non-steroidal anti inflammatory drugs are first line for acute gout in most patients and gastric protection addresses one of their risks. They can precipitate a further fall in glomerular filtration rate and hyperkalaemia at this level of renal function, particularly alongside an angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

options.text: Commence allopurinol at a low dose and titrate it upwards against the serum urate level
options.rationale: Urate lowering therapy is the correct long term treatment after three attacks and with chronic kidney disease, and it should be started once things settle. Introducing it during an acute flare can prolong or worsen the attack unless anti inflammatory cover is already running. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

options.text: Oral colchicine at the standard loading and maintenance dose used for an acute attack
options.rationale: Colchicine is genuinely useful in this situation but only at a substantially reduced dose, because it is renally cleared and accumulates. Standard dosing at an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 24 risks myelosuppression and neuromyopathy. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Oral flucloxacillin for seven days with elevation of the limb and review in forty eight hours
options.rationale: Antibiotic therapy treats cellulitis, the near pair, which spreads diffusely beyond the joint margins with a portal of entry or lymphangitis and does not confine itself precisely to one joint. Erythema sharply limited to the joint with an intact skin surface is inflammatory rather than infective. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Acute gout in chronic kidney disease is a common therapeutic bind because the two agents usually reached for first are both problematic. Non-steroidal anti inflammatory drugs reduce renal perfusion through prostaglandin inhibition and can cause a further decline in function and hyperkalaemia, especially alongside renin angiotensin blockade, and are generally avoided below an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 30. Colchicine is renally cleared, so dosing must be reduced substantially and it is avoided altogether in severe impairment or dialysis. That leaves corticosteroid as the pragmatic first choice for most patients with advanced kidney disease, given orally for a short course or injected intra articularly when a single large joint is involved and septic arthritis has been excluded. Once the flare settles, urate lowering therapy is indicated after recurrent attacks or with chronic kidney disease, starting allopurinol at a low dose appropriate to renal function and titrating to a target serum urate below 0.36 mmol/L.
key_points: Avoid non-steroidal agents below an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 30.
Colchicine is renally cleared and needs substantial dose reduction or avoidance.
Corticosteroid is the pragmatic first choice in advanced chronic kidney disease.
Aspirate the joint whenever fever, systemic upset or diagnostic doubt is present.
Start urate lowering therapy after the flare settles, targeting urate below 0.36 mmol/L.
explanation.pearls: Serum urate is frequently normal or low during an acute flare because urate shifts into the inflamed joint, so a normal level never excludes gout and the measurement that guides treatment is the one taken two to four weeks after the attack has settled.

subtopic_detail: older woman with an acutely swollen knee and a thin white line in the joint cartilage on radiograph
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 78-year-old woman admitted yesterday for management of community-acquired pneumonia, who has developed a painful swollen left knee overnight. She is on day two of intravenous benzylpenicillin and is improving from a respiratory point of view.

She has had no previous joint problems, no recent injury and no prosthetic joints. She takes no anticoagulant. On examination she is alert with a temperature of 37.8 degrees. The left knee is warm, swollen with a demonstrable effusion, and painful through the last 20 degrees of flexion, though she can straight leg raise. There is no overlying skin break, no rash and no other joint involvement. A plain radiograph of the knee shows a fine linear opacity within the meniscal cartilage and within the hyaline cartilage of both femoral condyles, with moderate joint space narrowing. C reactive protein is 88 mg/L (less than 5), white cell count 12.8 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0) and serum urate is 0.28 mmol/L (0.15 to 0.40).

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 128/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, SpO2 95 per cent on room air, temperature 37.8 degrees
data_table.Examination: Warm swollen left knee with demonstrable effusion, painful terminal flexion, able to straight leg raise, no skin break or rash
data_table.Imaging: Knee radiograph showing linear calcification within the meniscal and hyaline cartilage with moderate joint space narrowing
data_table.Investigations: C reactive protein 88 mg/L (less than 5), white cell count 12.8 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0), serum urate 0.28 mmol/L (0.15 to 0.40)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence oral colchicine at a reduced dose and reassess the knee again in forty eight hours
options.rationale: Colchicine is used for crystal arthritis including calcium pyrophosphate disease and would be reasonable once infection has been excluded. Her normal serum urate does not exclude gout during an attack either, and neither crystal has yet been demonstrated. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the knee to assess for osteomyelitis and a joint effusion
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance imaging is sensitive for bone marrow oedema and is useful when osteomyelitis is suspected or a joint cannot be accessed. It cannot distinguish crystal from infection in synovial fluid, which is the actual question, and it delays the answer by a day. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Septic arthritis)

options.text: Inject the joint with corticosteroid after confirming the radiographic calcification is present
options.rationale: Intra-articular corticosteroid is an excellent treatment for an acute calcium pyrophosphate flare in a single large joint and is what she is likely to need. Injecting steroid into an undiagnosed effusion in a febrile patient risks converting a treatable infection into a destroyed joint. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

options.text: Aspirate the joint and send fluid for cell count, Gram stain, culture and crystal examination
options.rationale: Cartilage calcification makes calcium pyrophosphate arthritis likely but never excludes infection, and a febrile inpatient with a hot joint and a raised C reactive protein must have septic arthritis ruled out. Aspiration answers both questions from one sample and must precede any treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

options.text: Broaden the antibiotic cover to intravenous flucloxacillin and arrange orthopaedic review today
options.rationale: Empirical antistaphylococcal cover is appropriate once septic arthritis is genuinely suspected, but treating before aspiration substantially reduces the yield of synovial culture. The organism is what determines the duration and the route of therapy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease produces chondrocalcinosis, the linear calcification of hyaline and fibrocartilage seen on plain films, and its acute inflammatory form was traditionally called pseudogout. The crucial management point is that radiographic chondrocalcinosis is common in the elderly and its presence never excludes septic arthritis, which in a native joint destroys cartilage within days and carries substantial mortality. Synovial fluid analysis is therefore mandatory, and a single aspirate gives the cell count, the Gram stain and culture, and the polarised light examination that identifies positively birefringent rhomboid crystals of calcium pyrophosphate or negatively birefringent needles of monosodium urate. Crystals and infection can coexist, so a positive crystal result does not close the question if the fluid also looks purulent or the cell count is very high. Once infection is excluded, treatment is intra-articular corticosteroid for a single joint, or oral corticosteroid or colchicine where several joints are involved, and secondary causes including hyperparathyroidism, haemochromatosis and hypomagnesaemia are worth considering in younger patients.
key_points: Chondrocalcinosis is common in older people and never excludes septic arthritis.
Acute flares are often triggered by intercurrent illness, surgery or trauma.
One aspirate provides cell count, Gram stain, culture and crystal analysis.
Calcium pyrophosphate crystals are rhomboid and positively birefringent.
Aspirate before starting antibiotics to preserve the culture yield.
explanation.pearls: A synovial fluid white cell count above 50 x10^9 per litre with a neutrophil predominance points strongly to septic arthritis whatever crystals are also seen, and the two can genuinely coexist, so the crystal result never overrides a purulent aspirate.

subtopic_detail: shallow ulcer above the inner ankle with brown staining that improves when the leg is raised
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 69-year-old retired nurse with an ulcer on her left lower leg that has been present for four months. It aches by the end of the day and the ache eases when she puts her feet up on the lounge in the evening.

She stood for long shifts for thirty years and has varicose veins on both legs. She has hypertension and a body mass index of 31 kg per square metre, and she has never smoked and has no diabetes. On examination there is a shallow ulcer 4 cm across with a sloping edge and a granulating base just above the medial malleolus. The surrounding skin is brown stained with pitting oedema and firm inelastic skin over the lower third of the calf. The foot is warm and pink with normal capillary refill, and dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are both palpable. Monofilament sensation is intact at all sites. The ankle brachial pressure index is 1.0 on the affected side.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Shallow 4 cm ulcer with sloping edge and granulating base above the medial malleolus, haemosiderin staining, pitting oedema, lipodermatosclerosis
data_table.Vascular: Warm pink foot, normal capillary refill, palpable dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses, ankle brachial pressure index 1.0
data_table.Neurological: Monofilament sensation intact at all tested sites, no deformity or callus

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Apply a hydrocolloid dressing with weekly review and referral for vascular surgical assessment
options.rationale: Venous duplex assessment with a view to superficial venous intervention is worthwhile and reduces recurrence, so referral belongs in the plan. A dressing without compression does not heal a venous ulcer, and omitting compression is the single commonest reason these ulcers persist for years. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Clinical Practice Guideline for Prevention and Management of Venous Leg Ulcers)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Clinical Practice Guideline for Prevention and Management of Venous Leg Ulcers

options.text: Arrange urgent arterial duplex imaging and refer to vascular surgery for consideration of bypass
options.rationale: This is the pathway for an arterial ulcer, the near pair, which sits over the toes, heel or lateral malleolus with a punched out edge, a pale base, absent pulses and an ankle brachial index below 0.8. Palpable pulses and an index of 1.0 exclude significant arterial disease. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Clinical Practice Guideline for Prevention and Management of Venous Leg Ulcers)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Clinical Practice Guideline for Prevention and Management of Venous Leg Ulcers

options.text: Take a wound swab for culture and commence oral cefalexin pending the microbiology result
options.rationale: All chronic ulcers are colonised, so a positive swab reflects surface flora rather than infection and prompts unnecessary antibiotics. Treatment is reserved for clinical infection with spreading erythema, increasing pain, purulence or systemic features, none of which is present. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Apply graduated multilayer compression bandaging with a simple non adherent wound dressing
options.rationale: A shallow sloping edged ulcer in the gaiter area with haemosiderin staining and lipodermatosclerosis is venous, and an ankle brachial pressure index of 1.0 confirms that compression is safe. Graduated compression is the intervention that heals venous ulcers, and the dressing choice itself makes little difference. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Clinical Practice Guideline for Prevention and Management of Venous Leg Ulcers)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Clinical Practice Guideline for Prevention and Management of Venous Leg Ulcers

options.text: Refer to a podiatrist for pressure offloading footwear and daily inspection of both feet
options.rationale: Offloading is the cornerstone of neuropathic ulcer management, which occurs at pressure points on the plantar surface in a patient with sensory loss. Intact monofilament sensation and an ulcer in the gaiter area rather than under the foot point away from that mechanism. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Wound care)

explanation.summary: Venous leg ulceration results from sustained ambulatory venous hypertension, and around 70 per cent of leg ulcers in Australia are venous in origin. The characteristic picture is a shallow ulcer with a sloping irregular edge in the gaiter region, most often above the medial malleolus, surrounded by haemosiderin staining, varicose eczema and lipodermatosclerosis, with an aching leg that is relieved by elevation. Graduated multilayer compression delivering around 40 mmHg at the ankle is the treatment that heals these ulcers, and dressing selection has repeatedly been shown to matter far less than whether compression is applied. Measuring the ankle brachial pressure index before compression is mandatory, because applying compression to a limb with significant arterial disease can cause tissue necrosis; an index between 0.8 and 1.3 permits full compression, lower values require modified or no compression with vascular referral, and values above 1.3 suggest incompressible calcified vessels needing a toe pressure instead. Early endovenous ablation of superficial reflux speeds healing and reduces recurrence, and lifelong compression hosiery after healing is what prevents the ulcer coming back.
key_points: Shallow sloping edged gaiter area ulcer with haemosiderin staining and lipodermatosclerosis.
Measure the ankle brachial pressure index before applying any compression.
Graduated multilayer compression is the intervention that heals; the dressing matters little.
Swabs reflect colonisation; treat only clinically infected ulcers with antibiotics.
Ongoing compression hosiery after healing prevents recurrence.
explanation.pearls: An ankle brachial pressure index above 1.3 does not mean excellent arterial supply but incompressible calcified vessels, most often in diabetes or chronic kidney disease, and a toe brachial index below 0.7 is what confirms arterial disease in that situation.

sources.label: Australian and New Zealand Clinical Practice Guideline for Prevention and Management of Venous Leg Ulcers

subtopic_detail: thickened crumbling discolouration of several toenails in a man who wants treatment before a holiday
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 54-year-old man who is embarrassed about his toenails and wants them treated before a beach holiday. Over about three years the nails have become thickened, yellow brown and crumbly, and the first, third and fourth toenails on the right foot and the first on the left are affected.

He has no diabetes, no peripheral vascular symptoms and takes no regular medications. He plays squash twice a week and uses communal changing rooms. On examination the affected nails are thickened with subungual debris lifting the nail plate from the bed at the free edge, and the discolouration runs from the distal edge proximally. There is fine scaling in the fourth toe web spaces bilaterally. The unaffected nails are normal, there is no nail pitting, no oil drop sign and no skin plaques at the elbows, knees or scalp. Pedal pulses are palpable, the feet are warm and monofilament sensation is intact.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Four thickened yellow brown nails with distal subungual hyperkeratosis and onycholysis, fine interdigital scaling in the fourth web spaces
data_table.Negative findings: No nail pitting, no oil drop discolouration, no cutaneous psoriatic plaques, no nail fold inflammation
data_table.Vascular and neurological: Palpable pedal pulses, warm feet, intact monofilament sensation, no diabetes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Send nail clippings with subungual debris for microscopy and culture before prescribing
options.rationale: Only about half of dystrophic nails are fungal, and oral terbinafine is a months long course requiring liver monitoring, so laboratory confirmation is required before treatment. Clippings taken from the proximal edge of the affected area with subungual debris give the best yield. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

options.text: Refer to a dermatologist for a nail matrix biopsy to establish the underlying diagnosis
options.rationale: Nail biopsy is reserved for suspected melanoma of the nail unit or for dystrophy that remains unexplained after negative mycology. It is invasive and painful compared with a clipping that answers the question here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

options.text: Prescribe a potent topical corticosteroid under occlusion to the nail folds for eight weeks
options.rationale: Topical corticosteroid is directed at nail psoriasis, the near pair, which is distinguished by pitting, an oil drop discolouration through the nail plate, and cutaneous plaques elsewhere. Distal onycholysis with subungual debris and coexisting tinea pedis points to a dermatophyte instead. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

options.text: Prescribe an amorolfine nail lacquer applied weekly for twelve months with regular nail filing
options.rationale: Topical lacquer is a reasonable option for superficial or distal disease affecting a small number of nails without matrix involvement, and it avoids systemic exposure. Cure rates are low for thickened nails with substantial subungual hyperkeratosis, and the diagnosis is still unconfirmed. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Commence oral terbinafine for three months with liver function testing at baseline and six weeks
options.rationale: This is the correct regimen and the correct monitoring for confirmed dermatophyte toenail disease, so the treatment plan itself is sound. Committing him to three months of systemic therapy without mycological confirmation is what the guidance specifically advises against. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

explanation.summary: Onychomycosis accounts for roughly half of all nail dystrophy, with the remainder caused by psoriasis, trauma, lichen planus and, rarely, subungual melanoma. Dermatophytes, principally Trichophyton rubrum, cause most cases, and coexisting tinea pedis is a useful supporting clue since the nail is usually infected from the adjacent skin. Because the appearance is not reliable enough to commit a patient to months of systemic antifungal therapy with its hepatic monitoring and drug interactions, confirmation by microscopy and culture on nail clippings is recommended before treatment. Sampling technique matters: clippings should be taken as proximally as possible within the affected area together with subungual debris, since the distal nail plate often contains only non viable organisms. Oral terbinafine is first line for dermatophyte nail disease, given for six weeks for fingernails and three months for toenails, and cure is judged by the growth of healthy nail rather than by immediate appearance, which takes twelve to eighteen months for a great toenail.
key_points: Only about half of dystrophic nails are fungal, so confirm before systemic treatment.
Coexisting tinea pedis supports a dermatophyte source; pitting suggests psoriasis instead.
Sample proximally within the affected nail and include subungual debris.
Oral terbinafine runs six weeks for fingernails and three months for toenails.
A single dark longitudinal band with proximal nail fold pigment needs melanoma exclusion.
explanation.pearls: Warn the patient that the nail will not look normal at the end of treatment: a great toenail grows about 1 mm a month, so a visually acceptable result takes twelve to eighteen months after a three month course and the absence of immediate change is not treatment failure.

subtopic_detail: woman with central facial flushing and papules whose eyes are gritty with crusted lid margins
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 46-year-old woman with two years of facial redness that she has treated as sensitive skin. She flushes with red wine, hot drinks and stepping into a warm room, and over the past six months small red bumps have appeared across her cheeks and nose.

She has used a topical corticosteroid cream prescribed for eczema intermittently over the past year, which helps for a few days before the redness returns worse. She also mentions that her eyes have felt gritty and dry for months and that her eyelids are crusted in the mornings. On examination there is persistent erythema with telangiectasia across the cheeks, nose and chin, with scattered papules and pustules and no comedones. The eyelid margins are thickened and erythematous with crusting at the lash bases, and the conjunctivae are mildly injected. Visual acuity is 6/6 in each eye and the corneas are clear on fluorescein staining.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Persistent central facial erythema with telangiectasia, papules and pustules across cheeks, nose and chin, no comedones
data_table.Ocular: Thickened erythematous lid margins with crusting at the lash bases, mild conjunctival injection
data_table.Ocular assessment: Visual acuity 6/6 each eye, corneas clear on fluorescein staining, no photophobia or eye pain

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Commence topical benzoyl peroxide with adapalene applied each evening to the affected areas
options.rationale: This combination treats acne vulgaris, the near pair, which is distinguished by comedones, involvement of the back and chest, and a younger age of onset. Both agents are irritant on rosacea skin and typically worsen the erythema. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

options.text: Cease the topical corticosteroid and commence an oral tetracycline with lid hygiene measures
options.rationale: Papulopustular rosacea with blepharitis is ocular rosacea, and an oral tetracycline treats both the cutaneous and the ocular disease where topical therapy treats only the skin. Withdrawing the corticosteroid is essential because it drives a steroid induced rosacea like eruption and causes rebound on cessation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

options.text: Cease the topical corticosteroid and commence topical metronidazole gel applied twice daily
options.rationale: Topical metronidazole or ivermectin is appropriate first line treatment for mild to moderate papulopustular rosacea confined to the skin, and stopping the steroid is right. Topical therapy does not treat ocular involvement, which is what makes this case need systemic treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

options.text: Continue the topical corticosteroid and add an oral antihistamine for the flushing episodes
options.rationale: Antihistamines target histamine mediated flushing such as that of mastocytosis or an allergic reaction, and they do not help rosacea. Continuing the corticosteroid perpetuates the atrophy and telangiectasia that are worsening her appearance. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Refer for pulsed dye laser treatment of the telangiectasia and background facial erythema
options.rationale: Vascular laser is genuinely effective for fixed erythema and telangiectasia and has a place once inflammation is controlled. It does nothing for papules, pustules or blepharitis, which are the active problems now. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

explanation.summary: Rosacea is a chronic inflammatory facial dermatosis of the central face, characterised by flushing, persistent erythema, telangiectasia, and in the papulopustular subtype inflammatory papules and pustules without comedones. Ocular involvement occurs in around half of patients and can precede the skin disease, presenting as blepharitis with lid margin telangiectasia, meibomian gland dysfunction, a gritty foreign body sensation, recurrent chalazia and conjunctival injection. Oral tetracyclines are the treatment of choice when ocular disease is present, and their benefit is largely anti inflammatory rather than antibacterial, which is why subantimicrobial dosing also works. Topical corticosteroids must be stopped, since prolonged use produces a steroid induced rosacea like dermatitis with atrophy and rebound flaring. Trigger avoidance, daily sun protection and gentle non soap cleansing are part of every management plan, and persistent corneal involvement or visual symptoms require ophthalmology referral.
key_points: Absence of comedones separates rosacea from acne vulgaris.
Ocular rosacea affects around half of patients and can precede the skin disease.
Oral tetracyclines treat both cutaneous and ocular disease; topicals treat only the skin.
Topical corticosteroids cause a steroid induced rosacea and must be withdrawn.
Refer to ophthalmology for corneal involvement, photophobia or reduced acuity.
explanation.pearls: Doxycycline at 40 mg daily in a modified release form is as effective as 100 mg for rosacea while remaining below the antimicrobial threshold, which reduces both resistance pressure and the gastrointestinal and candidal adverse effects of full dose therapy.

subtopic_detail: recurrent hours long spinning with fluctuating low frequency hearing loss and ear fullness on one side
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 44-year-old woman with recurrent attacks of the room spinning. Over the past eight months she has had six episodes, each building over minutes, lasting three to four hours, and leaving her unsteady for a day afterwards. She vomits during them and has to lie still in a dark room.

She describes a sense of pressure and fullness in the left ear before and during each attack, with a low pitched roaring noise on that side, and says her hearing in that ear is muffled during an attack and improves between episodes. She has no headache with the attacks, no photophobia or visual aura, and no history of migraine. There is no positional trigger and the attacks come without warning. Between attacks her examination is normal with no nystagmus, normal gait and a negative head impulse test bilaterally. Weber lateralises to the right and Rinne is positive bilaterally. A pure tone audiogram taken last week shows a 35 decibel sensorineural loss at 250 and 500 Hz on the left with normal thresholds above 2000 Hz.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Attack pattern: Six episodes over eight months, each lasting three to four hours, with vomiting and no headache or visual aura
data_table.Otological: Left aural fullness and low pitched roaring tinnitus during attacks, fluctuating muffled hearing on the left
data_table.Examination: No spontaneous nystagmus between attacks, negative head impulse test bilaterally, Weber lateralises to the right, Rinne positive bilaterally
data_table.Audiometry: 35 decibel sensorineural loss at 250 and 500 Hz on the left with normal thresholds above 2000 Hz

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer for intratympanic gentamicin injection to ablate vestibular function on the affected side
options.rationale: Chemical ablation is an effective option but is reserved for disabling attacks that persist despite medical therapy, because it carries a risk of further hearing loss. Offering it before any first line treatment has been tried is disproportionate. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Meniere disease)

options.text: Advise dietary salt restriction and commence betahistine with referral for otological review
options.rationale: Episodic vertigo lasting twenty minutes to twelve hours with documented low frequency sensorineural loss, aural fullness and roaring tinnitus is Meniere disease. Salt restriction with betahistine and specialist audiological follow up is the standard Australian first line approach. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Commence propranolol as migraine prophylaxis and provide a headache and vertigo diary
options.rationale: Vestibular migraine is the commonest cause of recurrent spontaneous vertigo and is the central near pair, so prophylaxis is a reasonable reflex. It requires a history of migraine and migrainous features with the attacks, and it does not produce a documented low frequency hearing loss. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Commence a tapering course of oral prednisolone and refer for vestibular rehabilitation therapy
options.rationale: This is the treatment for vestibular neuritis, which causes a single prolonged attack over days with a positive head impulse test on the affected side and normal hearing. Recurrent discrete attacks with a normal head impulse test between them do not fit. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Perform the Epley particle repositioning manoeuvre and teach her the Brandt Daroff exercises
options.rationale: Repositioning treats benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, which gives seconds long positionally triggered spinning with a positive Dix Hallpike test and no auditory symptoms at all. Attacks lasting hours without a positional trigger are a different mechanism. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Meniere disease is thought to result from endolymphatic hydrops and is diagnosed on a clinical triad backed by audiometry: two or more spontaneous episodes of vertigo lasting twenty minutes to twelve hours, audiometrically documented low to mid frequency sensorineural hearing loss in the affected ear on at least one occasion, and fluctuating aural symptoms of hearing loss, tinnitus or fullness. The low frequency pattern of hearing loss is the feature that most reliably separates it from vestibular migraine, which is far commoner and produces episodic vertigo without any documented hearing loss but with migrainous features. Attack duration is the most useful single discriminator across the episodic vertigo syndromes: seconds for benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, twenty minutes to twelve hours for Meniere disease, and days for vestibular neuritis. First line management is salt restriction with attention to caffeine and alcohol, betahistine, and a diuretic in some protocols, with vestibular sedatives used only for acute attacks because they impair central compensation. Escalation for refractory disabling disease includes intratympanic corticosteroid, intratympanic gentamicin and surgical procedures, and progressive hearing loss is managed with amplification.
key_points: Attack duration of twenty minutes to twelve hours is the Meniere window.
Low to mid frequency sensorineural loss on audiometry is required for the diagnosis.
Vestibular migraine is commoner, needs migrainous features, and spares the audiogram.
Vestibular sedatives are for acute attacks only, as they impede central compensation.
Ablative treatment is reserved for disabling disease refractory to medical therapy.
explanation.pearls: The low frequency pattern of hearing loss is what makes Meniere disease unusual, because almost every other cause of sensorineural loss, including presbyacusis, noise exposure and acoustic neuroma, takes the high frequencies first.

subtopic_detail: daily itchy weals for five months resolving within a day each and no response to a standard antihistamine dose
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 34-year-old woman with itchy raised weals that have appeared almost every day for five months. Individual weals come up on the trunk and limbs, are intensely itchy, and fade completely within about twelve hours leaving no mark behind.

She has been taking cetirizine 10 mg once daily for three months with only partial benefit and is losing sleep. She has identified no food, drug or physical trigger, and the weals appear at rest as often as with exercise. She has had no lip, tongue or throat swelling, no abdominal pain and no breathing difficulty. She takes no other medications including no non-steroidal anti inflammatory drugs. On examination there are scattered pink weals of varying size on the trunk and thighs, each blanching on pressure, with no purpura, no residual pigmentation and no scaling. There is no wheeze, the joints are not swollen, and she is afebrile with no weight loss. Full blood examination, C reactive protein and thyroid function are within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Scattered blanching pink weals of varying size on trunk and thighs, no purpura, no residual pigmentation, no angioedema
data_table.Symptom pattern: Daily weals for five months, each individual lesion resolving within twelve hours without bruising
data_table.Investigations: Full blood examination, C reactive protein and thyroid function within normal limits
data_table.Current treatment: Cetirizine 10 mg once daily for three months with partial benefit

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Commence a maintenance course of oral prednisolone with review of the dose every month
options.rationale: Short corticosteroid courses are occasionally used for severe exacerbations lasting a few days, so steroids are not entirely absent from the algorithm. Maintenance corticosteroid for a condition lasting years produces predictable and serious harm and is explicitly discouraged. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Increase the cetirizine dose up to fourfold the standard dose and review her response
options.rationale: Chronic spontaneous urticaria is treated with a second generation antihistamine, and updosing to up to four times the standard dose before escalating further is the established next step. Around half of patients who fail the standard dose respond to updosing, which is far safer than the alternatives. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

options.text: Refer for omalizumab therapy after documenting her failure of standard antihistamine treatment
options.rationale: Omalizumab is highly effective and is the correct escalation, but Australian access requires documented failure of antihistamine at up to four times the standard dose. Referring before updosing means the step she most likely needs has not been tried. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

options.text: Arrange a punch biopsy of a fresh lesion to look for a leucocytoclastic vasculitic pattern
options.rationale: Biopsy is indicated for urticarial vasculitis, the near pair, which is suggested by individual weals lasting more than 24 hours, painful or burning rather than itchy lesions, and residual bruising or pigmentation. Her weals clear within twelve hours leaving normal skin. (Source: ASCIA: Chronic urticaria)

options.text: Arrange specific immunoglobulin E allergy testing to a panel of common foods and aeroallergens
options.rationale: Allergen testing is useful when the history points to a specific reproducible trigger with lesions appearing within an hour of exposure. Daily spontaneous weals over months are not allergic, and indiscriminate panel testing generates false positives that lead to unnecessary dietary restriction. (Source: ASCIA: Chronic urticaria)

explanation.summary: Chronic spontaneous urticaria is defined by weals, angioedema or both occurring for six weeks or longer without a consistent external trigger, and it affects around one per cent of the population with a strong female predominance. Most cases are autoimmune, mediated by immunoglobulin G autoantibodies against the high affinity immunoglobulin E receptor or against immunoglobulin E itself, and extensive allergy testing is therefore unhelpful and often misleading. The essential clinical discriminator is the life of an individual weal: a lesion that lasts under 24 hours and resolves without a mark is urticaria, while one that persists beyond 24 hours, burns rather than itches, or leaves bruising or pigmentation should be biopsied for urticarial vasculitis. The treatment ladder is a second generation antihistamine at standard dose, updosing to up to four times standard, then omalizumab, then ciclosporin, and maintenance oral corticosteroid has no place at any rung. Most cases remit spontaneously, around half within a year, which is a genuinely useful thing to tell a distressed patient.
key_points: Six weeks or more of weals without a consistent trigger defines the chronic spontaneous form.
Individual weals lasting under 24 hours without residual marks distinguish it from vasculitis.
Allergy testing is unhelpful because most cases are autoimmune rather than allergic.
Updose the second generation antihistamine to up to four times standard before escalating.
Maintenance oral corticosteroid is not part of the treatment ladder.
explanation.pearls: Ask the patient to circle a single weal with a pen and check it the next day, because a lesion still present at 24 hours or leaving pigmentation within the circle is the finding that turns an antihistamine prescription into a skin biopsy for urticarial vasculitis.

subtopic_detail: distinguishing a post enteric inflammatory arthritis from septic arthritis when the synovial white cell count is raised
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 27-year-old man in the emergency department. Three weeks ago he had five days of profuse watery diarrhoea after a camping trip with friends, which settled without treatment. For the past five days his right knee has been swollen and painful and his left ankle has become sore, and this morning he could not put his heel to the ground.

He also describes both eyes being red and gritty for a week and pain where the back of his heel meets the bone. He injects no drugs, has no skin breaks and no indwelling lines. You aspirate the knee at the bedside and send the fluid urgently. The aspirate results return while he is still in the department.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84, blood pressure 124/76, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99 per cent in air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Right knee effusion with full but painful flexion, left ankle swollen, tenderness at the Achilles insertion, bilateral conjunctival injection
data_table.Investigations: Synovial fluid white cells 18 x10^9/L, Gram stain shows no organisms, no crystals seen under polarised light, C reactive protein 62 mg/L (less than 5), white cell count 9.8 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: High dose oral naproxen with review of the joints in two weeks
options.rationale: An asymmetrical lower limb oligoarthritis with enthesitis and conjunctivitis following a dysenteric illness is treated first with a full dose non-steroidal anti inflammatory drug, which controls symptoms in most patients while the self-limiting course runs. Culture negative fluid without crystals supports a reactive rather than infective process. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

options.text: Arthroscopic washout with intravenous flucloxacillin for fourteen days
options.rationale: A synovial white cell count of 18 x10^9/L sits well below the range that usually accompanies pyogenic infection, and with no fever, a negative Gram stain and no portal of entry the pretest probability of a septic joint is low. This option would be correct if he were febrile with a synovial count above 50 x10^9/L or if the Gram stain were positive. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Oral doxycycline for three months to treat the triggering infection
options.rationale: Prolonged antibiotics have a possible role only where a genital chlamydial trigger is identified, and even then the evidence is contested. His trigger was enteric rather than urogenital, and antibiotics do not alter the course of the enteric form. (Source: Australian STI Management Guidelines)

options.text: Oral prednisolone 50 mg daily tapered over four weeks from today
options.rationale: Systemic corticosteroid is reserved for polyarticular or refractory disease after a non-steroidal anti inflammatory drug has been given an adequate trial. Starting it now commits him to a taper before the natural history has been observed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

options.text: Weekly oral methotrexate with folic acid as initial disease control
options.rationale: A disease modifying agent is considered only when symptoms persist beyond about three to six months or the course becomes chronic and erosive. Reaching for it in the first week treats a condition that most often remits on its own. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association)

explanation.summary: An asymmetrical lower limb oligoarthritis appearing one to four weeks after an enteric or urogenital infection sits within the seronegative spondyloarthritis family, and enthesitis, dactylitis, conjunctivitis and mucocutaneous lesions are the extra articular clues that separate it from an isolated septic joint. Joint aspiration remains mandatory in any acute monoarthritis because the consequences of a missed infection are severe, but the fluid interpretation is what steers management rather than the decision to aspirate. Synovial counts above 50 x10^9/L with a neutrophil predominance point to infection, while counts in the 5 to 30 x10^9/L band with negative culture fit an inflammatory process. Most cases settle within three to six months, and HLA B27 positivity predicts a more protracted course rather than confirming the diagnosis. Persistent disease beyond six months warrants a disease modifying agent and rheumatology involvement.
key_points: Aspirate every acute monoarthritis, but read the count rather than assuming infection
Enthesitis at the Achilles insertion and conjunctivitis point away from a pyogenic joint
Full dose non-steroidal anti inflammatory therapy is the first line treatment
Antibiotics do not shorten the post enteric form of the illness
Escalate to a disease modifying agent only if disease persists beyond three to six months
explanation.pearls: A synovial white cell count between 5 and 30 x10^9/L with a negative Gram stain and no crystals is the band where an inflammatory arthritis is far more likely than infection; above 50 x10^9/L treat as septic until culture proves otherwise.

subtopic_detail: first line medical therapy for a pituitary macroadenoma causing chiasmal compression
stem:
You are the endocrinology registrar seeing a 34-year-old woman referred by her general practitioner. Her periods stopped eight months ago and she has noticed a milky discharge from both breasts when she showers. Over the past two months she has twice walked into the left hand door frame of her kitchen.

She takes no regular medicines, has never taken an antipsychotic or metoclopramide, and a urinary pregnancy test in the clinic is negative. Formal perimetry shows loss in both upper outer quadrants. Her results and imaging are available at the consultation.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Bitemporal upper quadrant field loss on confrontation and on formal perimetry, visual acuity 6/6 bilaterally, no ophthalmoplegia
data_table.Investigations: Prolactin 9800 mIU/L (less than 500), thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, free thyroxine within normal limits, creatinine within normal limits
data_table.Imaging: Magnetic resonance imaging shows an 18 mm pituitary adenoma with suprasellar extension abutting and elevating the optic chiasm

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Urgent transsphenoidal surgical decompression of the pituitary lesion
options.rationale: Surgery is the first line approach for most other pituitary macroadenomas causing chiasmal compression, which is exactly why this option is tempting, but the lactotroph tumour is the exception because it shrinks reliably on medical therapy. Surgery is reserved for dopamine agonist resistance, intolerance, or apoplexy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Oral cabergoline twice weekly with visual fields repeated at six weeks
options.rationale: A dopamine agonist normalises prolactin and shrinks tumour volume in the large majority of these adenomas, with field improvement often evident within weeks, so it is first line even when the chiasm is already compressed. Cabergoline is preferred over bromocriptine for efficacy and tolerability. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Stereotactic radiotherapy to the pituitary with endocrine follow up
options.rationale: Radiotherapy works slowly over years and carries a high rate of subsequent hypopituitarism, so it has no role as initial treatment when vision is threatened now. It is a third line option after both medical and surgical therapy have failed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Combined oral contraceptive alone with repeat imaging in six months
options.rationale: Replacing oestrogen treats the consequence of the hypogonadism but does nothing to the tumour, and leaving an adenoma that is already lifting the chiasm for six months risks permanent field loss. Oestrogen replacement is appropriate only once the tumour is controlled. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Observation with repeat prolactin and pituitary imaging in six months
options.rationale: Watchful waiting is reasonable for a small intrasellar lesion with normal fields, not for a lesion that has already produced a bitemporal defect. The field loss is the indication to treat now. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia)

explanation.summary: Prolactin secreting adenomas are the commonest functioning pituitary tumour and are unique among them in responding to medical therapy well enough that drugs displace surgery as first line, even for large lesions compressing the chiasm. Before accepting the diagnosis the treating doctor must exclude the common secondary causes of a raised prolactin, principally dopamine antagonist drugs, pregnancy, primary hypothyroidism and renal failure, because these produce modest elevations that do not need imaging. The height of the prolactin helps: levels above about 5000 mIU/L are almost always tumoural, whereas a mild rise alongside a large adenoma suggests stalk compression by a non lactotroph mass, a distinction that changes management entirely. Field defects typically improve within weeks of starting a dopamine agonist and perimetry is the practical early measure of response. Long term issues include the need to monitor for impulse control disorders on dopamine agonists and consideration of cardiac valve surveillance at higher cumulative doses.
key_points: Exclude drugs, pregnancy, hypothyroidism and renal failure before attributing a raised prolactin to a tumour
Levels above about 5000 mIU/L with a macroadenoma indicate a lactotroph tumour rather than stalk effect
A dopamine agonist is first line even with chiasmal compression, unlike other pituitary macroadenomas
Repeat perimetry at about six weeks is the practical early marker of response
Reserve surgery for resistance, intolerance or apoplexy
explanation.pearls: A prolactin of only 1000 to 2000 mIU/L alongside a large pituitary mass argues against a prolactinoma and for stalk compression by a non secreting tumour, which will not shrink on cabergoline and needs surgery instead.

subtopic_detail: acting on a frailty assessment rather than chronological age before major elective surgery
stem:
You are the registrar in the pre admission clinic assessing an 82-year-old woman listed for elective open repair of a 6.1 cm abdominal aortic aneurysm. The vascular surgeon has asked for a medical opinion on her fitness.

She lives alone in a unit and uses a four wheeled frame indoors. Her daughter does her shopping and manages her medicines in a dose administration aid, and she has stopped going to her weekly card group because she tires. She has lost 6 kg over the past year without trying. She tells you she wants to do whatever will let her stay in her own home. Her cardiac and respiratory examination is unremarkable and her recent bloods are unremarkable.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Timed up and go test 22 seconds, grip strength reduced, no murmurs, chest clear
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 118 g/L (115 to 165), creatinine within normal limits, albumin 31 g/L (35 to 50), electrocardiogram sinus rhythm
data_table.Functional assessment: Clinical Frailty Scale score 6, requires assistance with shopping and medicines, independent with personal care

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Proceed to surgery as listed since age alone does not preclude repair
options.rationale: The principle is correct but it is being applied to the wrong variable. The concern here is not her age but a Clinical Frailty Scale score of 6 with unintentional weight loss and a slow timed up and go, all of which independently predict postoperative mortality and loss of independence. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Society for Geriatric Medicine)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Society for Geriatric Medicine

options.text: Cancel the operation and refer to the palliative care service instead
options.rationale: A frailty score of 6 raises operative risk substantially but does not make repair futile, and a 6.1 cm aneurysm carries a real rupture risk if left. Withdrawing the surgical option outright forecloses a decision that has not yet been properly informed. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Society for Vascular Surgery)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Society for Vascular Surgery

options.text: Refer for comprehensive geriatric assessment before the operation is listed
options.rationale: Structured multidimensional assessment with targeted optimisation of nutrition, function, medicines and cognition reduces postoperative complications and length of stay in frail surgical patients, and it generates the risk information she needs to weigh repair against her stated goal of remaining at home. It also frames the endovascular alternative properly. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Society for Geriatric Medicine)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Society for Geriatric Medicine

options.text: Arrange dobutamine stress echocardiography before making any decision
options.rationale: Functional cardiac testing is indicated when there are active cardiac symptoms or poor exercise tolerance of cardiac origin, neither of which is present. Ordering it here adds delay and answers a question that is not the one limiting her. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.text: Start oral nutritional supplements and re-review in the clinic in six weeks
options.rationale: Addressing the low albumin and weight loss is a legitimate part of prehabilitation, but delivering it as an isolated intervention without assessing function, cognition, medicines and goals leaves most of the modifiable risk untouched. It is one component of the fuller assessment rather than a substitute for it. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Society for Geriatric Medicine)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Society for Geriatric Medicine

explanation.summary: Frailty is a state of reduced physiological reserve that predicts adverse surgical outcomes far better than age or than any single organ based risk score, and it is now routinely assessed before major elective surgery in Australian practice. The Clinical Frailty Scale grades from 1 for very fit to 9 for terminally ill, with 5 and above denoting increasing degrees of frailty and 6 indicating dependence for all outside activities and some personal care. Comprehensive geriatric assessment examines medical, functional, cognitive, nutritional, medication and social domains together and pairs the findings with a targeted intervention plan, and randomised evidence in older surgical and orthopaedic populations shows reductions in delirium, complications and length of stay. The assessment also surfaces what matters to the patient, which is decisive when the choice is between an intervention that prevents a future rupture and one that preserves current independence. For aortic disease specifically, the assessment output often reframes the discussion toward an endovascular approach with a shorter recovery.
key_points: Frailty predicts postoperative outcome better than chronological age
Clinical Frailty Scale 5 and above signals frailty, with 6 indicating dependence for outside activities
Comprehensive geriatric assessment reduces delirium, complications and length of stay in frail surgical patients
Unintentional weight loss, slow gait speed and weak grip are individually prognostic
Assessment output should be tied to the patient's own stated goals
explanation.pearls: A timed up and go of more than 15 seconds before major elective surgery predicts a markedly increased rate of postoperative complications and one year mortality, and is a two minute bedside test that outperforms most preoperative bloods.

sources.label: Australian and New Zealand Society for Geriatric Medicine
Australian and New Zealand Society for Vascular Surgery
Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand

subtopic_detail: prioritising which medicine to withdraw first after recurrent falls when there is no postural drop
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar reviewing a 79-year-old man admitted after his second fall in six weeks. Both falls happened at home in the early hours when he got up to pass urine. He did not lose consciousness on either occasion and remembers hitting the floor.

His daughter has brought in his dose administration aid. He takes perindopril, amlodipine, temazepam nightly which he has taken for about six years, sertraline, aspirin, atorvastatin, metformin, pantoprazole, docusate and regular paracetamol. He drinks no alcohol. Lying and standing blood pressures have been recorded on the ward over two days.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72, blood pressure 138/78, respiratory rate 15, SpO2 97 per cent in air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Timed up and go 18 seconds, no postural drop on repeated lying and standing measurement, no focal neurological deficit, mini mental state examination 28 out of 30
data_table.Investigations: Electrocardiogram sinus rhythm with normal intervals, 24 hour Holter monitor shows no pauses or arrhythmia, creatinine within normal limits, vitamin B12 and thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: Which single medication change is the highest priority?

options.text: Stop pantoprazole, which has had no documented indication for six years
options.rationale: Indefinite proton pump inhibitor therapy without indication is worth unwinding and carries its own risks including fracture and hypomagnesaemia, but those act over years rather than explaining two falls in six weeks. It ranks below the sedative on urgency. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

options.text: Stop amlodipine and review the blood pressure in the clinic in two weeks
options.rationale: Withdrawing an antihypertensive is the reflex answer in a faller, but the lying and standing measurements were repeated and show no postural drop, which removes the mechanism this change would address. It would be correct if he had a symptomatic drop of 20 mmHg systolic or 10 mmHg diastolic on standing. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Stop atorvastatin given his age and the absence of vascular disease
options.rationale: Reviewing a statin for ongoing benefit is a reasonable part of a broader medication review, but statins do not cause falls and stopping one changes nothing about tonight's risk. Deprescribing is prioritised by harm, and this drug is not the one causing harm. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Wean and cease the nightly temazepam over the next four to eight weeks
options.rationale: Long term benzodiazepine use is among the strongest modifiable medication risks for falls and hip fracture in older people, and the nocturnal timing of both falls fits residual sedation on rising. Abrupt cessation after six years risks withdrawal, so a structured taper is the correct method. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Stop aspirin as primary prevention and review in the clinic in two weeks
options.rationale: Aspirin for primary prevention in this age group has an unfavourable balance of bleeding against benefit and is a fair target for review, particularly in someone who is falling. It reduces the consequence of a fall rather than the chance of one, so it is second order here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

explanation.summary: Medication review after a fall is most useful when it is prioritised rather than exhaustive, and the drug classes with the strongest causal link to falls are benzodiazepines and Z drugs, antipsychotics, antidepressants, opioids and anticholinergics, collectively described as fall risk increasing drugs. Orthostatic hypotension is the other major reversible contributor, but it must be demonstrated rather than assumed, because withdrawing antihypertensives from an older person who does not have a postural drop exposes them to cardiovascular risk for no fall benefit. Benzodiazepine withdrawal after years of use requires a gradual taper, typically reducing by about an eighth to a quarter of the dose every one to two weeks with slower steps at the end, and it is helped by explaining that the drug has long since stopped improving sleep architecture. A structured falls assessment should run in parallel, covering vision, footwear, home hazards, vitamin D and strength and balance exercise. Sertraline is also a fall risk increasing drug and is a legitimate second target once the sedative is addressed.
key_points: Benzodiazepines, Z drugs, antipsychotics, antidepressants, opioids and anticholinergics are the main fall risk increasing drugs
Demonstrate orthostatic hypotension before withdrawing antihypertensives in a faller
Taper long term benzodiazepines rather than ceasing abruptly
Prioritise deprescribing by the harm actually operating, not by list length
Run a structured falls assessment covering vision, footwear, home hazards and exercise alongside the medication change
explanation.pearls: Orthostatic hypotension is defined as a fall of 20 mmHg systolic or 10 mmHg diastolic within three minutes of standing; without that measured drop, stopping an antihypertensive after a fall treats a mechanism that has not been shown to exist.

subtopic_detail: changing opioid and route when the oral route fails and renal function is deteriorating at the end of life
stem:
You are the registrar on the community palliative care service visiting a 68-year-old woman with metastatic pancreatic cancer at home. Her pain has been well controlled on modified release oral morphine 60 mg twice daily for the past two months.

Over the past three days she has vomited after most doses and has not reliably kept a tablet down. Her husband says she has become much drowsier and that her hands and arms twitch in short jerks when she dozes, which is new. Bloods were taken yesterday by the visiting nurse. She wishes to remain at home and a subcutaneous syringe driver is available through the service.
