data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96, blood pressure 104/64, respiratory rate 12, SpO2 95 per cent in air, temperature 36.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Rousable to voice, multifocal myoclonic jerks of the upper limbs, pinpoint pupils, abdomen soft with hepatomegaly
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 218 micromol/L (60 to 110), estimated glomerular filtration rate 22 mL/min/1.73m2 (greater than 60), corrected calcium within normal limits, sodium within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her analgesia?

options.text: Convert to a continuous subcutaneous morphine infusion at the same daily dose
options.rationale: Changing route solves the vomiting but keeps the drug whose active metabolites are accumulating. Morphine 6 glucuronide is renally cleared and is the direct cause of the myoclonus and sedation, so this option would relieve one problem while worsening the other. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Palliative Care)

options.text: Increase the oral morphine dose and add regular oral metoclopramide
options.rationale: Drowsiness with myoclonus and pinpoint pupils indicates too much opioid effect rather than too little, so increasing the dose accelerates the toxicity. Her pain was controlled until the route failed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Palliative Care)

options.text: Apply a transdermal fentanyl patch today and stop all other opioid therapy
options.rationale: Fentanyl is metabolically a sound choice in renal impairment, so the drug is not the error here. The patch takes twelve to twenty four hours to reach useful concentrations and cannot be titrated quickly, which makes it unsuitable when pain control must be maintained from today and the clinical situation is changing. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Continue oral morphine and add subcutaneous haloperidol for the vomiting
options.rationale: An antiemetic is appropriate alongside whatever opioid is chosen, but she is not absorbing the tablets, so continuing the oral route leaves her analgesia unreliable. It also leaves the accumulating metabolite in place. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Palliative Care)

options.text: Convert to a continuous subcutaneous hydromorphone infusion at a reduced dose
options.rationale: Hydromorphone has a far smaller burden of renally cleared active metabolite than morphine, which makes it the preferred switch when the estimated glomerular filtration rate falls and neurotoxicity has appeared. The dose is reduced below strict equianalgesic calculation because cross tolerance between opioids is incomplete. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Palliative Care)

explanation.summary: Opioid rotation is prompted either by inadequate analgesia despite titration or, as here, by dose limiting toxicity, and declining renal function at the end of life is the commonest trigger in practice. Morphine is metabolised to morphine 3 glucuronide and morphine 6 glucuronide, both renally cleared, and their accumulation produces the recognisable picture of increasing sedation, multifocal myoclonus, pinpoint pupils and sometimes hyperalgesia or delirium. Hydromorphone and fentanyl carry a much lighter metabolite load and are the preferred agents once the estimated glomerular filtration rate falls below about 30 mL/min/1.73m2. Because cross tolerance between opioids is incomplete, the calculated equianalgesic dose is reduced, conventionally by around a quarter to a half, with breakthrough doses written and the patient reviewed within twenty four hours. A continuous subcutaneous infusion through a syringe driver is the standard way to deliver this at home when swallowing fails, and it allows antiemetic and anxiolytic to be combined in the same device.
key_points: Renally cleared morphine metabolites cause sedation, multifocal myoclonus and pinpoint pupils
Switch to hydromorphone or fentanyl when the estimated glomerular filtration rate falls below about 30 mL/min/1.73m2
Reduce the calculated equianalgesic dose because cross tolerance between opioids is incomplete
A subcutaneous syringe driver maintains analgesia when the oral route fails at home
Rising sedation with myoclonus signals opioid excess, not undertreated pain
explanation.pearls: New multifocal myoclonus in a patient stable on morphine is opioid neurotoxicity from metabolite accumulation until proven otherwise, and it should trigger a check of renal function and a switch of opioid rather than a dose increase.

subtopic_detail: choosing the starting corticosteroid dose for girdle pain when cranial arteritis features are absent
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 71-year-old woman with six weeks of aching and stiffness across both shoulders and both hips. She is worst on waking and says it takes about two hours before she can move freely. She has been unable to lift her arms high enough to brush her own hair or to reach a shelf above her head.

She has taken atorvastatin for three years without previous problems. She has no jaw pain on chewing, no scalp tenderness and no visual symptoms, and her temporal arteries are not tender or thickened. There is no swelling of the small joints of her hands.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Painful restriction of active shoulder and hip abduction with full passive range, no synovitis of the hands or wrists, temporal arteries non-tender with normal pulsation
data_table.Investigations: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate 68 mm/h (less than 30), C reactive protein 54 mg/L (less than 5), creatine kinase within normal limits, rheumatoid factor negative, anti cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody negative, thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Commence prednisolone 15 mg daily and review the response in one week
options.rationale: Bilateral girdle pain with prolonged morning stiffness, raised inflammatory markers and normal muscle enzymes in this age group is treated with low dose corticosteroid, and a dose in the 12.5 to 25 mg range is the accepted starting point. The dramatic response within days is itself part of the diagnostic assessment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

options.text: Cease atorvastatin and review the symptoms in the clinic in six weeks
options.rationale: Statin associated muscle symptoms would be a reasonable consideration, but a creatine kinase within normal limits alongside a markedly raised erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C reactive protein points away from a myopathy, since statin muscle injury does not raise inflammatory markers. Six weeks of observation also leaves her functionally disabled. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Commence prednisolone 50 mg daily and refer for temporal artery biopsy
options.rationale: High dose corticosteroid with urgent biopsy is the pathway when cranial arteritis is suspected, signalled by jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, temporal artery abnormality or any visual symptom. None of those is present, and this dose commits her to the toxicity of high dose steroid without the indication. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

options.text: Commence weekly methotrexate 10 mg with folic acid supplementation
options.rationale: Methotrexate is used as a steroid sparing agent for relapsing disease or where corticosteroid toxicity is a particular concern, not as initial monotherapy. It works too slowly to address her current disability. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association)

options.text: Commence regular naproxen 500 mg twice daily and refer to physiotherapy
options.rationale: Non-steroidal anti inflammatory drugs give only partial relief in this condition and carry gastrointestinal and renal risk in her age group. A failure to respond to them is sometimes what delays the correct diagnosis for months. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

explanation.summary: Girdle pain with prolonged morning stiffness and raised inflammatory markers in a patient over 50 is a clinical diagnosis supported by the exclusion of mimics rather than by any confirmatory test. The important mimics are inflammatory myopathy, which raises creatine kinase, late onset seronegative rheumatoid arthritis, which produces peripheral synovitis, hypothyroidism and statin myopathy, and each is addressed by a small targeted panel rather than a broad screen. The cardinal linked concern is cranial arteritis, which shares the underlying vasculopathy and occurs in a substantial minority, and any jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, temporal artery abnormality or visual disturbance mandates immediate high dose corticosteroid before biopsy because vision loss is irreversible. Treatment response is expected to be rapid and near complete within a few days, and a poor response should prompt reconsideration of the diagnosis rather than dose escalation. Tapering is slow over one to two years with bone protection and monitoring for steroid related harm.
key_points: Start at 12.5 to 25 mg prednisolone daily for isolated girdle disease
A creatine kinase within normal limits argues against statin myopathy and inflammatory myositis
Jaw claudication, scalp tenderness or visual symptoms demand high dose steroid immediately
A poor response within a week should prompt diagnostic review rather than dose escalation
Plan bone protection and a slow taper over one to two years
explanation.pearls: Expect near complete relief within three to five days of starting prednisolone 15 mg daily; failure to respond by one week is a diagnostic red flag that should send you back to myositis, malignancy or late onset seronegative rheumatoid arthritis rather than upward on the dose.

subtopic_detail: recognising sight threatening orbitopathy when the thyroid biochemistry has already been corrected
stem:
You are the medical registrar seeing a 46-year-old woman in the emergency department. She has been taking carbimazole for three months for hyperthyroidism and her most recent clinic bloods were reported as satisfactory.

For the past two weeks the vision in her right eye has been blurred, and this week she noticed that a red traffic light looks washed out and grey compared with how it appears through the left eye. She has forward protrusion of both eyes and cannot look up fully on the right. She is a current smoker of fifteen cigarettes daily.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Bilateral proptosis with lid retraction, restricted elevation of the right eye, right relative afferent pupillary defect, red desaturation in the right eye, corneas intact
data_table.Investigations: Visual acuity 6/18 right and 6/6 left, thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, free thyroxine within normal limits, free triiodothyronine within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Increase the carbimazole dose and review in the clinic in four weeks
options.rationale: Her thyroid function tests are already within normal limits, so there is no residual thyrotoxicosis to treat, and the orbitopathy runs a course partly independent of the biochemistry. Escalating the antithyroid drug risks hypothyroidism, which itself worsens eye disease. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Refer the same day for intravenous methylprednisolone under ophthalmology
options.rationale: Reduced acuity with a relative afferent pupillary defect and red desaturation indicates optic nerve compromise, which is the sight threatening form of the disease and a medical emergency. High dose intravenous corticosteroid is the immediate treatment, with orbital decompression if the response is inadequate within one to two weeks. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Prescribe lubricant eye drops and review in the clinic in six weeks
options.rationale: Ocular surface lubrication is the right supportive measure for mild disease with grittiness and exposure symptoms. It does nothing for compression of the optic nerve at the orbital apex, and a six week delay in that setting risks permanent loss. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Ophthalmologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Ophthalmologists

options.text: Refer for radioactive iodine ablation of the thyroid within two weeks
options.rationale: Radioiodine is relatively contraindicated while the orbitopathy is active because it can precipitate deterioration, and where it is unavoidable it is given under corticosteroid cover. Choosing it as the response to failing vision inverts the priority. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Refer for routine orbital radiotherapy at the next available appointment
options.rationale: Orbital radiotherapy has a place in moderate to severe active disease, usually in combination with corticosteroid, but its effect develops over weeks to months. A routine referral does not match the tempo of an optic neuropathy. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Ophthalmologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Ophthalmologists

explanation.summary: Thyroid associated orbitopathy is driven by autoantibody mediated inflammation of orbital fat and extraocular muscle and follows its own active then inactive course, which is why it can progress or first appear after the thyroid biochemistry has been normalised. Severity is graded by the impact on sight, and the two sight threatening manifestations are compressive optic neuropathy from apical muscle crowding and corneal breakdown from failure of lid closure. Reduced acuity, a relative afferent pupillary defect, impaired colour vision with red desaturation and optic disc swelling are the findings that define the emergency, and they must be sought explicitly because proptosis severity correlates poorly with nerve compromise. Smoking is the strongest modifiable risk factor for progression and for treatment failure, so cessation support is part of the management rather than an aside. Both hyperthyroidism and hypothyroidism worsen the eye disease, so restoring and maintaining euthyroidism matters even though it does not by itself treat the orbit.
key_points: Orbitopathy can progress after the thyroid biochemistry has normalised
Relative afferent pupillary defect and red desaturation define compressive optic neuropathy
High dose intravenous methylprednisolone is the immediate treatment, with decompression for non response
Smoking is the strongest modifiable driver of progression and treatment failure
Radioiodine can worsen active eye disease and needs corticosteroid cover if unavoidable
explanation.pearls: Loss of red colour saturation tested by asking the patient to compare a red object between the two eyes detects optic nerve compression in thyroid eye disease before visual acuity falls, and it takes about thirty seconds at the bedside.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Ophthalmologists

subtopic_detail: interpreting a normal random growth hormone in suspected somatotroph excess and choosing the screening test
stem:
You are the endocrinology registrar reviewing a 48-year-old man referred with a two year history of headaches and increasing daytime sleepiness. A sleep study last year showed obstructive sleep apnoea and he uses continuous positive airway pressure.

He tells you that his wedding ring had to be cut off last year and that he has gone up three shoe sizes since his thirties. He has noticed new gaps appearing between his lower teeth and his dentist has remarked on the change in his bite. He has bilateral hand tingling that wakes him at night. His referring doctor has already sent one blood test.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78, blood pressure 156/94, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 96 per cent in air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Coarse facial features with prominent supraorbital ridges, macroglossia, spade like hands, bilateral positive Tinel sign at the wrists, visual fields full to confrontation
data_table.Investigations: Random serum growth hormone 1.8 mIU/L, glycated haemoglobin 7.2 per cent (less than 6.0), fasting glucose 7.4 mmol/L (3.0 to 5.4), calcium within normal limits, prolactin within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Repeat the random serum growth hormone level on three separate mornings
options.rationale: Growth hormone is secreted in pulses with troughs that reach undetectable levels even in active disease, so a random value cannot exclude the condition however many times it is repeated. This is the reasoning trap that the single normal result sets. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Oral glucose tolerance test with serial growth hormone measurements
options.rationale: Failure of growth hormone to suppress after a glucose load is the confirmatory test, and it is the correct next step only once the screening result is raised or equivocal. Running it before the screening test reverses the established sequence and uses a more demanding test than the situation requires. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia)

options.text: Measure serum insulin like growth factor 1 against an age matched range
options.rationale: Insulin like growth factor 1 integrates growth hormone exposure over days and has a long half life, so it is stable across the day and is the screening test of choice. The result must be read against an age and sex matched reference range because normal values fall with age. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia)

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary fossa with contrast now
options.rationale: Imaging follows biochemical confirmation rather than preceding it, because incidental pituitary lesions are found in around one in ten adults and a scan done first cannot distinguish a functioning tumour from an incidentaloma. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Measure 24 hour urinary free cortisol on two separate collections
options.rationale: Cortisol excess can also produce hypertension, glucose intolerance and changed facial appearance, which makes it a reasonable differential to hold. It does not explain acral enlargement, increasing shoe size, dental separation or macroglossia, which are specific to growth hormone excess. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Somatotroph excess develops insidiously over years and the diagnosis is typically delayed by close to a decade, so the presenting complaints are usually its complications rather than the appearance itself. Obstructive sleep apnoea, carpal tunnel syndrome, hypertension, glucose intolerance, arthropathy and colonic polyps cluster together and should raise suspicion when they appear in combination in middle age. The biochemical pathway is fixed: insulin like growth factor 1 is the screening test because it reflects integrated secretion, a glucose load with serial growth hormone measurement is the confirmatory test, and pituitary imaging comes last to localise the source once the biochemistry is established. The excess mortality is largely cardiovascular and is reversed when the growth hormone axis is controlled, which is why finding the diagnosis matters even after years of slow change. Transsphenoidal surgery is first line treatment, with somatostatin analogues, dopamine agonists and growth hormone receptor antagonists for residual disease.
key_points: A normal random growth hormone never excludes somatotroph excess because secretion is pulsatile
Insulin like growth factor 1 read against an age matched range is the screening test
Growth hormone suppression after an oral glucose load is the confirmatory test
Image the pituitary only after the biochemistry is established
Sleep apnoea, carpal tunnel syndrome, hypertension and glucose intolerance cluster as presenting complications
explanation.pearls: Ask the patient whether their ring size or shoe size has changed in adulthood and whether gaps have appeared between the teeth; acral and jaw change over years is more discriminating than facial appearance, which the treating doctor and family both adapt to gradually.

subtopic_detail: interpreting a markedly raised ferritin when the transferrin saturation is normal
stem:
You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 52-year-old man who came in for a fatigue check. He works long hours, sleeps poorly and has gained weight steadily since his forties. His body mass index is 33 kg/m2 and his waist circumference is 112 cm.

He has type 2 diabetes managed on metformin. He drinks four standard drinks a week and has done so for years. There is no family history of liver disease and no arthralgia, and he has no skin pigmentation change. His initial blood results have come back and his general practice colleague has flagged the ferritin.

data_table.Vital signs: Blood pressure 146/90, remaining vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 33 kg/m2, waist circumference 112 cm, no hepatomegaly, no stigmata of chronic liver disease, no skin bronzing
data_table.Investigations: Ferritin 980 micrograms/L (30 to 300), transferrin saturation 31 per cent (15 to 45), alanine aminotransferase 78 U/L (less than 40), aspartate aminotransferase 52 U/L (less than 35), C reactive protein within normal limits, full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Send HFE genotyping for the C282Y and H63D variants before anything else
options.rationale: Genotyping is indicated when the transferrin saturation is persistently raised, conventionally above about 45 per cent, because saturation rather than ferritin is the marker of true iron loading. A saturation of 31 per cent makes hereditary iron overload very unlikely and a positive genotype here would more likely be an incidental carrier state than the explanation. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia)

options.text: Begin weekly therapeutic venesection and recheck the ferritin at ten weeks
options.rationale: Venesection treats established iron overload, which has not been demonstrated. Removing blood will lower the ferritin in almost anyone, so the falling number would falsely appear to confirm a diagnosis he does not have while the actual liver disease goes unaddressed. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia)

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging for hepatic iron quantification now
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance iron quantification is an accurate non-invasive measure and is the right test when iron overload is genuinely suspected but the biochemistry is ambiguous. Ordering it when the saturation is normal spends a scarce resource on a question the saturation has already answered. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Radiologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Radiologists

options.text: Arrange liver ultrasound with viral serology and fasting iron studies
options.rationale: Ferritin is an acute phase protein that rises with hepatic inflammation, adiposity, insulin resistance and alcohol, and with a normal saturation the raised value is far more likely to reflect one of these than iron loading. Imaging the liver, excluding viral hepatitis and repeating iron studies fasting addresses the probable causes and the transaminase rise together. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia)

options.text: Refer for percutaneous liver biopsy to quantify the hepatic iron index
options.rationale: Biopsy has largely been displaced by genotyping and magnetic resonance quantification for the assessment of iron, and it carries a small risk of significant bleeding. It may still have a role later for staging fibrosis, but it is not the step that follows this result. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia)

explanation.summary: A raised ferritin is one of the commonest abnormal results in Australian general practice and the great majority of raised values do not represent iron overload. Ferritin behaves as an acute phase reactant and rises with inflammation, infection, malignancy, alcohol use, hepatocellular injury and the insulin resistant state, so the result must always be read alongside the transferrin saturation, which is the marker that actually tracks body iron stores. Persistent saturation above about 45 per cent is the threshold that prompts HFE genotyping, whereas a normal saturation with a raised ferritin redirects the workup toward liver disease, alcohol and metabolic factors. Dysmetabolic iron overload syndrome describes the pattern of modestly raised ferritin with normal saturation in the setting of metabolic syndrome, and it is managed by treating the metabolic drivers rather than by venesection. Where transaminases are also raised, the assessment must proceed to imaging, viral serology and a fibrosis estimate, because the fibrosis stage is what determines prognosis.
key_points: Transferrin saturation, not ferritin, is the marker of true iron loading
Ferritin rises with inflammation, adiposity, insulin resistance, alcohol and hepatocyte injury
Genotype only when the saturation is persistently above about 45 per cent
Venesection lowers ferritin in anyone and can falsely appear to confirm the wrong diagnosis
A raised transaminase alongside a raised ferritin needs imaging, viral serology and fibrosis staging
explanation.pearls: Repeat iron studies fasting before acting on them, because transferrin saturation rises after a meal and after iron supplements and can push a normal result above the 45 per cent genotyping threshold on a non fasting sample.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Radiologists

subtopic_detail: post exercise facilitation and autonomic features distinguishing a presynaptic neuromuscular disorder from myasthenia
stem:
You are the neurology registrar assessing a 63-year-old man referred with four months of difficulty getting out of a low chair and climbing the stairs at home. He has smoked twenty cigarettes daily since he was twenty three.

He volunteers that his mouth has been persistently dry, that he has become constipated and that he has had difficulty with erections over the same period. He denies double vision and says his eyelids do not droop as the day goes on. On testing, his knee reflexes are absent, but after he holds a sustained quadriceps contraction for fifteen seconds they become obtainable, and his grip feels briefly stronger after repeated effort.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88, blood pressure 128/80 lying with a 14 mmHg systolic fall on standing, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 95 per cent in air, temperature 36.5 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Symmetrical proximal lower limb weakness, absent knee and ankle reflexes at rest which return after sustained contraction, no ptosis, no ophthalmoplegia, dry oral mucosa
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase within normal limits, full blood count within normal limits, electrolytes within normal limits, thyroid function within normal limits, chest radiograph reported as no focal abnormality

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Serum acetylcholine receptor antibodies with repetitive nerve stimulation
options.rationale: This pairing targets the postsynaptic disorder, in which fatigable ptosis and diplopia dominate, reflexes are preserved and strength worsens rather than improves with repeated effort. The two conditions are distinguished by the direction of the response to exercise, and here strength and reflexes both improve. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists

options.text: Nerve conduction studies with a lumbar puncture for oligoclonal bands
options.rationale: Oligoclonal bands support a central demyelinating process, which would give upper motor neuron signs rather than absent reflexes. Nerve conduction studies alone, without repetitive stimulation protocols, will not capture the presynaptic abnormality. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the whole spine with gadolinium contrast
options.rationale: A cord or cauda equina lesion could produce lower limb weakness with areflexia and bladder or bowel disturbance, which gives this option some surface plausibility. It would not produce dry mouth, would not improve with sustained contraction and would be expected to give sensory and sphincter findings that he does not have. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists

options.text: Creatine kinase with electromyography and a subsequent muscle biopsy
options.rationale: An inflammatory myopathy is a standard differential for subacute proximal weakness, but the creatine kinase is already within normal limits and a primary muscle disease does not explain the autonomic symptoms or the facilitation. Biopsy would subject him to a procedure that does not address the discriminating findings. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association)

options.text: Chest computed tomography with voltage gated calcium channel antibodies
options.rationale: Proximal weakness with autonomic features and post exercise facilitation of reflexes indicates a presynaptic defect of acetylcholine release, which in a heavy smoker of this age is paraneoplastic in around half of cases and most often driven by a small cell lung carcinoma. The tumour frequently precedes the neurological presentation and a plain radiograph is insufficiently sensitive to exclude it. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists

explanation.summary: Presynaptic failure of acetylcholine release produces a triad of proximal weakness, autonomic dysfunction and reduced or absent tendon reflexes, and the reflexes characteristically return after ten to fifteen seconds of sustained voluntary contraction because repeated activity increases calcium entry at the nerve terminal. This post exercise facilitation is the bedside finding that separates it from the postsynaptic disorder, where sustained effort worsens weakness. Around half of cases are paraneoplastic and the tumour is almost always small cell lung carcinoma, with the neurological syndrome preceding the cancer by months to years, so a normal chest radiograph does not close the question and computed tomography is required, with consideration of positron emission tomography and repeated surveillance over two years if the initial imaging is clear. Antibodies to the P and Q type voltage gated calcium channel are found in most patients and confirm the diagnosis. Treatment of the tumour often improves the neurology, with amifampridine used symptomatically alongside immunotherapy for the non paraneoplastic form.
key_points: Proximal weakness plus autonomic features plus areflexia is the presynaptic triad
Post exercise facilitation of reflexes is the discriminating bedside sign
Around half of cases are paraneoplastic, almost always small cell lung carcinoma
A normal chest radiograph does not exclude the tumour and computed tomography is required
Voltage gated calcium channel antibodies confirm the diagnosis
explanation.pearls: Test for post exercise facilitation by eliciting an absent reflex, having the patient sustain a maximal contraction of that muscle group for ten to fifteen seconds, then immediately re-testing; return of the reflex points to a presynaptic disorder and should trigger chest imaging for small cell lung cancer.

sources.label: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists

subtopic_detail: screening for the diabetes of cystic fibrosis when the glycated haemoglobin is within normal limits
stem:
You are the registrar in the adult cystic fibrosis clinic reviewing a 24-year-old woman at her routine appointment. Her forced expiratory volume in one second is 62 per cent predicted and she has been established on modulator therapy for two years.

She has lost 4 kg over the past four months. She takes her pancreatic enzyme replacement with every meal and snack and her dietitian confirms her adherence and her intake have not changed. She has needed two courses of intravenous antibiotics for exacerbations in the past six months, up from none in the preceding year. She has noticed she is thirstier than usual but has not changed her diet.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 19.1 kg/m2 down from 20.6 kg/m2 four months ago, scattered coarse crackles bilaterally, no clubbing change
data_table.Investigations: Glycated haemoglobin 5.9 per cent (less than 6.0), random plasma glucose 8.1 mmol/L (3.0 to 7.7), faecal elastase low consistent with known pancreatic insufficiency, liver function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Two hour 75 gram oral glucose tolerance test arranged in the next week
options.rationale: The oral glucose tolerance test is the standard annual screen from adolescence in this population and is the appropriate test now, because the characteristic early abnormality is postprandial hyperglycaemia with a preserved fasting glucose. Unexplained weight loss and a rising exacerbation frequency are the classic prompts to test outside the annual schedule. (Source: Cystic Fibrosis Australia)

options.text: Repeat the glycated haemoglobin in three months and review the weight
options.rationale: Glycated haemoglobin is unreliable in this population because shortened red cell survival from chronic inflammation and recurrent infection falsely lowers the result, so a value within normal limits does not exclude the diagnosis. Repeating an insensitive test after a further three months of weight loss compounds the delay. (Source: Cystic Fibrosis Australia)

options.text: Fasting plasma glucose on two separate mornings in the coming fortnight
options.rationale: The fasting glucose remains within normal limits until relatively late in this condition because residual insulin secretion covers the basal state while failing to cover meals. Relying on it misses the window in which treatment protects lung function and weight. (Source: Australian Diabetes Society)

options.text: Two weeks of continuous glucose monitoring with a clinic review after
options.rationale: Continuous monitoring detects postprandial excursions sensitively and is increasingly used in this group, which makes it a genuine near miss. It has not replaced the glucose tolerance test as the diagnostic standard, and the diagnostic thresholds that direct insulin therapy are defined against the tolerance test. (Source: Australian Diabetes Society)

options.text: Random plasma glucose with urinary ketones at the next clinic review
options.rationale: A random glucose lacks the sensitivity to establish the diagnosis and ketosis is characteristically absent in this form of diabetes because insulin deficiency is partial rather than complete. A negative result would provide false reassurance. (Source: Australian Diabetes Society)

explanation.summary: Cystic fibrosis related diabetes arises from progressive destruction of the pancreatic islets by the same fibrotic process that causes exocrine insufficiency, and it affects a substantial proportion of adults with the condition, with prevalence rising steeply with age. It sits apart from both type 1 and type 2 diabetes: insulin deficiency is partial so ketoacidosis is rare, insulin resistance fluctuates with infection and corticosteroid use, and the earliest abnormality is postprandial rather than fasting hyperglycaemia. Its clinical importance is that unexplained weight loss, a decline in lung function and increasing exacerbation frequency precede the diagnosis by up to several years, and these outcomes improve with insulin therapy, which is the treatment of choice rather than oral agents. Annual screening with an oral glucose tolerance test from about ten years of age is standard, with additional testing whenever there is unexplained decline. Glycated haemoglobin is specifically not recommended as the screening test because red cell turnover in this population makes it falsely reassuring.
key_points: Glycated haemoglobin is unreliable in cystic fibrosis because of shortened red cell survival
The oral glucose tolerance test is the annual screen and the diagnostic standard
Postprandial hyperglycaemia precedes any fasting abnormality
Unexplained weight loss, falling lung function and more frequent exacerbations are the clinical prompts
Insulin, not an oral agent, is the treatment of choice
explanation.pearls: In cystic fibrosis related diabetes the decline in weight and forced expiratory volume in one second begins two to four years before the glucose tolerance test becomes diagnostic, so an unexplained fall in either is itself the indication to test regardless of the annual schedule.

subtopic_detail: new mononeuritis multiplex with marked eosinophilia in a patient carrying an asthma label
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 44-year-old man in the emergency department. He has carried a diagnosis of asthma for six years, takes a high dose inhaled corticosteroid with a long-acting beta agonist, and has had nasal polyps removed twice.

Three weeks ago he developed a right foot drop that has not improved, and over the past week the ring and little fingers of his left hand have become numb and weak. He has a non blanching purple rash over both shins. He has not travelled overseas and has not started any new medication in the past year. His bloods and chest film are back.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96, blood pressure 138/84, respiratory rate 20, SpO2 94 per cent in air, temperature 37.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Right foot drop with weak ankle dorsiflexion, sensory loss in the left ulnar distribution with weak finger abduction, palpable purpura over both shins, expiratory wheeze
data_table.Investigations: Eosinophils 4.8 x10^9/L (0.0 to 0.5), white cell count 14.2 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0), C reactive protein 66 mg/L (less than 5), creatinine within normal limits, urinalysis within normal limits, troponin mildly raised
data_table.Imaging: Chest radiograph shows patchy bilateral migratory infiltrates

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Escalate the inhaled therapy and add a monoclonal anti interleukin 5 agent
options.rationale: Treating this as refractory eosinophilic asthma addresses the wheeze while leaving a vasculitis to infarct further nerves and myocardium. Biologic therapy targeting interleukin 5 does have a role in this condition, but as a steroid sparing agent after remission is induced, not as the acute response to progressive nerve and cardiac involvement. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association)

options.text: Commence high dose oral corticosteroid today with urgent specialist referral
options.rationale: Late onset asthma with nasal polyps, marked eosinophilia, palpable purpura and mononeuritis multiplex constitutes an eosinophilic small vessel vasculitis with active neurological and probable cardiac involvement, which is an indication for immediate corticosteroid while specialist assessment and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody testing proceed. Cardiac involvement is the leading cause of death in this condition and drives the urgency. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association)

options.text: Arrange nerve conduction studies and review in the clinic in six weeks
options.rationale: Nerve conduction studies will confirm the pattern of multiple separate named nerve lesions and are worth obtaining, but the tempo is wrong. Each week of untreated disease risks a further infarcted nerve with incomplete recovery, and the raised troponin signals organ involvement that will not wait. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists

options.text: Send strongyloides serology and treat with ivermectin before any steroid
options.rationale: Excluding strongyloides before immunosuppression is genuinely important because hyperinfection can be fatal, and serology should be sent today, but it is drawn in parallel rather than used to delay treatment. He has no overseas travel or endemic residence, and the neurological progression will not pause for a serology result. (Source: Australian Society for Infectious Diseases)

options.text: Refer for skin prick allergy testing and commence a leukotriene antagonist
options.rationale: Allergy testing addresses the atopic label he has carried rather than the vasculitic process now causing his deficits. Leukotriene antagonists have historically been associated with unmasking this condition when corticosteroid is reduced, and they have no therapeutic role in the acute vasculitis. (Source: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy)
source_refs: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy

explanation.summary: Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis evolves through three overlapping phases: an allergic phase with adult onset asthma and sinonasal disease, an eosinophilic phase with peripheral eosinophilia and tissue infiltration producing migratory pulmonary infiltrates or eosinophilic gastroenteritis, and a vasculitic phase with neuropathy, purpura, cardiac and renal involvement. The asthma label typically precedes the vasculitis by several years, which is why the condition is so often first recognised at the moment a patient labelled asthmatic develops a neurological deficit. Mononeuritis multiplex, meaning deficits in two or more separately named peripheral nerves, is the classic neurological signature and occurs in the majority. Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies are positive in only about forty per cent and a negative result therefore cannot exclude the diagnosis, which is a frequent source of delay. Cardiac involvement, which may present with only a raised troponin, is the principal cause of mortality and shifts treatment toward combined corticosteroid and cyclophosphamide or rituximab.
key_points: Adult onset asthma with nasal polyps plus eosinophilia plus neuropathy is the defining combination
Mononeuritis multiplex means deficits in two or more separately named nerves
Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies are positive in only about forty per cent
Cardiac involvement is the leading cause of death and may show only as a raised troponin
Send strongyloides serology in parallel with, not instead of, starting corticosteroid
explanation.pearls: A peripheral eosinophil count above 1.5 x10^9/L in someone carrying an asthma label who develops a new foot drop should prompt same day corticosteroid and vasculitis referral, because an infarcted nerve left untreated beyond a few weeks recovers poorly.

sources.label: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy
Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists

subtopic_detail: low voltage electrocardiogram with increased wall thickness and nephrotic range proteinuria in an infiltrative cardiomyopathy
stem:
You are the cardiology registrar assessing a 64-year-old man referred with five months of breathlessness on exertion and ankle swelling. He has lost 8 kg without trying and feels light headed whenever he stands up quickly.

His wife mentions that he has twice woken with purple marks around his eyes after a bout of coughing, and that his tongue looks bigger than it used to. He has never had hypertension and his blood pressure has in fact been running lower than his usual over the past year, so his general practitioner stopped his only antihypertensive six months ago. There is no family history of cardiac disease or sudden death. His investigations are back.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92, blood pressure 98/64 lying with a 28 mmHg systolic fall on standing, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 96 per cent in air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Elevated jugular venous pressure, bilateral pitting oedema to the knees, macroglossia with lateral dental indentations, periorbital purpura
data_table.Investigations: Urine protein to creatinine ratio 420 mg/mmol (less than 30), serum albumin 24 g/L (35 to 50), estimated glomerular filtration rate 55 mL/min/1.73m2 (greater than 60), N terminal pro B type natriuretic peptide markedly raised, high sensitivity troponin persistently mildly raised without a rise and fall pattern
data_table.Electrocardiogram: Sinus rhythm with low voltage QRS complexes in the limb leads and poor R wave progression
data_table.Echocardiogram: Left ventricular wall thickness 16 mm, ejection fraction 52 per cent, grade 2 diastolic dysfunction, biatrial enlargement, apical sparing on longitudinal strain imaging

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Technetium labelled bone scintigraphy to characterise the cardiac deposits
options.rationale: Bone avid tracer uptake identifies the transthyretin form of the disease and is an excellent non-invasive test for it, which makes this the strongest competing answer. It must not be used alone, because a positive scan is only interpretable as transthyretin disease once a plasma cell disorder has been excluded, and the extracardiac features here point to the light chain form. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.text: Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging with late gadolinium enhancement now
options.rationale: Diffuse subendocardial late enhancement with abnormal gadolinium kinetics supports infiltration and refines the cardiac assessment, so this is a reasonable investigation at some point. It cannot distinguish the light chain from the transthyretin form, and that distinction is the one that changes treatment. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.text: Serum free light chain assay with serum and urine immunofixation studies
options.rationale: Macroglossia, periorbital purpura and nephrotic range proteinuria alongside an infiltrative cardiomyopathy indicate light chain deposition from an underlying plasma cell disorder, and the light chain assay with immunofixation is both the most sensitive screen and the test that determines treatment. Identifying the clonal process is what separates a haematologically treatable disease from an untreatable one, and it must precede or accompany any bone scintigraphy. (Source: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.text: Percutaneous renal biopsy to establish the cause of the proteinuria
options.rationale: A renal biopsy would demonstrate the deposits and is sometimes how the diagnosis is first made, but it is invasive and carries bleeding risk that is increased in this disease by factor X deficiency and vascular fragility. A blood and urine based assay answers the same question first. (Source: Kidney Health Australia)

options.text: Invasive coronary angiography to exclude an ischaemic cardiomyopathy
options.rationale: The persistently raised troponin without a rise and fall pattern reflects ongoing myocardial injury from infiltration rather than plaque rupture, and the preserved ejection fraction with marked wall thickening and biatrial enlargement is not an ischaemic pattern. Angiography also exposes him to contrast with an already reduced filtration rate. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand

explanation.summary: Infiltrative cardiomyopathy should be suspected whenever increased left ventricular wall thickness coexists with low QRS voltages, because hypertensive and hypertrophic disease both produce high voltages in proportion to muscle mass and the discordance signals that the thickening is deposited material rather than myocyte hypertrophy. Apical sparing on longitudinal strain imaging, biatrial enlargement, a persistently raised troponin without a rise and fall pattern and disproportionately elevated natriuretic peptides complete the echocardiographic and biochemical picture. The critical fork is between the light chain form arising from a clonal plasma cell population and the transthyretin form, because the first is treated with anti plasma cell therapy and carries a far worse untreated prognosis measured in months, while the second is treated with a transthyretin stabiliser. Extracardiac features separate them: macroglossia, periorbital purpura and nephrotic range proteinuria are essentially specific to the light chain form, while bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome and lumbar spinal stenosis years earlier suggest transthyretin disease. A further trap is that blood pressure often falls and antihypertensives are withdrawn in the year before diagnosis, and autonomic involvement produces the postural drop seen here.
key_points: Increased wall thickness with low QRS voltage is the signature discordance of infiltration
Apical sparing on strain imaging and biatrial enlargement support the diagnosis
Macroglossia, periorbital purpura and nephrotic proteinuria indicate the light chain form
Exclude a plasma cell disorder before interpreting bone scintigraphy as transthyretin disease
A persistently raised troponin without a rise and fall pattern reflects infiltration, not plaque rupture
explanation.pearls: Serum free light chains with serum and urine immunofixation together detect over ninety per cent of light chain amyloidosis, whereas serum protein electrophoresis alone misses roughly a third, so ordering electrophoresis by itself is the commonest way this diagnosis is delayed.

sources.label: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand
Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand

subtopic_detail: bilateral leg pain with a large post void residual and reduced perianal sensation five days after a lifting injury
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar seeing a 42-year-old warehouse worker who developed severe low back pain five days ago while lifting a pallet. Over the past two days the pain has begun shooting down the back of both legs.

Since yesterday morning he has had to wait and strain to start passing urine and feels he never empties. This morning he noticed that the paper felt strange when he wiped himself. He has had no fevers, night sweats or weight loss, has never had cancer, uses no injected drugs and has no indwelling lines. His bowels last opened normally two days ago. A bladder scan in the department shows a post-void residual volume of 620 mL.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84, blood pressure 132/78, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 98 per cent in air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Reduced sensation over both buttocks and the perineum, reduced voluntary anal squeeze, ankle jerks absent bilaterally, power 4 out of 5 in ankle plantarflexion on both sides, no spinal tenderness to percussion
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 8.4 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0), C reactive protein 4 mg/L (less than 5), creatinine 88 micromol/L (60 to 110)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Emergency magnetic resonance imaging of the lumbosacral spine today
options.rationale: Bilateral radicular pain with saddle sensory loss, reduced anal tone and urinary retention is a surgical emergency, and magnetic resonance imaging is the only study that shows the disc, the thecal sac and the nerve roots well enough to plan decompression. Outcomes for bladder and sexual function deteriorate with every hour of delay, so the scan is arranged now rather than booked. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Computed tomography of the lumbar spine without intravenous contrast today
options.rationale: Computed tomography shows bone well but resolves the disc, ligament and neural elements poorly, so a normal study cannot exclude compression and an abnormal one rarely gives the surgeon what is needed. It is the fallback only when magnetic resonance imaging is contraindicated or unavailable. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Radiologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Radiologists

options.text: Intravenous dexamethasone commenced before any imaging is arranged for him
options.rationale: High dose corticosteroid is given ahead of imaging for malignant spinal cord compression to reduce peritumoural oedema, and the absence of any cancer history, fever, weight loss or raised inflammatory markers argues against that mechanism here. Steroid does not relieve mechanical compression by disc material. (Source: eviQ Cancer Treatments Online)

options.text: Plain radiographs of the lumbar spine in two planes including flexion views
options.rationale: Plain films do not image neural tissue at all and change management in acute back pain only when a fracture or gross instability is suspected. Ordering them here consumes time in a condition measured in hours. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Radiologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Radiologists

options.text: Simple analgesia with physiotherapy and general practitioner review in one week
options.rationale: Conservative management is right for mechanical back pain without neurological compromise, but retention with a 620 mL residual and saddle anaesthesia are the specific findings that take this out of that category. Missing them is the commonest cause of permanent bladder dysfunction in this condition. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Cauda equina syndrome results from compression of the lumbosacral nerve roots below the conus, most often by a large central disc prolapse, and it is one of the few genuine neurosurgical emergencies arising from a common presentation. The features to elicit are bilateral radicular pain or weakness, saddle sensory disturbance, reduced anal tone, and bladder dysfunction that progresses from difficulty initiating micturition and loss of the sense of fullness to painless retention with overflow. Painless retention with overflow incontinence indicates established damage and carries a far worse prognosis than the earlier phase of altered urinary sensation, which is why asking about the quality of bladder sensation matters more than asking only about incontinence. A post-void residual measured by bladder scan is a quick objective addition to the examination. Red flags for other serious causes of back pain, namely fever, injected drug use, known malignancy, unexplained weight loss, age over fifty with new pain and prolonged corticosteroid use, are screened for at the same time.
key_points: Bilateral symptoms, saddle anaesthesia, reduced anal tone and urinary change define the syndrome
Magnetic resonance imaging is the only adequate study and is arranged emergently
Painless retention with overflow already indicates established injury
A bladder scan residual is a fast objective bedside measure
Corticosteroid before imaging belongs to malignant cord compression, not disc prolapse
explanation.pearls: Ask specifically whether the patient can feel urine passing and whether they feel the bladder filling, because loss of urethral and filling sensation precedes retention by hours to days and identifies the window in which decompression preserves continence.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Radiologists

subtopic_detail: fixed airflow obstruction with lower zone predominant emphysema in a woman in her forties with a light smoking history
stem:
You are the respiratory registrar reviewing a 41-year-old primary school teacher referred with two years of breathlessness on exertion. She can no longer carry shopping up the stairs to her flat without stopping.

She smoked about five cigarettes a day for five years in her twenties and stopped eleven years ago. She has never worked in dusty or fume exposed environments, keeps no birds and has no mould in her home. She had no childhood asthma and uses no inhaler. Her brother died at forty five of liver failure that the family were told was cirrhosis without a cause being found. Her computed tomography shows emphysematous change concentrated in the lower zones of both lungs with relative sparing of the apices.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 23 kg/m2, quiet breath sounds with prolonged expiration, no clubbing, no crackles, no wheeze
data_table.Investigations: Forced expiratory volume in one second 48 per cent predicted, ratio to forced vital capacity 0.52, no significant bronchodilator response, diffusing capacity reduced, alanine aminotransferase 62 U/L (less than 35), gamma glutamyl transferase 88 U/L (less than 40)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate investigation to establish the underlying cause?

options.text: Serum total immunoglobulin E with Aspergillus specific antibody testing
options.rationale: This combination investigates allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, which arises in people with asthma or cystic fibrosis and produces central bronchiectasis with mucus plugging rather than basal emphysema. She has no history of asthma and no wheeze. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.text: Serum alpha one antitrypsin concentration with phenotyping if it is reduced
options.rationale: Emphysema before fifty with a trivial smoking history, a lower zone rather than apical distribution, and unexplained liver disease in a first degree relative is the pattern of this inherited protease inhibitor deficiency. Phenotyping is added because the level alone can be misleading during any acute phase response. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.text: Sweat chloride testing followed by an extended cystic fibrosis gene panel
options.rationale: Late presenting cystic fibrosis is a real entity but produces bronchiectasis with chronic productive cough, sinus disease and pancreatic insufficiency rather than isolated basal emphysema with a normal body mass index. Her computed tomography shows destruction rather than airway dilatation. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.text: Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody testing with proteinase 3 and myeloperoxidase
options.rationale: Small vessel vasculitis of the lung presents with haemoptysis, nodules or cavities, alveolar haemorrhage and usually renal involvement, none of which is present, and it does not cause fixed airflow obstruction with basal emphysema. The absence of systemic features argues against it. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association)

options.text: Cardiopulmonary exercise testing with arterial blood gases taken at peak exercise
options.rationale: Exercise testing quantifies the limitation and distinguishes cardiac from respiratory causes of breathlessness, but the spirometry and imaging have already established that the problem is emphysema. It measures severity rather than identifying an aetiology. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand

explanation.summary: Alpha one antitrypsin deficiency is an inherited disorder of the principal circulating antiprotease, and without it neutrophil elastase released in the lung destroys alveolar tissue unopposed. The severe deficiency phenotype is the commonest clinically significant form, and smoking accelerates decline so steeply that smoking status largely determines whether an affected person presents in their forties or remains well into old age. The radiological signature is panlobular emphysema with a basal predominance, which contrasts with the apical centrilobular pattern of ordinary smoking related disease and is one of the most useful discriminators available. Liver disease arises by a different mechanism, from polymerisation and accumulation of the abnormal protein within hepatocytes, and it can present as neonatal cholestasis, childhood liver disease or adult cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma. Diagnosis matters for the patient's own management, for smoking cessation emphasis and occupational advice, and because first degree relatives should be offered testing and counselling.
key_points: Suspect it in emphysema before fifty, in never or light smokers, and with a basal distribution
Unexplained liver disease in the patient or a relative is a strong pointer
Measure the level and phenotype, since the level rises as an acute phase reactant
Lung disease comes from unopposed elastase; liver disease from protein accumulation in hepatocytes
Test first degree relatives once a severe deficiency phenotype is confirmed
explanation.pearls: The basal panlobular distribution is the single most useful radiological clue, because ordinary smoking related emphysema is centrilobular and apical, so a lower zone predominant pattern should prompt the test even when the smoking history seems adequate to explain the disease.

sources.label: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand

subtopic_detail: a magnetic gait with urinary urgency and mild forgetfulness in an older man with ventriculomegaly and no parkinsonian signs
stem:
You are the geriatric medicine registrar seeing a 74-year-old retired surveyor referred after two falls at home in the past three months. His wife says he has changed over about eight months.

He describes his feet as feeling stuck to the floor when he starts to walk and has most trouble turning in the kitchen and getting going after standing. For the past three months he has had to rush to the toilet and has twice not made it. His wife says he repeats himself and has become slower in conversation, but he manages the household accounts and knows the date and where he is. There is no resting tremor, no rigidity and no reduction in the amplitude of repeated finger tapping. His posture is upright, his arm swing is preserved and there is no postural drop in blood pressure.

data_table.Examination: Broad based shuffling gait with reduced step height and difficulty turning, normal tone and power, Mini Mental State Examination 25 of 30, no tremor or rigidity, no postural hypotension
data_table.Investigations: Computed tomography of the brain shows enlarged lateral ventricles with an Evans index of 0.38 and no disproportionate cortical atrophy, vitamin B12, thyroid stimulating hormone, syphilis serology, urea electrolytes and creatinine all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Carotid duplex ultrasound to assess for haemodynamically significant stenosis
options.rationale: Carotid disease causes focal hemispheric events rather than a symmetrical gait disorder with urinary and cognitive change, and he has had no transient ischaemic attack or stroke. The study would not explain a progressive eight month syndrome. (Source: Stroke Foundation Australia)

options.text: Trial of levodopa titrated over six weeks with formal reassessment of his gait
options.rationale: A levodopa trial is reasonable where parkinsonism is suspected, but bradykinesia, rigidity and rest tremor are all absent and his arm swing is preserved, so the cardinal features are not there to respond. Lower body predominant gait failure without upper limb signs points away from Parkinson disease. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: High volume lumbar puncture with timed gait testing before and afterwards
options.rationale: Removing thirty to fifty millilitres of cerebrospinal fluid and measuring gait speed and step length before and several hours afterwards is the standard test of whether shunting is likely to help, and the gait component is the feature that responds best. Objective timed measurement is essential because subjective impressions of improvement are unreliable. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Society for Geriatric Medicine)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Society for Geriatric Medicine

options.text: Referral for insertion of a ventriculoperitoneal shunt on the imaging findings alone
options.rationale: Ventriculomegaly is common in older people and much of it reflects atrophy rather than a treatable disturbance of cerebrospinal fluid dynamics, so operating on the scan alone subjects many patients to a procedure with real infection, haemorrhage and over drainage risks for no benefit. The correct answer is the test that selects who will respond. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Society for Geriatric Medicine)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Society for Geriatric Medicine

options.text: Electroencephalography to exclude a non convulsive seizure disorder as the cause
options.rationale: Non convulsive status can cause fluctuating confusion but does not produce a steadily progressive gait disorder with urinary urgency over eight months. His clear orientation and preserved handling of the household accounts argue against an ongoing ictal state. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Normal pressure hydrocephalus is characterised by ventricular enlargement with a normal opening pressure and the triad of gait disturbance, urinary dysfunction and cognitive slowing, and it matters disproportionately because it is one of the few causes of dementia and gait failure that can be improved by treatment. The gait is the earliest and most responsive element, described as magnetic or apraxic, with a broad base, reduced step height, difficulty initiating and marked trouble turning. Cognitive change is typically subcortical, with slowing, apathy and reduced attention rather than the amnesia of Alzheimer disease, and urinary urgency precedes frank incontinence. Ventriculomegaly alone is not sufficient for the diagnosis because it is common in ageing brains, so response to cerebrospinal fluid removal is used to identify who will benefit from shunting. Reversible mimics including vitamin B12 deficiency, hypothyroidism, neurosyphilis, cervical myelopathy and medication effects are excluded first.
key_points: Gait disturbance is the earliest feature and the most likely to improve with treatment
Cognitive impairment is subcortical slowing rather than early amnesia
Ventriculomegaly alone does not make the diagnosis
High volume cerebrospinal fluid removal with objective gait testing predicts shunt response
Exclude vitamin B12 deficiency, thyroid disease and cervical myelopathy first
explanation.pearls: Time a ten metre walk and count steps before and about two to four hours after removing thirty to fifty millilitres of cerebrospinal fluid, because a fall in walking time of more than about ten to twenty per cent is the objective threshold used to select patients for shunting.

sources.label: Australian and New Zealand Society for Geriatric Medicine

subtopic_detail: confirming the haemodynamic diagnosis before treatment when echocardiography has already estimated a high right ventricular systolic pressure
stem:
You are the cardiology registrar seeing a 36-year-old woman with twelve months of breathlessness that has progressed from long walks to the distance between her car and her front door. Three weeks ago she blacked out briefly while carrying washing up a flight of stairs.

She has never smoked, takes no appetite suppressants and uses no stimulant drugs. She has no rash, no Raynaud phenomenon, no joint swelling and no dysphagia. She snores rarely and her partner has seen no pauses in her breathing. Her computed tomography pulmonary angiogram shows no filling defect and clear lung parenchyma, and a ventilation perfusion scan shows no mismatched defects. Her connective tissue serology and human immunodeficiency virus test are negative and her liver ultrasound is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96, blood pressure 106/68, respiratory rate 20, SpO2 94 per cent in air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Jugular venous pressure raised 6 cm with a prominent v wave, loud pulmonary component of the second heart sound, pansystolic murmur at the left sternal edge increasing on inspiration, pitting oedema to mid shin
data_table.Investigations: Echocardiogram shows estimated right ventricular systolic pressure 68 mmHg with a dilated hypokinetic right ventricle, normal left ventricular function and structurally normal valves; spirometry normal with a reduced diffusing capacity; brain natriuretic peptide elevated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Overnight polysomnography to assess for sleep disordered breathing as a cause
options.rationale: Sleep apnoea can contribute to pulmonary hypertension but rarely produces pressures of this magnitude with right ventricular failure in a young non obese woman, and her partner reports no witnessed apnoea. It is a contributor to look for, not the explanation for this picture. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.text: Repeat transthoracic echocardiography in six months to assess the rate of change
options.rationale: Serial imaging defers action in a woman who has already had exertional syncope, which is a marker of severely limited cardiac output and of high short term mortality. Untreated disease of this type progresses over months, so waiting is itself a decision against treatment. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.text: Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging with gadolinium to assess the right ventricle
options.rationale: Cardiac magnetic resonance characterises right ventricular volumes and function superbly and is used for prognostication and follow up, but it does not measure pressures directly and so cannot establish the haemodynamic diagnosis. The distinction from the correct answer is measured pressure against inferred structure. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.text: Right heart catheterisation with vasoreactivity testing in a specialist centre
options.rationale: Echocardiography estimates rather than measures pressure and cannot separate pre from post capillary disease, so catheterisation with direct measurement of mean pulmonary artery pressure, wedge pressure and pulmonary vascular resistance is required before any targeted therapy is started. Acute vasoreactivity testing at the same sitting identifies the small group who respond to calcium channel blockade. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.text: Empirical sildenafil started now with reassessment of her exercise capacity later
options.rationale: Pulmonary vasodilators given without a confirmed haemodynamic diagnosis can precipitate pulmonary oedema if the elevation turns out to be post capillary from left heart disease, and they are prescribed in Australia through specialist centres after catheterisation. Treating before measuring risks harming the patient it is meant to help. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand

explanation.summary: Pulmonary hypertension is defined haemodynamically by a mean pulmonary artery pressure above 20 mmHg measured at right heart catheterisation, and the pre capillary form additionally requires a wedge pressure at or below 15 mmHg with an elevated pulmonary vascular resistance. Echocardiography is the screening test and estimates right ventricular systolic pressure from the tricuspid regurgitant jet, but it systematically over and under estimates in individual patients and cannot distinguish the groups that require entirely different treatment. The classification into five groups drives management: arterial disease, disease due to left heart failure, disease due to lung disease or hypoxia, chronic thromboembolic disease, and multifactorial causes. Chronic thromboembolic disease is specifically excluded with a ventilation perfusion scan rather than a computed tomography angiogram, because the scan is more sensitive for the chronic organised thrombus that is potentially curable by surgical endarterectomy. Exertional syncope, right heart failure and a rapidly falling exercise capacity all mark high risk disease requiring urgent specialist referral.
key_points: Catheterisation defines the diagnosis; echocardiography only screens
A wedge pressure at or below 15 mmHg separates pre from post capillary disease
Ventilation perfusion scanning, not computed tomography, excludes chronic thromboembolic disease
Exertional syncope indicates severely limited cardiac output and high mortality
Targeted pulmonary vasodilators are started only after haemodynamic confirmation
explanation.pearls: A ventilation perfusion scan showing mismatched segmental defects identifies chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension, the one form that is potentially curable by pulmonary endarterectomy, which is why it is never omitted even when a computed tomography angiogram is clean.

sources.label: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand
Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand

subtopic_detail: a cord lesion spanning six vertebral segments with negative oligoclonal bands after an episode of painful visual loss
stem:
You are the neurology registrar admitting a 34-year-old woman with six days of progressive weakness in both legs, now unable to stand unaided, with a band of altered sensation across her trunk and difficulty passing urine.

Two months ago she had a painful right eye with loss of colour vision over several days, which recovered only partially, and she was told it was probably a viral problem. She has had no rash, no oral or genital ulceration, no dry eyes or mouth and no joint swelling. Magnetic resonance imaging of her spine shows a contiguous cord lesion extending from the fourth to the ninth thoracic vertebral level with swelling and patchy enhancement. Imaging of her brain shows no periventricular or juxtacortical lesions. Cerebrospinal fluid shows 40 white cells per microlitre with a neutrophil component, protein 0.82 g/L and no oligoclonal bands.

data_table.Examination: Power 2 out of 5 in both legs, sensory level at T6, brisk knee and ankle reflexes with extensor plantar responses, right relative afferent pupillary defect, visual acuity 6 out of 24 on the right
data_table.Investigations: Cerebrospinal fluid white cells 40 per microlitre, protein 0.82 g/L (0.15 to 0.45), glucose within normal limits, no oligoclonal bands, spinal magnetic resonance imaging shows a lesion spanning six vertebral segments

lead_in: What is the most appropriate investigation?

options.text: Visual evoked potentials in both eyes to demonstrate subclinical optic pathway delay
options.rationale: Evoked potentials can document a previous optic neuritis but her clinical history and afferent pupillary defect have already done so, and the test does not distinguish between the conditions under consideration. It would add confirmation of something already known. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Repeat magnetic resonance imaging of the brain with gadolinium in three months
options.rationale: Serial brain imaging is the approach to demonstrating dissemination in time in multiple sclerosis, but a cord lesion spanning six segments, a cerebrospinal fluid pleocytosis of this degree with neutrophils, and absent oligoclonal bands are all atypical for that disease. Waiting three months in a relapsing condition that causes stepwise permanent disability is also unsafe. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Extractable nuclear antigen antibody panel including anti Ro and anti La antibodies
options.rationale: Connective tissue disease can cause a myelitis and the panel is reasonable to include in a broad screen, but she has none of the sicca, cutaneous, mucosal or articular features that would suggest it. It does not test the leading diagnosis. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association)

options.text: Commence interferon beta and arrange neurology follow up within the next month
options.rationale: Beyond being a treatment rather than an investigation, interferon beta is specifically harmful in the condition that this presentation suggests and has been reported to precipitate relapses. Starting a multiple sclerosis therapy before distinguishing the two diseases is the central error to avoid here. (Source: Royal Australasian College of Physicians)

options.text: Serum aquaporin four immunoglobulin G antibody assayed by a cell based method
options.rationale: A longitudinally extensive cord lesion of three or more vertebral segments with optic neuritis, absent oligoclonal bands and a marked cerebrospinal fluid pleocytosis is the pattern of aquaporin four antibody disease, and the cell based assay is substantially more sensitive and specific than older enzyme immunoassays. A positive result changes acute and long term treatment immediately. (Source: Royal Australasian College of Physicians)

explanation.summary: Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder is an antibody mediated astrocytopathy directed at the aquaporin four water channel, and separating it from multiple sclerosis is one of the more consequential diagnostic distinctions in neurology because the treatments diverge and several multiple sclerosis therapies make it worse. The features that point away from multiple sclerosis are a cord lesion extending three or more vertebral segments, severe and often bilateral optic neuritis with poor recovery, area postrema syndrome with intractable hiccups or vomiting, absent oligoclonal bands, and a cerebrospinal fluid pleocytosis above fifty cells or containing neutrophils. Attacks are more severe and recover less completely than multiple sclerosis relapses, so disability accumulates through attacks rather than through progression between them, which makes rapid attack treatment and effective relapse prevention the whole of management. Acute attacks are treated with high dose methylprednisolone and plasma exchange for severe or steroid refractory episodes. A separate antibody against myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein defines an overlapping but distinct disease with a different prognosis, and is tested when the aquaporin four antibody is negative.
key_points: Three or more contiguous vertebral segments defines a longitudinally extensive cord lesion
Absent oligoclonal bands and a neutrophilic pleocytosis argue against multiple sclerosis
Interferon beta and some other multiple sclerosis therapies worsen this disease
Disability accrues through incomplete recovery from attacks rather than by progression
Test myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody when the aquaporin four antibody is negative
explanation.pearls: Intractable hiccups or vomiting lasting more than forty eight hours, from a lesion in the area postrema of the dorsal medulla, is a recognised presenting syndrome and is frequently investigated as a gastrointestinal problem for weeks before the neurological diagnosis is considered.
