subtopic_detail: the order of volume replacement and bone directed therapy in a drowsy dehydrated woman whose creatinine has risen with the calcium
stem:
You are the medical registrar called to see a 68-year-old woman with breast cancer metastatic to bone who was brought in by her daughter. Over five days she has become increasingly drowsy, has vomited several times and has not opened her bowels.

Her daughter says she has been passing large volumes of urine and drinking very little, and that she slept most of yesterday. She takes no thiazide, no lithium and no calcium or vitamin D supplement, and she has had no recent imaging with contrast. Her creatinine three months ago was 78 micromol/L. She is rousable to voice and oriented to person only. Her mucous membranes are dry, her skin turgor is reduced and her jugular venous pressure is not visible with her lying flat.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108, blood pressure 96/58, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 97 per cent in air, temperature 36.5 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Dry mucous membranes, reduced skin turgor, jugular venous pressure not visible supine, chest clear, no focal neurological deficit
data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 3.42 mmol/L (2.15 to 2.55), creatinine 168 micromol/L (45 to 90), urea 14.2 mmol/L (3.0 to 8.0), albumin 28 g/L (35 to 50), parathyroid hormone less than 0.5 pmol/L (1.6 to 6.9), phosphate 1.1 mmol/L (0.75 to 1.50)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Intravenous sodium chloride 0.9 per cent given at a brisk rate with close monitoring
options.rationale: Hypercalcaemia drives a nephrogenic concentrating defect and vomiting, so these patients are always profoundly volume depleted, and restoring circulating volume alone lowers calcium by improving glomerular filtration and urinary calcium excretion. It must precede bone directed therapy because a bisphosphonate given to a hypovolaemic patient with an acute kidney injury risks worsening renal function. (Source: eviQ Cancer Treatments Online)

options.text: Intravenous zoledronic acid at full dose given as a single infusion immediately
options.rationale: A bisphosphonate is the definitive treatment and will be given, but it takes two to four days to work, requires dose reduction in renal impairment and is relatively contraindicated until volume has been restored. Giving it first treats the number while leaving the physiology that caused it uncorrected. (Source: eviQ Cancer Treatments Online)

options.text: Intravenous furosemide given regularly to promote a calcium diuresis from the outset
options.rationale: Loop diuretics were once routine but worsen volume depletion and electrolyte disturbance, and they are now reserved for fluid overload developing during rehydration in a patient with cardiac or renal impairment. Using one in a hypotensive hypovolaemic patient will make both the kidney injury and the calcium worse. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Oral prednisolone at high dose with review of the calcium after forty eight hours
options.rationale: Corticosteroids are effective where the mechanism is excess calcitriol production, as in lymphoma, myeloma and granulomatous disease, but her suppressed parathyroid hormone with bone metastases indicates a parathyroid hormone related peptide or local osteolytic mechanism. The steroid is aimed at the wrong pathway. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Urgent haemodialysis against a low calcium bath arranged through the renal unit
options.rationale: Dialysis is reserved for life threatening hypercalcaemia with established kidney failure or heart failure that prevents adequate fluid loading, and her kidney injury is pre renal and expected to reverse with fluid. Escalating to dialysis before a saline challenge subjects her to an invasive procedure she is likely not to need. (Source: Kidney Health Australia)

explanation.summary: Hypercalcaemia of malignancy occurs in a substantial minority of patients with advanced cancer and carries a poor prognosis, marking disease progression as often as it marks a treatable metabolic emergency. Three mechanisms account for nearly all cases: secretion of parathyroid hormone related peptide by solid tumours, local osteolysis from bone metastases or myeloma, and excess calcitriol production in lymphoma and granulomatous disease, and the last of these is the one that responds to corticosteroid. A suppressed parathyroid hormone distinguishes these from primary hyperparathyroidism, which remains the commonest cause of hypercalcaemia overall and is usually mild and chronic rather than acute. The clinical syndrome of drowsiness, confusion, nausea, constipation, polyuria and polydipsia is explained by a calcium induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus that produces a vicious cycle of volume depletion and rising calcium. Management is therefore sequential: restore volume first, then give a bisphosphonate or denosumab to switch off osteoclastic resorption, then treat the underlying cancer.
key_points: Volume replacement comes before any bone directed agent
A suppressed parathyroid hormone separates malignant from primary hyperparathyroid hypercalcaemia
Bisphosphonates take two to four days to act and need renal dose adjustment
Corticosteroids work only in calcitriol mediated disease such as lymphoma or sarcoidosis
Loop diuretics are reserved for fluid overload during rehydration
explanation.pearls: Denosumab is the alternative when renal impairment precludes a bisphosphonate or when hypercalcaemia recurs despite one, because it is not renally cleared, but it carries a substantial risk of delayed hypocalcaemia and calcium must be monitored for several weeks afterwards.

subtopic_detail: a widespread rash with facial swelling, fever, eosinophilia and hepatitis appearing five weeks after starting a urate lowering drug
stem:
You are the medical registrar seeing a 62-year-old man who was started on allopurinol by his general practitioner five weeks ago after a third attack of gout. He has had four days of feeling hot and shivery and a rash that began on his trunk and has spread.

He says his face feels tight and his wife says his eyelids and cheeks look puffy. The rash is itchy rather than painful. He has not taken any other new medication, has had no recent travel and no unwell contacts. On examination there is a confluent red rash covering most of his trunk and limbs with facial swelling, and there are enlarged tender nodes in both sides of his neck and in his axillae. His lips, mouth, eyes and genitals are normal with no erosions, and the skin does not shear when firm lateral pressure is applied.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 104, blood pressure 128/76, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 97 per cent in air, temperature 38.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Confluent morbilliform rash over more than half the body surface, periorbital and facial oedema, cervical and axillary lymphadenopathy, no mucosal erosions, Nikolsky sign negative
data_table.Investigations: Eosinophils 2.4 x10^9/L (less than 0.5), atypical lymphocytes present on film, alanine aminotransferase 320 U/L (less than 45), creatinine 118 micromol/L (60 to 110), C reactive protein 62 mg/L (less than 5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue allopurinol and add a sedating antihistamine with topical corticosteroid
options.rationale: Continuing the responsible drug in a reaction with fever, organ involvement and eosinophilia allows it to progress, and the mortality of this syndrome is around ten per cent, driven largely by liver failure. Antihistamine and topical treatment is the management of a simple morbilliform drug eruption, which this is not. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists)

options.text: Cease allopurinol and commence systemic corticosteroid with staged organ monitoring
options.rationale: Withdrawal of the causative drug plus systemic corticosteroid is the standard treatment when there is significant organ involvement, and his transaminases at seven times the upper limit qualify. Monitoring continues for weeks after the drug is stopped because relapse and late thyroiditis are characteristic. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists)

options.text: Cease allopurinol and arrange urgent transfer to the regional burns unit for care
options.rationale: Burns unit transfer is the pathway for epidermal necrolysis, which presents with painful dusky skin, mucosal erosions and a positive Nikolsky sign, all of which are explicitly absent here. His rash is inflammatory rather than necrolytic and his skin barrier is intact. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists)

options.text: Cease allopurinol and commence intravenous immunoglobulin over the next five days
options.rationale: Immunoglobulin has been used in refractory cases and in epidermal necrolysis but has no established first line role in this syndrome, and it carries thrombotic and renal risks. It would be considered only after corticosteroid failure. (Source: National Blood Authority Australia)

options.text: Cease allopurinol and commence intravenous flucloxacillin for a presumed cellulitis
options.rationale: Cellulitis is unilateral, tender and sharply demarcated rather than a symmetrical confluent eruption with facial oedema, and it does not cause eosinophilia, atypical lymphocytes or hepatitis. Adding a new beta lactam during a severe drug reaction also risks a second sensitisation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms is a severe delayed hypersensitivity reaction distinguished from ordinary drug exanthems by fever, facial oedema, lymphadenopathy, haematological abnormality and internal organ involvement. Its defining feature is a long latency of two to eight weeks from starting the drug, far longer than the four to fourteen days of a simple morbilliform eruption, so the drug started most recently is frequently exonerated wrongly and an older one overlooked. Allopurinol, the aromatic anticonvulsants including carbamazepine, lamotrigine and phenytoin, sulfonamides, vancomycin and minocycline account for most cases. The liver is the organ most often involved and hepatitis is the usual cause of death, while kidney, lung, heart and thyroid involvement also occur. Reactivation of human herpesvirus 6 and other herpesviruses is characteristic and contributes to the prolonged and relapsing course, which is why corticosteroid is weaned slowly over weeks to months and follow up thyroid function is checked months after apparent recovery.
key_points: Latency of two to eight weeks separates it from a simple drug exanthem
Fever, facial oedema, lymphadenopathy and eosinophilia are the recognition tetrad
Liver involvement is commonest and drives the mortality
Absent mucosal erosions and a negative Nikolsky sign exclude epidermal necrolysis
Relapse on steroid weaning and late autoimmune thyroid disease are characteristic
explanation.pearls: Check thyroid function two to three months after apparent recovery, because autoimmune thyroiditis develops weeks to months later in a recognised minority of patients and is easily missed once the rash has settled and the patient has been discharged.

subtopic_detail: multiple vertebral fractures fourteen months after the last six monthly injection in a woman who simply stopped attending
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 71-year-old woman who has had four days of severe pain between her shoulder blades that began as she lifted a box while unpacking after moving house.

She was treated with six monthly denosumab injections for five years for osteoporosis. She moved interstate fourteen months ago, did not transfer her care, and has had no injection since. She takes calcium and colecalciferol daily. She has had no fevers, no night sweats and no weight loss. Radiographs today show new wedge compression fractures at the seventh and ninth thoracic vertebrae that were not present on a film taken two years ago. Her serum and urine protein electrophoresis, corrected calcium, thyroid function and myeloma screen are all normal.

data_table.Examination: Tender over the mid thoracic spinous processes, increased thoracic kyphosis, normal lower limb neurology, height 4 cm less than recorded five years ago
data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 2.32 mmol/L (2.15 to 2.55), 25 hydroxyvitamin D 78 nmol/L (greater than 50), thyroid stimulating hormone, creatinine and protein electrophoresis all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of her osteoporosis now?

options.text: Continue calcium and colecalciferol alone and repeat bone densitometry in two years
options.rationale: Supplements support but do not substitute for antiresorptive therapy, and a woman who has already sustained two vertebral fractures has severe established disease with a high risk of further fractures within the next twelve months. Doing nothing active is the option with the highest short term fracture risk. (Source: Healthy Bones Australia)

options.text: Withhold all antiresorptive treatment until the acute fractures have healed fully
options.rationale: Fracture healing is not impaired by antiresorptive therapy and delaying treatment prolongs exactly the window of accelerated bone turnover that produced these fractures. The rebound is time limited but intense, so the delay is the harm. (Source: Healthy Bones Australia)

options.text: Recommence denosumab now and plan a bisphosphonate before it is ever stopped again
options.rationale: Stopping denosumab releases a burst of osteoclast activity that produces rapid bone loss and multiple vertebral fractures within one to two years, and the treatment is to restore antiresorptive suppression without further delay. The lasting fix is that denosumab is never simply ceased, and a bisphosphonate is given as follow on therapy whenever it is discontinued. (Source: Healthy Bones Australia)

options.text: Refer for percutaneous vertebroplasty of both fractured levels before any drug change
options.rationale: Vertebral augmentation has not shown consistent benefit over sham in randomised trials and is considered only for intractable pain unresponsive to conservative measures. It also addresses the two fractures already sustained rather than the accelerated bone loss that will cause the next ones. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Radiologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Radiologists

options.text: Commence teriparatide alone as she has fractured while on antiresorptive treatment
options.rationale: Anabolic therapy has a place in severe osteoporosis with multiple fractures, but given immediately after denosumab and without antiresorptive cover it produces transient loss of hip bone density because it amplifies the already elevated turnover. The sequence of agents matters as much as the choice. (Source: Healthy Bones Australia)

explanation.summary: Denosumab is a monoclonal antibody against the receptor activator of nuclear factor kappa B ligand, and unlike bisphosphonates it is not incorporated into bone, so its effect disappears entirely once dosing stops. The result is a rebound in osteoclast activity that overshoots baseline, producing rapid loss of the bone mineral density gained and a characteristic pattern of multiple vertebral fractures appearing within one to two years of the last injection. The risk is highest in those who had vertebral fractures before treatment and in those treated for longer, and a single late or missed dose is enough to begin the process. This makes denosumab a treatment that should not be started unless continuity can be assured, and it means a missed appointment carries a clinical consequence rather than an administrative one. When denosumab is deliberately stopped, a bisphosphonate is given as follow on therapy, usually starting around six months after the last injection, and bone turnover markers or densitometry are used to check that the rebound has been suppressed.
key_points: The denosumab effect ends completely when dosing stops, unlike a bisphosphonate
Rebound produces multiple vertebral fractures within one to two years
A single missed or delayed dose can initiate the rebound
Follow on bisphosphonate is mandatory whenever denosumab is ceased
Anabolic therapy given straight after denosumab without cover loses hip bone density
explanation.pearls: Denosumab injections are due every six months and are given within a four week window, so a patient who is more than a month overdue needs active recall rather than being left until the next routine visit.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Radiologists

subtopic_detail: dusky coalescing macules with skin shearing and erosions at three mucosal sites three weeks after a rapidly titrated mood stabiliser
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar seeing a 29-year-old woman who started lamotrigine three weeks ago for bipolar affective disorder and was titrated up quickly because of a transcription error on the prescription.

For two days she has had fever, a gritty burning sensation in both eyes and increasing pain in her mouth so that she cannot swallow her own saliva. Yesterday dusky flat spots appeared on her chest and have since joined together, and this morning the skin over her upper back and chest has begun to lift away in sheets. She describes the skin as burning and exquisitely painful rather than itchy. Gentle lateral pressure on apparently intact skin adjacent to a blister causes the epidermis to shear. Erosions are present on her lips, conjunctivae and vulva, and you estimate about twelve per cent of her body surface has detached.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118, blood pressure 102/62, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 97 per cent in air, temperature 38.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Dusky coalescing macules with flaccid blisters, epidermal detachment over about twelve per cent of body surface, positive Nikolsky sign, erosions of the lips, conjunctivae and vulva
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 4.2 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0), urea 9.8 mmol/L (3.0 to 8.0), bicarbonate 19 mmol/L (22 to 32), glucose 6.8 mmol/L (3.0 to 7.7), creatinine 96 micromol/L (45 to 90)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Cease lamotrigine and start oral prednisolone with review in clinic in two days
options.rationale: Ambulatory management is unsafe with twelve per cent epidermal detachment, since fluid loss, hypothermia, infection and ocular scarring all progress over the following days. The role of systemic corticosteroid in epidermal necrolysis also remains contested, unlike its accepted role in the eosinophilic drug syndrome. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists)

options.text: Cease lamotrigine and apply potent topical corticosteroid with oral antihistamine
options.rationale: Topical treatment is appropriate for inflammatory drug eruptions with an intact epidermis, whereas she has lost her skin barrier across a large area and needs the fluid, thermal, analgesic and ocular care of a specialist unit. Applying steroid to denuded dermis does not address any of those problems. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists)

options.text: Cease lamotrigine and start intravenous flucloxacillin for staphylococcal skin disease
options.rationale: Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome is the near diagnosis to exclude, but it occurs almost entirely in young children, spares the mucosae and splits the epidermis at a very superficial level without the dusky targetoid macules seen here. Prophylactic antibiotics are also avoided in epidermal necrolysis because they select resistant organisms. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Cease lamotrigine and transfer urgently to a specialist burns or dermatology unit
options.rationale: Immediate withdrawal of the causative drug improves survival, and detachment of this extent requires the fluid balance, temperature control, analgesia, wound handling and ophthalmic review that only a specialist unit provides. Ocular involvement in particular causes permanent scarring and vision loss unless assessed within the first days. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists)

options.text: Arrange a skin biopsy for frozen section before deciding on any transfer or treatment
options.rationale: Biopsy confirms the level of the split and is usually performed, but it is done alongside rather than before the decisions that determine survival. Waiting for histology delays drug withdrawal and transfer in a condition whose mortality tracks with how quickly the drug is stopped. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists)

explanation.summary: Stevens Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis are a single disease separated by the extent of epidermal detachment, under ten per cent for the former, over thirty per cent for the latter, and the overlap band between them. Onset is typically one to four weeks after starting the responsible drug, with the aromatic anticonvulsants, allopurinol, sulfonamides, nevirapine and oxicam anti inflammatories the commonest culprits. A prodrome of fever, sore throat and painful eyes precedes the rash by one to three days and is routinely mistaken for a viral illness. Lamotrigine is a particular risk when titrated faster than the recommended schedule or combined with valproate, which inhibits its metabolism, so titration errors are a recurring cause. Mortality is predicted by the SCORTEN score using age, malignancy, heart rate, detached surface area, urea, bicarbonate and glucose, and early withdrawal of the causative drug is one of the few interventions with a clear survival benefit.
key_points: Detachment under ten per cent, ten to thirty per cent and over thirty per cent define the spectrum
Latency is one to four weeks and a febrile prodrome precedes the rash
Mucosal involvement at two or more sites with a positive Nikolsky sign is characteristic
Stopping the drug early is one of the few interventions that improves survival
Ophthalmology review within days prevents permanent ocular scarring
explanation.pearls: Lamotrigine must be titrated slowly over at least six weeks, and the starting dose is halved when it is combined with valproate, because valproate inhibits lamotrigine glucuronidation and roughly doubles its concentration.

subtopic_detail: recurrent severe abdominal pain with a soft abdomen, hyponatraemia and new proximal weakness after a sulfonamide antibiotic
stem:
You are the medical registrar asked to see a 27-year-old woman in the emergency department with four days of severe generalised abdominal pain and repeated vomiting. She has been unable to keep anything down and has eaten almost nothing.

This is her third presentation with the same pain in eighteen months. A diagnostic laparoscopy eight months ago was entirely normal and she was told the pain was functional. Five days ago her general practitioner started trimethoprim with sulfamethoxazole for a urinary tract infection. She has also been following a strict low carbohydrate diet for three weeks. Today she cannot lift her arms above her head to tie her hair and her grip has weakened. She is agitated and tearful and keeps asking to go home. Her partner mentions that the urine in the bottle by her bed went a deep reddish brown after sitting on the windowsill overnight.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118, blood pressure 156/94, respiratory rate 20, SpO2 99 per cent in air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft with generalised tenderness but no guarding or rebound, bowel sounds present, proximal upper limb power 3 out of 5 with reduced biceps and supinator reflexes, sensation intact, no rash and no basophilic stippling reported on film
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 121 mmol/L (135 to 145), potassium 3.6 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.2), creatinine 64 micromol/L (45 to 90), lipase and amylase within normal limits, haemoglobin 134 g/L (120 to 160), beta human chorionic gonadotropin negative, computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis with contrast reported as normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Repeat computed tomography of the abdomen with oral and intravenous contrast
options.rationale: A normal contrast study three days into the illness, a soft abdomen without peritonism and a previously normal laparoscopy together make an intra abdominal structural cause very unlikely. Repeating the scan will not explain the hyponatraemia, the hypertension or the motor weakness. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Radiologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Radiologists

options.text: Venous blood lead concentration with a blood film examined for basophilic stippling
options.rationale: Lead poisoning is the closest mimic, causing colicky abdominal pain with a motor neuropathy, but it produces a microcytic anaemia with basophilic stippling and does not cause a syndrome of inappropriate antidiuresis, and her haemoglobin and film are normal. It is also not precipitated by starting a drug or by fasting. (Source: Royal College of Pathologists of Australasia)
source_refs: Royal College of Pathologists of Australasia

options.text: Lumbar puncture for cerebrospinal fluid protein and cell count to assess her weakness
options.rationale: An acute motor neuropathy makes Guillain Barre syndrome a reasonable thought, but that illness is ascending and predominantly distal, does not begin with four days of abdominal pain, and does not cause hypertension with hyponatraemia. Her weakness is proximal and upper limb predominant, which is the opposite of the usual pattern. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Urine drug screen with paired serum and urine osmolality to explain the low sodium
options.rationale: Paired osmolalities would confirm inappropriate antidiuresis but stop at describing a mechanism that is itself a manifestation of the underlying disease rather than an answer. Investigating the sodium in isolation leaves the pain, the hypertension and the weakness unexplained. (Source: Kidney Health Australia)

options.text: Urinary porphobilinogen measured on a fresh sample protected from light exposure
options.rationale: Recurrent severe abdominal pain with a soft abdomen and normal imaging, autonomic features of tachycardia and hypertension, a motor neuropathy, hyponatraemia and psychiatric disturbance, all following a sulfonamide and a period of carbohydrate restriction, is the acute neurovisceral attack of a hepatic porphyria. Porphobilinogen rises markedly during an attack and the sample is shielded from light because the porphyrins degrade on exposure. (Source: Royal College of Pathologists of Australasia)
source_refs: Royal College of Pathologists of Australasia

explanation.summary: Acute intermittent porphyria is the commonest of the acute hepatic porphyrias and results from partial deficiency of hydroxymethylbilane synthase, so that induction of hepatic haem synthesis floods the pathway with neurotoxic porphyrin precursors. Attacks are provoked by anything that induces the rate limiting enzyme, principally drugs including sulfonamides, barbiturates, carbamazepine, phenytoin, rifampicin and progestogens, along with fasting or carbohydrate restriction, alcohol, infection and the luteal phase of the menstrual cycle. The attack is neurovisceral rather than cutaneous: severe abdominal pain with a soft abdomen and no peritonism, autonomic overactivity with tachycardia and hypertension, a predominantly motor and often proximal neuropathy that can ascend to respiratory failure, hyponatraemia from inappropriate antidiuresis, and psychiatric disturbance ranging from anxiety to frank psychosis. Patients are characteristically investigated repeatedly and frequently undergo a negative laparotomy or laparoscopy before the diagnosis is considered, so a history of recurrent unexplained abdominal pain with normal imaging is itself a diagnostic clue. Treatment is withdrawal of the precipitant, high carbohydrate intake, and intravenous haem arginate, with careful attention to using only drugs known to be safe in porphyria.
key_points: Pain out of proportion with a soft abdomen and normal imaging is the hallmark
Autonomic features, motor neuropathy, hyponatraemia and psychiatric change complete the syndrome
Sulfonamides, anticonvulsants, rifampicin, progestogens, fasting and alcohol precipitate attacks
Urinary porphobilinogen during the attack is the diagnostic test and the sample must be light protected
Treatment is removal of the precipitant, carbohydrate loading and intravenous haem arginate
explanation.pearls: Every drug prescribed during and after an attack must be checked against a porphyria safe list, and among the analgesics morphine and paracetamol are safe while among the antiemetics ondansetron is safe but metoclopramide is a recognised precipitant.

sources.label: Royal College of Pathologists of Australasia
Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Radiologists

subtopic_detail: deciding what must be excluded before iron is replaced in a middle aged man with microcytic anaemia
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 58-year-old man who has become breathless walking up the hill to his house over the past three months. He puts it down to getting older and having given up cycling.

He has no abdominal pain, has not noticed any blood in his stool and says his bowels are unchanged. He takes no aspirin, no anti-inflammatory medication and no anticoagulant. He drinks four standard drinks a week and has never had a gastroscopy or colonoscopy. He has not been invited to bowel screening because he moved address. His father had a colectomy in his sixties for a reason he was never told. His weight is stable and he has no night sweats. His examination shows conjunctival pallor with no abdominal mass, no organomegaly and a normal rectal examination.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 86/min, blood pressure 132/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Conjunctival pallor, no jaundice, no koilonychia, abdomen soft with no mass or organomegaly, rectal examination normal with brown stool
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 96 g/L (130-175), mean cell volume 72 fL (80-100), ferritin 7 micrograms/L (30-300), transferrin saturation 6 percent (16-45), C reactive protein 2 mg/L (less than 5), coeliac serology negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start oral iron and recheck the full blood count after three months of therapy
options.rationale: Iron replacement is certainly needed and will correct the haemoglobin, and giving it without investigating the cause allows a colonic malignancy to progress while the blood count normalises and falsely reassures both of you. Replacement and investigation proceed together rather than one instead of the other. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Iron deficiency anaemia)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Iron deficiency anaemia

options.text: Refer for gastroscopy and colonoscopy while commencing iron replacement
options.rationale: Iron deficiency anaemia in a man or a postmenopausal woman is gastrointestinal blood loss until proven otherwise, and bidirectional endoscopy is the standard investigation because a right sided colonic carcinoma can bleed occultly for months without altering bowel habit or producing visible blood. His family history of colectomy in his sixties raises that risk further, and iron is started at the same time rather than afterwards. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Iron deficiency anaemia)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Iron deficiency anaemia

options.text: Request a faecal occult blood test and investigate further only if it is positive
options.rationale: Faecal occult blood testing is a population screening tool for asymptomatic people, and using it in someone who already has established iron deficiency anaemia adds nothing, because the anaemia is itself the evidence of blood loss. A negative result would not exclude a tumour and would delay endoscopy. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Iron deficiency anaemia)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Iron deficiency anaemia

options.text: Perform haemoglobin electrophoresis before any endoscopic investigation is arranged
options.rationale: Electrophoresis distinguishes thalassaemia trait from iron deficiency in an unexplained microcytosis, and that question is already answered here by a ferritin of 7 micrograms/L with a transferrin saturation of 6 percent. Thalassaemia trait also does not deplete iron stores. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Iron deficiency anaemia)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Iron deficiency anaemia

options.text: Arrange an intravenous iron infusion and review his symptoms again in six weeks
options.rationale: Intravenous iron is appropriate where oral iron has failed or is not tolerated, or where rapid correction is needed, and the route of replacement is not the issue in this case. Whichever route is chosen, the underlying source of loss still has to be found. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Iron deficiency anaemia)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Iron deficiency anaemia

explanation.summary: Iron deficiency anaemia in an adult man or a postmenopausal woman is gastrointestinal blood loss until proven otherwise, and the absence of visible bleeding or altered bowel habit is expected rather than reassuring. Right sided colonic tumours characteristically present exactly this way, with occult blood loss and anaemia rather than obstruction, because the caecum is capacious and the stool is liquid there. Bidirectional endoscopy is the standard investigation, because upper and lower tract lesions are both common and synchronous pathology occurs. Coeliac serology should be checked, as here, since coeliac disease is a treatable non bleeding cause. Iron replacement is started at the same time as referral, never instead of it.
key_points: Iron deficiency anaemia in men and postmenopausal women mandates investigation of the gastrointestinal tract.
Right sided colonic tumours bleed occultly without altering bowel habit or producing visible blood.
Bidirectional endoscopy is required because upper and lower lesions are both common and may coexist.
Faecal occult blood testing adds nothing once iron deficiency anaemia is established.
Coeliac serology should be checked as a treatable non bleeding cause of iron deficiency.
explanation.pearls: Never accept a normal rectal examination and a normal bowel habit as a reason to skip colonoscopy in a man with iron deficiency anaemia, because a caecal carcinoma bleeds into liquid stool in a capacious lumen and typically declares itself only as breathlessness and a low ferritin.

sources.label: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Iron deficiency anaemia
Cancer Council Australia: Colorectal cancer guidelines

subtopic_detail: completing assessment of a discrete breast lump when the imaging report is reassuring but the clinical findings are not
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 47-year-old woman who found a lump in her left breast three weeks ago while showering. She has no breast pain and no nipple discharge.

She has no family history of breast or ovarian cancer and has never taken hormonal contraception. She had a screening mammogram eighteen months ago that was reported as normal. On examination there is a 2 cm firm irregular mass in the upper outer quadrant of the left breast that does not move freely within the breast tissue, and there is mild tethering of the overlying skin when she raises her arm. There is no palpable axillary lymphadenopathy. Bilateral mammography and targeted ultrasound arranged by a colleague last week are both reported as showing no discrete abnormality in dense breast tissue.

data_table.Examination: 2 cm firm irregular mass in the left upper outer quadrant with reduced mobility and skin tethering on arm elevation, no nipple retraction or discharge, no axillary or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy, right breast normal
data_table.Investigations: Bilateral mammography reports heterogeneously dense breast tissue with no discrete abnormality, targeted left breast ultrasound reports no discrete lesion identified

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer for core biopsy of the palpable abnormality despite the imaging result
options.rationale: Triple assessment requires clinical examination, imaging and tissue sampling to be concordant, and when any one component is suspicious the assessment is incomplete until tissue has been obtained regardless of how reassuring the others are. Mammographic sensitivity falls substantially in dense breast tissue and some cancers, particularly invasive lobular carcinoma, infiltrate diffusely without forming a discrete sonographic mass, so a negative scan cannot override a tethered irregular lump. (Source: Cancer Australia: Investigation of a new breast symptom)
source_refs: Cancer Australia: Investigation of a new breast symptom

options.text: Reassure her that both imaging tests are normal and review her in three months
options.rationale: Interval review is appropriate for a clinically benign finding such as a soft mobile lump in a younger woman with concordant normal imaging. Discordance between a suspicious examination and negative imaging is the specific situation in which reassurance is unsafe, and three months allows nodal progression. (Source: Cancer Australia: Investigation of a new breast symptom)
source_refs: Cancer Australia: Investigation of a new breast symptom

options.text: Repeat the mammogram with tomosynthesis views in a further six months' time
options.rationale: Tomosynthesis does improve cancer detection in dense tissue and would be a sensible adjunct at the time of assessment rather than a reason to wait half a year. Repeating imaging also cannot substitute for the histology that a palpable suspicious mass requires. (Source: Cancer Australia: Investigation of a new breast symptom)
source_refs: Cancer Australia: Investigation of a new breast symptom

options.text: Arrange fine needle aspiration cytology of the mass in the practice this week
options.rationale: Fine needle aspiration can confirm malignancy but cannot distinguish invasive carcinoma from ductal carcinoma in situ, and it does not provide receptor status or grade, which now guide neoadjuvant decisions. Core biopsy has superseded it as the sampling method for a solid breast mass. (Source: Cancer Australia: Investigation of a new breast symptom)
source_refs: Cancer Australia: Investigation of a new breast symptom

options.text: Check her serum tumour markers and refer only if the results are abnormal
options.rationale: Serum markers such as CA15-3 have no role in the diagnosis of breast cancer because they lack both sensitivity and specificity in early disease, and they are used only for monitoring established metastatic disease. A normal result would wrongly reassure everyone involved. (Source: Cancer Australia: Investigation of a new breast symptom)
source_refs: Cancer Australia: Investigation of a new breast symptom

explanation.summary: Triple assessment of a breast lump comprises clinical examination, imaging and tissue sampling, and its central principle is concordance: if any component raises suspicion, the workup continues until that suspicion is resolved by histology. This woman has a firm irregular tethered mass, which is a clinically suspicious finding regardless of what the imaging shows. Mammographic sensitivity is substantially reduced in heterogeneously dense breast tissue, and invasive lobular carcinoma characteristically infiltrates in single file without forming a discrete mass on either mammography or ultrasound. A normal screening mammogram eighteen months earlier does not exclude an interval cancer. Core biopsy rather than fine needle aspiration is the sampling method, because it distinguishes invasive from in situ disease and provides grade and receptor status.
key_points: Triple assessment requires concordance, and any suspicious component mandates tissue sampling.
Mammographic sensitivity is substantially reduced in dense breast tissue.
Invasive lobular carcinoma may infiltrate without forming a discrete mass on mammography or ultrasound.
Core biopsy is preferred over fine needle aspiration because it provides grade, invasion status and receptor status.
Serum tumour markers have no role in diagnosing early breast cancer.
explanation.pearls: Refer a clinically suspicious breast lump for core biopsy even when mammography and ultrasound are both reported as normal, because discordance is resolved by histology and invasive lobular carcinoma in dense tissue is the classic cancer that both imaging modalities miss.

subtopic_detail: separating an arrhythmic cause of collapse from a benign faint using the history and electrocardiogram
stem:
You are the emergency registrar seeing a 34-year-old man who collapsed while playing indoor soccer an hour ago. His teammates say he dropped without warning, was briefly stiff with a few jerks, and was fully alert within thirty seconds.

He had no warmth, nausea, tunnel vision or sweating beforehand, and he does not remember falling. He has had two similar episodes in the past year, one while sprinting for a bus and one while swimming, both of which he attributed to dehydration. He has no tongue biting, no incontinence and no confusion afterwards. His father died suddenly at 41 while jogging and was never autopsied. He takes no medication and uses no drugs. He is currently asymptomatic with normal observations, and his examination reveals a systolic murmur that becomes louder when he stands up from squatting.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 72/min, blood pressure 124/76 mmHg lying and 122/74 mmHg standing, respiratory rate 15/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Ejection systolic murmur at the left sternal edge increasing on standing from squatting and on Valsalva, jerky carotid upstroke, no ankle oedema, chest clear, neurological examination normal
data_table.Investigations: Electrocardiogram shows voltage criteria for left ventricular hypertrophy with deep T wave inversion in the lateral leads, electrolytes and troponin within normal limits, capillary glucose 5.1 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Discharge with advice on hydration and salt intake for a vasovagal tendency
options.rationale: Reflex syncope is common and is managed this way, and it is identified by a prodrome of warmth, nausea, sweating or visual greying, by an upright provoking situation such as prolonged standing or venepuncture, and by a normal heart and electrocardiogram. Syncope occurring during exertion without any prodrome is the opposite pattern and is never attributed to a reflex cause. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Arrange outpatient tilt table testing to confirm a neurally mediated mechanism
options.rationale: Tilt testing is used for recurrent unexplained syncope where a reflex mechanism is suspected and the cardiac workup is clean. Using it in a man with exertional syncope, a family history of sudden death and an abnormal electrocardiogram risks a falsely reassuring positive result while he remains at risk of sudden death. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Load with an antiepileptic and refer to neurology for outpatient investigation
options.rationale: Brief stiffening with a few jerks is common in syncope of any cause once cerebral perfusion falls, and it is not evidence of epilepsy. A genuine seizure is suggested by tongue biting, incontinence and postictal confusion lasting minutes, and he recovered fully within thirty seconds. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Admit for continuous cardiac monitoring with urgent inpatient echocardiography
options.rationale: Syncope during exertion with no prodrome, a family history of sudden death under 50, a murmur that increases with reduced preload and an electrocardiogram showing hypertrophy with lateral T wave inversion together identify a structural cardiac cause with a real risk of ventricular arrhythmia. Admission with telemetry protects him while echocardiography defines the outflow tract and wall thickness, and this pathway also captures the family screening that a heritable cardiomyopathy requires. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Fit a 24 hour ambulatory monitor and review him in the clinic next week
options.rationale: Ambulatory monitoring is reasonable for infrequent palpitations or for syncope judged to be low risk, and a 24 hour recording is very unlikely to capture an event that has occurred three times in a year. Sending him home while awaiting the result leaves him unmonitored during the interval in which he is most at risk. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

explanation.summary: Most syncope is reflex and benign, so the clinical task is to identify the minority in whom it signals a risk of sudden death. The high risk features present here are syncope occurring during exertion rather than after it, complete absence of a prodrome, recurrence, and a family history of sudden death under 50 years. Examination adds a murmur that becomes louder on standing from squatting and on Valsalva, which indicates dynamic left ventricular outflow tract obstruction because reduced preload worsens it, in contrast to aortic stenosis where the murmur softens. The electrocardiogram showing left ventricular hypertrophy with deep lateral T wave inversion supports hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Brief myoclonic jerking during syncope is common and does not indicate epilepsy, and these patients need admission, telemetry and echocardiography rather than outpatient investigation.
key_points: Syncope during exertion, without prodrome, or with a family history of sudden death is high risk.
A murmur that increases with reduced preload indicates dynamic outflow obstruction rather than valvular stenosis.
Left ventricular hypertrophy with deep lateral T wave inversion suggests hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
Brief stiffening and jerking occur commonly in syncope and do not indicate a seizure.
Tongue biting, incontinence and prolonged postictal confusion distinguish a genuine seizure from syncope.
explanation.pearls: Ask whether the collapse happened during exertion or after it, because syncope during exertion points to a structural or arrhythmic cause needing admission, whereas syncope immediately after stopping exercise is usually reflex and benign.

subtopic_detail: managing a small solid pulmonary nodule found incidentally in a former smoker with no prior imaging
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 64-year-old woman after a computed tomography scan of the abdomen performed for suspected renal colic, which incidentally captured the lung bases and reported a 7 mm solid nodule in the right lower lobe with smooth margins.

She smoked fifteen cigarettes a day from age eighteen until she stopped nine years ago. She has no cough, no haemoptysis, no chest pain and no weight loss, and her exercise tolerance is unchanged. She has never had a chest radiograph or chest computed tomography before, so there is no earlier imaging for comparison. She has no history of malignancy and no known asbestos exposure. Her examination is normal with no lymphadenopathy, no clubbing and a clear chest. The radiologist notes no mediastinal lymphadenopathy and no pleural abnormality.

data_table.Examination: No clubbing, no cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy, chest clear on auscultation with equal expansion, no chest wall tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Computed tomography reports a 7 mm solid nodule in the right lower lobe with smooth margins, no mediastinal lymphadenopathy, no pleural effusion, full blood count and electrolytes within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer for computed tomography guided percutaneous biopsy of the nodule
options.rationale: Percutaneous biopsy is used for larger or more suspicious peripheral lesions where a tissue diagnosis will direct treatment, and at 7 mm the target is small enough that the non diagnostic rate is high while the pneumothorax risk is unchanged. Sampling is not justified before surveillance has shown whether the nodule is growing. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Lung cancer)

options.text: Arrange positron emission tomography to characterise the metabolic activity
options.rationale: Functional imaging is valuable for nodules above about 8 to 10 mm, and below that size its spatial resolution produces frequent false negatives because partial volume effects understate uptake. A negative scan at 7 mm would provide false reassurance rather than information. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Lung cancer)

options.text: Refer for bronchoscopy with endobronchial ultrasound and transbronchial sampling
options.rationale: Bronchoscopic sampling is suited to central lesions and to mediastinal nodal staging, and the yield for a small peripheral nodule without a bronchus leading to it is poor. There is also no nodal disease here to stage. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Lung cancer)

options.text: Reassure her that a nodule of this size in a former smoker requires no follow up
options.rationale: Discharge without follow up is appropriate for a nodule below about 5 mm in a low risk person, or for one with benign features such as dense central or laminated calcification or macroscopic fat. A 7 mm solid nodule in a former smoker with a substantial history sits above the threshold at which surveillance is recommended. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Lung cancer)

options.text: Interval computed tomography surveillance determined by nodule diameter
options.rationale: A solid nodule of this size carries a low but not negligible malignancy risk, and growth over time is the most useful discriminator available, so serial thin section computed tomography at intervals set by size and risk is the accepted approach. Surveillance continues for around two years because stability of a solid nodule over that period effectively excludes malignancy, whereas any interval growth prompts escalation to functional imaging or sampling. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Lung cancer)

explanation.summary: Incidental pulmonary nodules are found frequently as computed tomography use increases, and management is determined by nodule size, attenuation, morphology and the patient's risk of lung cancer. Comparison with any earlier imaging is the single most valuable first step because documented stability over two years effectively excludes malignancy in a solid nodule, and here no earlier imaging exists. For a solid nodule of this size in a person with a smoking history, interval computed tomography surveillance is recommended, with the interval determined by diameter and risk. Positron emission tomography is unreliable below about 8 to 10 mm because of partial volume effects, and biopsy of a 7 mm target has a high non diagnostic rate. Subsolid and part solid nodules follow different and longer surveillance schedules because indolent adenocarcinoma can grow very slowly.
key_points: Nodule size, attenuation, margin morphology and smoking history together determine management.
Documented stability of a solid nodule over two years effectively excludes malignancy.
Positron emission tomography is unreliable below about 8 to 10 mm because of partial volume effects.
Spiculated margins, upper lobe location and larger size increase the probability of malignancy.
Subsolid and part solid nodules require longer surveillance because indolent adenocarcinoma grows slowly.
explanation.pearls: Hunt for any previous chest imaging before arranging surveillance for an incidental nodule, because two years of documented stability on an old scan resolves a solid nodule immediately and spares the patient a further two years of interval computed tomography.

subtopic_detail: preventing acute urate nephropathy before treating a bulky haematological malignancy
stem:
You are the medical registrar admitting a 34-year-old man with a three week history of rapidly enlarging cervical and abdominal lymphadenopathy and night sweats. Biopsy has confirmed a high grade B cell lymphoma with a very high proliferation index, and chemotherapy is planned to start tomorrow.

He has a large abdominal nodal mass and hepatosplenomegaly. He has no history of gout and takes no regular medication. He is of Southern European background and his glucose 6 phosphate dehydrogenase level has been requested but has not yet returned. He is passing urine normally. His lactate dehydrogenase is markedly raised, his urate is elevated, his potassium and phosphate are at the upper end of normal and his corrected calcium is at the lower end. His creatinine is mildly raised and his urine output has been adequate.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 98/min, blood pressure 124/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 37.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Bulky cervical and axillary lymphadenopathy, abdominal mass palpable in the left upper quadrant, liver edge 4 cm below the costal margin, no oedema, no rash
data_table.Investigations: Lactate dehydrogenase 1 840 U/L (120-250), urate 0.58 mmol/L (0.20-0.42), potassium 5.1 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), phosphate 1.48 mmol/L (0.80-1.50), corrected calcium 2.12 mmol/L (2.10-2.60), creatinine 118 micromol/L (60-110)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management before chemotherapy begins?

options.text: Oral allopurinol with encouragement to increase his oral fluid intake
options.rationale: Allopurinol inhibits xanthine oxidase and so prevents the formation of new urate, which makes it appropriate prophylaxis for low and intermediate risk disease. It cannot remove the urate that has already accumulated, and oral fluids are inadequate for a patient whose urate is already raised with a rising creatinine. (Source: eviQ: Tumour lysis syndrome)

options.text: Prophylactic haemodialysis via a temporary catheter before the first cycle
options.rationale: Dialysis is used for established tumour lysis syndrome with refractory hyperkalaemia, severe acidosis, fluid overload or oliguric renal failure. Inserting a line and dialysing prophylactically exposes him to procedural risk when pharmacological prevention has not yet been tried. (Source: eviQ: Tumour lysis syndrome)

options.text: Intravenous sodium bicarbonate to alkalinise the urine and improve urate clearance
options.rationale: Urinary alkalinisation was standard practice and has been abandoned because raising the urinary pH increases the deposition of calcium phosphate in the renal tubules, worsening nephrocalcinosis in a patient who is already hyperphosphataemic. It also exacerbates the hypocalcaemia. (Source: eviQ: Tumour lysis syndrome)

options.text: Delay chemotherapy for one week and repeat the biochemistry before proceeding
options.rationale: Delay would be reasonable for a slow growing tumour requiring optimisation, and a high grade lymphoma with this proliferation index can double in days, so waiting increases both the tumour burden and the eventual lysis risk. The metabolic risk is managed alongside treatment rather than by postponing it. (Source: eviQ: Tumour lysis syndrome)

options.text: Intravenous hydration with rasburicase once the enzyme result has returned
options.rationale: Bulky rapidly proliferating disease with a markedly raised lactate dehydrogenase, an elevated urate and impaired renal function places him at high risk, and rasburicase converts existing urate to the far more soluble allantoin rather than merely preventing further production. Vigorous intravenous hydration to maintain high urine output is given alongside, and confirming glucose 6 phosphate dehydrogenase status first matters because rasburicase causes severe haemolysis and methaemoglobinaemia in deficient patients. (Source: eviQ: Tumour lysis syndrome)

explanation.summary: Tumour lysis syndrome occurs when rapid cell death releases intracellular contents, producing hyperkalaemia, hyperphosphataemia, hyperuricaemia and consequent hypocalcaemia, with acute kidney injury from urate and calcium phosphate deposition in the tubules. Risk is determined by tumour bulk, proliferation rate, baseline lactate dehydrogenase and urate, and pre-existing renal impairment, and this man is high risk on every count. Allopurinol prevents new urate formation and suits lower risk patients, whereas rasburicase enzymatically degrades urate already present and is indicated for high risk disease. Glucose 6 phosphate dehydrogenase status must be established first because rasburicase generates hydrogen peroxide and causes severe haemolysis in deficient individuals, who are more commonly of Mediterranean, African or South East Asian ancestry. Urinary alkalinisation has been abandoned because it promotes calcium phosphate precipitation, and vigorous hydration with close biochemical monitoring remains the foundation of prevention.
key_points: The metabolic signature is hyperkalaemia, hyperphosphataemia, hyperuricaemia and hypocalcaemia.
Allopurinol prevents new urate formation while rasburicase degrades urate already present.
Glucose 6 phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency is a contraindication to rasburicase because of severe haemolysis.
Urinary alkalinisation is no longer recommended because it promotes calcium phosphate deposition.
Vigorous intravenous hydration with frequent biochemical monitoring is the foundation of prevention.
explanation.pearls: Check glucose 6 phosphate dehydrogenase status before giving rasburicase, because the drug generates hydrogen peroxide and causes life threatening haemolysis and methaemoglobinaemia in deficient patients, who are disproportionately of Mediterranean, African or South East Asian ancestry.

subtopic_detail: preventing viral reactivation before rituximab in a patient with resolved hepatitis B infection
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 58-year-old man newly diagnosed with diffuse large B cell lymphoma who is due to start rituximab based chemotherapy next week.

He was born in Vietnam and came to Australia at nineteen. He has never had jaundice and has never been told he has a liver problem. His pre treatment screening shows hepatitis B surface antigen negative, hepatitis B core antibody positive and hepatitis B surface antibody positive at a protective level, with hepatitis B viral load undetectable. His alanine aminotransferase is normal, his liver ultrasound is normal and his hepatitis C and human immunodeficiency virus serology are negative. The haematology team have asked whether anything is needed before the first cycle.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 78/min, blood pressure 128/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: No jaundice, no stigmata of chronic liver disease, liver edge not palpable, no splenomegaly, cervical lymphadenopathy consistent with his lymphoma
data_table.Investigations: Hepatitis B surface antigen negative, core antibody positive, surface antibody positive at a protective level, hepatitis B viral load undetectable, alanine aminotransferase 24 U/L (less than 45), liver ultrasound normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management before starting his chemotherapy?

options.text: No specific action, since a negative surface antigen indicates cleared infection
options.rationale: A negative surface antigen with positive core antibody means the virus is controlled by the immune system rather than eradicated, because covalently closed circular viral DNA persists in hepatocyte nuclei indefinitely. Removing B cell mediated immune control is precisely what allows that reservoir to reactivate. (Source: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine)
source_refs: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine

options.text: Give a hepatitis B vaccine booster course before the first cycle of treatment
options.rationale: Vaccination generates surface antibody, which he already has at a protective level, and it does nothing about the intranuclear viral reservoir that reactivation arises from. Response to vaccination is also poor once chemotherapy has begun. (Source: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine)
source_refs: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine

options.text: Commence antiviral prophylaxis before the immunosuppression begins
options.rationale: Rituximab depletes B cells and carries one of the highest risks of hepatitis B reactivation of any agent, including reverse seroconversion in people whose surface antigen is negative and core antibody positive, and the resulting hepatitis can be fulminant and fatal. Entecavir or tenofovir started before the first cycle prevents this and is continued for at least twelve months after the last dose, because the risk persists while B cell recovery is incomplete. (Source: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine)
source_refs: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine

options.text: Monitor liver enzymes monthly and start an antiviral if the enzymes rise
options.rationale: Monitoring with on demand treatment is an accepted strategy only for patients at low reactivation risk, and it fails with rituximab because the viral load rises before the transaminases and the hepatitis can progress to liver failure faster than a monthly test detects. Waiting for enzyme rise means waiting for hepatocyte destruction to have begun. (Source: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine)
source_refs: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine

options.text: Replace rituximab with a regimen that avoids B cell depleting monoclonal therapy
options.rationale: Rituximab substantially improves survival in this lymphoma and omitting it would trade a curable cancer outcome for a risk that effective prophylaxis reduces to a very low level. The hepatitis risk is managed pharmacologically rather than by compromising the oncological regimen. (Source: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine)
source_refs: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine

explanation.summary: Hepatitis B is never fully eradicated after infection, because covalently closed circular viral DNA persists in hepatocyte nuclei and is held in check by immune surveillance rather than removed. A surface antigen negative, core antibody positive pattern therefore represents resolved rather than absent infection, and immunosuppression can allow reverse seroconversion with reappearance of surface antigen and a viral load. Rituximab and other B cell depleting agents carry among the highest reactivation risks, and the resulting hepatitis may be severe or fatal. All patients should be screened for surface antigen, core antibody and surface antibody before immunosuppression, and those at high risk receive entecavir or tenofovir prophylaxis started before treatment and continued for at least twelve months afterwards. Monitoring alone is reserved for low risk regimens, because viral load rises before transaminases do.
key_points: Covalently closed circular viral DNA persists in hepatocytes for life, so infection is controlled rather than cleared.
Core antibody positivity with a negative surface antigen indicates resolved infection at risk of reactivation.
Rituximab and other B cell depleting agents carry the highest reactivation risk.
Prophylaxis starts before immunosuppression and continues at least twelve months after the last dose.
Screening before immunosuppression should include surface antigen, core antibody and surface antibody.
explanation.pearls: Order hepatitis B core antibody rather than surface antigen alone before any B cell depleting therapy, because a patient who has cleared surface antigen still harbours intranuclear viral DNA and rituximab can drive reverse seroconversion into a fulminant hepatitis.

subtopic_detail: applying the diameter and growth thresholds for repair to an incidentally found aortic aneurysm in a fit older man
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 71-year-old man after an abdominal ultrasound arranged for intermittent right upper quadrant discomfort, which showed gallstones and an incidental infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm measuring 4.8 cm in maximum anteroposterior diameter.

He has no back pain and no abdominal pain related to the aneurysm, and his abdomen is not tender. He smoked twenty cigarettes a day for forty years and stopped two years ago. He has hypertension treated with perindopril and his blood pressure today is 138/82 mmHg. He walks his dog for an hour daily without limitation and lives independently. He has no family history of aneurysm. A scan performed eleven months ago for renal colic reported the aorta as 4.6 cm, which no one had mentioned to him.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 70/min, blood pressure 138/82 mmHg, respiratory rate 15/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft and non-tender with a pulsatile mass palpable above the umbilicus, femoral and pedal pulses present and equal, no abdominal bruit, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: Current ultrasound 4.8 cm infrarenal aneurysm, ultrasound eleven months ago reported 4.6 cm, total cholesterol 5.4 mmol/L (less than 5.5), creatinine 84 micromol/L (60-110)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer for urgent vascular surgical repair within the next two weeks
options.rationale: Urgent repair is indicated for a symptomatic, tender or ruptured aneurysm, and he has no pain and no tenderness with a stable growth rate. Operating at 4.8 cm exposes him to perioperative mortality that exceeds his current annual rupture risk. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Society for Vascular Surgery)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Society for Vascular Surgery

options.text: Reassure him and repeat the ultrasound only if he develops abdominal symptoms
options.rationale: Symptom triggered imaging fails because the first symptom of an abdominal aortic aneurysm is frequently rupture, which carries a mortality of around eighty percent when all prehospital deaths are counted. Surveillance exists precisely because the condition is silent until it is catastrophic. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Society for Vascular Surgery)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Society for Vascular Surgery

options.text: Arrange interval ultrasound surveillance with cardiovascular risk factor treatment
options.rationale: Repair is offered at 5.5 cm in men, for growth exceeding 1 cm in a year, or for symptoms, and at 4.8 cm growing 0.2 cm over eleven months he meets none of these, so surveillance at intervals of around six months is correct. The active part of management is cardiovascular, since smoking cessation is the single most effective measure for slowing expansion and statin and antihypertensive treatment address the coronary disease that is the commonest cause of death in these patients. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Society for Vascular Surgery)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Society for Vascular Surgery

options.text: Start a beta blocker specifically to slow the rate of aneurysm expansion
options.rationale: Beta blockade was studied for this purpose on the rationale of reducing aortic wall stress and randomised trials showed no reduction in expansion rate or rupture. It remains appropriate if indicated for another reason such as ischaemic heart disease, which he does not have. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Society for Vascular Surgery)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Society for Vascular Surgery

options.text: Order computed tomography angiography now to plan endovascular stent grafting
options.rationale: Computed tomography angiography is the planning study once the repair threshold is reached, as it defines neck anatomy and iliac access for stent grafting. Performing it eight months before he is likely to need it adds contrast and radiation exposure without changing anything today. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Society for Vascular Surgery)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Society for Vascular Surgery

explanation.summary: Elective repair of an infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm is offered at a maximum diameter of 5.5 cm in men, at around 5.0 cm in women, for expansion exceeding 1 cm per year, or for symptoms or tenderness regardless of size. Below those thresholds the annual rupture risk is lower than the perioperative mortality of repair, so surveillance is the correct approach, with ultrasound intervals shortening as the diameter increases. This man is at 4.8 cm with 0.2 cm of growth over eleven months, which is well within the surveillance range. The most effective intervention available to him is smoking cessation, which slows expansion and reduces rupture risk, and he has already achieved it. Optimising blood pressure and lipids matters because most patients with an aneurysm die of coronary disease rather than of rupture.
key_points: Repair thresholds are 5.5 cm in men, around 5.0 cm in women, growth over 1 cm per year, or symptoms.
Below the threshold the perioperative mortality of repair exceeds the annual rupture risk.
Smoking cessation is the single most effective measure for slowing aneurysm expansion.
Beta blockers have been trialled for expansion and do not slow it.
Most patients with an abdominal aortic aneurysm die of coronary disease rather than of rupture.
explanation.pearls: Treat an incidentally found aneurysm below 5.5 cm as a cardiovascular diagnosis rather than a surgical one, because the patient is statistically far likelier to die of coronary disease than of rupture, and smoking cessation does more to slow expansion than any drug that has been trialled.

sources.label: Australian and New Zealand Society for Vascular Surgery

subtopic_detail: investigating persistent symptoms twelve months after starting a gluten free diet for coeliac disease
stem:
You are the gastroenterology registrar reviewing a 42-year-old woman diagnosed with coeliac disease twelve months ago on duodenal biopsy showing subtotal villous atrophy. She started a gluten free diet immediately after diagnosis.

She reports that her bloating and loose stools improved for about four months and have since returned, occurring most days. She has not lost weight, has no nocturnal diarrhoea, no rectal bleeding and no fever. She eats out two or three times a week and buys packaged foods, and she has not seen a dietitian since the month after her diagnosis. Her tissue transglutaminase antibody was 128 units at diagnosis, fell to 34 at six months and is 41 units today. Her haemoglobin and ferritin have normalised on oral iron and her albumin is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 74/min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 15/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft and non-tender with mild distension, no mass, no lymphadenopathy, no dermatitis herpetiformis, body mass index 24 kg/m2 and unchanged from diagnosis
data_table.Investigations: Tissue transglutaminase antibody 128 units at diagnosis, 34 at six months and 41 today, haemoglobin 134 g/L (115-155), ferritin 68 micrograms/L (30-300), albumin 40 g/L (35-50), C reactive protein 3 mg/L (less than 5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer to a specialist dietitian to review adherence and hidden exposure
options.rationale: Continuing gluten exposure, usually inadvertent, accounts for the great majority of persistent symptoms after diagnosis, and a serology that has plateaued and then risen rather than normalising is the objective marker of ongoing exposure. Cross contamination in restaurant kitchens, shared toasters and gluten in sauces, medications and supplements are not identifiable without a specialist dietary history, which is why this precedes any further investigation. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Coeliac disease)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Coeliac disease

options.text: Start oral budesonide for presumed refractory coeliac disease and reassess
options.rationale: Refractory coeliac disease is treated with corticosteroid and is diagnosed only after persistent villous atrophy is demonstrated on repeat biopsy with strict adherence confirmed, which has not been established here. It is also rare, affecting a very small proportion of patients, and her rising serology points to exposure rather than to true refractoriness. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Coeliac disease)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Coeliac disease

options.text: Arrange computed tomography enterography to exclude small bowel lymphoma
options.rationale: Enteropathy associated T cell lymphoma is a recognised complication and is sought when there are alarm features such as weight loss, fever, night sweats, abdominal pain or a falling albumin. She has none of these and her weight, albumin and inflammatory markers are all normal. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Coeliac disease)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Coeliac disease

options.text: Trial a low fermentable carbohydrate diet for coexisting irritable bowel syndrome
options.rationale: Functional gut symptoms genuinely coexist with coeliac disease and a low fermentable carbohydrate approach helps those patients, and it is considered only once ongoing gluten exposure has been excluded. Layering a second restrictive diet onto an incompletely implemented first one makes both harder to follow. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Coeliac disease)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Coeliac disease

options.text: Repeat duodenal biopsy now to assess whether the villous architecture has recovered
options.rationale: Repeat biopsy has a place in assessing mucosal healing and is essential before diagnosing refractory disease, and performed while adherence is unverified it cannot distinguish ongoing exposure from true refractoriness. The dietary assessment should come first so the biopsy, if still needed, can be interpreted. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Coeliac disease)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Coeliac disease

explanation.summary: Persistent or recurrent symptoms after a coeliac diagnosis are common, and continuing gluten exposure accounts for the large majority of cases. Serology is the most useful objective guide: antibody titres should fall progressively and normalise within about twelve months of strict adherence, so a plateau or a rise indicates ongoing exposure even when the patient believes the diet is strict. Common sources are cross contamination in shared kitchens and restaurants, and gluten in sauces, thickeners, medications and supplements, none of which emerge without a detailed dietary review. Refractory coeliac disease and enteropathy associated T cell lymphoma are important but rare, and both are pursued only after adherence has been verified or when alarm features are present. Coexisting functional gut symptoms are considered once exposure has been excluded.
key_points: Ongoing gluten exposure explains most persistent symptoms after a coeliac diagnosis.
Antibody titres should fall progressively and normalise within about twelve months of strict adherence.
A plateau or rise in serology is objective evidence of continuing exposure.
Refractory coeliac disease requires demonstrated persistent villous atrophy with verified adherence.
Weight loss, fever, night sweats, pain or falling albumin are alarm features prompting imaging for lymphoma.
explanation.pearls: Plot the coeliac serology trend rather than reading a single value, because a titre that falls and then plateaus or rises is objective evidence of continuing gluten exposure and sends the patient to a dietitian rather than to repeat endoscopy.

sources.label: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Coeliac disease

subtopic_detail: lowering an extreme triglyceride concentration after an episode of pancreatitis with lipaemic serum
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 38-year-old man on day four of an admission with acute pancreatitis. His abdominal pain has settled and he has resumed a light oral diet.

The laboratory reported his admission serum as grossly lipaemic. His abdominal ultrasound showed no gallstones and no biliary dilatation, and his admission alcohol history is twelve standard drinks most evenings for several years. He has type 2 diabetes managed with metformin alone and has not attended review for two years. His admission triglycerides were 46 mmol/L and are 18 mmol/L today after fasting and insulin infusion. His amylase peaked at four times the upper limit of normal. He has eruptive xanthomas over both elbows and his father had pancreatitis in his forties.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 84/min, blood pressure 132/82 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Crops of yellow papules over both elbows and knees, no tendon xanthomas, no corneal arcus, abdomen soft with mild epigastric tenderness, body mass index 33 kg/m2, hepatomegaly 3 cm below the costal margin
data_table.Investigations: Triglycerides 46 mmol/L on admission and 18 mmol/L today (less than 2.0), total cholesterol 9.8 mmol/L (less than 5.5), haemoglobin A1c 82 mmol/mol (less than 53), alanine aminotransferase 74 U/L (less than 45), thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, lipase raised

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment to prevent a further episode?

options.text: Fenofibrate with alcohol abstinence, dietary fat restriction and glycaemic control
options.rationale: Fibrates activate peroxisome proliferator activated receptor alpha and are the most effective agents for lowering triglycerides, reducing them by up to half, which is what is needed to move him below the threshold at which pancreatitis recurs. The drug alone is insufficient because alcohol, uncontrolled diabetes and dietary fat are each driving the hypertriglyceridaemia, so treating all four factors together is what prevents another episode. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: High intensity statin therapy titrated to a target low density lipoprotein level
options.rationale: Statins are the cornerstone of cardiovascular risk reduction and lower triglycerides only modestly, typically by ten to thirty percent, which is insufficient at this concentration. He will need one for cardiovascular protection, but it does not address the pancreatitis risk that is the immediate problem. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Ezetimibe added to dietary modification with lipid review in three months
