options.rationale: Ezetimibe inhibits intestinal cholesterol absorption and lowers low density lipoprotein cholesterol with minimal effect on triglycerides. It addresses the wrong lipid fraction for a man whose risk comes from chylomicronaemia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Regular therapeutic plasma exchange arranged as an ongoing outpatient program
options.rationale: Apheresis removes triglycerides rapidly and has a role in severe acute hypertriglyceridaemic pancreatitis, particularly with organ failure, and in refractory familial chylomicronaemia. As ongoing outpatient therapy it is invasive and resource intensive when modifiable drivers have not yet been addressed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Cholecystectomy on this admission to remove the likely source of the pancreatitis
options.rationale: Gallstones are the commonest cause of pancreatitis in Australia and cholecystectomy would be correct if they were present, and his ultrasound shows no stones and no biliary dilatation. Operating would not address the triglyceride concentration that caused this episode. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

explanation.summary: Hypertriglyceridaemia is the third commonest cause of acute pancreatitis after gallstones and alcohol, and the risk becomes appreciable above about 10 mmol/L and substantial above 20 mmol/L, when chylomicrons obstruct pancreatic capillaries and liberated free fatty acids injure acinar cells. Grossly lipaemic serum, eruptive xanthomas and a family history point to an underlying genetic predisposition unmasked by acquired factors, which here are alcohol, poorly controlled diabetes and obesity. Fibrates are the most effective triglyceride lowering drugs and are first line for preventing recurrence, with omega 3 fatty acids as a possible adjunct. Statins lower triglycerides only modestly and are prescribed for cardiovascular risk rather than for pancreatitis prevention. Controlling the acquired drivers is as important as the drug, because the genetic component alone rarely produces these concentrations.
key_points: Pancreatitis risk rises above about 10 mmol/L and becomes substantial above 20 mmol/L.
Eruptive xanthomas and lipaemic serum indicate chylomicronaemia.
Fibrates lower triglycerides by up to half and are first line for preventing recurrence.
Statins lower triglycerides only modestly and address cardiovascular rather than pancreatitis risk.
Alcohol, uncontrolled diabetes, obesity and certain drugs are the acquired drivers that must be corrected.
explanation.pearls: Treat the alcohol and the diabetes with the same urgency as the fibrate after hypertriglyceridaemic pancreatitis, because a genetic predisposition rarely produces a triglyceride concentration above 20 mmol/L without an acquired driver, and the drug alone will not keep him below the threshold for recurrence.

subtopic_detail: separating drug induced prolactin elevation from a lactotroph adenoma when the level sits in an ambiguous range
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 28-year-old woman whose periods stopped seven months ago. She has a negative pregnancy test and has noticed a milky discharge from both nipples.

She was started on risperidone 3 mg daily fourteen months ago for a psychotic illness and has been stable on it since, with no relapse and good adherence. She takes no other medication, no herbal preparations and no opioids. She has no headache and no visual symptoms. Her thyroid function is normal, her renal function is normal and she has no features of polycystic ovary syndrome. Her prolactin measured on two occasions without venepuncture stress is 2 400 mIU/L and then 2 550 mIU/L. Her formal visual field testing is normal and her body mass index is 23 kg/m2.

data_table.Examination: Bilateral expressible galactorrhoea, no goitre, no hirsutism or acne, visual fields full on formal perimetry, no cranial nerve abnormality, body mass index 23 kg/m2
data_table.Investigations: Prolactin 2 400 mIU/L and 2 550 mIU/L on two occasions (less than 500), thyroid stimulating hormone 1.8 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), creatinine 64 micromol/L (45-90), beta human chorionic gonadotrophin negative, oestradiol low

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange pituitary magnetic resonance imaging and liaise with her psychiatrist
options.rationale: Antipsychotic induced elevation usually sits below about 2 000 mIU/L, so a level above that range does not safely exclude a coexisting adenoma and imaging is required before the elevation is attributed to the drug. The psychiatrist must be involved because the alternatives, switching to a prolactin sparing agent such as aripiprazole or adding a dopamine agonist, both carry a risk of destabilising a psychotic illness that has been well controlled for over a year. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Stop the risperidone today and recheck the prolactin level in four weeks
options.rationale: Withdrawing the antipsychotic does test the hypothesis, and stopping it unilaterally in a woman whose psychotic illness has been stable for fourteen months risks relapse with far greater consequences than amenorrhoea. Any change to her antipsychotic belongs to a shared decision with the prescriber. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Start cabergoline to restore her menstrual cycle and continue the risperidone
options.rationale: Dopamine agonists lower prolactin effectively and are first line for a true lactotroph adenoma, and in a patient on an antipsychotic they directly oppose the dopamine blockade that is treating her illness and can precipitate psychotic relapse. They are used in this setting only with psychiatric agreement and after imaging. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Reassure her that this is an expected drug effect and no further action is needed
options.rationale: Attributing it to the drug without imaging accepts a diagnosis that the level does not support, and it also leaves prolonged hypo-oestrogenism untreated, which causes accelerated bone loss in a woman of 28. An expected adverse effect still requires management when it is causing harm. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Request macroprolactin screening on the stored sample before doing anything further
options.rationale: Macroprolactin is a biologically inactive complex that causes a spuriously high result and is worth excluding in an asymptomatic patient with an unexplained elevation. She has galactorrhoea, amenorrhoea and a low oestradiol, which demonstrate that the circulating prolactin is biologically active. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Antipsychotics that block the dopamine D2 receptor remove the tonic inhibition of lactotrophs by hypothalamic dopamine and raise prolactin, with risperidone, paliperidone and amisulpride the worst offenders while aripiprazole, quetiapine and clozapine are comparatively sparing. The difficulty is that drug induced elevation and a prolactinoma present identically with amenorrhoea and galactorrhoea, so the magnitude of the elevation is used as a guide. Drug induced levels usually remain below about 2 000 mIU/L, and levels above that range warrant pituitary imaging before the elevation is attributed to medication. Prolonged hypo-oestrogenism carries real consequences for bone density, so the problem cannot simply be accepted. Management requires collaboration with the psychiatrist, since both switching the antipsychotic and adding a dopamine agonist risk destabilising the underlying illness.
key_points: Dopamine D2 blockade removes tonic inhibition of lactotrophs and raises prolactin.
Risperidone, paliperidone and amisulpride raise prolactin most, while aripiprazole and quetiapine spare it.
Drug induced elevation usually stays below about 2 000 mIU/L, and higher levels warrant pituitary imaging.
Macroprolactin causes spuriously raised results but does not cause galactorrhoea or amenorrhoea.
Prolonged hypo-oestrogenism from hyperprolactinaemia accelerates bone loss and must be addressed.
explanation.pearls: Image the pituitary rather than blaming the antipsychotic when prolactin exceeds about 2 000 mIU/L, and never stop or add to a psychotropic regimen unilaterally, because both switching the agent and starting a dopamine agonist can precipitate relapse of a psychotic illness that has been stable for a year.

subtopic_detail: selecting which medicine to withdraw first in a frail older woman with recurrent falls and postural hypotension
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing an 84-year-old woman who has fallen three times in two months, most recently sustaining a skin tear to her forearm. She lives alone with daily assistance from her daughter.

She describes light headedness on standing from a chair and says the falls all happened shortly after she got up. Her medicines are perindopril 5 mg daily, amlodipine 5 mg daily, temazepam 10 mg at night taken intermittently, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, pantoprazole 40 mg daily and doxazosin 4 mg daily, which was started three months ago for nocturia. Her blood pressure is 142/80 mmHg sitting and 106/62 mmHg standing with reproduction of her symptoms. Her cognition is intact, her gait is steady when she is not light headed, her vitamin D is replete and her vision was checked this year.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 68/min, blood pressure 142/80 mmHg sitting and 106/62 mmHg standing with symptoms reproduced, respiratory rate 15/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Timed up and go 14 seconds, no focal neurological deficit, no cerebellar signs, no peripheral neuropathy, heart sounds dual with no murmur, skin tear dressed on the left forearm
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes and renal function within normal limits, 25 hydroxyvitamin D 76 nmol/L (50-150), electrocardiogram sinus rhythm with no conduction abnormality, morning cortisol within normal limits

lead_in: Which medication would you withdraw first?

options.text: Atorvastatin, since its benefit at her age is limited and it may cause myalgia
options.rationale: Statins are frequently reviewed in frail older people and may reasonably be stopped where life expectancy is short or the indication is primary prevention. They do not cause orthostatic hypotension, so withdrawing the statin would not address the mechanism producing her falls. (Source: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Deprescribing)
source_refs: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Deprescribing

options.text: Pantoprazole, since long term use is associated with fracture and infection risk
options.rationale: Long term proton pump inhibitor use without a continuing indication is a legitimate deprescribing target, associated with hip fracture, hypomagnesaemia and enteric infection. It is not a cause of postural blood pressure drop and is therefore not the first priority in a patient falling because of orthostatic symptoms. (Source: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Deprescribing)
source_refs: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Deprescribing

options.text: Amlodipine, since calcium channel blockade causes vasodilatation and ankle oedema
options.rationale: Amlodipine contributes to her overall blood pressure lowering and is a reasonable later target as her regimen is simplified. Dihydropyridines cause considerably less orthostatic hypotension than alpha blockade because they do not impair the reflex vasoconstriction that maintains pressure on standing. (Source: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Deprescribing)
source_refs: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Deprescribing

options.text: Doxazosin, since alpha blockade directly impairs the vasoconstrictor reflex on standing
options.rationale: Alpha one blockade prevents the peripheral vasoconstriction that normally maintains blood pressure on standing, making it the drug most specifically responsible for a symptomatic 36 mmHg systolic drop, and the temporal link to its introduction three months ago matches the onset of her falls. It also has the weakest indication in the list, having been started for nocturia in a woman for whom safer alternatives exist. (Source: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Deprescribing)
source_refs: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Deprescribing

options.text: Temazepam, since benzodiazepines roughly double the risk of falls in older adults
options.rationale: Benzodiazepine withdrawal is an important goal in anyone over 65 who is falling and this drug should certainly come out in due course. It is taken only intermittently and at night, whereas her falls occur on standing during the day with a reproducible postural drop, which points to a different mechanism. (Source: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Deprescribing)
source_refs: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Deprescribing

explanation.summary: Deprescribing in frail older people works best when it is mechanism driven rather than list driven, starting with the drug most closely linked to the presenting harm. This woman has symptomatic orthostatic hypotension with a 36 mmHg systolic drop that reproduces her symptoms, and her falls all occur on standing. Alpha one blockers such as doxazosin and prazosin directly prevent the reflex vasoconstriction that maintains blood pressure on standing, which makes them the most potent orthostatic offenders among common antihypertensives. The temporal association with its introduction three months ago and the weakness of its indication strengthen the case further. Several of her other medicines are legitimate deprescribing targets and should be addressed sequentially afterwards, changing one drug at a time so that the effect of each withdrawal can be judged.
key_points: Alpha one blockers impair reflex vasoconstriction and are potent causes of orthostatic hypotension.
A symptomatic postural drop of 20 mmHg systolic or 10 mmHg diastolic defines orthostatic hypotension.
Deprescribing should start with the drug most closely linked to the presenting harm.
Temporal association between starting a drug and the onset of symptoms is strong supporting evidence.
Withdraw one drug at a time so that the effect of each change can be attributed.
explanation.pearls: Measure lying and standing blood pressure before choosing which medicine to stop in a falling older patient, and start with the alpha blocker when there is a symptomatic postural drop, because alpha one blockade abolishes the reflex vasoconstriction that other antihypertensives leave intact.

sources.label: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Deprescribing

subtopic_detail: choosing therapy for amiodarone associated thyrotoxicosis when the gland shows absent vascularity
stem:
You are the endocrinology registrar asked to see a 68-year-old man who has taken amiodarone 200 mg daily for fourteen months for recurrent ventricular tachycardia after an infarct. His implanted defibrillator has fired twice in the past fortnight.

Over three months he has lost 9 kg despite a good appetite, and he has a fine tremor and heat intolerance. He grew up in Adelaide and has no history of iodine deficiency or previous thyroid disease. There is no neck swelling and no eye signs. His thyroid stimulating hormone is suppressed with a raised free thyroxine and free triiodothyronine. His thyroid peroxidase and thyrotrophin receptor antibodies are both negative, and colour flow Doppler of the thyroid shows a normal sized gland with absent parenchymal vascularity.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 108/min irregular, blood pressure 138/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 37.2 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Fine resting tremor, warm moist palms, no goitre or thyroid bruit, no proptosis or lid retraction, no pretibial change, defibrillator generator palpable below the left clavicle
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone less than 0.01 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), free thyroxine 42 pmol/L (10-20), free triiodothyronine 11.8 pmol/L (3.5-6.5), thyroid peroxidase and thyrotrophin receptor antibodies negative, colour flow Doppler shows absent parenchymal vascularity, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 48 mm/h (less than 20)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: High dose carbimazole alone titrated against repeat thyroid function testing
options.rationale: Thionamides block new hormone synthesis and are the treatment where excess iodine drives an overactive gland, typically in a patient with a pre-existing nodular goitre or latent Graves disease and preserved or increased Doppler flow. They cannot help where the gland is not synthesising hormone at all but is releasing preformed stores as it is destroyed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Oral corticosteroid for destructive thyroiditis with cardiology review of the amiodarone
options.rationale: Absent parenchymal vascularity with negative antibodies, no goitre and a raised erythrocyte sedimentation rate in an iodine replete patient indicates a destructive thyroiditis releasing preformed hormone, which responds to corticosteroid rather than to synthesis blockade. Whether to stop amiodarone is a separate cardiological judgement rather than an automatic step, because its half life of around one hundred days means cessation gives no rapid biochemical benefit while withdrawal risks recurrence of the ventricular tachycardia his defibrillator is already treating. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Cease amiodarone and observe, since the thyrotoxicosis will settle once it clears
options.rationale: Stopping the drug is often appropriate in principle and achieves nothing quickly, because amiodarone is highly lipophilic with a half life measured in months, so tissue iodine loading persists long after the last dose. Observation also leaves a thyrotoxic state that is actively destabilising his ventricular arrhythmia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Radioactive iodine ablation of the thyroid arranged as an outpatient procedure
options.rationale: Radioiodine requires the gland to take up iodine, and the enormous iodine load delivered by amiodarone saturates the sodium iodide symporter and suppresses radioiodine uptake to negligible levels for many months. The treatment is therefore ineffective in this setting regardless of which subtype is present. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Potassium perchlorate with lithium carbonate to block further iodide uptake
options.rationale: Perchlorate competitively inhibits iodide transport into the thyroid and is used as an adjunct in the iodine induced subtype or in mixed disease unresponsive to first line therapy, often alongside a thionamide. Blocking uptake is illogical in a destructive process where stored hormone is leaking from a gland that is not trapping iodide. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Amiodarone contains a large iodine load and is highly lipophilic, and it causes thyrotoxicosis by two mechanisms that require opposite treatments. Type 1 is iodine induced excess synthesis in a gland with pre-existing pathology such as a nodular goitre or latent Graves disease, and it shows normal or increased vascularity on colour flow Doppler with often positive antibodies, responding to thionamides with or without perchlorate. Type 2 is a destructive thyroiditis in which preformed hormone leaks from a damaged gland, showing absent vascularity, negative antibodies, no goitre and often a raised erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and it responds to corticosteroid. Mixed forms occur and are treated with both. Radioiodine is ineffective because the iodine load suppresses uptake, and stopping amiodarone produces no rapid benefit given a half life of around one hundred days, so the decision to continue it rests on the cardiac indication.
key_points: Type 1 is iodine induced hormone synthesis in an abnormal gland with preserved or increased Doppler vascularity.
Type 2 is a destructive thyroiditis with absent vascularity, negative antibodies and no goitre.
Thionamides treat type 1 and corticosteroid treats type 2, with both used in mixed disease.
Radioiodine is ineffective because the amiodarone iodine load suppresses thyroidal uptake for months.
Amiodarone has a half life of about one hundred days, so cessation gives no rapid biochemical benefit.
explanation.pearls: Use colour flow Doppler to separate the two forms of amiodarone induced thyrotoxicosis before prescribing, because absent parenchymal vascularity means a destructive thyroiditis that needs corticosteroid rather than carbimazole, and stopping the amiodarone changes nothing for months while risking the arrhythmia it was prescribed for.

subtopic_detail: sequencing thiamine and glucose in a high anion gap acidosis where the blood sugar is not raised
stem:
You are the emergency registrar seeing a 49-year-old man brought in by ambulance with two days of vomiting and abdominal pain. He drinks a bottle of spirits most days and has eaten almost nothing for three days since his last drink.

He is alert and oriented but looks unwell and dehydrated, with dry mucous membranes and reduced skin turgor. He has no focal abdominal tenderness, no guarding and no organomegaly. He has no history of diabetes and takes no medication. He has not taken any paracetamol, aspirin, antifreeze or methylated spirits, and his partner confirms there were no tablets or unusual containers at home. His venous gas shows a metabolic acidosis with a raised anion gap, his blood glucose is 4.1 mmol/L, his serum ketones are strongly positive, his lactate is mildly raised and his osmolar gap is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 114/min, blood pressure 104/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 26/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Dry mucous membranes with reduced skin turgor, alert and oriented with Glasgow coma scale 15, no ophthalmoplegia or nystagmus, gait not tested, abdomen soft with generalised mild tenderness, no asterixis
data_table.Investigations: pH 7.24 with bicarbonate 12 mmol/L (22-32) and anion gap 24 mmol/L, blood glucose 4.1 mmol/L (3.0-5.4), beta hydroxybutyrate strongly positive, lactate 3.1 mmol/L (less than 2.0), osmolar gap normal, ethanol not detected, paracetamol and salicylate not detected

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.text: Commence an intravenous insulin infusion with hourly blood glucose monitoring
options.rationale: Insulin is the treatment for diabetic ketoacidosis, where hyperglycaemia drives the osmotic diuresis and insulin deficiency drives the ketogenesis. This man has a normal blood glucose and is not insulin deficient, so an insulin infusion would cause profound hypoglycaemia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

options.text: Give intravenous sodium bicarbonate to correct the metabolic acidosis directly
options.rationale: Bicarbonate is reserved for severe acidaemia below a pH of about 7.1 with haemodynamic compromise, and it does not address the underlying ketogenesis. In this condition the acidosis resolves rapidly once substrate and volume are restored, so bicarbonate would risk rebound alkalosis and hypokalaemia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

options.text: Start fomepizole and arrange urgent haemodialysis for presumed toxic alcohol ingestion
options.rationale: Toxic alcohol poisoning produces a high anion gap acidosis and must always be considered, and it characteristically raises the osmolar gap and is not accompanied by strongly positive ketones. His osmolar gap is normal and there is no history of ingestion, which together make this very unlikely. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

options.text: Give oral carbohydrate and observe him for symptomatic improvement overnight
options.rationale: Restoring carbohydrate is the right principle and the oral route is unreliable in a man who has been vomiting for two days and is clinically dehydrated. He needs intravenous volume and substrate, and observation alone would leave both the ketosis and the volume deficit uncorrected. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

options.text: Intravenous thiamine followed by glucose containing fluid with volume replacement
options.rationale: Starvation and alcohol deplete glycogen and raise the ratio of reduced nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide, driving ketogenesis with a normal glucose, so the treatment is carbohydrate and volume rather than insulin. Thiamine must be given before the glucose because it is the cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase and a glucose load in a depleted patient consumes the remaining stores and can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

explanation.summary: Alcoholic ketoacidosis develops when a person with alcohol dependence stops eating and drinking, typically because of vomiting, and presents with a high anion gap metabolic acidosis, strongly positive ketones and a blood glucose that is normal or even low. The mechanism is glycogen depletion combined with a raised ratio of reduced nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide from ethanol metabolism, which suppresses gluconeogenesis and shifts the redox state towards beta hydroxybutyrate. Because beta hydroxybutyrate predominates, urine ketone dipsticks that detect acetoacetate may substantially understate the ketosis. Treatment is intravenous glucose and saline, which suppresses ketogenesis by restoring substrate and stimulating insulin, together with potassium, magnesium and phosphate replacement. Thiamine must precede the glucose, and toxic alcohol ingestion should be excluded by checking the osmolar gap.
key_points: A high anion gap ketoacidosis with a normal or low glucose distinguishes this from diabetic ketoacidosis.
Glycogen depletion and a raised reduced nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide ratio drive the ketogenesis.
Beta hydroxybutyrate predominates, so acetoacetate based urine dipsticks understate the ketosis.
Treatment is glucose and saline rather than insulin, with potassium, magnesium and phosphate replacement.
A normal osmolar gap argues against toxic alcohol ingestion as the cause of the acidosis.
explanation.pearls: Give thiamine before any glucose containing fluid in a patient with alcohol dependence, because glucose consumes the last of the thiamine as a cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase and can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy in someone who arrived neurologically intact.

subtopic_detail: the rebound that follows stopping a monoclonal antiresorptive without replacing it
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 68-year-old woman who has had six monthly denosumab injections for three years after a wrist fracture. She tells you she has decided to stop because she dislikes injections and feels her bones must be stronger now. Her last injection was five months ago and the next is due in four weeks.

She has had no new fractures and no back pain. Her repeat bone density scan last month showed a lumbar spine T score improved from minus 2.9 to minus 2.2. Her renal function is normal, her corrected calcium is normal and her vitamin D is adequate on supplementation. She has no history of dental problems and no upper gastrointestinal symptoms, and she takes no corticosteroids.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: No spinal tenderness, height unchanged from two years ago, no kyphosis, dentition in good condition
data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 2.35 mmol/L (2.10-2.60), creatinine 68 micromol/L (45-90), estimated glomerular filtration rate above 60, 25 hydroxyvitamin D 78 nmol/L (above 50), lumbar spine T score minus 2.2
data_table.Medications: Denosumab 60 mg subcutaneously six monthly, colecalciferol 1000 units daily, calcium from diet

lead_in: What should you recommend?

options.text: Stop now and start teriparatide instead, given her improved bone density result
options.rationale: Teriparatide is an anabolic agent reserved for severe osteoporosis with fractures despite antiresorptive treatment, and it is not funded in this situation. Giving it after this drug also produces a transient fall in bone density at the hip, which makes it a poor choice for the sequence. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Osteoporosis)

options.text: Start an oral bisphosphonate to begin when the next injection would have been due
options.rationale: Stopping this drug without replacement produces a rebound in bone turnover that returns density to baseline within a year and causes multiple vertebral fractures in a substantial minority of women. Following it with a bisphosphonate started around the time the next dose was due preserves the gain she has made and is the specific measure that prevents the rebound. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Osteoporosis)

options.text: Extend the dosing interval to twelve monthly as a compromise she may find acceptable
options.rationale: The suppression of bone turnover wanes markedly by about seven months after a dose, so a twelve monthly interval delivers a rebound period twice a year rather than avoiding one. Delay of more than a month beyond the due date is itself associated with vertebral fracture. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Denosumab)

options.text: Continue the injections indefinitely because stopping is never appropriate with this drug
options.rationale: Long term continuation is a reasonable plan for many patients and avoids the problem altogether, but it is not the only safe option and it disregards a clear preference she has expressed. The requirement is not that she continues forever, only that she does not stop without cover. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Osteoporosis)

options.text: Agree to stop and repeat her bone density scan in two years to check for any loss
options.rationale: Simply stopping is safe with the bisphosphonates, where the drug remains bound to bone for years and a drug holiday is a recognised strategy. It is unsafe with this agent, whose effect disappears entirely once dosing ceases, and a scan in two years would document the fractures rather than prevent them. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Osteoporosis)

explanation.summary: Denosumab inhibits osteoclast formation but is not incorporated into bone, so its effect depends entirely on continued dosing and disappears once it stops. Cessation is followed by a sharp rebound in bone turnover, loss of the accumulated density within about twelve months, and multiple vertebral fractures in a meaningful proportion of patients, often occurring together. This distinguishes it sharply from the bisphosphonates, which bind to bone mineral and continue to act for years after the last dose, allowing a planned drug holiday. Anyone stopping denosumab therefore needs an antiresorptive to follow it, usually an oral bisphosphonate or a zoledronic acid infusion, started around the time the next injection would have fallen due. Even routine delays of more than a month beyond the due date are associated with increased vertebral fracture risk.
key_points: Denosumab is not incorporated into bone and its effect stops when dosing stops.
Cessation causes rebound turnover and multiple vertebral fractures in a substantial minority.
Bisphosphonates bind to bone and permit a planned drug holiday, which this drug does not.
Follow on antiresorptive treatment is started around the time the next dose was due.
Delaying a dose beyond about a month is itself associated with vertebral fracture.
explanation.pearls: Treat a missed denosumab appointment as urgent rather than routine, because the fractures that follow cluster in the months after a delayed or abandoned dose and typically present as several vertebral fractures at once in a woman who had been doing well.

subtopic_detail: the fourth agent to add once three classes at maximum tolerated dose have not reached target
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 58-year-old man whose blood pressure remains above target despite three medicines. His home readings over the past fortnight average 158/94 mmHg, and his clinic reading today is 162/96 mmHg in both arms.

He takes perindopril 10 mg daily, amlodipine 10 mg daily and indapamide 2.5 mg daily, all at maximum tolerated doses, and his dispensing history confirms he collects all three every month. He does not use non-steroidal anti inflammatories, decongestants or liquorice, drinks two standard drinks a week and does not snore or have witnessed apnoeas. His renal artery imaging last year was normal and his aldosterone to renin ratio was not suggestive of primary aldosteronism. His potassium today is 3.9 mmol/L and his estimated glomerular filtration rate is above 60.

data_table.Vital signs: Blood pressure 162/96 mmHg both arms, pulse rate 72/min regular, other observations within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 29, no radiofemoral delay, no abdominal bruit, fundoscopy shows arteriovenous nipping without haemorrhage
data_table.Investigations: Potassium 3.9 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), sodium 140 mmol/L (135-145), creatinine 82 micromol/L (60-110), estimated glomerular filtration rate above 60, aldosterone to renin ratio not elevated
data_table.Medications: Perindopril 10 mg daily, amlodipine 10 mg daily, indapamide 2.5 mg daily

lead_in: Which medicine should you add next?

options.text: Spironolactone 25 mg daily with electrolytes rechecked within one to two weeks
options.rationale: In resistant hypertension where adherence is confirmed and secondary causes have been addressed, a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist lowers blood pressure more than a beta blocker or an alpha blocker added at the same point. His potassium at 3.9 mmol/L and preserved renal function make it safe to start, with a check within a fortnight because the combination with an angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor raises the risk of hyperkalaemia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Resistant hypertension)

options.text: Candesartan 16 mg daily in addition to his current angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor
options.rationale: Combining an angiotensin receptor blocker with an angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor gives little additional blood pressure reduction while significantly increasing hyperkalaemia, acute kidney injury and hypotension. This combination is avoided in current practice. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Hypertension)

options.text: Prazosin 1 mg twice daily, increasing the dose according to his tolerance
options.rationale: An alpha blocker is an accepted later line option and is useful where prostatic symptoms coexist. It is less effective than the preferred agent at this step and causes postural hypotension, so it sits behind it in the sequence. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Resistant hypertension)

options.text: Bisoprolol 5 mg daily, titrating upward according to his heart rate response
options.rationale: A beta blocker is a reasonable fourth agent where there is a compelling indication such as angina, prior myocardial infarction or heart failure, and it remains an option if the preferred agent cannot be used. Compared head to head at this point in the sequence it produces a smaller blood pressure reduction. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Resistant hypertension)

options.text: Substitute hydrochlorothiazide for the indapamide before adding any further agent
options.rationale: Swapping between thiazide type diuretics is worth considering when the current one is poorly tolerated, and indapamide is at least as effective as hydrochlorothiazide. Exchanging one for the other adds no blood pressure reduction and delays the step that will. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Hypertension)

explanation.summary: Resistant hypertension is defined as blood pressure above target despite three agents from different classes, including a diuretic, at maximum tolerated doses. Before adding a fourth drug, three things must be established: that the readings are real rather than white coat, that the patient is actually taking the medicines, and that contributing causes such as non-steroidal anti inflammatories, alcohol, sleep apnoea, renal artery disease and primary aldosteronism have been considered. Once that groundwork is done, a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist is the fourth agent with the best evidence, outperforming both a beta blocker and an alpha blocker when tested directly in this population. The main hazard is hyperkalaemia, particularly alongside an angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor or in renal impairment, so electrolytes are checked within one to two weeks of starting and after any dose increase. A starting potassium at the lower end of normal, as here, makes the choice comfortable.
key_points: Resistant hypertension means above target on three agents including a diuretic.
Confirm adherence and exclude contributing causes before adding a fourth drug.
A mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist outperforms a beta blocker or alpha blocker at this step.
Hyperkalaemia is the main hazard, so electrolytes are checked within one to two weeks.
Combining an angiotensin receptor blocker with a converting enzyme inhibitor is avoided.
explanation.pearls: Check the dispensing history before calling any hypertension resistant, because roughly half the patients referred for resistant hypertension are not taking what is on the list, and adding a fourth drug to a regimen nobody is taking achieves nothing but hyperkalaemia risk.

subtopic_detail: committing an asymptomatic patient to lifelong replacement on the strength of a single abnormal result
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 41-year-old woman who had thyroid function tested by an after hours service three weeks ago when she attended with a viral illness and fatigue. She feels completely well now and has come for the result.

Her thyroid stimulating hormone is 11.4 mIU/L with a free thyroxine of 14 pmol/L. She has no cold intolerance, constipation, weight change, hair loss or menstrual change, and her energy has returned to normal since the illness settled. She is not pregnant, is not trying to conceive and uses an intrauterine device. She takes no amiodarone, lithium or iodine containing preparation and has had no neck surgery or radiation. Her pulse is 68 beats per minute and there is no goitre or nodule palpable.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 68/min, blood pressure 116/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: No goitre or palpable nodule, no periorbital puffiness, reflexes normal with normal relaxation phase, no dry skin
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone 11.4 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), free thyroxine 14 pmol/L (10-20), full blood count and electrolytes within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start thyroxine 50 micrograms daily now and recheck the thyroid function in eight weeks
options.rationale: Persistent elevation above 10 mIU/L is an accepted indication to treat, so this is the right destination if the result is confirmed. Starting on a single sample taken during an acute illness commits an asymptomatic woman to lifelong medicine on a result that may well normalise by itself. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Thyroid disorders)

options.text: Arrange thyroid ultrasound to look for the structural cause of the abnormal result
options.rationale: Ultrasound assesses a palpable nodule or goitre and does not contribute to the assessment of thyroid function, since the biochemistry and antibodies establish the diagnosis. She has a normal neck on examination. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Thyroid disorders)

options.text: Repeat the thyroid function tests in six to eight weeks with thyroid peroxidase antibodies
options.rationale: A raised thyroid stimulating hormone with a normal free thyroxine resolves spontaneously in up to a third of people, particularly when the sample was taken during or shortly after an acute illness, which is what happened here. Confirming that the elevation persists before starting lifelong replacement is the point of the repeat, and the antibody result predicts who will progress to overt disease and therefore how closely to follow her. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Thyroid disorders)

options.text: Reassure her that she is well and repeat the thyroid function only if symptoms appear
options.rationale: Waiting for symptoms is appropriate for a mildly raised result in the range up to about 7 mIU/L in an older person, where the finding often reflects normal ageing. At this level the chance of progression to overt disease is considerably higher, so the result needs following up rather than discarding. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Thyroid disorders)

options.text: Measure free triiodothyronine now to establish whether her thyroid function is adequate
options.rationale: Free triiodothyronine is useful in suspected thyrotoxicosis, where it can be raised while thyroxine remains normal. It stays within range until hypothyroidism is far advanced and adds nothing to the assessment of an underactive gland. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Thyroid hormones)

explanation.summary: Subclinical hypothyroidism is a biochemical diagnosis defined by a raised thyroid stimulating hormone with a normal free thyroxine, and it is common enough that the first question is always whether the result is real and persistent. Up to a third of elevations resolve spontaneously, and acute illness in particular disturbs the axis, so a single abnormal sample taken during a viral illness cannot support a decision about lifelong treatment. The repeat is taken after six to eight weeks, alongside thyroid peroxidase antibodies, which identify autoimmune disease and predict progression to overt hypothyroidism. If the elevation persists above 10 mIU/L, treatment is generally offered even without symptoms. Different thresholds apply in pregnancy or when conception is planned, where treatment is started at lower levels and sooner.
key_points: Subclinical hypothyroidism means a raised stimulating hormone with a normal free thyroxine.
Up to a third of elevations resolve spontaneously, particularly after acute illness.
Confirm persistence at six to eight weeks before committing to lifelong replacement.
Thyroid peroxidase antibodies predict progression to overt hypothyroidism.
Pregnancy and planned conception use lower thresholds and earlier treatment.
explanation.pearls: Ask why the test was ordered before you act on it, because a thyroid stimulating hormone measured during an acute illness is the commonest reason a well person ends up on thyroxine for life, and the repeat six weeks later is normal surprisingly often.

subtopic_detail: numb feet in a patient whose long standing medicine interferes with absorption of a vitamin
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 63-year-old man with type 2 diabetes who has taken metformin 1 g twice daily for nine years. Over the past eight months he has noticed numbness and pins and needles in both feet, and more recently in his fingertips.

His most recent glycated haemoglobin was 6.8 per cent and has stayed below 7 per cent for six years. He drinks one beer on weekends and has no history of alcohol misuse. He has no back pain, no bladder symptoms and no weight loss. On examination he has reduced vibration sense to the mid shin bilaterally, absent ankle reflexes with preserved knee reflexes, and a positive Romberg test. His full blood count shows a mean cell volume of 103 fL with a normal haemoglobin, and his renal function, liver function and thyroid function are normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 74/min, blood pressure 128/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 15/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Reduced vibration and proprioception to mid shin, absent ankle reflexes with preserved knee reflexes, Romberg positive, no pallor, tongue normal
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 141 g/L (130-180), mean cell volume 103 fL (80-100), glycated haemoglobin 6.8 per cent, creatinine 78 micromol/L (60-110), thyroid stimulating hormone within range
data_table.Medications: Metformin 1 g twice daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, perindopril 5 mg daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Arrange nerve conduction studies to characterise the distribution of the neuropathy
options.rationale: Nerve conduction studies are valuable where the pattern is atypical, asymmetrical or progressing rapidly and the diagnosis remains unclear after blood tests. They cannot identify the cause of a symmetrical sensory neuropathy, and doing them first delays a result that is available from a single tube of blood. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Peripheral neuropathy)

options.text: Intensify glycaemic control, since neuropathy reflects inadequate long term diabetes management
options.rationale: Poor glycaemic control is the usual driver of diabetic neuropathy and improving it slows progression, which makes this a reflex answer in a diabetic patient. His control has been excellent for six years, and diabetic neuropathy does not explain a raised mean cell volume or prominent proprioceptive loss. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Diabetic neuropathy)

options.text: Measure serum vitamin B12 with folate and consider methylmalonic acid if borderline
options.rationale: Metformin reduces ileal absorption of vitamin B12 and the risk rises with dose and duration, making deficiency likely after nine years of treatment. The raised mean cell volume, the dorsal column signs with a positive Romberg test and the upper limb involvement all point away from diabetic neuropathy and toward a treatable deficiency that causes irreversible cord damage if missed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Vitamin B12 deficiency)

options.text: Check serum protein electrophoresis and free light chains for a paraproteinaemic cause
options.rationale: A paraprotein is a recognised cause of neuropathy and belongs in the second line workup, particularly in an older patient when the common causes have been excluded. It does not account for the macrocytosis and is far less likely than the deficiency his medicine predicts. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Peripheral neuropathy)

options.text: Request magnetic resonance imaging of the lumbar spine to exclude a compressive cause
options.rationale: Spinal imaging is indicated for asymmetrical signs, a sensory level, bladder or bowel disturbance or upper motor neurone findings, none of which he has. A symmetrical length dependent pattern with fingertip involvement does not localise to the lumbar spine. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Peripheral neuropathy)

explanation.summary: Metformin interferes with calcium dependent uptake of the vitamin B12 and intrinsic factor complex in the terminal ileum, and the resulting deficiency becomes common after several years of treatment, with risk rising with both dose and duration. Three features here argue against attributing the neuropathy to diabetes: glycaemic control has been excellent for years, the mean cell volume is raised, and the examination shows dorsal column involvement with a positive Romberg test and upper limb symptoms rather than a purely distal small fibre pattern. Deficiency is confirmed with a serum level, and methylmalonic acid or homocysteine resolve borderline results, because the serum assay is insensitive at the lower end of the range. Treatment is straightforward and neurological recovery depends heavily on how early it starts, since subacute combined degeneration of the cord becomes irreversible. Haematological abnormalities may be entirely absent even with established neurological disease.
key_points: Metformin impairs ileal absorption of vitamin B12 with risk rising over years of use.
Dorsal column signs and a positive Romberg test point away from diabetic neuropathy.
Macrocytosis may be present without anaemia, and may be absent altogether.
Methylmalonic acid or homocysteine clarify borderline serum levels.
Neurological recovery depends on early treatment before cord damage becomes fixed.
explanation.pearls: Check vitamin B12 in anyone who has taken metformin for more than four years and develops numb feet, because attributing it to diabetic neuropathy is the default that lets subacute combined degeneration progress to a deficit that replacement will never reverse.

subtopic_detail: recurrent falls where the medication list rather than a new diagnosis explains the symptom
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing an 81-year-old man who has fallen four times in three months, twice in the bathroom on getting up at night and twice when standing from a chair after lunch. He has not been injured beyond bruising and has not lost consciousness.

He describes feeling lightheaded and greying out for a few seconds on standing, which resolves if he sits back down. There is no chest pain, palpitation or exertional symptom, and the episodes never happen while he is sitting or walking. He takes perindopril, amlodipine, indapamide, temazepam for sleep and oxybutynin for urinary urgency. His lying blood pressure is 142/80 mmHg falling to 108/62 mmHg after three minutes standing, with a pulse rate rising only from 68 to 74 beats per minute. His electrocardiogram shows sinus rhythm with no conduction abnormality and his neurological examination is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Lying blood pressure 142/80 mmHg, standing blood pressure 108/62 mmHg at three minutes, pulse rate 68/min lying and 74/min standing, other observations within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Normal gait when observed unhurried, no cerebellar signs, proprioception intact, no cogwheel rigidity, timed up and go 14 seconds
data_table.Investigations: Electrocardiogram sinus rhythm with normal intervals, haemoglobin 137 g/L (130-180), sodium 138 mmol/L (135-145), creatinine 96 micromol/L (60-110), glucose within range
data_table.Medications: Perindopril 5 mg daily, amlodipine 5 mg daily, indapamide 2.5 mg daily, temazepam 10 mg at night, oxybutynin 5 mg twice daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange a 24 hour Holter monitor and an echocardiogram before changing any medicine
options.rationale: Cardiac investigation is warranted for syncope without warning, exertional symptoms, palpitations or an abnormal electrocardiogram, since arrhythmia and outflow obstruction are dangerous causes. His symptoms occur only on standing, reproduce with a documented postural drop and come with a normal trace, so the cause is already demonstrated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Syncope)

options.text: Start fludrocortisone to raise his standing blood pressure and continue the current regimen
options.rationale: Fludrocortisone has a place in orthostatic hypotension that persists after culprit drugs have been removed, usually where there is autonomic failure. Using it to counteract medicines that could simply be reduced adds supine hypertension, oedema and hypokalaemia to the problem. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Falls in older people)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Falls in older people

options.text: Request computed tomography of the brain to exclude an intracranial cause for the falls
options.rationale: Imaging is indicated after a fall with head injury on anticoagulation, with focal neurological signs or with unexplained cognitive decline. A normal neurological examination and a clear postural mechanism do not justify it, and a chronic subdural collection would not produce symptoms confined to the act of standing. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Falls in older people)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Falls in older people

options.text: Reduce his antihypertensive burden and plan a staged withdrawal of the sedative and the anticholinergic
options.rationale: A fall of 34 mmHg systolic on standing without a compensatory rise in heart rate confirms orthostatic hypotension, and three antihypertensives together with a sedative and an anticholinergic explain it entirely. Medication reduction is the intervention with the best evidence for preventing falls in this situation, and the withdrawal is staged because stopping a benzodiazepine abruptly causes its own problems. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Falls in older people)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Falls in older people

options.text: Refer for a falls prevention exercise program as the single intervention needed
options.rationale: Strength and balance exercise reduces falls in older people and should form part of his plan alongside the medication review. On its own it does nothing about a blood pressure that drops 34 mmHg every time he stands up at night. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Falls in older people)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Falls in older people

explanation.summary: Orthostatic hypotension is defined as a fall of at least 20 mmHg systolic or 10 mmHg diastolic within three minutes of standing, and the absence of a compensatory tachycardia here suggests the response is blunted by his medicines. Five of his drugs contribute: three lower blood pressure directly, the benzodiazepine impairs postural reflexes and increases night time falls, and the anticholinergic adds cognitive impairment and further postural drop. Medication review with staged withdrawal has the strongest evidence of any single intervention for falls of this kind, and the timing of his falls at night and after meals fits the pattern precisely. Exercise programs, home hazard assessment and vitamin D where deficient are complementary rather than alternatives. Cardiac and neurological investigation is reserved for syncope without warning, exertional symptoms or focal signs.
key_points: Orthostatic hypotension is a drop of 20 mmHg systolic or 10 mmHg diastolic within three minutes.
An absent compensatory tachycardia suggests drugs or autonomic impairment.
Benzodiazepines and anticholinergics contribute to falls independently of blood pressure.
Medication reduction has the strongest single evidence for preventing falls of this type.
Postprandial and nocturnal timing supports a postural rather than a cardiac mechanism.
explanation.pearls: Measure lying and standing blood pressure at three minutes rather than immediately, because the drop that explains the falls frequently appears only after the first minute and a normal reading taken straight after standing sends the patient off for a Holter monitor they do not need.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Falls in older people

subtopic_detail: an evening urge to move the legs where a routine blood test changes the treatment entirely
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 55-year-old woman with eighteen months of an uncomfortable crawling sensation in both legs that comes on when she sits down in the evening and is worse in bed. She has to get up and walk around, which relieves it completely until she lies down again.

She is losing about two hours of sleep most nights and is exhausted at work. The sensation is not painful and there is no burning or numbness. She has heavy periods that she has never had investigated. She takes no antihistamines, antidepressants or antiemetics. Her neurological examination is normal with intact reflexes, power and sensation, and her peripheral pulses are present. Her full blood count shows a haemoglobin of 119 g/L with a mean cell volume of 78 fL, and her ferritin is 22 micrograms/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Normal power, tone, reflexes and sensation in both legs, pedal pulses present, no varicosities, no calf tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 119 g/L (115-155), mean cell volume 78 fL (80-100), ferritin 22 micrograms/L (30-200), transferrin saturation 14 per cent (15-45), creatinine 66 micromol/L (45-90), thyroid stimulating hormone within range

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first treatment?

options.text: Start pramipexole at a low dose taken two hours before her symptoms usually begin
options.rationale: Dopamine agonists work quickly and were once first line, which is why they remain a tempting answer. Long term use causes augmentation, in which symptoms begin earlier in the day, spread to the arms and become more severe than before treatment, so they are no longer preferred and are never started before iron status is corrected. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Drugs for restless legs)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook: Drugs for restless legs

options.text: Replace iron with the aim of raising the ferritin well above the lower limit of normal
options.rationale: Iron deficiency is the commonest reversible cause of these symptoms because brain iron is required for dopamine synthesis, and replacement often resolves them without any specific drug. The treatment target is higher than the laboratory lower limit, around 75 micrograms per litre or more, and her heavy periods with a low mean cell volume explain the deficiency and need addressing in their own right. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Restless legs syndrome)

options.text: Prescribe temazepam at night to restore her sleep while the symptoms are investigated
options.rationale: Sedatives may help a patient sleep through mild symptoms and are occasionally used as an adjunct in specialist practice. They do not address the urge to move, and starting a benzodiazepine in a woman facing months of symptoms risks dependence for a condition with a treatable cause. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Restless legs syndrome)

options.text: Arrange overnight polysomnography to document periodic limb movements during sleep
options.rationale: The diagnosis is clinical, resting on an urge to move with an unpleasant sensation, worse at rest and in the evening and relieved by movement. A sleep study is reserved for suspected coexisting sleep apnoea or an unclear picture, and periodic limb movements are neither necessary nor sufficient for the diagnosis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Restless legs syndrome)

options.text: Start gabapentin at night, titrating the dose upward according to her symptom response
options.rationale: An alpha 2 delta ligand is an appropriate pharmacological first line when symptoms persist after iron repletion, and it does not cause augmentation. Starting it now would treat the symptom while leaving the deficiency that is generating it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Restless legs syndrome)

explanation.summary: Restless legs syndrome is diagnosed clinically from an urge to move the legs with an unpleasant sensation that is worse at rest, worse in the evening and relieved by movement. Iron status is the single most useful investigation because brain iron is a cofactor for dopamine synthesis, and deficiency is the commonest reversible cause even when the patient is not anaemic. Replacement is aimed at a ferritin well above the laboratory lower limit, commonly taken as at least 75 micrograms per litre, and often resolves symptoms without any further treatment. Where drug treatment is needed, an alpha 2 delta ligand such as gabapentin or pregabalin is preferred over a dopamine agonist, because agonists cause augmentation over time, with symptoms starting earlier in the day, spreading to the arms and becoming worse than before treatment. Contributing medicines such as antihistamines, antidepressants and dopamine blocking antiemetics are reviewed at the same time.
key_points: The diagnosis is clinical: urge to move, worse at rest and in the evening, relieved by movement.
Iron deficiency is the commonest reversible cause and occurs without anaemia.
Replacement targets a ferritin above about 75 micrograms per litre, not merely within range.
Dopamine agonists cause augmentation and are no longer first line.
Antihistamines, antidepressants and dopamine blocking antiemetics can precipitate symptoms.
explanation.pearls: A ferritin of 22 micrograms per litre is reported as only mildly low but is emphatically abnormal for this condition, where the treatment target is 75 or above, so read the number against the neurological target rather than against the laboratory range.

sources.label: Australian Medicines Handbook: Drugs for restless legs

subtopic_detail: the size of creatinine rise after starting renin angiotensin blockade that should not stop the drug
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 62-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes and albuminuria who started ramipril 5 mg daily two weeks ago. She has come for the follow up blood test you arranged and feels entirely well.

Her creatinine has risen from 88 micromol/L before starting to 106 micromol/L today, and her potassium is 4.7 mmol/L. She has had no vomiting or diarrhoea, is drinking normally and has not started any anti inflammatory medicine. Her blood pressure today is 128/74 mmHg sitting, with no postural drop, and she has no oedema. Her urine albumin to creatinine ratio before starting was 42 mg/mmol. Her renal ultrasound last year showed normal sized kidneys with no obstruction and no asymmetry.

data_table.Vital signs: Blood pressure 128/74 mmHg sitting with no postural drop, pulse rate 76/min, other observations within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Euvolaemic with moist mucous membranes, no ankle oedema, no abdominal bruit, chest clear
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 106 micromol/L (45-90) risen from 88, potassium 4.7 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), sodium 139 mmol/L (135-145), bicarbonate 25 mmol/L (22-32), urine albumin to creatinine ratio 42 mg/mmol
data_table.Medications: Ramipril 5 mg daily, metformin 1 g twice daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, empagliflozin 10 mg daily

lead_in: What should you do?

options.text: Halve the dose to 2.5 mg daily and recheck her renal function in four weeks
options.rationale: Dose reduction is a reasonable response when the rise approaches the threshold or when symptomatic hypotension limits treatment. Here it sacrifices part of the dose-dependent reduction in albuminuria for a change that is within the expected range. (Source: KHA Kidney Disease: Chronic kidney disease management in primary care)
source_refs: KHA Kidney Disease: Chronic kidney disease management in primary care

options.text: Stop the empagliflozin, since it is the more likely explanation for the creatinine rise
options.rationale: Sodium glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors do cause an initial dip in filtration rate through a similar haemodynamic mechanism, and that dip is likewise expected and reversible. Both drugs reduce kidney disease progression and neither is stopped for the anticipated early change. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Chronic kidney disease)

options.text: Arrange urgent renal artery imaging, since this degree of rise suggests arterial stenosis
options.rationale: A steep rise, often above thirty per cent and occurring within days, does raise the possibility of bilateral renal artery stenosis and warrants imaging. Her ultrasound showed symmetrical kidneys of normal size and her rise is within the expected range, so this is not indicated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Chronic kidney disease)

options.text: Keep her on the current dose and confirm the result has plateaued on repeat testing
options.rationale: A creatinine rise of about twenty per cent reflects the expected fall in intraglomerular pressure that produces the long term kidney protection, and rises of up to thirty per cent that stabilise are acceptable and are not a reason to stop. Her potassium is within range and she is euvolaemic, so the drug continues and the result is simply confirmed as stable. (Source: KHA Kidney Disease: Chronic kidney disease management in primary care)
source_refs: KHA Kidney Disease: Chronic kidney disease management in primary care

options.text: Stop the ramipril permanently and record it as having caused acute kidney injury
options.rationale: Cessation is warranted when the rise exceeds thirty per cent, when it keeps climbing on repeat testing or when potassium rises above the acceptable range. Stopping for a stable twenty per cent rise removes the treatment that most reduces her progression to kidney failure and is the commonest error made at this point. (Source: KHA Kidney Disease: Chronic kidney disease management in primary care)
source_refs: KHA Kidney Disease: Chronic kidney disease management in primary care

explanation.summary: Angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors dilate the efferent arteriole, which lowers intraglomerular pressure and produces an immediate fall in filtration rate alongside the long term reduction in albuminuria and in progression to kidney failure. A creatinine rise of up to thirty per cent within the first two to four weeks is therefore expected and is a marker that the drug is working rather than a sign of injury. The drug is continued and the result rechecked to confirm it has stabilised. Cessation is warranted when the rise exceeds thirty per cent, continues to climb, or is accompanied by hyperkalaemia above the acceptable range, and a steep early rise raises the possibility of bilateral renal artery stenosis or volume depletion. Stopping for a stable rise within the expected range removes one of the few treatments that alters the trajectory of diabetic kidney disease.
key_points: Efferent arteriolar dilatation lowers intraglomerular pressure and raises creatinine acutely.
A stable rise up to thirty per cent is expected and the drug is continued.
Recheck renal function and potassium within two weeks to confirm stability.
A rise above thirty per cent, a continuing climb or hyperkalaemia prompt cessation.
A steep early rise suggests bilateral renal artery stenosis or volume depletion.
explanation.pearls: Calculate the percentage rise rather than reacting to the absolute number, because 88 to 106 micromol/L looks alarming on a report and is twenty per cent, which is exactly what a drug that is protecting her kidneys is supposed to do.

sources.label: KHA Kidney Disease: Chronic kidney disease management in primary care

subtopic_detail: why a hypoglycaemic episode that has already corrected still requires admission
stem:
You are the emergency registrar seeing a 78-year-old woman brought in by ambulance after her daughter found her confused and sweating at home. The paramedics recorded a blood glucose of 1.8 mmol/L and gave intravenous glucose, after which she recovered completely within minutes.

Four hours later in the department she has become drowsy again with a blood glucose of 2.4 mmol/L, which responded to a further dose of glucose. She takes gliclazide modified release 120 mg daily and metformin, and her daughter says she has been eating poorly for three days because of a sore throat. She takes no insulin. Her creatinine is 142 micromol/L, risen from a baseline of 96. She lives alone and her daughter is returning interstate tonight.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 92/min, blood pressure 124/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable during the second episode, alert between episodes, no focal neurology, mildly dry mucous membranes, chest clear
data_table.Investigations: Blood glucose 2.4 mmol/L during the second episode, creatinine 142 micromol/L (45-90) risen from 96, potassium 4.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), glycated haemoglobin 6.4 per cent
data_table.Medications: Gliclazide modified release 120 mg daily, metformin 1 g twice daily, perindopril 5 mg daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Give intramuscular glucagon and arrange review by her general practitioner tomorrow
options.rationale: Glucagon mobilises hepatic glycogen and is valuable where intravenous access is difficult, particularly in the community. Its effect is brief, glycogen stores are already depleted in someone who has been eating poorly for days, and it can provoke further insulin release in sulfonylurea hypoglycaemia. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Sulfonylureas)

options.text: Give a carbohydrate meal and discharge her once her glucose has been stable for two hours
options.rationale: Two hours of stability is a reasonable discharge rule after hypoglycaemia caused by short-acting insulin, where the effect is over and the cause is understood. It is unsafe with a long-acting sulfonylurea in renal impairment, since the drug continues to stimulate insulin release long after the observation period ends. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Hypoglycaemia)

options.text: Admit for a glucose infusion with regular monitoring and withhold the gliclazide
options.rationale: The modified release preparation acts for well over twenty four hours and her reduced renal clearance prolongs it further, so a single correction treats the reading rather than the cause and the recurrence at four hours confirms it. Admission with a glucose infusion and regular monitoring covers the many hours of continuing insulin secretion, and she cannot be observed at home with her daughter leaving tonight. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Hypoglycaemia)

options.text: Halve the gliclazide dose and discharge her with instructions to monitor at home
options.rationale: Reducing or stopping the sulfonylurea is certainly part of the plan, and a glycated haemoglobin of 6.4 per cent indicates she is overtreated for her age in any case. Dose adjustment does nothing about the drug already circulating, which will keep causing hypoglycaemia through tonight. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Hypoglycaemia)

options.text: Start octreotide now as the specific antidote and observe her in the short stay unit
options.rationale: Octreotide suppresses pancreatic insulin release and is the targeted treatment for sulfonylurea hypoglycaemia, used when episodes recur despite adequate glucose. It is reserved for refractory cases rather than started at the first recurrence, and it does not remove the need for admission and monitoring. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Hypoglycaemia)

explanation.summary: Sulfonylurea induced hypoglycaemia differs from insulin induced hypoglycaemia in that the drug continues to stimulate endogenous insulin secretion for as long as it remains in the circulation, and correcting the glucose does nothing to shorten that. The modified release preparation acts for more than twenty four hours, and acute kidney injury from poor intake prolongs it further, so recurrence is the rule rather than the exception. Anyone with sulfonylurea hypoglycaemia needs admission for a glucose infusion and regular monitoring for at least twenty four hours, and longer if renal function is impaired. Octreotide suppresses insulin release and is reserved for episodes that recur despite adequate glucose replacement. A glycated haemoglobin of 6.4 per cent in a frail older woman indicates overtreatment, and relaxing the glycaemic target is part of preventing the next episode.
key_points: Sulfonylureas keep stimulating insulin release long after the glucose has been corrected.
Modified release preparations act for more than twenty four hours.
Renal impairment prolongs the effect and makes recurrence more likely.
Octreotide is reserved for hypoglycaemia recurring despite adequate glucose replacement.
A low glycated haemoglobin in a frail older person indicates overtreatment.
explanation.pearls: Never discharge a sulfonylurea hypoglycaemia from the emergency department on the strength of a normal glucose, because the drug outlasts the observation period by a day or more and the second episode typically happens overnight at home with nobody there.

subtopic_detail: maintaining time critical dopaminergic dosing in a patient who cannot take anything by mouth
stem:
You are the surgical resident admitting a 72-year-old man with Parkinson disease of eleven years duration who has a small bowel obstruction and is being kept nil by mouth pending theatre tomorrow. A nasogastric tube is in place on free drainage.

He takes levodopa with carbidopa at 6 am, 10 am, 2 pm, 6 pm and 10 pm, and he tells you his movement becomes very difficult within an hour of a late dose. The intern has charted his usual doses as three times daily with meals and has added metoclopramide for nausea. It is now 9 am and his 6 am dose was not given because he was in the emergency department. He is currently rigid, barely able to turn in bed and speaking softly, and he was walking independently at home yesterday.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 96/min, blood pressure 138/82 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 37.1 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Marked rigidity with bradykinesia, soft hypophonic speech, unable to turn unaided in bed, abdomen distended with tinkling bowel sounds
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 88 micromol/L (60-110), potassium 4.1 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), abdominal computed tomography showing small bowel obstruction with a transition point
data_table.Medications: Levodopa with carbidopa five times daily, metoclopramide charted as required, nil by mouth

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Withhold all his medicines until after theatre and restart them when he is eating again
options.rationale: Withholding oral medicines is standard for most drugs before an operation and is what the nil by mouth order is usually taken to mean. Levodopa is a specific exception because interruption for even a day risks an akinetic crisis, aspiration and a syndrome resembling neuroleptic malignant syndrome. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Parkinson disease)

options.text: Convert him to a rotigotine patch at an equivalent dose and leave the metoclopramide charted
options.rationale: A transdermal dopamine agonist is the accepted alternative when no enteral route is available at all, and calculating the equivalent dose requires specialist input. He has a working nasogastric tube, and leaving a centrally acting dopamine antagonist charted undermines whatever dopaminergic treatment is given. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Parkinson disease)

options.text: Accept the three times daily charting as close enough and give the doses with the drug round
options.rationale: Standard ward drug rounds are convenient and adequate for most medicines, which is exactly how this error is made. In advanced disease the interval between doses determines whether the patient can move at all, and shifting a five times daily schedule onto the ward round produces hours of immobility each day. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Parkinson disease)

options.text: Give intravenous apomorphine as a bolus now and reassess his rigidity in thirty minutes
options.rationale: Apomorphine is a potent dopamine agonist given subcutaneously rather than intravenously, and it is used for sudden off periods under specialist supervision with premedication against severe vomiting. It is not a ward level substitute for restoring the regular schedule. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Drugs for Parkinson disease)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook: Drugs for Parkinson disease

options.text: Give the levodopa through the nasogastric tube at his exact home times and cease the metoclopramide
options.rationale: Missed or delayed doses in advanced Parkinson disease cause rapid deterioration and can precipitate an akinetic crisis with rigidity, swallowing failure and aspiration, so the home schedule is maintained through the tube with the tube clamped briefly after each dose. Metoclopramide is a dopamine antagonist that crosses into the brain and will worsen his rigidity, so it is replaced with an antiemetic that does not. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Parkinson disease)

explanation.summary: Levodopa has a short plasma half life and in advanced Parkinson disease the response follows the dosing schedule closely, so delays of even an hour produce disabling off periods. Interrupting treatment altogether can precipitate an akinetic crisis, with severe rigidity, inability to swallow, hyperthermia and a picture resembling neuroleptic malignant syndrome, which carries a real mortality. A nil by mouth order therefore does not extend to levodopa, which is given through a nasogastric tube at the patient's own times, or delivered by a rotigotine patch when no enteral route exists. Dopamine antagonists must be avoided, so metoclopramide, prochlorperazine and haloperidol are replaced by ondansetron or domperidone for nausea and by quetiapine if an antipsychotic is unavoidable. Charting the home regimen exactly, rather than mapping it onto standard ward drug rounds, is the single most important prescribing decision at admission.
key_points: Levodopa has a short half life and the dosing schedule determines mobility.
Interruption can precipitate an akinetic crisis resembling neuroleptic malignant syndrome.
Nil by mouth does not include levodopa, which is given by nasogastric tube.
A rotigotine patch is the alternative when no enteral route is available.
Metoclopramide, prochlorperazine and haloperidol are avoided as central dopamine antagonists.
explanation.pearls: Chart the patient's own times rather than three times daily on admission, and cross off any metoclopramide, because those two entries on the drug chart cause more avoidable deterioration in Parkinson disease than anything that happens in theatre.

sources.label: Australian Medicines Handbook: Drugs for Parkinson disease

subtopic_detail: Antibiotic choice for moderate community acquired pneumonia in a man with a documented anaphylactic reaction to penicillin
stem:
A 62-year-old man presents to your emergency department with four days of fever, productive cough and right sided pleuritic chest pain. He is admitted under your medical team.

His medical record documents an episode ten years ago in which amoxicillin caused urticaria, lip swelling and hypotension requiring adrenaline in an emergency department. He has no other allergies. On examination he has bronchial breathing at the right base with dullness to percussion. His chest radiograph shows right lower lobe consolidation without effusion. His severity assessment places him in the moderate category requiring inpatient intravenous therapy.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 108/min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 26/min, SpO2 92% on room air, temperature 38.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Bronchial breathing and dullness to percussion at the right base, no signs of effusion
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 16.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), C-reactive protein 186 mg/L (<5), urea 7.2 mmol/L (3.0-8.0), chest radiograph shows right lower lobe consolidation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Intravenous ceftriaxone with oral doxycycline and review when culture results return
options.rationale: Cephalosporins retain a beta lactam ring and, although cross reactivity with later generation agents is lower than once believed, they are avoided after a documented anaphylactic reaction. The atypical cover is appropriate but the primary agent is not. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Intravenous benzylpenicillin with oral doxycycline and review when culture results return
