Management comprises oxygen and escalating respiratory support, antibiotics that cover atypical organisms, cautious fluid balance, adequate analgesia and incentive spirometry to counter splinting. The transfusion decision turns on severity: simple transfusion suffices for milder disease, while hypoxia, multilobar involvement or clinical deterioration calls for exchange transfusion, which lowers the haemoglobin S fraction without the viscosity penalty of simply adding red cells.
key_points: New infiltrate with fever or respiratory symptoms defines the syndrome
It commonly develops two to three days into a vaso-occlusive admission
Opioid induced hypoventilation and chest splinting are contributors
Exchange transfusion is used for hypoxia, multilobar disease or deterioration
Incentive spirometry during painful crises reduces the incidence
explanation.pearls: Incentive spirometry prescribed routinely during a vaso-occlusive crisis reduces the incidence of acute chest syndrome, making it one of the few genuinely preventive bedside interventions in this disease.

subtopic_detail: Treatment of raised intracranial pressure with papilloedema and normal neuroimaging
stem:
A 28-year-old woman is referred to your general medical clinic with four months of daily headache that is worst when she first wakes and when she bends forward. She has also noticed brief greying of vision in both eyes when she stands up quickly, lasting a few seconds each time.

She describes a whooshing sound in both ears in time with her pulse. Her body mass index is 36 kg/m2 and she has gained 14 kg over two years. She takes no medication other than the combined oral contraceptive pill and has never taken tetracyclines or vitamin A derivatives. Fundoscopy shows bilateral swollen optic discs with blurred margins. Formal visual field testing shows an enlarged blind spot on both sides with otherwise preserved fields.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Bilateral papilloedema, no focal neurological deficit, no meningism, visual acuity 6/6 bilaterally
data_table.Imaging: Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and magnetic resonance venography both reported as normal with no mass, hydrocephalus or venous sinus thrombosis
data_table.Lumbar puncture: Opening pressure 32 cmH2O, cerebrospinal fluid cell count, protein and glucose all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Repeated therapeutic lumbar punctures as the mainstay of treatment
options.rationale: Pressure reverts within hours of drainage so repeated punctures give only transient relief, and the procedure is uncomfortable and carries its own risks. It is used as a temporising measure in pregnancy or while awaiting surgery rather than as ongoing treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Acetazolamide with weight management and visual field monitoring
options.rationale: Acetazolamide reduces cerebrospinal fluid production through carbonic anhydrase inhibition and is the first line drug, with randomised evidence supporting its combination with weight reduction for improving visual field outcomes. Serial perimetry is essential because visual loss rather than headache determines the need to escalate. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Referral for urgent optic nerve sheath fenestration this admission
options.rationale: Surgical decompression is reserved for rapidly progressive or severe visual loss that threatens sight despite medical therapy, and her acuity and fields are currently preserved apart from an enlarged blind spot. Proceeding now would expose her to operative risk without indication. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Prednisolone at high dose with a slow taper over three months
options.rationale: Corticosteroids produce rebound elevation of pressure on withdrawal and contribute to the weight gain that drives the condition, so they are not used for maintenance. They are occasionally used briefly as a bridge before urgent surgery. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Topiramate alone with review of the headache in three months
options.rationale: Topiramate has weak carbonic anhydrase activity and assists with weight loss, making it a reasonable second line or adjunctive option, but the evidence base favours acetazolamide first. Reviewing only at three months would also miss deteriorating fields. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension typically affects women of reproductive age with a raised body mass index and recent weight gain, and presents with headache that is worse on waking and on bending, pulsatile tinnitus and transient visual obscurations. Diagnosis follows the modified Dandy criteria: signs and symptoms of raised intracranial pressure, no focal neurological deficit other than a sixth nerve palsy, normal neuroimaging including venography to exclude cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, a raised opening pressure on lumbar puncture, and normal cerebrospinal fluid constituents. The threat is to vision rather than to life, and papilloedema can progress to irreversible optic atrophy while the headache is unremarkable, so serial formal perimetry rather than symptom report drives management. Treatment combines acetazolamide with sustained weight reduction, and offending drugs including tetracyclines, retinoids and excess vitamin A are stopped where relevant.
key_points: Venography is required to exclude cerebral venous sinus thrombosis
Normal cerebrospinal fluid constituents with a raised opening pressure are required
Vision rather than headache determines urgency and escalation
Acetazolamide with weight reduction is first line therapy
Serial formal visual field testing is the key monitoring tool
explanation.pearls: A sixth nerve palsy is the only focal deficit permitted by the diagnostic criteria, because it is a false localising sign produced by the raised pressure itself rather than evidence of a structural lesion.

sources.label: RANZCO: Papilloedema and idiopathic intracranial hypertension

subtopic_detail: Opioid rotation when morphine metabolites accumulate as renal function declines
stem:
You are the registrar on the palliative care ward looking after a 71-year-old man with metastatic prostate cancer and painful bone disease. He has been comfortable for six weeks on sustained release oral morphine with occasional immediate release doses.

Over the past three days his family have noticed he is drowsy through the day, and twice they have seen sudden brief jerks of his arms while he dozes. Overnight he became restless and was briefly confused about where he was. His pain is no worse than before. His creatinine has risen progressively over the past fortnight and his urine output has fallen. His calcium is within normal limits, he is not hypoxic and his blood glucose is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 82/min, blood pressure 108/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 12/min, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable, intermittent multifocal myoclonic jerks, pupils 2 mm bilaterally, no focal neurological deficit
data_table.Biochemistry: Creatinine 268 micromol/L (60-110), estimated glomerular filtration rate 18 mL/min/1.73m2, corrected calcium and glucose within normal limits
data_table.Medication: Sustained release oral morphine with immediate release breakthrough doses, unchanged for six weeks

lead_in: What is the most appropriate change to his analgesia?

options.text: Increase the morphine dose to control the increasing agitation
options.rationale: The agitation and myoclonus are features of metabolite toxicity rather than uncontrolled pain, which his family confirm is no worse. Increasing the dose would deepen the neurotoxicity and could precipitate respiratory depression. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Palliative Care)

options.text: Add midazolam and continue the morphine at the current dose
options.rationale: Sedation would mask the myoclonus and confusion while the accumulating metabolites continue to build, and it adds to his drowsiness. Benzodiazepines may be used symptomatically alongside rotation but not instead of it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Palliative Care)

options.text: Add haloperidol for the agitation and continue the morphine unchanged
options.rationale: Haloperidol treats delirium from other causes but does not remove the accumulating metabolite that is driving this picture. Treating the symptom while leaving the cause in place will not resolve the neurotoxicity. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Palliative Care)

options.text: Stop the morphine and rotate to fentanyl or hydromorphone
options.rationale: Morphine-6-glucuronide and morphine-3-glucuronide are renally cleared, and as the filtration rate falls they accumulate to produce exactly this triad of sedation, myoclonus and delirium with preserved analgesia. Fentanyl has no active renally cleared metabolites and hydromorphone is substantially safer in renal impairment, so rotation removes the cause. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Palliative Care)

options.text: Continue morphine but give it by subcutaneous infusion instead
options.rationale: Changing the route does not change the metabolism, so the same metabolites continue to accumulate in renal impairment. A route change is useful when swallowing fails rather than when toxicity has developed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Palliative Care)

explanation.summary: Morphine is metabolised in the liver to morphine-3-glucuronide and morphine-6-glucuronide, both of which are cleared by the kidney, so declining renal function allows them to accumulate even when the prescribed dose has not changed. Morphine-6-glucuronide is a potent opioid agonist producing sedation and respiratory depression, while morphine-3-glucuronide is neuroexcitatory and causes myoclonus, hyperalgesia and delirium. The clinical signature is a patient whose pain control is unchanged but who becomes drowsy, twitchy and confused as the creatinine climbs, and recognising the pattern prevents the reflex dose increase that makes it worse. Fentanyl is the safest opioid in significant renal impairment because its metabolites are inactive, with hydromorphone a reasonable alternative, and equianalgesic conversion should be done with a dose reduction of around a quarter to a third because of incomplete cross tolerance.
key_points: Morphine metabolites are renally cleared and accumulate as filtration falls
Sedation, myoclonus and delirium with unchanged pain is the signature
Fentanyl has no active renally cleared metabolites
Exclude hypercalcaemia, hypoxia and other delirium causes at the same time
Reduce the calculated equianalgesic dose for incomplete cross tolerance
explanation.pearls: Multifocal myoclonus in a patient on morphine whose pain is well controlled should prompt a creatinine check rather than a dose increase, because it is usually the first sign of metabolite accumulation.

subtopic_detail: Classifying a pleural effusion when the absolute protein and the protein ratio disagree
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 55-year-old man who has had three weeks of breathlessness on exertion and a dull ache in the right chest. He has smoked twenty cigarettes daily for thirty years and has lost 5 kg.

He has no orthopnoea or ankle swelling, his jugular venous pressure is not elevated and his echocardiogram shows normal ventricular function. He takes no diuretics and has never taken any. His liver function and albumin are within normal limits and there is no ascites. A diagnostic pleural tap has been performed and the fluid and paired serum results are now available. The resident tells you the fluid must be a transudate because the protein is under 30 g/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 92/min, blood pressure 128/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 95% on room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Stony dull percussion note and reduced breath sounds at the right base, no peripheral oedema, jugular venous pressure not elevated
data_table.Pleural fluid: Protein 28 g/L, lactate dehydrogenase 210 U/L, straw coloured, cytology pending
data_table.Paired serum: Protein 46 g/L, lactate dehydrogenase 295 U/L with a laboratory upper reference limit of 250 U/L, albumin within normal limits

lead_in: How should the fluid be classified and why?

options.text: An exudate, because the protein and lactate dehydrogenase ratios are raised
options.rationale: The fluid to serum protein ratio is 0.61 and the lactate dehydrogenase ratio is 0.71, each exceeding the thresholds of 0.5 and 0.6 respectively, so the criteria classify this as an exudate on two counts. Meeting any one of the three criteria is sufficient, and the absolute protein value is not one of them. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pleural disease)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pleural disease

options.text: A transudate, because the pleural fluid protein is below 30 g/L
options.rationale: The absolute protein cut off is an older rule that misclassifies a substantial minority of effusions, which is precisely why the ratio based criteria replaced it. A serum protein at the lower end of normal drags the absolute pleural value down while the ratio stays exudative. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pleural disease)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pleural disease

options.text: A transudate, so he should be treated with diuretics and observation
options.rationale: This compounds a misclassification with a treatment that would delay diagnosis in a smoker with weight loss and a unilateral effusion. There is also no clinical or echocardiographic evidence of a transudative cause. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pleural disease)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pleural disease

options.text: Indeterminate, so the tap should be repeated in one week to classify it
options.rationale: The available paired results already allow definitive classification, so repeating the procedure adds risk and delay without new information. Repeat sampling is for inadequate volume or to pursue cytology, not to reclassify. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pleural disease)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pleural disease

options.text: Indeterminate, so the fluid glucose and pH should be used to classify it
options.rationale: Glucose and pH help characterise an effusion once it is known to be exudative, particularly in suspected empyema where a low pH drives drainage. They do not perform the transudate and exudate separation. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pleural disease)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pleural disease

explanation.summary: The first branch point in assessing any pleural effusion is whether it is a transudate, produced by altered hydrostatic or oncotic pressures across an intact pleura, or an exudate, produced by increased capillary permeability or impaired lymphatic drainage from pleural disease itself. Light criteria classify an effusion as exudative if any one of three conditions is met: a pleural to serum protein ratio above 0.5, a pleural to serum lactate dehydrogenase ratio above 0.6, or a pleural lactate dehydrogenase greater than two thirds of the upper limit of the serum reference range. Because only one criterion need be satisfied, the rule is deliberately sensitive and will occasionally label a transudate as an exudate, most often in heart failure treated with diuretics, where a serum to pleural albumin gradient above 12 g/L correctly reclassifies it. The absolute protein concentration is not part of the criteria and misleads whenever the serum protein is itself abnormal, and an exudative unilateral effusion in a smoker with weight loss demands cytology and further imaging.
key_points: Any one of the three Light criteria is sufficient to define an exudate
The criteria use ratios rather than the absolute pleural protein
Paired serum samples must be taken at the same time as the tap
Diuretic treated heart failure can be misclassified as an exudate
A serum to pleural albumin gradient above 12 g/L reclassifies such cases
explanation.pearls: When Light criteria label an effusion exudative but the clinical picture is clearly heart failure on diuretics, calculate the serum minus pleural albumin gradient, because a value above 12 g/L identifies the transudate the criteria misclassified.

sources.label: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pleural disease

subtopic_detail: Sequencing joint aspiration and antibiotics in a monoarthritis in an immunosuppressed patient
stem:
You are the medical registrar in the emergency department assessing a 62-year-old woman with a two day history of a hot, swollen and exquisitely painful right knee that she cannot bear weight on.

She has seropositive rheumatoid arthritis and takes weekly methotrexate and low dose prednisolone. Her other joints are at their usual baseline and none is acutely inflamed. She is febrile and her inflammatory markers are markedly raised. She is haemodynamically stable with no hypotension or features of shock. The resident has drawn up intravenous flucloxacillin and is about to administer it while the orthopaedic registrar is being contacted about aspiration.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 104/min, blood pressure 132/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 38.5 °C
data_table.Examination: Right knee hot, swollen and tense with a large effusion, all movement severely restricted by pain, other joints at baseline
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 17.4 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), C reactive protein 268 mg/L (less than 5), urate within normal limits, blood cultures taken
data_table.Medication: Weekly methotrexate and low dose prednisolone

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Give the intravenous flucloxacillin now and aspirate the knee tomorrow
options.rationale: Antibiotics given before sampling substantially reduce the yield of synovial fluid culture, which is what identifies the organism and directs definitive therapy. Antibiotics do take precedence when the patient is septic and shocked, which she is not. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Start oral prednisolone for a presumed inflammatory arthritis flare
options.rationale: Attributing an acute hot joint to a flare of her known rheumatoid disease is a classic and dangerous error, because immunosuppression both raises the risk of septic arthritis and blunts its presentation. A single acutely inflamed joint against a quiescent background should be treated as infection until proven otherwise. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the knee before any aspiration
options.rationale: Imaging cannot distinguish septic from inflammatory effusion and delays the only test that can, while cartilage is being destroyed within days. It is useful for suspected osteomyelitis or a periarticular collection after the joint has been sampled. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Start colchicine for a presumed crystal arthropathy and review later
options.rationale: Crystal arthritis is a genuine differential and can produce an identical picture with fever and high inflammatory markers, but a normal urate does not exclude infection and crystals can coexist with sepsis. Only synovial fluid examination distinguishes them. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Aspirate the joint for urgent culture before antibiotics are given
options.rationale: Synovial fluid for urgent Gram stain, culture and crystal examination should be obtained before antibiotics whenever the patient is stable, because prior antibiotics markedly reduce culture yield and leave subsequent therapy unguided. Treatment then starts immediately after the sample is taken rather than waiting for the result. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Septic arthritis destroys articular cartilage within days and carries appreciable mortality, so an acutely hot single joint is an emergency regardless of what else the patient has. The diagnostic pathway is synovial fluid aspiration for urgent Gram stain, culture and polarised light microscopy, together with blood cultures, obtained before antibiotics whenever the patient is haemodynamically stable, since prior antibiotic exposure is the commonest reason cultures return negative and therapy remains empirical. Patients on immunosuppression and those with pre-existing joint disease are at the highest risk and the most likely to have the diagnosis missed, because the presentation is attributed to a flare of the underlying condition. Staphylococcus aureus is the commonest organism, empirical therapy in Australia is usually intravenous flucloxacillin adjusted for local resistance patterns, and definitive management requires joint washout or repeated aspiration alongside antibiotics.
key_points: Aspirate before antibiotics unless the patient is septic and unstable
Send fluid for Gram stain, culture and polarised light microscopy together
Crystals in the fluid do not exclude coexisting infection
Immunosuppression raises risk and masks the usual clinical signs
Joint washout or repeated aspiration accompanies antibiotic therapy
explanation.pearls: A normal serum urate during an acute attack neither confirms nor excludes gout, because urate commonly falls during the acute inflammatory episode, so it can never be used to avoid aspirating a hot joint.

subtopic_detail: Order of agents when controlling blood pressure in acute aortic dissection
stem:
You are the medical registrar called urgently to the emergency department to see a 58-year-old man who developed severe tearing pain between his shoulder blades while getting out of his car two hours ago. The pain was maximal at onset.

He has long standing hypertension and has not taken his medication for several weeks. He is alert and in obvious distress. Peripheral pulses are present and symmetrical and there is no aortic regurgitant murmur or neurological deficit. His computed tomography aortogram has just been reported. On arriving you find that a glyceryl trinitrate infusion was started ten minutes ago and is being titrated upwards, and his heart rate has risen since it began.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 116/min, blood pressure 194/108 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Symmetrical peripheral pulses, no diastolic murmur, no focal neurological deficit, chest clear
data_table.Imaging: Computed tomography aortogram shows an intimal flap arising distal to the left subclavian artery extending to the level of the diaphragm, with no branch vessel compromise
data_table.Current treatment: Glyceryl trinitrate infusion commenced ten minutes ago and being titrated upwards, morphine given

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate change to his management?

options.text: Continue the nitrate infusion alone and titrate it to the blood pressure
options.rationale: A vasodilator given without rate control causes a reflex tachycardia and a rise in the rate of pressure change against the aortic wall, which propagates the dissection even as the recorded pressure falls. His rising heart rate since the infusion started is that reflex occurring. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Start intravenous beta blockade before continuing the vasodilator
options.rationale: The aim is to reduce the shearing force on the aortic wall, which depends on the rate of rise of pressure as well as its absolute value, so heart rate must be brought to about 60 per minute with an intravenous beta blocker first. A vasodilator is then added to reach a target systolic pressure of roughly 100 to 120 mmHg once the reflex tachycardia has been prevented. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Start a dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker as the single agent
options.rationale: Dihydropyridines are vasodilators without rate limiting effect, so used alone they reproduce the same reflex tachycardia problem as the nitrate. A rate limiting calcium channel blocker is an alternative only when beta blockade is contraindicated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Give intravenous hydralazine boluses to bring the pressure down fast
options.rationale: Hydralazine is a direct arterial dilator that causes marked reflex tachycardia and produces unpredictable stepwise falls that are difficult to titrate. It is specifically avoided in dissection for these reasons. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Withhold all antihypertensives until surgical review has been completed
options.rationale: Medical control of heart rate and blood pressure is the primary treatment for an uncomplicated dissection distal to the left subclavian artery and is started immediately rather than after review. Delay allows extension of the flap. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

explanation.summary: Acute aortic dissection presents with severe pain that is maximal at onset, classically tearing and interscapular, and is classified by whether the ascending aorta is involved. A Stanford type A dissection involving the ascending aorta is a surgical emergency, whereas a type B dissection beginning distal to the left subclavian artery without malperfusion, rupture or refractory pain is managed medically in the first instance. The therapeutic target is not simply the blood pressure but the shearing stress on the aortic wall, which is determined by the rate of rise of arterial pressure as well as its peak, and that rate of rise is driven by ventricular contractility and heart rate. Rate control with an intravenous beta blocker therefore always precedes vasodilatation, aiming for a heart rate near 60 per minute and a systolic pressure of about 100 to 120 mmHg, with adequate analgesia because pain itself drives catecholamine release.
key_points: Pain maximal at onset distinguishes dissection from evolving ischaemic pain
Type A involves the ascending aorta and requires urgent surgery
Uncomplicated type B dissection is managed medically at first
Shearing stress depends on rate of pressure rise, not just peak pressure
Beta blockade precedes vasodilators to prevent reflex tachycardia
explanation.pearls: Target a heart rate of about 60 per minute before adding any vasodilator, because a vasodilator given first produces reflex tachycardia that raises the rate of pressure rise and can extend the dissection while the recorded blood pressure looks better.

subtopic_detail: Recognising respiratory failure in myasthenia gravis when oxygen saturation remains normal
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 63-year-old woman with myasthenia gravis, maintained on pyridostigmine and azathioprine, who was admitted yesterday with a chest infection. She was started on a macrolide antibiotic by the admitting team.

Since this morning her voice has become nasal, she is struggling to swallow her tablets, and she describes her breathing as feeling like hard work although she does not feel short of breath lying still. She is anxious and using her accessory muscles intermittently. The nursing staff report that her oxygen saturation has remained normal throughout. Serial bedside spirometry performed by the physiotherapist shows her forced vital capacity has fallen from 1.9 L on admission to 1.4 L this morning and 0.9 L twenty minutes ago.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 108/min, blood pressure 138/82 mmHg, respiratory rate 26/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 37.4 °C
data_table.Examination: Nasal speech, weak cough, bilateral ptosis, poor palatal elevation, intermittent accessory muscle use, chest clear to auscultation
data_table.Serial vital capacity: 1.9 L on admission, 1.4 L this morning, 0.9 L twenty minutes ago
data_table.Medication: Pyridostigmine and azathioprine maintained, macrolide antibiotic commenced yesterday

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Increase the pyridostigmine dose and observe on the ward overnight
options.rationale: Escalating an anticholinesterase in a deteriorating patient risks excessive secretions that compromise an already weak cough, and ward observation is unsafe with a vital capacity falling this fast. Pyridostigmine does not arrest an evolving crisis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Give high flow oxygen and repeat the vital capacity in the morning
options.rationale: Oxygen corrects the saturation without addressing ventilatory failure and removes the one warning sign that would otherwise appear late, masking progressive hypercapnia. Deferring reassessment until morning ignores a trajectory measured in hours. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Start high dose prednisolone alone and continue the antibiotic course
options.rationale: High dose corticosteroid can transiently worsen weakness in the first one to two weeks and takes days to help, so it is not the immediate answer to impending ventilatory failure. Continuing the precipitating antibiotic also leaves the trigger in place. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Arrange ventilatory support and plasma exchange, ceasing the antibiotic
options.rationale: A vital capacity falling below about 1 L or 15 mL/kg with bulbar weakness defines myasthenic crisis and requires intensive care admission for ventilatory support, alongside plasma exchange or intravenous immunoglobulin as definitive treatment. The macrolide is a recognised precipitant through impaired neuromuscular transmission and should be changed to an alternative that covers her infection. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Administer intravenous edrophonium to distinguish the type of crisis
options.rationale: The edrophonium test is of historical interest and carries risks of bradycardia and increased secretions, and it does not alter the immediate need for airway and ventilatory support. Cholinergic crisis is rare at standard pyridostigmine doses and would present with additional muscarinic features. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Myasthenic crisis is respiratory failure from neuromuscular weakness, and its central trap is that oxygen saturation stays normal until very late because the problem is ventilation rather than gas exchange across normal lung. Monitoring therefore relies on serial forced vital capacity and negative inspiratory force rather than on pulse oximetry, with a vital capacity below roughly 15 mL/kg or 1 L, or a rapidly falling trend, indicating the need for intensive care. Bulbar weakness compounds the risk because a weak cough and impaired swallow lead to aspiration, and arterial carbon dioxide rises only as a preterminal event. Definitive treatment is plasma exchange or intravenous immunoglobulin, with corticosteroids often started concurrently while recognising they may transiently worsen weakness. Common precipitants include infection, surgery and a long list of drugs, among them aminoglycosides, macrolides, fluoroquinolones, beta blockers and magnesium, so the medication chart should be reviewed in every deteriorating patient.
key_points: Oxygen saturation remains normal until ventilatory failure is advanced
Serial vital capacity is the monitoring tool, not pulse oximetry
A vital capacity below about 1 L or a rapid fall indicates intensive care
Plasma exchange or immunoglobulin is the definitive acute treatment
Macrolides, aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones and magnesium can precipitate crisis
explanation.pearls: Ask the patient to count aloud from one on a single breath as a bedside surrogate for vital capacity, since reaching fewer than about twenty suggests significant impairment and warrants formal spirometry immediately.

subtopic_detail: Order of drug administration in decompensated thyrotoxicosis precipitated by infection
stem:
You are the medical registrar called to the emergency department to see a 44-year-old woman brought in by her partner because she has become confused and agitated over the past day.

She was diagnosed with Graves disease eight months ago but stopped attending appointments and has not taken her tablets for several months. She has had a productive cough for five days. On examination she is agitated and disoriented, with warm sweaty skin, a fine tremor and a smooth goitre with a bruit. Her heart is irregularly irregular at a rapid rate and she has bibasal crackles. Her thyroid function has been sent urgently and cultures have been taken.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 158/min and irregularly irregular, blood pressure 106/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 28/min, SpO2 93% on room air, temperature 39.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Agitated and disoriented, smooth goitre with a bruit, fine tremor, warm peripheries, bibasal crackles
data_table.Investigations: Electrocardiogram shows atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response, liver function mildly deranged, thyroid function pending
data_table.Other: Chest radiograph shows right lower lobe consolidation, blood cultures taken

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial pharmacological management?

options.text: Give iodine first to block release then add a thionamide afterwards
options.rationale: Iodine given before a thionamide supplies substrate to a gland that is still actively organifying it, which can transiently increase hormone synthesis and worsen the crisis. The order of these two drugs is the specific point being tested. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Give a beta blocker and a thionamide before any iodine is administered
options.rationale: A beta blocker controls the adrenergic features and the ventricular rate while a thionamide blocks new hormone synthesis, and iodine is given only afterwards, conventionally at least an hour later, to inhibit release of stored hormone. Corticosteroid is added to reduce peripheral conversion and cover possible relative adrenal insufficiency, alongside treatment of the precipitating pneumonia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Give intravenous levothyroxine with supportive care and active cooling
options.rationale: Thyroid hormone replacement is the treatment for myxoedema coma, which presents with hypothermia, bradycardia and obtundation, and giving it here would add to an already excessive hormone load. This is the opposite endocrine emergency. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Start amiodarone for rate control of the atrial fibrillation
options.rationale: Amiodarone carries a very high iodine load and can itself cause or worsen thyrotoxicosis, making it an unsuitable choice in this setting. Rate control here is achieved with a beta blocker as part of the definitive treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Arrange urgent thyroidectomy before starting any medical therapy
options.rationale: Operating on an uncontrolled thyrotoxic patient carries very high mortality, and surgery is reserved for the rare case refractory to maximal medical therapy after biochemical control has been attempted. Medical stabilisation always comes first. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Thyroid storm is decompensated thyrotoxicosis with organ dysfunction, typically precipitated in a patient with untreated or poorly controlled Graves disease by infection, surgery, trauma, childbirth or iodine exposure. It is a clinical diagnosis made on fever, tachyarrhythmia, cardiac failure, gastrointestinal and hepatic dysfunction and altered mental state, and treatment must begin before confirmatory thyroid function returns because mortality remains appreciable. Therapy attacks the problem at several points in sequence: a beta blocker for the adrenergic manifestations and rate control, a thionamide to block new hormone synthesis, iodine at least an hour after the thionamide to inhibit release of preformed hormone, and a corticosteroid to reduce peripheral conversion of thyroxine to triiodothyronine and to cover relative adrenal insufficiency. The sequencing of thionamide before iodine is the point most often tested and most often reversed, because iodine given to a gland still capable of organification can transiently increase hormone production. Identifying and treating the precipitant is as important as the endocrine treatment itself.
key_points: Thyroid storm is a clinical diagnosis treated before confirmatory results return
Infection is the commonest precipitant and must be treated concurrently
Beta blocker and thionamide precede iodine by at least an hour
Corticosteroid reduces peripheral conversion and covers adrenal insufficiency
Amiodarone is avoided because of its large iodine load
explanation.pearls: Give the thionamide at least one hour before iodine, because iodine reaching a gland that can still organify it acts as substrate and transiently increases hormone synthesis, a phenomenon that can worsen the crisis.

subtopic_detail: Asymmetric oligoarthritis with nail pitting and a scaly rash
stem:
A 42-year-old plumber attends your general practice with four months of pain and swelling in his right knee, left ankle and the whole of his left fourth toe, which he says looks like a sausage.

He has morning stiffness lasting about an hour that eases as the day goes on. He has had scaly patches behind his ears and at his hairline for years which he treats with a shampoo from the chemist. His fingernails have small dents in them and one is lifting away from the nail bed. Rheumatoid factor and anti cyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies are both negative, and urate is normal. Plain radiographs of the hands show no erosion.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Swollen right knee with effusion, swollen left ankle, diffuse swelling of the entire left fourth toe, nail pitting with onycholysis, scaly plaques at the hairline and retroauricular area
data_table.Investigations: C reactive protein 28 mg/L (less than 5), rheumatoid factor negative, anti cyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies negative, urate 0.32 mmol/L (0.20-0.42), hand radiographs show no erosion
data_table.Symptom pattern: Morning stiffness of one hour improving with activity, asymmetric joint involvement

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start colchicine and arrange joint aspiration for crystal analysis
options.rationale: Crystal arthropathy is worth considering in an acutely swollen joint but does not produce dactylitis of an entire digit, months of inflammatory morning stiffness or nail changes, and his urate is normal. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

options.text: Start a non-steroidal anti inflammatory drug and review in a year
options.rationale: Anti inflammatory drugs provide symptomatic relief and are a reasonable adjunct, but they do not modify the disease, and a year of delay is long enough for irreversible erosive change to develop. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

options.text: Reassure him that seronegative tests exclude an inflammatory cause
options.rationale: Psoriatic arthritis is characteristically seronegative, so negative rheumatoid factor and citrullinated peptide antibodies are the expected finding rather than evidence against inflammatory disease. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

options.text: Start methotrexate and refer him to a rheumatology service
options.rationale: Asymmetric oligoarthritis with dactylitis, nail pitting and onycholysis on a background of skin psoriasis is psoriatic arthritis, and a conventional disease modifying agent should be started early with specialist referral to prevent erosive damage. Methotrexate has the advantage of treating both the joint and skin disease. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

options.text: Refer him to dermatology for management of the psoriatic skin disease
options.rationale: Skin treatment alone leaves the joint disease untreated, and topical therapy has no effect on synovitis or on the progression to joint destruction. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

explanation.summary: Psoriatic arthritis affects roughly a fifth to a third of people with psoriasis and is frequently missed because the skin disease may be mild, hidden at the scalp, natal cleft or behind the ears, and because the serology is negative. The features that distinguish it are asymmetric oligoarticular involvement, dactylitis producing uniform swelling of an entire digit, enthesitis, and nail changes such as pitting and onycholysis that correlate strongly with joint disease. Inflammatory pattern stiffness lasting more than 30 minutes and easing with activity separates it from mechanical pain. Early disease modifying treatment with rheumatology referral prevents the erosive damage that develops in a substantial proportion of untreated patients.
key_points: Dactylitis of a whole digit is highly suggestive and rarely caused by rheumatoid arthritis
Seronegativity is expected and does not argue against the diagnosis
Nail pitting and onycholysis correlate with the presence of joint disease
Absence of erosions on early radiographs does not justify delaying treatment
explanation.pearls: Examine the scalp, umbilicus, natal cleft and nails in anyone with unexplained inflammatory arthritis: the psoriasis is often a patch the patient has never mentioned or considered relevant, and finding it changes the diagnosis and the drug.

sources.label: Australian Rheumatology Association: Patient medicine information

subtopic_detail: Raised transferrin saturation with fatigue and arthralgia in a middle aged man
stem:
A 46-year-old man of northern European ancestry attends your general practice with a year of tiredness and aching in the second and third knuckles of both hands. He drinks about six standard drinks a week.

He has no known liver disease and takes no supplements, including no iron tablets. His brother was told at the age of fifty that he had too much iron and now has regular venesection. Examination shows no hepatomegaly, no spider naevi and no skin pigmentation. His fasting transferrin saturation is 68 percent on two separate occasions and his ferritin is 940 micrograms per litre. His C reactive protein is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 26 kg/m2, tenderness of the second and third metacarpophalangeal joints bilaterally, no hepatomegaly, no spider naevi, no skin pigmentation
data_table.Investigations: Fasting transferrin saturation 68 percent (less than 45), ferritin 940 micrograms per litre (30-300), alanine aminotransferase 58 U/L (less than 45), C reactive protein 2 mg/L (less than 5), fasting glucose 5.2 mmol/L
data_table.Family history: Brother diagnosed with iron overload at fifty and on venesection

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Request a liver biopsy
options.rationale: Biopsy was the historical standard for quantifying hepatic iron but has been superseded by genotyping and magnetic resonance imaging, and it is now reserved for assessing fibrosis when the ferritin is very high or the transaminases are abnormal. (Source: GESA: Haemochromatosis clinical update)

options.text: Repeat his ferritin level
options.rationale: Ferritin is an acute phase reactant, but his C reactive protein is normal and the measurement has already been supported by a persistently raised transferrin saturation, so repeating it simply delays diagnosis. (Source: GESA: Haemochromatosis clinical update)

options.text: Arrange hepatitis serology
options.rationale: Viral hepatitis causes a raised ferritin through hepatic inflammation but does not raise the transferrin saturation to this degree, and his history has no risk factors for viral acquisition. (Source: GESA: Haemochromatosis clinical update)

options.text: Advise alcohol cessation
options.rationale: Alcohol raises ferritin and worsens iron related liver injury, and reduction should be advised, but six standard drinks a week does not explain a transferrin saturation of 68 percent and an affected sibling. (Source: GESA: Haemochromatosis clinical update)

options.text: Request HFE genotyping
options.rationale: A fasting transferrin saturation above 45 percent with a raised ferritin and a normal C reactive protein in a man of northern European ancestry with an affected sibling indicates hereditary haemochromatosis, and genotyping confirms it non invasively. Confirmation also identifies the need to screen first degree relatives. (Source: GESA: Haemochromatosis clinical update)

explanation.summary: Hereditary haemochromatosis is the commonest inherited disorder in Australians of northern European ancestry and is usually detected through iron studies rather than through the classic late triad of cirrhosis, diabetes and skin pigmentation. The screening test that matters is the fasting transferrin saturation, because ferritin alone is a non-specific acute phase reactant that rises in inflammation, alcohol use and metabolic liver disease. A raised saturation with a raised ferritin and a normal C reactive protein should prompt HFE genotyping rather than biopsy. Early diagnosis matters because venesection begun before cirrhosis develops restores a normal life expectancy.
key_points: Fasting transferrin saturation is the discriminating test; ferritin alone is too non-specific
Genotyping has replaced liver biopsy for diagnosis
Arthropathy of the second and third metacarpophalangeal joints is a characteristic early feature
First degree relatives should be offered screening once the diagnosis is confirmed
explanation.pearls: Venesection prevents cirrhosis and diabetes if started early but does not reverse established arthropathy or hypogonadism, which is why the joint symptoms that often bring the patient in are also the ones least likely to improve with treatment.

subtopic_detail: Episodic flushing with diarrhoea and a right sided cardiac murmur
stem:
A 58-year-old woman attends your clinic with two years of episodes in which her face and upper chest become hot and deep red for several minutes, sometimes several times a week. They are not associated with sweating and often follow a glass of wine or a cheese board.

She also has loose stools four to six times daily that have been attributed to irritable bowel syndrome, and she has lost 5 kg. She has not had night sweats. She is not menopausal, having had regular periods until last year, and a trial of an oestrogen preparation made no difference to the episodes. On auscultation there is a systolic murmur at the left sternal edge that increases on inspiration, and her jugular venous pressure shows prominent v waves.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 84 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Systolic murmur at the left sternal edge increasing on inspiration, prominent jugular venous v waves, hepatomegaly 3 cm below the costal margin, telangiectasia over the cheeks
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, renal function, thyroid function and coeliac serology all within normal limits, C reactive protein 4 mg/L (less than 5), faecal calprotectin within normal limits
data_table.Symptom pattern: Dry flushing lasting minutes, often triggered by alcohol and aged cheese, with chronic loose stools and weight loss

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Measure urinary five hydroxyindoleacetic acid
options.rationale: Dry flushing triggered by alcohol and tyramine containing foods, secretory diarrhoea, weight loss and right sided valvular disease with hepatomegaly constitute carcinoid syndrome from a metastatic neuroendocrine tumour, and measurement of the serotonin metabolite in urine is the standard biochemical screening test. The right sided murmur reflects the classic pattern of valve involvement. (Source: eviQ: Neuroendocrine tumours)

options.text: Measure plasma free metanephrine levels
options.rationale: Catecholamine excess causes flushing but characteristically with sweating, palpitations, headache and paroxysmal hypertension, and it does not cause secretory diarrhoea or right sided valvular disease. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Measure serum follicle stimulating hormone
options.rationale: Vasomotor flushing of the menopause is a reasonable initial thought in a woman of this age, but her periods were regular until recently, an oestrogen trial made no difference, and menopause does not cause diarrhoea, weight loss or a tricuspid murmur. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Measure serum tryptase during an episode
options.rationale: Mast cell disorders cause flushing, but the flushing is typically accompanied by urticaria, pruritus and hypotension, and they do not produce right sided cardiac valve fibrosis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Immunology)

options.text: Measure serum vasoactive intestinal peptide
options.rationale: This hormone causes profuse watery diarrhoea with hypokalaemia and achlorhydria rather than episodic flushing with valvular heart disease, and the electrolytes here are normal. (Source: eviQ: Neuroendocrine tumours)

explanation.summary: Carcinoid syndrome arises when a neuroendocrine tumour releases vasoactive mediators into the systemic circulation, which for a midgut primary requires hepatic metastases because the liver otherwise inactivates them on first pass. The syndrome is characteristically dry flushing without sweating, often precipitated by alcohol, aged cheese and other tyramine containing foods, together with secretory diarrhoea, and over time fibrotic right sided valvular heart disease producing tricuspid regurgitation and pulmonary stenosis. Left sided valves are spared because the mediators are inactivated in the pulmonary circulation. Screening is by urinary five hydroxyindoleacetic acid, with chromogranin A and specialised imaging to follow.
key_points: Dry flushing without sweating distinguishes it from menopausal and catecholamine driven flushing
Right sided valve involvement with sparing of left sided valves is characteristic
Diarrhoea is frequently misattributed to irritable bowel syndrome for years
Hepatic metastases are usually required for a midgut primary to produce the syndrome
explanation.pearls: Warn the patient and the anaesthetic team about carcinoid crisis before any procedure: anaesthesia, tumour handling or contrast can precipitate profound vasodilatory shock that does not respond to catecholamines and requires octreotide, so the diagnosis must be flagged preoperatively.

subtopic_detail: Nocturnal leg restlessness with a ferritin in the low normal range
stem:
A 52-year-old woman attends your general practice with eighteen months of an unpleasant crawling sensation deep in both calves that comes on when she sits down in the evening and is worse when she goes to bed.

She describes an overwhelming need to move her legs, and says that walking around the house relieves it completely while she is moving. Her partner reports that she kicks in her sleep. She is exhausted during the day. She has no numbness, no weakness and no back pain, and her ankle reflexes and pedal pulses are normal. Her renal function and thyroid function are normal and she is not pregnant. She takes no antidepressant, antihistamine or antipsychotic.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Normal power, normal sensation to light touch and pinprick, ankle reflexes present, pedal pulses palpable, no varicosities
data_table.Investigations: Ferritin 30 micrograms per litre (30-300), transferrin saturation 18 percent, haemoglobin 128 g/L (115-155), creatinine 66 micromol/L (45-90), thyroid function within normal limits
data_table.Symptom pattern: Onset at rest in the evening, relieved completely by movement, worse at night, partner reports periodic limb movements

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first treatment?

options.text: Start pramipexole at a low dose and titrate to her symptoms
options.rationale: Dopamine agonists are effective but carry a substantial risk of augmentation, in which symptoms become earlier, more intense and more widespread over time, so they are no longer first line and are reserved for cases where iron repletion has failed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Start oral iron replacement and recheck her iron studies
options.rationale: Brain iron deficiency is the central mechanism in this condition, and iron replacement is recommended whenever the ferritin is at or below 75 micrograms per litre or the transferrin saturation is below 20 percent, even when these values fall within the standard laboratory reference range. Treating the iron first often resolves symptoms and avoids committing her to long term dopaminergic therapy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Start pregabalin at night and review her symptoms in four weeks
options.rationale: Alpha 2 delta ligands are a reasonable pharmacological option, particularly where pain is prominent, but they should follow correction of iron status rather than precede it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Start a low dose benzodiazepine at night for the sleep disturbance
options.rationale: Sedatives may improve sleep continuity but do nothing for the sensory urge itself, and regular use in a chronic condition risks tolerance and dependence. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Refer for nerve conduction studies before any treatment is started
options.rationale: Neurophysiology is indicated when examination suggests a peripheral neuropathy, but her sensation, power, reflexes and pulses are all normal and the history is characteristic, so testing would delay effective treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Restless legs syndrome is a clinical diagnosis resting on an urge to move the legs with unpleasant sensations, beginning or worsening at rest, relieved by movement, and worse in the evening or at night. Iron status is the first thing to assess and correct, because brain iron deficiency drives the disorder and the thresholds for treatment are higher than those used for anaemia: replacement is recommended at a ferritin of 75 micrograms per litre or below, or a transferrin saturation below 20 percent. This means a result reported as within the normal range still warrants treatment. Dopamine agonists, once standard, have fallen out of first line use because of augmentation, and alpha 2 delta ligands are generally preferred when drug treatment is needed.
key_points: Ferritin at or below 75 micrograms per litre is the treatment threshold, well above the anaemia threshold
Augmentation makes dopamine agonists a later line option than they once were
Review medications that provoke symptoms, including antidepressants, antihistamines and antipsychotics
Periodic limb movements in sleep frequently accompany the condition and support the diagnosis
explanation.pearls: A ferritin reported as normal is the commonest reason this condition goes untreated; read the actual number rather than the flag, because anything at or below 75 micrograms per litre is an indication for iron in a patient with these symptoms.

sources.label: Sleep Health Foundation: Restless legs syndrome

subtopic_detail: Cholestatic liver enzymes with a positive antimitochondrial antibody
stem:
A 54-year-old woman attends your general practice with nine months of tiredness and itching that is worst at night and affects her whole body. She scratches until she bleeds and has not slept properly for months.

She drinks two standard drinks a week and takes no regular medication, herbal preparation or supplement. She has no jaundice, no abdominal pain and no pale stools or dark urine. Her alkaline phosphatase and gamma glutamyl transferase are raised with only a mild rise in transaminases. An abdominal ultrasound shows a normal liver texture with no biliary dilatation and no gallstones. Antimitochondrial antibody is positive at a high titre and her immunoglobulin M is raised.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Widespread excoriations, no jaundice, no hepatomegaly, no splenomegaly, no xanthelasma, no ascites
data_table.Investigations: Alkaline phosphatase 420 U/L (30-110), gamma glutamyl transferase 310 U/L (less than 40), alanine aminotransferase 62 U/L (less than 35), bilirubin 14 micromol/L (less than 20), antimitochondrial antibody positive at high titre, immunoglobulin M raised, viral hepatitis serology negative
data_table.Imaging: Abdominal ultrasound shows normal liver texture, no biliary dilatation, no gallstones

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Start prednisolone and azathioprine and monitor her biochemistry
options.rationale: Immunosuppression is the treatment for autoimmune hepatitis, which produces a hepatitic rather than cholestatic pattern with high transaminases, positive smooth muscle or antinuclear antibodies and raised immunoglobulin G. It is ineffective here and adds steroid toxicity. (Source: GESA: Primary biliary cholangitis)

options.text: Refer for endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography urgently
options.rationale: Biliary intervention is directed at large duct obstruction, and her ultrasound shows no dilatation, so the procedure carries a risk of pancreatitis with no diagnostic or therapeutic yield. (Source: GESA: Primary biliary cholangitis)

options.text: Start ursodeoxycholic acid and monitor her liver biochemistry
options.rationale: A cholestatic pattern with a high titre antimitochondrial antibody and normal biliary imaging in a middle aged woman is primary biliary cholangitis, and ursodeoxycholic acid is first line because it slows progression to cirrhosis and improves transplant free survival. Biochemical response at twelve months guides whether second line therapy is required. (Source: GESA: Primary biliary cholangitis)

options.text: Start colestyramine alone and review her symptoms in three months
options.rationale: A bile acid sequestrant is the first line treatment for the pruritus and should be offered, but symptom control alone leaves the underlying disease to progress towards cirrhosis. (Source: GESA: Primary biliary cholangitis)

options.text: Arrange a liver biopsy before committing her to any drug treatment
options.rationale: Biopsy is not required when the cholestatic biochemistry and antimitochondrial antibody are both present, and is reserved for atypical cases or suspected overlap with autoimmune hepatitis. (Source: GESA: Primary biliary cholangitis)

explanation.summary: Primary biliary cholangitis is a chronic autoimmune cholangiopathy that predominantly affects middle aged women and typically presents with fatigue and pruritus long before jaundice appears. The diagnosis can be made without biopsy when a cholestatic biochemical pattern is accompanied by a positive antimitochondrial antibody and imaging excludes large duct obstruction. Ursodeoxycholic acid is first line and improves transplant free survival, with response assessed biochemically at around twelve months and second line agents added for non responders. Pruritus is treated separately, usually beginning with a bile acid sequestrant, and patients need surveillance for osteoporosis, fat soluble vitamin deficiency and, once cirrhotic, for varices and hepatocellular carcinoma.
key_points: Cholestatic pattern plus antimitochondrial antibody plus normal ducts on imaging is sufficient for diagnosis
Ursodeoxycholic acid modifies disease; antipruritic therapy only treats the symptom
Biochemical response at twelve months determines the need for second line treatment
Screen for osteoporosis, because metabolic bone disease is a common and treatable complication
explanation.pearls: Separate colestyramine from ursodeoxycholic acid by at least four hours: the sequestrant binds the therapeutic bile acid as readily as the ones causing the itch, and co administration quietly abolishes the benefit of the disease modifying drug.

subtopic_detail: Muscle aches with a moderately raised creatine kinase on a statin
stem:
A 61-year-old man attends your general practice with six weeks of aching and heaviness in both thighs and shoulders that makes getting out of a low chair harder than it used to be. He started atorvastatin 40 mg daily four months ago after a myocardial infarction.

He has not changed his exercise, has done no unaccustomed heavy work and has not started any new medication, including no antifungal, macrolide or fibrate. He drinks minimal alcohol. His urine is normal in colour and his renal function is unchanged from baseline. He is worried because he has been told he must never stop the tablet after a heart attack.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Mild symmetrical proximal weakness of hip flexors and shoulder abductors, no rash, no muscle tenderness, reflexes normal
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 840 U/L (less than 200), creatinine 82 micromol/L (60-110) unchanged from baseline, potassium 4.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), urinalysis negative for blood
data_table.Medication: Atorvastatin 40 mg daily for four months, aspirin, metoprolol, perindopril, no new interacting drug

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Halve the statin dose and recheck his creatine kinase in two weeks
options.rationale: Dose reduction is a reasonable strategy for muscle symptoms with a normal or only mildly raised enzyme, but with a creatine kinase over four times the upper limit and objective proximal weakness the drug should be withheld entirely until the enzyme normalises. Continuing at any dose also leaves a reversible contributor unexamined. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Continue the statin unchanged and review his symptoms in three months
options.rationale: Continuing at full dose while the creatine kinase is over four times the upper limit with objective proximal weakness risks progression to rhabdomyolysis and acute kidney injury. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Stop the statin permanently and record a statin allergy in his file
options.rationale: Labelling him permanently intolerant after one episode denies effective secondary prevention to a man who has had a myocardial infarction, when most patients tolerate rechallenge at a lower dose or with a different agent. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Withhold the statin and check his thyroid function before rechallenge
options.rationale: A creatine kinase between four and ten times the upper limit with proximal symptoms warrants temporary cessation, and hypothyroidism is a common and readily reversible contributor that must be excluded before the drug is blamed permanently. Once symptoms and enzymes normalise, rechallenge at a lower dose or with an alternative agent is appropriate because his cardiovascular indication is strong. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Add a fibrate to allow the statin dose to be reduced immediately
options.rationale: Combining a fibrate with a statin increases the risk of myopathy substantially, particularly with gemfibrozil, so it is the wrong direction in a patient who already has muscle symptoms. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

explanation.summary: Muscle symptoms are the commonest reason statins are stopped, and most are manageable without abandoning the drug. The creatine kinase level stratifies the response: symptoms with a normal or mildly raised enzyme can often be managed by dose reduction or a change of agent, a rise of four to ten times the upper limit warrants temporary cessation and investigation, and a rise above ten times or any evidence of rhabdomyolysis requires immediate cessation and assessment of renal function. Before attributing symptoms permanently to the statin, look for reversible contributors, particularly hypothyroidism, vitamin D deficiency, interacting drugs and unaccustomed exertion. Rechallenge succeeds in most patients and matters because the secondary prevention benefit is large.
key_points: Check thyroid function before accepting a diagnosis of statin intolerance
Interacting drugs such as macrolides, azole antifungals and fibrates raise statin exposure
Persisting weakness with a very high creatine kinase after cessation raises immune mediated necrotising myopathy
Most patients tolerate rechallenge at a lower dose or with an alternative statin
explanation.pearls: If the creatine kinase keeps rising or the weakness persists weeks after stopping the drug, test for antibodies to 3 hydroxy 3 methylglutaryl coenzyme A reductase: immune mediated necrotising myopathy does not resolve on withdrawal and needs immunosuppression rather than watchful waiting.

subtopic_detail: Responding when an inpatient asks about lawfully ending their own life
stem:
You are the medical registrar on a ward in a Victorian hospital caring for a 68-year-old man with metastatic pancreatic cancer. He has declined further chemotherapy and is receiving palliative care with reasonable symptom control.

During your morning review he asks you directly whether there is a legal way for him to end his life at a time of his choosing, and says he has been thinking about it for several weeks. He is alert and orientated, his mood is not depressed on assessment, and he has no delirium. He has decision making capacity. His pain is controlled and he is not requesting a change to his analgesia. He asks what he needs to do next.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Cachectic, alert and orientated, abbreviated mental test score normal, no features of delirium
data_table.Assessment: Decision making capacity intact, no depressive disorder on assessment, pain adequately controlled
data_table.Disease status: Metastatic pancreatic cancer, further chemotherapy declined, receiving palliative care

lead_in: What is the most appropriate response to his question?

options.text: Tell him you are prohibited from discussing this subject with him
options.rationale: The prohibition is on a practitioner initiating the conversation, not on responding when a patient raises it, and refusing to engage abandons a man who has asked a direct question about his own care. (Source: Victorian Voluntary Assisted Dying Act 2017)

options.text: Start an antidepressant and reassess his request in four weeks
options.rationale: Treating depression is essential when it is present and can change a request entirely, but he has been assessed as not depressed, and presuming psychiatric illness from the request alone is both inaccurate and dismissive. (Source: Victorian Voluntary Assisted Dying Act 2017)

options.text: Increase his opioid dose with the intention of shortening his life
options.rationale: Administering medication with the intention of ending life outside the legislated process is unlawful, and it is quite distinct from proportionate symptom relief that may incidentally shorten life. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Palliative Care)

options.text: Refer him to psychiatry for a formal capacity assessment first
options.rationale: Routine psychiatric referral is not required when capacity is clearly intact, and making it a precondition implies that wanting to consider this option is itself evidence of disorder. (Source: Victorian Voluntary Assisted Dying Act 2017)

options.text: Answer his question and refer him for a first eligibility assessment
options.rationale: Victorian law prohibits a health practitioner from initiating a discussion about voluntary assisted dying, but once the patient raises it the practitioner may respond, provide information and facilitate access. Referral to a practitioner trained and willing to conduct the assessment is the appropriate next step for a patient with capacity who has asked directly. (Source: Victorian Voluntary Assisted Dying Act 2017)

explanation.summary: Voluntary assisted dying is lawful in all Australian states under legislation that varies in detail between jurisdictions. The Victorian legislation contains a distinctive provision prohibiting registered health practitioners from initiating a discussion about voluntary assisted dying with a patient, a restriction that does not apply in several other states. That prohibition does not prevent a practitioner from responding fully when the patient raises the subject themselves, which is the distinction this scenario tests. A practitioner with a conscientious objection may decline to participate but should not obstruct access, and the appropriate step is referral to a practitioner trained to conduct the assessment.
key_points: The Victorian restriction is on initiating the discussion, not on responding to it
Requirements generally include an advanced progressive condition expected to cause death within a defined period, decision making capacity, and a voluntary enduring request
Conscientious objection permits non participation but not obstruction of access
Assess for depression and uncontrolled symptoms, because both can drive a request and both are treatable
explanation.pearls: A request of this kind is frequently a request for reassurance about how dying will be managed rather than a settled decision, so explore what specifically he fears; unaddressed fear of pain, breathlessness or loss of dignity is treatable and often changes what the person wants.

subtopic_detail: Abdominal pain with hyponatraemia and a raised urinary porphobilinogen
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 27-year-old woman admitted with four days of severe generalised abdominal pain requiring repeated opioid doses. Two surgical reviews have found a soft abdomen with no guarding and no rebound, and computed tomography of her abdomen is normal.

She has vomited repeatedly and is constipated. She is anxious and mildly confused this morning and has developed weakness of both arms that is worse proximally. She started a new medication three weeks ago for acne. A nurse notes that the urine sample left on the bench has turned a dark reddish brown over several hours. Her white cell count and C reactive protein are normal and her lipase is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 118 beats per minute, blood pressure 162/96 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Soft abdomen with no peritonism despite severe pain, proximal weakness of both arms, reduced reflexes, mild confusion, no rash
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 121 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 3.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), white cell count 7.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), C reactive protein 3 mg/L (less than 5), lipase within normal limits, computed tomography of abdomen normal, urinary porphobilinogen markedly raised
data_table.Medication: New agent started three weeks ago for acne

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Give intravenous haem arginate with a high carbohydrate load
options.rationale: Severe unexplained abdominal pain without peritonism, autonomic instability, hyponatraemia, neuropsychiatric features and a motor neuropathy with a raised urinary porphobilinogen indicate an acute porphyric attack. Haem arginate suppresses the rate limiting enzyme that drives precursor accumulation and is given alongside carbohydrate loading and withdrawal of the precipitating drug. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

options.text: Give intravenous hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone replacement
options.rationale: Adrenal insufficiency also causes abdominal pain with hyponatraemia, but it produces hypotension rather than hypertension and tachycardia, and does not cause a motor neuropathy or discoloured urine. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Give hypertonic saline to correct the sodium concentration rapidly
options.rationale: The hyponatraemia is a consequence of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion during the attack and improves as the attack is treated, and rapid correction risks osmotic demyelination in a patient with a chronic low sodium. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Give intravenous immunoglobulin for the ascending motor weakness
options.rationale: Immunoglobulin treats Guillain Barre syndrome, which does not cause severe abdominal pain, hypertension, hyponatraemia or discoloured urine, and delay would allow the underlying attack to progress to respiratory failure. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Give a phenobarbital loading dose to control her agitation overnight
options.rationale: Barbiturates are among the most potent inducers of the pathway driving the attack and will worsen it substantially, which is why drug safety review is a central part of management. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

explanation.summary: Acute porphyria is rare but is a classic cause of severe abdominal pain with a soft abdomen and normal imaging, in a young adult, accompanied by autonomic features, hyponatraemia from inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion, neuropsychiatric disturbance and a predominantly motor neuropathy. Attacks are commonly precipitated by drugs that induce the haem synthesis pathway, by fasting, alcohol, infection and hormonal fluctuation. Diagnosis rests on a raised urinary porphobilinogen during the attack, and urine characteristically darkens on standing in light. Treatment is intravenous haem arginate with carbohydrate loading, withdrawal of precipitants, and careful selection of safe analgesics and antiemetics.
key_points: Severe pain with a soft abdomen and normal imaging should raise the diagnosis
Hyponatraemia during an attack is usually from inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion
Many common drugs are unsafe, including barbiturates, several anticonvulsants and some antibiotics
Progression to respiratory muscle weakness is the feared complication and requires monitoring of vital capacity
explanation.pearls: Check a drug safety database before prescribing anything in a suspected attack: opioids, paracetamol, ondansetron and gabapentin are generally safe, but reaching for an anticonvulsant or a barbiturate to manage agitation or seizures can convert a treatable attack into a respiratory arrest.

subtopic_detail: Mucositis and pancytopenia after an inadvertent daily methotrexate dose
stem:
You are the medical registrar admitting a 71-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis who has had six days of worsening mouth ulceration so severe she cannot eat, and two days of fever.

She has taken methotrexate 15 mg once weekly for four years with stable blood counts. Her daughter brings in the dose administration aid, which a new pharmacy packed nine days ago, and you see methotrexate 15 mg packed into every single day rather than into one day each week. She takes no trimethoprim and no non-steroidal anti inflammatory drug. Her renal function is mildly impaired. She has been taking folic acid 5 mg on a different day of the week as usual.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 110 beats per minute, blood pressure 106/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, SpO2 96 percent on room air, temperature 38.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Extensive confluent oral ulceration, dry mucous membranes, no rash, no focal chest signs, no lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 0.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0) with neutrophils 0.2 x10^9/L (2.0-7.5), haemoglobin 88 g/L (115-155), platelets 42 x10^9/L (150-400), creatinine 128 micromol/L (45-90) rising from a baseline of 82, alanine aminotransferase 92 U/L (less than 35)
data_table.Medication error: Methotrexate 15 mg packed daily rather than weekly for the past nine days

lead_in: What is the most important specific treatment?

options.text: Give colony stimulating factor and antibiotics
options.rationale: Both are indicated in febrile neutropenia and should be given, but neither addresses the ongoing intracellular folate blockade that is continuing to poison every dividing cell line including gut and marrow. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

options.text: Give folinic acid by intravenous injection now
options.rationale: Folinic acid is reduced folate that bypasses the enzyme blocked by methotrexate and is the specific antidote, restoring the folate pool to dividing cells, and it must be given urgently and continued until the toxicity resolves. Ordinary folic acid cannot be used because it requires the very enzyme that methotrexate has inhibited. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

options.text: Give high dose intravenous folic acid instead
options.rationale: Folic acid must be reduced by dihydrofolate reductase before it can be used, and that is precisely the enzyme methotrexate inhibits, so increasing the dose or changing the route achieves nothing. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

options.text: Give a sodium bicarbonate infusion to alkalinise
options.rationale: Alkalinisation increases methotrexate solubility and is used to prevent crystal nephropathy after high dose intravenous therapy, but it does not reverse the established cellular toxicity in this chronic oral overdose. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

options.text: Give platelet and red cell transfusion support
options.rationale: Stopping the drug is essential and blood product support may be required, but supportive transfusion alone allows the toxicity to run its course over weeks with high mortality when an antidote is available. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

explanation.summary: Inadvertent daily rather than weekly methotrexate is one of the most lethal medication errors in Australian practice and typically presents after about a week with severe mucositis, then pancytopenia, often with renal and hepatic impairment. Methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, so the antidote must be a reduced folate that bypasses the blocked enzyme, which is folinic acid rather than folic acid. Treatment is stopping the drug, urgent folinic acid rescue continued until counts and mucositis recover, aggressive hydration to maintain renal clearance, and management of febrile neutropenia. Renal impairment prolongs elimination and worsens toxicity, creating a vicious cycle.
key_points: Folinic acid bypasses the blocked enzyme; folic acid does not and is useless as an antidote
Mucositis usually precedes the nadir in blood counts by several days
Renal impairment reduces clearance and compounds the toxicity
Treat concurrent febrile neutropenia with broad spectrum antibiotics in parallel with the antidote
